Use `ProgressView(timerInterval:)` to animate between two dates with no timer code.

```swift
@State private var countdown = Date.now...Date.now.addingTimeInterval(30)

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    ProgressView(timerInterval: countdown) {
        Text("Code expires")
    }
    Button("Restart") {
        countdown = Date.now...Date.now.addingTimeInterval(30)
    }
}
.onAppear {
    countdown = Date.now...Date.now.addingTimeInterval(30)
}
```

**Note:** Pass `countsDown: false` to fill up instead. The same view works in widgets and Live Activities.

### Loading overlay

Put a large spinner in an `.overlay` on a material, so the layout doesn't jump while content loads.

```swift
RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 16)
    .fill(.fill.tertiary)
    .frame(height: 140)
    .overlay {
        ProgressView("Loading photos")
            .controlSize(.large)
            .padding(20)
            .background(.regularMaterial, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 14))
    }
```

## Related

`gauge`, `slider`, `async-image`


<!-- topic: gauge -->
---
id: gauge
title: Gauge
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, watchOS 7.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/gauge.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/gauges.md
---

# Gauge

Shows where a value sits within a range, like a battery level or a speedometer.

Also called: meter, <meter>, ring, progress ring, dial, speedometer, battery, level indicator, donut.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Gauge(value: 21, in: 0...40) {
    Text("Temperature")
} currentValueLabel: {
    Text("21°")
}
.gaugeStyle(.accessoryCircular)
```

**Note:** The `accessory` styles are sized for widgets and the Lock Screen. On an app screen, keep them next to text or enlarge them with `.scaleEffect(_:)`.

## Rules

- **Label the value and both ends.** Short labels tell people what the range means, and VoiceOver reads them for people who can't see the gauge.
- **Use a gradient when the color carries meaning.** Blue to red for cold to hot, or green to purple for air quality, tells people whether a value is good before they read it.
- **Use a gauge to show a value, not to set one.** People can't drag a gauge. When they should change the value, use a Slider (`slider`).

## Key APIs

- `Gauge(value:in:label:)`: Shows a value in a range; `0...1` by default.
- `currentValueLabel:`: The value as text, often in the middle of a ring.
- `minimumValueLabel:` / `maximumValueLabel:`: Labels for the two ends.
- `.gaugeStyle(_:)`: A bar, a ring, or a widget-style look.
- `.tint(_:)`: A color, or a `Gradient` across the range.

## Variants

### Battery ring

Use the `.accessoryCircularCapacity` style for a ring that fills, with the value in the middle.

```swift
@State private var battery = 0.8

VStack(spacing: 20) {
    Gauge(value: battery) {
        Image(systemName: "iphone")
    } currentValueLabel: {
        Text(battery.formatted(.percent.precision(.fractionLength(0))))
    }
    .gaugeStyle(.accessoryCircularCapacity)
    .tint(battery < 0.2 ? .red : .green)
    .scaleEffect(1.4)

    Slider(value: $battery)
}
```

**Note:** This is the filling ring people often expect from `ProgressView`. On iOS, a circular `ProgressView` only spins.

### Storage bar

Use `.gaugeStyle(.linearCapacity)` for a labeled bar that shows usage, like storage or a data plan.

```swift
@State private var storage = 182.0

Gauge(value: storage, in: 0...256) {
    Text("iPhone Storage")
} currentValueLabel: {
    Text("\(Int(storage)) GB of 256 GB used")
}
.gaugeStyle(.linearCapacity)
.tint(.orange)
```

### Air quality scale

Use `.accessoryLinear` with a `Gradient` tint, so the marker's color shows whether a value is good.

```swift
Gauge(value: 42, in: 0...200) {
    Text("AQI")
} currentValueLabel: {
    Text("42")
} minimumValueLabel: {
    Text("Good")
} maximumValueLabel: {
    Text("Poor")
}
.gaugeStyle(.accessoryLinear)
.tint(Gradient(colors: [.green, .yellow, .orange, .red, .purple]))
```

## Related

`progress-view`, `slider`, `charts`


<!-- topic: link -->
---
id: link
title: Link
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/link.md
---

# Link

A control that opens a URL, in Safari or in the app that handles it.

Also called: <a>, href, anchor, hyperlink, url, open url, window.open, openURL, deep link, mailto.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Link("Terms of Service",
     destination: URL(string: "https://www.apple.com/legal/")!)

// Or inline, with Markdown
Text("Read our [Privacy Policy](https://www.apple.com/privacy/).")
```

**Important:** Markdown links only work in string literals. A `String` variable shows the brackets as typed; use `Text(LocalizedStringKey(string))` instead.

## Pitfalls

- **Web links leave your app.** They open in Safari. Other schemes open their own app: `mailto:` opens Mail, `tel:` the phone, and universal links the matching app.
- **A `Link` is a button.** `.buttonStyle(_:)`, `.tint(_:)`, and `.font(_:)` work on it like on any Button (`button`).

## Key APIs

- `Link(_:destination:)`: A text link that opens a URL.
- `Link(destination:label:)`: Use any view, like a `Label`, as the link.
- `Text("[title](url)")`: Markdown links inside text.
- `@Environment(\.openURL)`: Opens a URL from your own code.
- `prefersInApp:`: Opens a web page in a Safari sheet inside your app (iOS 26).
- `OpenURLAction`: Intercepts every link tap below it.

## Variants

### Links inside text

Write Markdown links in a `Text` literal for inline links, and color them with `.tint(_:)`.

```swift
Text("By continuing you agree to our [Terms](https://www.apple.com/legal/) and [Privacy Policy](https://www.apple.com/privacy/).")
    .font(.footnote)
    .multilineTextAlignment(.center)
    .tint(.purple)
```

### Open a URL from code

Read `openURL` from the environment to open a link from any action, like a button or list row.

```swift
@Environment(\.openURL) private var openURL

Button("Visit swift.org", systemImage: "safari") {
    if let url = URL(string: "https://www.swift.org") {
        openURL(url)
    }
}
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
```

**Note:** On iOS 26, call `openURL(url, prefersInApp: true)` to show a web page in a Safari sheet without leaving your app.

### Intercept links

Set an `OpenURLAction` in the environment to handle every link tap below it yourself.

```swift
@State private var lastTapped = "Nothing yet"

VStack {
    Text("Open [Settings](myapp://settings) or [Help](myapp://help)")
    Text("Tapped: \(lastTapped)")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.environment(\.openURL, OpenURLAction { url in
    lastTapped = url.host() ?? url.absoluteString
    return .handled
})
```

**Note:** Return `.handled` to stay in the app, or `.systemAction` to open the link normally. Try it: nothing here leaves the app.

### Email and phone

Use `mailto:` and `tel:` URLs to start an email in Mail or a call in Phone.

```swift
HStack {
    Link(destination: URL(string: "mailto:hello@example.com")!) {
        Label("Email", systemImage: "envelope")
    }
    Link(destination: URL(string: "tel:+15555550123")!) {
        Label("Call", systemImage: "phone")
    }
}
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
```

**Note:** The Simulator has no Mail or Phone app, so test these on a device.

## On macOS

Text that opens a web page in the person's default browser when clicked.

### Default code

```swift
Link("Privacy Policy", destination: URL(string: "https://www.apple.com/privacy/")!)
```

**Note:** Like an `<a href>`, but the page opens in the default browser, outside your app. Use a Button (`button`) for actions that stay inside.

### Pitfalls

- **Universal Links open their app.** For a link that belongs to an installed app, the system opens it there; everything else goes to the default browser.
- **Markdown links in `Text` work too.** A string literal like `"See [our site](https://…)"` becomes a clickable link, and it goes through the same `openURL` action.

### Key APIs

- `OpenURLAction { url in … }`: Handles links yourself.
- `.environment(\.openURL, …)`: Installs your action for the views inside.

### Variants

#### A link inside a sentence

Write the link in Markdown inside a `Text` to link a few words in the middle of a sentence.

```swift
Text("By continuing, you agree to the [Privacy Policy](https://www.apple.com/privacy/).")
```

#### A link with a symbol

`Link(destination:label:)` takes any view as its label, such as a `Label` with an SF Symbol.

```swift
Link(destination: URL(string: "https://developer.apple.com/swift/")!) {
    Label("Learn Swift", systemImage: "swift")
}
```

#### Open a URL from code

Read `openURL` from the environment when a button needs to do something first, then open the page.

```swift
@Environment(\.openURL) private var openURL

Button("Open Website", systemImage: "safari") {
    logVisit()
    openURL(URL(string: "https://www.apple.com/")!)
}
```

#### Handle links yourself

Set your own `OpenURLAction` to catch links before the browser does, for example to open a help topic inside the app.

```swift
Text("Stuck? Read [Getting Started](help:getting-started) or [Shortcuts](help:shortcuts).")
    .environment(\.openURL, OpenURLAction { url in
        guard url.scheme == "help" else { return .systemAction }
        showHelpTopic(url.absoluteString)
        return .handled
    })
```

**Note:** Return `.systemAction` for links you don't handle, so they still open normally.

## Related

`button`, `share-link`, `text`, `text-label`, `copy-paste`


<!-- topic: share-link -->
---
id: share-link
title: ShareLink
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/sharelink.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/activity-views.md
---

# ShareLink

A button that opens the share sheet to send a link, text, or image.

Also called: share sheet, share button, navigator.share, web share, UIActivityViewController, activity view, export, send, AirDrop.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
let article = URL(string: "https://www.swift.org")!

ShareLink(item: article)

ShareLink(item: article) {
    Label("Share Article", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up")
}
```

**Important:** Only `URL` and `String` items work without a preview. For an `Image` or your own type, also pass a `preview:` made with `SharePreview`.

## Rules

- **Use the standard Share symbol.** People look for `square.and.arrow.up` when they want to send something. A different icon makes them hunt for it.
- **Don't rebuild actions the share sheet already has.** Copy, Print, AirDrop, and Save to Files are built in. Your own versions would sit next to them and confuse people.
- **Give shared items a clear preview.** A `SharePreview` with a title and image shows people what they're about to send at the top of the sheet.

## Pitfalls

- **You can share anything `Transferable`.** `URL`, `String`, `Image`, and `Data` work out of the box; make your own types conform to share them too.

## Key APIs

- `ShareLink(item:)`: A Share button for a `URL` or `String`.
- `ShareLink(item:preview:)`: Shares any `Transferable` item, like an `Image`.
- `SharePreview(_:image:)`: The title and thumbnail at the top of the sheet.
- `subject:` / `message:`: Email subject and extra text, where apps support them.
- `ShareLink(items:)`: Shares several items at once.
- `label:`: A custom label instead of the standard Share button.

## Variants

### Share button in a toolbar

Put a `ShareLink` in `.toolbar` on a detail screen, where people look for sharing first.

```swift
NavigationStack {
    Text("Article")
        .navigationTitle("Article")
        .toolbar {
            ShareLink(item: URL(string: "https://www.swift.org")!)
        }
}
```

**Note:** In a toolbar, `ShareLink` shows only its icon. It's the same button people see in Safari and Photos.

### Share an image

Pass an `Image` as `item:` with a `SharePreview` that names it and shows a thumbnail in the sheet.

```swift
let photo = Image(systemName: "mountain.2.fill")

VStack {
    photo
        .font(.system(size: 60))
        .foregroundStyle(.teal)
    ShareLink(
        item: photo,
        preview: SharePreview("Mountains", image: photo)
    ) {
        Label("Share Photo", systemImage: "photo")
    }
    .buttonStyle(.bordered)
}
```

### Share several items

Pass an array to `items:`, and build a `SharePreview` for each one in the closure.

```swift
let links = [
    URL(string: "https://www.swift.org")!,
    URL(string: "https://developer.apple.com")!,
]

ShareLink(items: links) { url in
    SharePreview(url.host() ?? "Link")
} label: {
    Label("Share 2 Links", systemImage: "link")
}
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
```

## On macOS

A Share button that sends a link, text, or your own data to other apps.

### Default code

```swift
ShareLink(item: URL(string: "https://developer.apple.com/xcode/swiftui/")!)
```

**Note:** `ShareLink` makes the button and shows the system's sharing services when people click it. You only supply what to share.

### Rules

- **Use the standard Share button.** People know its symbol and what it does. `ShareLink` gives you that button, so don't build another way to reach the same services.
- **Put Share where Mac users look for it.** On the Mac, people find sharing in a window's toolbar and in the context menu of the item they want to share.
- **Share the richest data you have.** List your type's representations from most to least specific. Each service picks the best one it understands.

### Pitfalls

- **Some services want a file.** Mail, Messages, AirDrop, and Notes may not appear for every data type. If one is missing, add a `FileRepresentation` to your type.
- **A preview skips the wait.** For a URL, the system fetches the page's title and icon over the network. A `SharePreview` you supply shows right away.

### Key APIs

- `ShareLink(_:item:)`: The same, with your own title.
- `subject:`, `message:`: Fill in a subject and message, like for Mail.
- `Transferable`: Makes your own type shareable.

### Variants

#### In the toolbar

Put a `ShareLink` in the toolbar for whatever the window shows, icon-only with a `.help` tooltip.

```swift
.toolbar {
    ShareLink(item: photo, preview: SharePreview("Sunset", image: photo))
        .help("Share this photo")
}
```

**Note:** A real `.toolbar` here would land in this window's own toolbar, so the preview draws one. The Share button is real.

#### In a context menu

A `ShareLink` works as a context menu item too, so people can share the item they Control-click.

```swift
NoteCard(note)
    .contextMenu {
        Button("Duplicate") { duplicate(note) }
        ShareLink(item: note.text)
    }
```

#### Share your own type

Make your type `Transferable`, like this tip, which shares as plain text with a title in the preview.

```swift
struct GardenTip: Transferable {
    let title: String
    let body: String

    static var transferRepresentation: some TransferRepresentation {
        ProxyRepresentation { tip in "\(tip.title)\n\n\(tip.body)" }
    }
}

ShareLink(item: tip, preview: SharePreview(tip.title, image: Image(systemName: "leaf")))
```

## Related

`link`, `button`, `toolbar`, `image`, `drag-drop`, `copy-paste`, `file-import-export`, `context-menu`


<!-- topic: text-field -->
---
id: text-field
title: TextField
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/textfield.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/text-fields.md
---

# TextField

A box people type a short piece of text or a number into.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var name = ""

TextField("Name", text: $name)
    .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
```

**Important:** Outside a `Form` or `List`, the default style has no border, so the field can look invisible. Add `.textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)` or a background of your own.

## Rules

- **Keep a visible label once people start typing.** The placeholder disappears with the first keystroke. A label beside or above the field still says what each value is.
- **Show the keyboard that fits the content.** An email field with `.emailAddress` puts @ on the first screen, and a price with `.decimalPad` shows only digits. It saves taps and typos.
- **Validate at the right moment.** Check an email address when people leave the field, not on the first letter. Show the problem right under the field, in words.
- **Size the field to the text you expect.** A short field for a ZIP code and a wide one for a street address tell people how much to type.

## Pitfalls

- **The field edits a string you own.** Pass a `@State` property with `$`, like a controlled `<input>` in React. It updates on every keystroke.
- **Let it grow for longer text.** `TextField(_:text:axis: .vertical)` wraps onto new lines as people type; cap it with `.lineLimit(1...5)`. For a full page of text, use TextEditor (`text-editor`).
- **Focus and the keyboard are state too.** To move between fields on Return or hide the keyboard, see Keyboard & Focus (`focus-state`).

## Key APIs

`TextField(_:text:)`, `TextField(_:value:format:)`, `axis: .vertical`, `.textFieldStyle(_:)`, `.keyboardType(_:)`, `.textContentType(_:)`, `.autocorrectionDisabled()`, `.onSubmit { }`

## Variants

### In a Form

Inside a `Form`, fields need no style. Wrap one in `LabeledContent` to show a label beside it.

```swift
@State private var name = "Taylor"
@State private var city = ""

Form {
    TextField("Name", text: $name)
    LabeledContent("City") {
        TextField("Required", text: $city)
            .multilineTextAlignment(.trailing)
    }
}
```

## On macOS

A single-line field for short text, like a name, an email address, or a number.

### Default code

```swift
@State private var name = ""

TextField("Name", text: $name, prompt: Text("Jane Appleseed"))
    .onSubmit {
        print("Hello, \(name)")
    }
```

**Note:** The binding updates on every keystroke, like a controlled `<input>`. `onSubmit` runs when people press Return.

### Rules

- **Size the field for what goes in it.** The width hints at how much to type. A ZIP code needs a short field; a street address needs a long one.
- **Keep a label next to the field.** Placeholder text disappears as soon as people type, so a label beside the field keeps reminding them what it's for.
- **Check input at the right moment.** Check an email address when people move to the next field. Check a new user name before they move on, so they can fix it right away.
- **Let Tab move through fields in order.** People expect focus to go top to bottom and leading to trailing. SwiftUI does this for you; see Focus & keyboard navigation (`focus-keyboard`) when you need more.

### Pitfalls

- **A `String` updates as people type; other values wait.** A field bound with `value:format:` changes its value only when people commit the edit, such as by pressing Return.
- **On macOS 27 and later, use `.bordered` for a border.** It replaces `.roundedBorder`; pair it with `.textInputBorderShape(_:)`, such as `.capsule`, to choose the shape.

### Key APIs

`TextField(_:text:prompt:)`, `TextField(_:text:axis:)`, `.textInputSuggestions { }`

### Variants

#### Labels in a form

In a `Form`, the Mac puts each field's label at the leading edge and shows the `prompt` inside the field.

```swift
@State private var name = ""
@State private var email = ""

Form {
    TextField(text: $name, prompt: Text("Required")) {
        Text("Name")
    }
    TextField(text: $email, prompt: Text("Optional")) {
        Text("Email")
    }
}
```

#### Add an item with Return

Use `.onSubmit` to act when people press Return, then clear the field so they can type the next one.

```swift
@State private var newTag = ""
@State private var tags = ["Travel", "Family"]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    TextField("New Tag", text: $newTag)
        .onSubmit {
            let tag = newTag.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)
            guard !tag.isEmpty else { return }
            tags.append(tag)
            newTag = ""
        }
    Text(tags.joined(separator: ", "))
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.frame(width: 260)
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Email with validation, Numbers and currency, Search field with clear button, A price with a format (macOS), A field that grows (macOS), Suggestions as people type (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/textfield.md

## Related

`secure-field`, `text-editor`, `focus-state`, `form`, `focus-keyboard`, `labeled-content`, `search`


<!-- topic: secure-field -->
---
id: secure-field
title: SecureField
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/securefield.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/text-fields.md
---

# SecureField

A text field that hides what people type, for passwords and PINs.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var password = ""

SecureField("Password", text: $password)
    .textContentType(.password)
    .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
```

**Note:** Use `.password` on a sign-in screen and `.newPassword` on a sign-up screen, so iOS fills in the saved password or suggests a strong one.

## Rules

- **Always hide passwords and other secrets.** Someone nearby can read a plain field over a shoulder or in a screen recording. A `SecureField` shows dots instead.
- **Support AutoFill.** With the right `.textContentType`, people sign in with Face ID instead of typing. Mark the username field too, so both fill at once.
- **Check a new password before people move on.** Show the rules and whether they're met while people type. Finding out after Submit means typing it all again.

## Pitfalls

- **It works like a `TextField`.** It takes the same styles and modifiers, and the string you bind holds the real text. Only the display is hidden.
- **iOS locks it down for you.** Autocorrect, dictation, and copying are off, and each character shows for a moment before it turns into a dot.

## Key APIs

`SecureField(_:text:)`, `.textContentType(.password)`, `.textContentType(.newPassword)`, `.textContentType(.oneTimeCode)`, `.textFieldStyle(_:)`, `.onSubmit { }`

## Variants

### Sign-in form

In a `Form`, fields need no style. Mark them `.username` and `.password` so AutoFill fills both.

```swift
@State private var username = ""
@State private var password = ""

Form {
    TextField("Username", text: $username)
        .textContentType(.username)
        .textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
    SecureField("Password", text: $password)
        .textContentType(.password)
    Button("Sign In") {
        // Sign in
    }
    .disabled(username.isEmpty || password.isEmpty)
}
```

## On macOS

A text field that hides what people type, for passwords and other secrets.

### Default code

```swift
@State private var password = ""

SecureField("Password", text: $password)
    .textContentType(.password)
    .onSubmit {
        print("Signing in…")
    }
```

**Note:** Like `TextField`, the binding updates on every keystroke, so you can check the length or enable a button as people type.

### Rules

- **Never fill in a password for people.** Ask people to type it each time, or use biometric or keychain authentication instead.
- **Turn on Sign In only when it can work.** Keep the button disabled until people fill in the required fields, so it's clear what's missing.
- **Use a secure field for anything sensitive.** Passwords, PINs, and recovery codes belong in a `SecureField`, never a plain `TextField`.

### Pitfalls

- **The field protects its text for you.** It shows a dot for each character, won't let people cut or copy the contents, and shows an indicator while Caps Lock is on.
- **Consider not asking for a password at all.** The HIG suggests Sign in with Apple, or passkeys, before an app-specific password.

### Key APIs

`SecureField(_:text:prompt:)`, `.textContentType(.username)`, `.keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)`

### Variants

#### A sign-in form

Mark the fields with `.textContentType` so the system can suggest saved accounts, and give Sign In `.keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)` so Return clicks it.

```swift
@State private var username = ""
@State private var password = ""
@State private var message = ""

Form {
    TextField("User Name", text: $username)
        .textContentType(.username)
    SecureField("Password", text: $password)
        .textContentType(.password)
    Button("Sign In") {
        message = "Signed in as \(username)"
    }
    .keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)
    .disabled(username.isEmpty || password.isEmpty)
    Text(message)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.frame(width: 320)
```

**Note:** On the Mac, the default button gets special coloring, so people can see that Return clicks it.

#### Create a password

Use `.textContentType(.newPassword)` for a password people are making, and check the two fields match as they type.

```swift
@State private var newPassword = ""
@State private var confirmation = ""

Form {
    SecureField("New Password", text: $newPassword)
        .textContentType(.newPassword)
    SecureField("Verify", text: $confirmation)
        .textContentType(.newPassword)
    if !confirmation.isEmpty && confirmation != newPassword {
        Text("The passwords don't match.")
            .foregroundStyle(.red)
    }
}
.frame(width: 320)
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Show / hide password, New password with strength meter, Show the password (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/securefield.md

## Related

`text-field`, `focus-state`, `login-form`, `focus-keyboard`, `form`, `keyboard-shortcuts`


<!-- topic: text-editor -->
---
id: text-editor
title: TextEditor
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/texteditor.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/text-views.md
---

# TextEditor

A scrolling, multi-line area for long text such as notes or a bio.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var notes = ""

TextEditor(text: $notes)
    .frame(height: 150)
```

**Important:** A `TextEditor` takes all the space it's offered. Outside a `Form`, give it a `.frame(height:)` or `minHeight`.

## Rules

- **Use a text editor for long text, and a text field for short text.** A bio or a note needs room to see several lines at once. A one-line field hides most of what people wrote.
- **Keep the text readable at every size.** Use a text style like `.body` rather than a fixed point size, so the editor follows Dynamic Type.
- **Tell people what to write when it's empty.** An empty box gives no hint. Add a placeholder, and a counter if there's a limit.

## Pitfalls

- **Hide the default background before adding your own.** `.background` alone has no effect until you add `.scrollContentBackground(.hidden)`.
- **Text modifiers style all of the text.** `.font`, `.foregroundStyle`, and `.lineSpacing` apply to the whole editor. For styled runs, bind an `AttributedString`.

## Key APIs

`TextEditor(text:)`, `.frame(height:)`, `.scrollContentBackground(.hidden)`, `.font(_:)`, `.lineSpacing(_:)`, `.onChange(of:)`

## Variants

### Placeholder

`TextEditor` has no placeholder, so overlay a `Text` and hide it once there's text.

```swift
@State private var notes = ""

TextEditor(text: $notes)
    .overlay(alignment: .topLeading) {
        if notes.isEmpty {
            Text("Write something…")
                .foregroundStyle(.tertiary)
                .padding(.top, 8)
                .padding(.leading, 5)
                .allowsHitTesting(false)
        }
    }
    .frame(height: 120)
```

**Note:** The padding lines the placeholder up with the editor's first line, and `.allowsHitTesting(false)` lets taps reach the editor.

### Character limit

Trim the text in `.onChange(of:)` to enforce a maximum, and show a counter below the editor.

```swift
@State private var bio = ""
let limit = 80

VStack(alignment: .trailing) {
    TextEditor(text: $bio)
        .frame(height: 100)
        .onChange(of: bio) {
            if bio.count > limit {
                bio = String(bio.prefix(limit))
            }
        }
    Text("\(bio.count)/\(limit)")
        .font(.caption.monospacedDigit())
        .foregroundStyle(bio.count == limit ? .red : .secondary)
}
```

### Rich text

Bind an `AttributedString` and people can make selected text bold, italic, or underlined from the edit menu.

```swift
@State private var text = AttributedString("Select a word, then tap Format to make it bold.")

TextEditor(text: $text)
    .frame(height: 120)
```

**Note:** Rich text editing needs iOS 26 or later. With a `String` binding, the editor stays plain text.

## On macOS

A scrolling area for long, multi-line text, plain or styled.

### Default code

```swift
@State private var notes = ""

TextEditor(text: $notes)
    .frame(minHeight: 120)
```

**Note:** A `TextEditor` scrolls when the text is longer than its frame, like a `<textarea>`. Give it a frame that fits a few lines.

### Rules

- **Use a text editor for long text.** Notes, messages, and descriptions need room for several lines. A single-line field cuts them off.
- **Keep the text easy to read.** You can mix fonts, colors, and alignment, but readability comes first. Check your text with accessibility settings such as Increase Contrast turned on.

### Pitfalls

- **A `String` gives plain text; an `AttributedString` gives styled text.** Bind an attributed string and the editor's context menu offers formatting controls.
- **Find applies to the editors in the view.** With more than one `TextEditor` under `.findNavigator`, which one shows the find bar isn't guaranteed.

### Key APIs

`TextEditor(text:selection:)`, `.findNavigator(isPresented:)`, `.findDisabled()`, `.replaceDisabled()`, `.autocorrectionDisabled()`

### Variants

#### Find and replace

Bind `.findNavigator(isPresented:)` to show the find bar from a button. It stays in sync when people close it themselves.

```swift
@State private var text = "Bring snacks, bring water, bring a map."
@State private var isFinding = false

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Button("Find…", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") {
        isFinding.toggle()
    }
    TextEditor(text: $text)
        .font(.body)
        .findNavigator(isPresented: $isFinding)
        .frame(width: 320, height: 120)
}
```

**Important:** Put `.findDisabled()` or `.replaceDisabled()` closer to the editor than `.findNavigator`, or they won't apply.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Growing TextField instead, Styled text (macOS), A code editor (macOS), A limit with a counter (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/texteditor.md

## Related

`text-field`, `focus-state`, `text`, `focus-keyboard`, `text-label`, `typography`


<!-- topic: focus-state -->
---
id: focus-state
title: Keyboard & Focus
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/focusstate.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/virtual-keyboards.md
---

# Keyboard & Focus

Choose which field is active, move between fields on Return, pick the right keyboard, and dismiss it.

Also called: focus(), blur(), autofocus, dismiss keyboard, hide keyboard, becomeFirstResponder, resignFirstResponder, enterkeyhint, inputmode, onSubmit.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Match the keyboard to the content.** An email keyboard puts @ up front and a number pad shows only digits. Add `.textContentType` too, so iOS can offer AutoFill.
- **Name the Return key for what it does.** “Next” moves to the next field, “Search” runs a search, and “Done” finishes. People know what happens before they tap.
- **Move focus in reading order.** Return should go from one field to the one below it, top to bottom, and dismiss the keyboard after the last one.
- **Always give people a way to hide the keyboard.** It covers half the screen. Add a Done button, scroll-to-dismiss, or a Return key that ends editing.

## Pitfalls

- **Set focus once the field is on screen.** Setting it in `init` does nothing. Set it in `.onAppear` or `.task` to focus a field when a screen opens.
- **In the Simulator, press ⌘K to show the keyboard.** With a hardware keyboard connected, the software one stays hidden.

## Guide

On the web you call `input.focus()` and `input.blur()`. In SwiftUI, **focus is state**: declare a `@FocusState` property, attach it to fields with `.focused(_:equals:)`, and read or set it like any other value.

### Focus is state

Use a `Bool` for one field, or an optional enum for several. Tap a field or pick one below: the readout shows `focusedField`, and Return moves to the next field. `nil` means nothing is focused, so the keyboard hides.

```swift
enum Field { case name, email, city }

@State private var name = ""
@State private var email = ""
@State private var city = ""
@FocusState private var focusedField: Field?

VStack {
    TextField("Name", text: $name)
        .focused($focusedField, equals: .name)
        .submitLabel(.next)
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .focused($focusedField, equals: .email)
        .submitLabel(.next)
    TextField("City", text: $city)
        .focused($focusedField, equals: .city)
        .submitLabel(.done)

    Button("Dismiss Keyboard") {
        focusedField = nil
    }
}
.textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
.onSubmit {
    // Return moves to the next field, then dismisses.
    switch focusedField {
    case .name: focusedField = .email
    case .email: focusedField = .city
    default: focusedField = nil
    }
}
```

**Note:** `.onSubmit` on the container runs for every field inside it, so one `switch` can move focus through the whole form.

### Pick the right keyboard

`.keyboardType` chooses the layout, `.submitLabel` names the Return key, and `.textContentType` lets iOS offer AutoFill. Change them, then tap the field.

```swift
@State private var text = ""

TextField("Email", text: $text)
    .keyboardType(.emailAddress)
    .textContentType(.emailAddress)
    .textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
    .autocorrectionDisabled()
    .submitLabel(.go)
    .onSubmit {
        // Runs when Return is tapped
    }
```

**Important:** `.submitLabel` only changes the key's title, and `.keyboardType` is only a hint: people can still paste anything. Do the work in `.onSubmit`, and validate the text.

### Dismissing the keyboard

iOS doesn't hide the keyboard when people tap elsewhere. Give them at least one of these ways out.

**Important:** Old Stack Overflow answers hide the keyboard with a UIKit `sendAction` trick. You don't need it: set your `@FocusState` to `nil` or `false`.

## Key APIs

- `@FocusState`: Holds which field is focused: a `Bool` or an optional enum.
- `.focused(_:equals:)`: Ties a field to one value of an enum focus state.
- `.focused(_:)`: Ties a single field to a `Bool` focus state.
- `.onSubmit { }`: Runs when people tap Return.
- `.submitLabel(_:)`: The Return key's title: `.next`, `.done`, `.search`, and more.
- `.keyboardType(_:)`: The keyboard layout, such as `.emailAddress` or `.numberPad`.
- `.scrollDismissesKeyboard(_:)`: Hides the keyboard when people scroll.
- `ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .keyboard)`: Buttons in a bar above the keyboard.

## Variants

### Done button above the keyboard

Put a button in the `.keyboard` toolbar placement that clears focus. Tap the field, then tap **Done**.

```swift
@State private var note = ""
@FocusState private var isFocused: Bool

TextField("Add a note", text: $note)
    .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
    .focused($isFocused)
    .toolbar {
        ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .keyboard) {
            Spacer()
            Button("Done") {
                isFocused = false
            }
        }
    }
```

### Dismiss by scrolling

Add `.scrollDismissesKeyboard(.interactively)` so people can drag the keyboard down, like in Messages.

```swift
@State private var items = ["Milk", "Eggs", "Coffee"]
@State private var newItem = ""

List {
    TextField("New item", text: $newItem)
        .onSubmit {
            items.append(newItem)
            newItem = ""
        }
    ForEach(items, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
}
.scrollDismissesKeyboard(.interactively)
```

## Related

`text-field`, `secure-field`, `form`, `login-form`


<!-- topic: text -->
---
id: text
title: Text
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/text.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.md
---

# Text

Shows read-only text, styled with fonts and colors, with built-in Markdown and formatting.

Also called: label, <p>, <span>, paragraph, string, UILabel, font, text-overflow, ellipsis, markdown.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 4) {
    Text("Weekend in Lisbon")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("3 nights · Arrives Friday at 6:40 PM")
        .font(.subheadline)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

**Note:** A bold title over a smaller, secondary line is the most common text pair in iOS apps.

## Rules

- **Use text styles, not fixed sizes.** `.headline` and `.body` grow with the person's text size setting. `.font(.system(size: 15))` stays the same and gets hard to read.
- **Show hierarchy with size, weight, and color.** A bold title over a smaller, secondary line tells people what to read first. Same-looking lines run together.
- **Avoid light weights for small text.** Thin strokes fade at small sizes. Use Regular or heavier for anything at body size or below.
- **Let important text wrap instead of truncating.** With larger text sizes, a one-line limit cuts off words people need. Truncate only when they can open the full text.

## Pitfalls

- **Text wraps by default.** It takes as many lines as it needs. `.lineLimit(2)` caps it and adds “…”, like CSS `text-overflow: ellipsis`.
- **Style a whole group at once.** `.font`, `.foregroundStyle`, and `.multilineTextAlignment` on a `VStack` apply to every `Text` inside it.
- **For fonts and the type scale, see Typography (`typography`).** It shows every text style at its real size.

## Key APIs

- `Text(_:)`: Shows a string. Literals support Markdown and are localized.
- `.font(_:)`: A text style like `.headline`, which scales with Dynamic Type.
- `.bold()`, `.italic()`: Quick weight and style changes. `.fontWeight(_:)` for others.
- `.foregroundStyle(_:)`: The color, such as `.secondary` for less important text.
- `.lineLimit(_:)`: The most lines to show before truncating.
- `.multilineTextAlignment(_:)`: `.leading`, `.center`, or `.trailing` for wrapped lines.
- `Text(_:format:)`: Formats a number or date for the person's locale.
- `.textSelection(.enabled)`: Lets people select and copy the text.

## Variants

### Markdown

A string literal in `Text` renders inline Markdown: bold, italic, code, strikethrough, and links.

```swift
Text("**Bold**, *italic*, `code`, ~~strike~~, and a [link](https://developer.apple.com).")
```

**Important:** Only literals are parsed. A `String` variable shows its asterisks as-is; use `Text(LocalizedStringKey(string))` to render its Markdown.

### Dates and numbers

Pass a value and a `format:` to `Text`, and it formats the value for the person's locale.

```swift
let price = 1299.0
let date = Date.now

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
    Text(price, format: .currency(code: "USD"))
    Text(0.427, format: .percent.precision(.fractionLength(1)))
    Text(1_250_000, format: .number.notation(.compactName))
    Text(date, format: .dateTime.weekday(.wide).month().day())
    Text(date, style: .time)
    Text(date.addingTimeInterval(-90), style: .relative)
}
```

**Note:** The `.relative` and `.timer` styles update themselves every second, with no timer code.

### Mixing styles in one line

Interpolate a styled `Text` inside another to style part of a sentence. It still wraps as one paragraph.

```swift
Text("Your order is \(Text("on its way").bold().foregroundStyle(.green)) and arrives \(Text("tomorrow").italic()).")
```

### Selectable text

Add `.textSelection(.enabled)` so people can long-press to copy an order number or address.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 4) {
    Text("Order number")
        .font(.subheadline)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Text("W-48213-7790")
        .font(.title3.monospaced())
}
.textSelection(.enabled)
```

## Related

`font`, `typography`, `label`, `text-field`


<!-- topic: label -->
---
id: label
title: Label
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/label.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/labels.md
---

# Label

An icon and a title together, which adapts its look to where it's used.

Also called: icon with text, icon text, list item, menu item, badge, chip, tag, labelStyle.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Label("Favorites", systemImage: "star.fill")

// Icon only, but VoiceOver still reads "Favorites"
Label("Favorites", systemImage: "star.fill")
    .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
```

## Rules

- **Pick a symbol that means the same as the title.** People recognize the standard symbols, like `square.and.arrow.up` for Share. A loose match makes them read twice.
- **Keep a title even when you show only the icon.** Use `.labelStyle(.iconOnly)` instead of a bare `Image`. VoiceOver reads the title, and toolbars can show it when there's room.
- **Use the system colors to rank importance.** Primary for the title, secondary for details. The colors adapt to Dark Mode and higher-contrast settings for you.

## Pitfalls

- **Prefer `Label` over an `HStack` of `Image` and `Text`.** Lists, menus, toolbars, and tab bars know how to lay it out, and VoiceOver reads the title.
- **Controls build labels for you.** `Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash")`, `Toggle`, and `Menu` take a title and a `systemImage:` directly.

## Key APIs

- `Label(_:systemImage:)`: A title with an SF Symbol.
- `Label(_:image:)`: A title with an image from your asset catalog.
- `Label { } icon: { }`: Any views as the title and icon.
- `.labelStyle(_:)`: `.titleAndIcon`, `.titleOnly`, or `.iconOnly`.
- `LabelStyle`: A protocol for your own reusable label layout.
- `.symbolRenderingMode(_:)`: Colors the symbol: `.hierarchical`, `.multicolor`, and more.

## Variants

### In a List

Put `Label`s in a `List` and the icons line up in one column, even at different widths.

```swift
List {
    Label("Wi-Fi", systemImage: "wifi")
    Label("Bluetooth", systemImage: "point.3.connected.trianglepath.dotted")
    Label("Battery", systemImage: "battery.100")
}
```

### In buttons and menus

`Button` and `Menu` take a title and `systemImage:` and build the `Label` for you.

```swift
Menu("Options", systemImage: "ellipsis.circle") {
    Button("Duplicate", systemImage: "plus.square.on.square") {}
    Button("Rename", systemImage: "pencil") {}
    Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash", role: .destructive) {}
}

Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") {}
    .buttonStyle(.bordered)
```

**Note:** Menus show the icon after the title, and toolbars show only the icon. The same `Label` adapts to each place.

### Settings-style icon

Use `Label { } icon: { }` to build any icon, such as a white symbol on a colored square.

```swift
Label {
    Text("Notifications")
} icon: {
    Image(systemName: "bell.badge.fill")
        .font(.footnote)
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .frame(width: 28, height: 28)
        .background(.red, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 7))
}
```

### Custom label style

Conform to `LabelStyle` to define a layout once and reuse it, here an icon over its title.

```swift
struct VerticalLabelStyle: LabelStyle {
    func makeBody(configuration: Configuration) -> some View {
        VStack(spacing: 6) {
            configuration.icon
                .font(.title2)
            configuration.title
                .font(.caption)
        }
    }
}

HStack(spacing: 28) {
    Label("Camera", systemImage: "camera")
    Label("Photos", systemImage: "photo")
    Label("Files", systemImage: "folder")
}
.labelStyle(VerticalLabelStyle())
```

## Related

`text`, `sf-symbols`, `image`, `list`


<!-- topic: image -->
---
id: image
title: Image
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/image.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/image-views.md
---

# Image

Shows a picture or an SF Symbol, and controls how it fills its frame.

Also called: <img>, img, picture, photo, UIImageView, object-fit, background-size: cover, contain, icon, aspect ratio.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Image("landscape")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .frame(width: 300, height: 200)
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

**Important:** Without `.resizable()`, an image draws at its own size and ignores the frame. Put it first, right after `Image(...)`.

## Rules

- **Keep text over images readable.** A busy photo can hide white text. Put a dark gradient or a material behind the text so it always contrasts.
- **Use SF Symbols for icons.** Symbols scale with Dynamic Type, match the text weight, and take the tint color. Save bitmap images for photos and art.
- **Make tappable images buttons.** Put the image in a `Button` label instead of adding `.onTapGesture`. It gets a pressed state and VoiceOver treats it as a button.
- **Provide images at @2x and @3x.** iPhone screens have two or three pixels per point. A single small bitmap looks blurry; a PDF or SVG asset scales cleanly.

## Pitfalls

- **Fit or fill, like CSS `object-fit`.** `.scaledToFit()` is `contain`: the whole image shows, with gaps. `.scaledToFill()` is `cover`: no gaps, but the edges overflow until you clip them.
- **Describe meaningful images for VoiceOver.** Add `.accessibilityLabel`, or use `Image(decorative:)` for images that are only decoration.
- **For an image from a URL, use AsyncImage (`async-image`).** `Image` only shows images that are already in your app or in memory.

## Key APIs

- `Image(_:)`: An image from your asset catalog, by name.
- `Image(systemName:)`: An SF Symbol, sized and colored like text.
- `.resizable()`: Lets the image stretch to its frame. Must come first.
- `.scaledToFit()`: Shows the whole image inside the frame.
- `.scaledToFill()`: Fills the frame, cropping the edges once clipped.
- `.aspectRatio(_:contentMode:)`: Keeps a set width-to-height ratio.
- `.clipShape(_:)`: Clips to a shape: `.circle`, `.rect(cornerRadius:)`, and more.
- `.accessibilityLabel(_:)`: What VoiceOver says for the image.

## Variants

### Avatar

Fill a square with `.scaledToFill()`, clip it with `.clipShape(.circle)`, and add a ring overlay.

```swift
Image("profile")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .frame(width: 88, height: 88)
    .clipShape(.circle)
    .overlay {
        Circle().stroke(.background, lineWidth: 3)
    }
    .shadow(radius: 4)
```

### Cover image with a fixed aspect ratio

Size a `Color.clear` box with `.aspectRatio(16 / 9)` and fill its overlay with the image.

```swift
Color.clear
    .aspectRatio(16 / 9, contentMode: .fit)
    .overlay {
        Image("landscape")
            .resizable()
            .scaledToFill()
    }
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

**Important:** A filled image is wider than its frame until it's clipped, and it can push the layout around. The overlay keeps the box in charge of the size.

### Sizing SF Symbols

Size an `Image(systemName:)` with `.font`, not `.resizable()`, so it lines up with nearby text.

```swift
HStack(alignment: .firstTextBaseline, spacing: 20) {
    Image(systemName: "heart.fill").font(.body)
    Image(systemName: "heart.fill").font(.title)
    Image(systemName: "heart.fill").font(.largeTitle)
    Image(systemName: "heart.fill").font(.system(size: 56))
}
.foregroundStyle(.pink)
```

**Note:** Browse every symbol, and its rendering modes, in SF Symbols (`sf-symbols`).

### Text over a photo

Add the caption in an `.overlay` with a dark `LinearGradient` behind it, so it stays readable.

```swift
Image("landscape")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .frame(height: 200)
    .overlay(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
        Text("Lake Bled at sunset")
            .font(.headline)
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .padding()
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
            .background(.linearGradient(colors: [.clear, .black.opacity(0.6)], startPoint: .top, endPoint: .bottom))
    }
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

## Related

`async-image`, `sf-symbols`, `clip-shape`, `frame`


<!-- topic: async-image -->
---
id: async-image
title: AsyncImage
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/asyncimage.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/image-views.md
---

# AsyncImage

Downloads and shows an image from a URL, with a placeholder while it loads.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
let url = URL(string: "https://example.com/photo.jpg")

AsyncImage(url: url) { image in
    image
        .resizable()
        .scaledToFill()
} placeholder: {
    ProgressView()
}
.frame(width: 200, height: 200)
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

**Important:** `.resizable()` and `.scaledToFill()` belong to `Image`, so they go on the `image` inside the closure, not on `AsyncImage`.

## Rules

- **Reserve the image's space before it loads.** A placeholder at the final size keeps text from jumping when the photo arrives, so people don't lose their place.
- **Show a clear failure state.** An empty box looks like the app is still loading. Say the image couldn't load, and offer a way to try again.
- **Keep text over remote images readable.** You don't know what the photo will look like. Put a gradient or material behind any text on top of it.

## Pitfalls

- **Use the `phase` version to handle errors.** It hands you `.empty` while loading, `.success(image)`, and `.failure(error)`, so you can show a real error state.
- **Fade images in instead of popping.** Pass `transaction: Transaction(animation: .easeInOut)` and the image animates in when it arrives.

## Key APIs

`AsyncImage(url:)`, `AsyncImage(url:content:placeholder:)`, `AsyncImage(url:transaction:content:)`, `AsyncImagePhase`, `.frame(width:height:)`, `.id(_:)`

## Variants

### Avatar

Give `AsyncImage` a fixed `.frame` and a person symbol as the placeholder, then clip it to a circle.

```swift
AsyncImage(url: URL(string: "https://picsum.photos/seed/avatar/200")) { image in
    image
        .resizable()
        .scaledToFill()
} placeholder: {
    Image(systemName: "person.fill")
        .font(.title)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
        .background(.fill.tertiary)
}
.frame(width: 72, height: 72)
.clipShape(.circle)
```

### Photo grid

Make square cells in a `LazyVGrid` with `Color.clear` and `.aspectRatio(1)`, then fill each with an image.

```swift
let columns = Array(repeating: GridItem(.flexible(), spacing: 4), count: 3)

LazyVGrid(columns: columns, spacing: 4) {
    ForEach(1...6, id: \.self) { index in
        Color.clear
            .aspectRatio(1, contentMode: .fit)
            .overlay {
                AsyncImage(url: URL(string: "https://picsum.photos/seed/grid\(index)/300")) { image in
                    image.resizable().scaledToFill()
                } placeholder: {
                    Rectangle().fill(.fill.tertiary)
                }
            }
            .clipped()
    }
}
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

**Important:** `AsyncImage` doesn't cache images itself. Cells that scroll away and back may download again, so large grids often use a caching library.

## On macOS

### Rules

- **Keep text over images readable.** You can't predict what a downloaded photo looks like. Put a scrim or material behind text that sits on it.
- **Make a clickable image a button.** On the Mac, show an image people click inside a `Button`, rather than as a plain image with a gesture.
- **Use a symbol for an icon.** SF Symbols are vector images you can tint with the accent color, so they suit interface icons better than downloaded pictures.

### Pitfalls

- **A sandboxed app needs the network entitlement.** Turn on Outgoing Connections (Client), `com.apple.security.network.client`, under App Sandbox, or every image fails to load.
- **In macOS 27 and later, `AsyncImage` caches downloads.** To change the cache policy, pass a `URLRequest` with `AsyncImage(request:)`.

### Variants

#### Avatar in a row

Give `AsyncImage` a fixed `.frame` and a person symbol as the placeholder, then clip it to a circle.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 10) {
    AsyncImage(url: URL(string: "https://picsum.photos/seed/avatar/200")) { image in
        image
            .resizable()
            .scaledToFill()
    } placeholder: {
        Image(systemName: "person.fill")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
            .background(.fill.tertiary)
    }
    .frame(width: 40, height: 40)
    .clipShape(.circle)
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Jordan Lee")
            .font(.headline)
        Text("Photographer")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
```

#### Photo grid

Make square cells in a `LazyVGrid` with `Color.clear` and `.aspectRatio(1)`, then fill each with an image.

```swift
let columns = Array(repeating: GridItem(.flexible(), spacing: 4), count: 4)

LazyVGrid(columns: columns, spacing: 4) {
    ForEach(1...8, id: \.self) { index in
        Color.clear
            .aspectRatio(1, contentMode: .fit)
            .overlay {
                AsyncImage(url: URL(string: "https://picsum.photos/seed/grid\(index)/300")) { image in
                    image.resizable().scaledToFill()
                } placeholder: {
                    Rectangle().fill(.fill.tertiary)
                }
            }
            .clipped()
    }
}
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 10))
.frame(maxWidth: 420)
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Failure with retry, Failure with retry (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/asyncimage.md

## Related

`image`, `progress-view`, `lazy-grids`, `list`, `image-symbols`, `app-sandbox`, `privacy-permissions`, `stacks-grid`


<!-- topic: layout-basics -->
---
id: layout-basics
title: How Layout Works
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/layout-fundamentals.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# How Layout Works

A parent offers its child a size, the child picks its own, and the parent places it.

Also called: box model, css layout, width 100%, sizing, auto layout, constraints, flexbox, proposed size.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Let text set its own size.** People can make text much larger with Dynamic Type. A hard-coded width or height cuts it off; a flexible frame lets it wrap.
- **Base layout on the space you have, not the device.** An iPhone app can run in a narrow iPad window or rotate. Read the size class or use `ViewThatFits` instead of checking the model.

## Pitfalls

- **Shapes and colors are greedy.** `Color.blue` and `Rectangle()` take all the space they're offered, so give them a `.frame` or put them in a `.background`.
- **Write your own container with the `Layout` protocol.** When stacks and grids aren't enough, it's the same propose, choose, place conversation, in code.

## Guide

Forget the CSS box model for a moment. SwiftUI layout is a short conversation between a parent and each child, in three steps:

### See it happen

Drag the slider to change the offer (the dashed box). The colored outline is the size the child chose. Each child answers the same offer differently.

```swift
Text("Hello, layout")
    .frame(width: 240, height: 120) // the parent's offer
```

**Note:** The child always has the last word on its size. That's why `Text` hugs its words while `Color` fills everything it's offered.

## Key APIs

- `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)`: Fills the offered width, like `width: 100%`.
- `.frame(width:height:)`: Offers its child an exact size.
- `.padding(_:)`: Offers less space in, reports a bigger size out.
- `.fixedSize()`: Ignores the offer and uses the view's ideal size.
- `.layoutPriority(_:)`: Gives a sibling first claim on space in a stack.
- `Layout`: A protocol for writing your own container.

## Variants

### Fill the width

Views hug their content, so use `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` to get CSS's `width: 100%`.

```swift
Text("Full width")
    .padding()
    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
    .background(.blue.opacity(0.2), in: .rect(cornerRadius: 10))
```

**Note:** Pass an `alignment:` such as `.leading` to keep the text at one edge of the wider frame.

### Text wraps when offered less

`Text` fits the width it's offered, wrapping onto more lines and growing taller.

```swift
Text("SwiftUI lays out text to fit the space it's offered.")
    .frame(width: 140)
    .border(.blue)
```

### Ignore the offer with fixedSize

`.fixedSize()` makes a view use its ideal size, so this text overflows instead of wrapping.

```swift
Text("This line never wraps, even when it is too long")
    .fixedSize()
    .frame(width: 140)
    .border(.blue)
```

**Note:** Pass `horizontal: false, vertical: true` to let text wrap onto more lines but never truncate.

### Modifiers are parents too

Each modifier wraps the view above it, so `.padding(20)` offers its child 40 points less.

```swift
// Each modifier wraps the line above it
Text("Padded")
    .foregroundStyle(.black)
    .padding(20)
    .background(.yellow)
    .border(.blue)
```

**Note:** That's why order matters: the background here covers the padding. See Modifier Order (`modifier-order`).

## Related

`stacks`, `frame`, `padding`, `modifier-order`


<!-- topic: stacks -->
---
id: stacks
title: Stacks
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/building-layouts-with-stack-views.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# Stacks

Arrange views in a column, a row, or layered on top of each other.

Also called: flexbox, flex-direction, row, column, div, UIStackView, z-index, position absolute, gap, align-items.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Alex Chen")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("Online now")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

**Note:** A stack is only as big as its children. To fill the screen's width, add `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` or a `Spacer`.

## Rules

- **Line related text up on one edge.** A shared leading edge is easy to scan. Centered text of different lengths makes the eye jump around.
- **Use space to show what belongs together.** Keep related items close and put more room between groups, so people see the structure without lines or boxes.
- **Leave room for larger text.** People can make text much bigger with Dynamic Type. Let rows grow taller, and switch an `HStack` to a `VStack` when it no longer fits.

## Pitfalls

- **Leave out `spacing` to get the system default.** SwiftUI picks spacing that suits the views and platform. Pass `0` only when children should touch.
- **`alignment` works across the stack's axis.** A `VStack` takes a horizontal alignment like `.leading`; an `HStack` takes a vertical one like `.top`.
- **Stacks are like flexbox with `flex-direction`.** `VStack` is a column, `HStack` a row, and `spacing` is `gap`. There's no wrapping; use Lazy Grids (`lazy-grids`) or ViewThatFits (`view-that-fits`) instead.

## Key APIs

- `VStack(alignment:spacing:)`: A column. Alignment is `.leading`, `.center`, or `.trailing`.
- `HStack(alignment:spacing:)`: A row. Alignment is `.top`, `.center`, `.bottom`, or a baseline.
- `ZStack(alignment:)`: Layers children; later ones draw on top.
- `LazyVStack` / `LazyHStack`: Create children only as they scroll on screen.
- `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)`: Stretches a stack to fill the width, like `width: 100%`.
- `.overlay(alignment:)`: Puts one view on top of another, sized to the base view.

## Variants

### Profile row

The most common iOS layout: an `HStack` with an icon, a leading `VStack` of text, and a `Spacer`.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 12) {
    Image(systemName: "person.crop.circle.fill")
        .font(.largeTitle)
        .foregroundStyle(.tint)
    VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 2) {
        Text("Alex Chen")
            .font(.headline)
        Text("Online now")
            .font(.subheadline)
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
    Spacer()
    Image(systemName: "chevron.right")
        .foregroundStyle(.tertiary)
}
```

### Badge on an icon

A `ZStack` with `.topTrailing` alignment pins a badge to the icon's corner, drawn on top.

```swift
ZStack(alignment: .topTrailing) {
    Image(systemName: "bell.fill")
        .font(.system(size: 44))
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Text("3")
        .font(.caption.bold())
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .padding(6)
        .background(.red, in: .circle)
        .offset(x: 8, y: -8)
}
```

**Note:** When one view only decorates another, `.overlay(alignment: .topTrailing)` does the same job and sizes itself to the icon instead of the larger of the two.

### Line up text on its baseline

Align an `HStack` on `.firstTextBaseline` so text of different sizes sits on one line, like a price.

```swift
HStack(alignment: .firstTextBaseline, spacing: 4) {
    Text("$")
        .font(.title3)
    Text("249")
        .font(.system(size: 56, weight: .bold))
    Text("/ year")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

### Long scrolling column

Put a `LazyVStack` in a `ScrollView` so rows are created only as they scroll into view.

```swift
ScrollView {
    LazyVStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
        ForEach(1...200, id: \.self) { i in
            Text("Message \(i)")
                .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
                .padding()
                .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 10))
        }
    }
    .padding()
}
.frame(height: 220)
```

**Note:** For rows with swipe actions, selection, and separators, use a List (`list`) instead.

## Related

`layout-basics`, `spacer-divider`, `grid`, `lazy-grids`


<!-- topic: spacer-divider -->
---
id: spacer-divider
title: Spacer & Divider
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/spacer.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# Spacer & Divider

Spacer pushes views apart in a stack; Divider draws a thin line between them.

Also called: justify-content, space-between, margin auto, flex-grow, hr, separator, line, gap.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
HStack {
    Text("Recent")
        .font(.headline)
    Spacer()
    Button("See All") {}
}
```

**Important:** A `Spacer` only works inside a stack. It grows along the stack's axis: sideways in an `HStack`, up and down in a `VStack`.

## Rules

- **Group with space before you reach for lines.** Extra space between groups already shows structure. A divider under every row adds noise without adding meaning.
- **Put the main item on the leading side.** People read from the leading edge, so put the title there and push secondary actions to the trailing edge with a `Spacer`.

## Pitfalls

- **Several spacers split the free space evenly.** One before, between, and after the views gives you `space-evenly`.
- **A spacer keeps a small gap by default.** Use `Spacer(minLength: 0)` when the views should be allowed to touch.
- **Lists and forms draw their own separators.** Don't add a `Divider` between `List` or `Form` rows.

## Key APIs

- `Spacer()`: Takes all the free space along the stack's axis.
- `Spacer(minLength:)`: Sets the smallest gap the spacer keeps.
- `Divider()`: A thin line: horizontal in a `VStack`, vertical in an `HStack`.
- `.frame(maxWidth:alignment:)`: Pushes a view to one edge without a spacer.
- `.fixedSize(horizontal:vertical:)`: Keeps a row with dividers only as tall as its content.

## Variants

### Pin a button to the bottom

A `Spacer` in a `VStack` pushes the button down, like a welcome screen's Continue button.

```swift
VStack(spacing: 12) {
    Image(systemName: "hand.wave.fill")
        .font(.system(size: 44))
        .foregroundStyle(.tint)
    Text("Welcome")
        .font(.title2.bold())
    Spacer()
    Button("Continue") {}
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
.padding()
.frame(height: 240)
```

### Stats with vertical dividers

In an `HStack`, a `Divider` is vertical and stretches to the stack's full height.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 20) {
    VStack {
        Text("128").font(.title3.bold())
        Text("Posts").font(.caption)
    }
    Divider()
    VStack {
        Text("4.2k").font(.title3.bold())
        Text("Followers").font(.caption)
    }
    Divider()
    VStack {
        Text("310").font(.title3.bold())
        Text("Following").font(.caption)
    }
}
.fixedSize(horizontal: false, vertical: true)
```

**Important:** Without `.fixedSize` on the vertical axis, the dividers grow as tall as the space offered. With it, the row is only as tall as its text.

### "Or" separator

Wrap each `Divider` in a `VStack` so it stays horizontal beside the word "or".

```swift
HStack(spacing: 12) {
    VStack { Divider() }
    Text("or")
        .font(.footnote)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    VStack { Divider() }
}
```

## Related

`stacks`, `layout-basics`, `frame`


<!-- topic: grid -->
---
id: grid
title: Grid
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/grid.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# Grid

Lines views up in rows and columns, sizing each column to its widest cell.

Also called: css grid, table, colspan, grid-column span, rows and columns, spreadsheet, UICollectionView, key value.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Grid(alignment: .leading) {
    GridRow {
        Text("Coffee")
        Text("$9.00")
    }
    GridRow {
        Text("Croissant")
        Text("$3.75")
    }
}
```

**Note:** `Grid` works like a set of `HStack`s in a `VStack`, except every column is as wide as its widest cell.

## Rules

- **Line values up in a column.** Aligned values are quick to scan and compare. Separate rows of text start wherever each label ends.
- **Use a list for long text.** A grid suits short, structured data. For many rows of text that people scroll, tap, or edit, a `List` is easier to read and use.

## Pitfalls

- **`Grid` isn't lazy.** It measures every cell up front so columns line up. For long or scrolling collections, use Lazy Grids (`lazy-grids`).
- **A view outside a `GridRow` spans every column.** That's how a `Divider` stretches across the whole grid.
- **Set alignment at three levels.** `Grid(alignment:)` for everything, `.gridColumnAlignment(_:)` for a column, and `.gridCellAnchor(_:)` for one cell.

## Key APIs

- `Grid(alignment:)`: The container. Also takes `horizontalSpacing` and `verticalSpacing`.
- `GridRow`: A row; each child view is one cell.
- `.gridCellColumns(_:)`: Spans a cell across columns, like `colspan`.
- `.gridColumnAlignment(_:)`: Aligns a whole column. Put it on any one cell.
- `.gridCellUnsizedAxes(_:)`: Stops a cell from widening its column or row.

## Variants

### Label and value pairs

Use `.gridColumnAlignment(.trailing)` on one label to right-align the whole label column.

```swift
Grid(alignment: .leading, horizontalSpacing: 16, verticalSpacing: 8) {
    GridRow {
        Text("Name")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            .gridColumnAlignment(.trailing)
        Text("Ada Lovelace")
    }
    GridRow {
        Text("Role")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        Text("Mathematician")
    }
    GridRow {
        Text("Member since")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        Text("1843")
    }
}
```

### Dashboard tiles with a wide cell

Flexible tiles share the width evenly, and `.gridCellColumns(2)` makes one tile twice as wide.

```swift
Grid(horizontalSpacing: 10, verticalSpacing: 10) {
    GridRow {
        Tile(title: "Steps", value: "8,204", color: .orange)
            .gridCellColumns(2)
        Tile(title: "Rings", value: "3/3", color: .pink)
    }
    GridRow {
        Tile(title: "Sleep", value: "7h", color: .indigo)
        Tile(title: "Heart", value: "62", color: .red)
        Tile(title: "Water", value: "1.2L", color: .blue)
    }
}
.frame(height: 170)

// At the top level of the file:
struct Tile: View {
    let title: String
    let value: String
    let color: Color

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Text(title).font(.caption)
            Spacer()
            Text(value).font(.title3.bold())
        }
        .padding(10)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .background(color.gradient, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
    }
}
```

**Note:** Each tile fills the height it's offered, so give the grid a fixed `.frame(height:)`.

## Related

`lazy-grids`, `stacks`, `view-that-fits`


<!-- topic: lazy-grids -->
---
id: lazy-grids
title: Lazy Grids
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/lazyvgrid.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/collections.md
---

# Lazy Grids

Scrolling grids of many items, like a photo library, built only as they appear.

Also called: UICollectionView, collection view, photo grid, gallery, grid-template-columns, auto-fill, minmax, masonry, tiles.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
let columns = [GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 100))]

ScrollView {
    LazyVGrid(columns: columns, spacing: 12) {
        ForEach(1...100, id: \.self) { i in
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 10)
                .fill(.blue.gradient)
                .frame(height: 100)
                .overlay { Text("\(i)").foregroundStyle(.white) }
        }
    }
    .padding()
}
```

**Important:** Lazy grids don't scroll on their own. Put a `LazyVGrid` in a `ScrollView`, and a `LazyHGrid` in a `ScrollView(.horizontal)`.

## Rules

- **Show text in a list, not a grid.** Grids are best for images. Text in tiles is harder to scan than the same text in rows.
- **Keep to a simple, regular grid.** People know how a grid of equal tiles works. An unusual layout draws attention to itself instead of the content.
- **Don't change the layout while people are using it.** Changing the column count mid-scroll makes people lose their place. Change it only when they ask, like with a zoom control.

## Pitfalls

- **`.adaptive` is CSS `auto-fill`.** `GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 100))` works like CSS `auto-fill` with `minmax(100px, 1fr)`: as many columns as fit.
- **Columns can't size to their content.** A lazy grid doesn't measure every cell. For a small table whose columns fit their text, use Grid (`grid`).

## Key APIs

- `LazyVGrid(columns:spacing:)`: Scrolls vertically; you describe the columns.
- `LazyHGrid(rows:spacing:)`: Scrolls sideways; you describe the rows.
- `GridItem(.flexible())`: One column that shares the width equally.
- `GridItem(.adaptive(minimum:))`: As many columns as fit, each at least this wide.
- `GridItem(.fixed(_:))`: One column of an exact width.
- `pinnedViews: [.sectionHeaders]`: Makes `Section` headers stick while scrolling.

## Variants

### Photo grid

Use `.adaptive` columns, 2-point spacing, and `.aspectRatio(1, contentMode: .fit)` for square photo cells.

```swift
let columns = [GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 80), spacing: 2)]

ScrollView {
    LazyVGrid(columns: columns, spacing: 2) {
        ForEach(0..<30, id: \.self) { i in
            Color(hue: Double(i) / 30, saturation: 0.5, brightness: 0.9)
                .aspectRatio(1, contentMode: .fit)
        }
    }
}
.frame(height: 240)
```

**Note:** Adaptive columns adjust themselves, so the grid gains columns when you rotate the phone or widen an iPad window.

### Sticky section headers

Wrap items in a `Section` and pass `pinnedViews: [.sectionHeaders]` so each header sticks while you scroll.

```swift
ScrollView {
    LazyVGrid(
        columns: [GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 60))],
        pinnedViews: [.sectionHeaders]
    ) {
        ForEach(["Fruit", "Vegetables", "Snacks"], id: \.self) { name in
            Section {
                ForEach(0..<8, id: \.self) { _ in
                    RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 8)
                        .fill(.fill.secondary)
                        .frame(height: 60)
                }
            } header: {
                Text(name)
                    .font(.headline)
                    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
                    .padding(.vertical, 6)
                    .background(.background)
            }
        }
    }
}
.frame(height: 240)
```

**Note:** Give a pinned header a background, or the cells scroll visibly behind its text.

### Two-row shelf

A `LazyHGrid` with two `.flexible()` rows scrolls sideways, like an App Store shelf.

```swift
let rows = [GridItem(.flexible()), GridItem(.flexible())]

ScrollView(.horizontal) {
    LazyHGrid(rows: rows, spacing: 12) {
        ForEach(0..<16, id: \.self) { i in
            Label("App \(i + 1)", systemImage: "app.fill")
                .frame(width: 140, alignment: .leading)
        }
    }
    .padding(.horizontal)
}
.scrollIndicators(.hidden)
.frame(height: 90)
```

## Related

`grid`, `scroll-view`, `stacks`


<!-- topic: scroll-view -->
---
id: scroll-view
title: ScrollView
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+, ScrollPosition macOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/scrollview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/scroll-views.md
---

# ScrollView

Lets content that's bigger than the screen scroll, vertically or sideways.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- On macOS
- Related

## Use when

- `ScrollView` shows content that's bigger than the space it has and lets people drag through it.
- It's as big as its parent offers, and its content is as long as it needs to be.
- Use it for custom layouts like cards, carousels, and feeds.

## Don't use when

- For rows of data with swipe actions, selection, and separators, use a List (`list`), which scrolls on its own.

## Default code

```swift
ScrollView {
    LazyVStack(spacing: 12) {
        ForEach(1...100, id: \.self) { i in
            Text("Row \(i)")
        }
    }
    .padding()
}
```

**Note:** A plain `VStack` inside builds every row up front. Use `LazyVStack` or `LazyHStack` for long content so rows are created as they scroll in.

## Built from

ScrollView(.horizontal)
├── LazyHStack
│   ├── ForEach → cards
│   └── .scrollTargetLayout()
├── .scrollTargetBehavior
├── .scrollPosition(id:)
└── .contentMargins

## Rules

- **Show that there's more to scroll.** Scroll bars aren't always visible. Let the next card peek in from the edge so people know they can swipe.
- **Don't nest scroll views on the same axis.** A vertical scroll view inside another vertical one is hard to control. A horizontal row inside a vertical feed is fine.
- **Pair paging with a page indicator.** When content scrolls a page at a time, show which page people are on, and hide the scroll bar on that axis so there aren't two indicators.

## Pitfalls

- **Snapping is CSS `scroll-snap`.** `.viewAligned` snaps to each view in a `.scrollTargetLayout()`; `.paging` snaps a whole screen at a time.
- **Pad the content, not the scroll view.** `.contentMargins` adds space that scrolls with the content, so cards can peek in from the edges. Plain `.padding` clips them.

## Key APIs

`ScrollView(_:)`, `.scrollTargetBehavior(_:)`, `.scrollTargetLayout()`, `.scrollPosition(id:)`, `.contentMargins(_:_:for:)`, `.scrollIndicators(_:)`, `.refreshable { }`, `.scrollTransition { }`

## On macOS

Scrolls content that's bigger than its frame, in one direction or both.

### Default code

```swift
ScrollView {
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        ForEach(1...50, id: \.self) { number in
            Text("Row \(number)")
        }
    }
    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
    .padding()
}
```

**Note:** A `ScrollView` takes all the space it's offered, like a `<div>` with `overflow: auto`. Give it a frame, or put it where its parent sets the size.

### Rules

- **Don't put a scroll view inside one that scrolls the same way.** Two vertical scroll views fight over every swipe. A horizontal row inside a vertical page is fine.
- **Scroll for people only when it helps them find their place.** Bring a search result or a new selection into view, and scroll only as far as it takes to show it.
- **Keep the standard scrolling gestures and keys.** People expect the gestures and keyboard shortcuts they scroll with everywhere else to work in your app too. If you build custom scrolling, keep the elastic bounce at the edges.

### Pitfalls

- **On the Mac, scroll bars follow the person's settings.** Whether they always show or appear only while scrolling depends on the Show scroll bars setting and on whether a mouse is connected, not just on your code.
- **Lists, tables, forms, and text editors already scroll.** Don't wrap them in a `ScrollView`; give them a frame instead.

### Key APIs

`.scrollIndicators(_:axes:)`, `.scrollPosition(_:anchor:)`, `.defaultScrollAnchor(_:)`

### Variants

#### Jump to a row with scrollPosition

Bind `.scrollPosition` to a `ScrollPosition` to scroll from code and to read which row is at the top.

```swift
struct Message: Identifiable {
    let id: Int
    var text: String { "Message \(id)" }
```
