```swift
}

@State private var position = ScrollPosition(idType: Int.self)
private let messages = (1...100).map(Message.init)

VStack {
    ScrollView {
        LazyVStack(alignment: .leading) {
            ForEach(messages) { Text($0.text) }
        }
        .scrollTargetLayout()
    }
    .scrollPosition($position)
    .frame(height: 140)

    HStack {
        Button("Top") { position.scrollTo(edge: .top) }
        Button("Message 50") { position.scrollTo(id: 50) }
        Button("Bottom") { position.scrollTo(edge: .bottom) }
    }
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Carousel with peeking cards, Scroll to top, Pull to refresh, Start in the middle of a canvas (macOS), A horizontal row with room at the edges (macOS), Keep scroll bars inside rounded corners (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/scrollview.md

## Related

`lazy-grids`, `stacks`, `geometry-reader`, `list`, `list-styles`, `table`, `stacks-grid`


<!-- topic: view-that-fits -->
---
id: view-that-fits
title: ViewThatFits
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/viewthatfits.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# ViewThatFits

Give it a few versions of a view, and it shows the first one that fits.

Also called: responsive, media query, container query, breakpoint, @media, adaptive layout, fallback, truncate.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
    Text("Free shipping on orders over $50")
    Text("Free shipping over $50")
    Text("Free shipping")
}
.font(.headline)
```

**Note:** List the options from largest to smallest. Each is measured at its ideal size, so text is checked on one line, unwrapped.

## Rules

- **Stack side-by-side items when they don't fit.** With large text or a narrow window, a row gets cramped. Switching to a column keeps every label on one line.
- **Show less, but keep every feature.** When space is tight, move actions into a menu rather than dropping them, so the app works the same at every size.

## Pitfalls

- **It's a container query, not a media query.** It reacts to the space its parent offers, not the screen. To adapt to the whole window, read the `horizontalSizeClass` environment value.
- **If nothing fits, you get the last option.** Make the last one the smallest, so it fits almost anywhere.

## Key APIs

`ViewThatFits { }`, `ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal)`, `.fixedSize()`, `\.horizontalSizeClass`, `AnyLayout`

## Variants

### Side by side, else stacked

Put an `HStack` first and a `VStack` second, so buttons sit in a row only when there's room.

```swift
ViewThatFits {
    HStack {
        Button("Not now") {}
            .buttonStyle(.bordered)
        Button("Turn on notifications") {}
            .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
    }
    VStack {
        Button("Turn on notifications") {}
            .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        Button("Not now") {}
            .buttonStyle(.bordered)
    }
}
```

### Scroll only when needed

Use `ViewThatFits(in: .vertical)` with a `ScrollView` fallback, so only text that's too tall scrolls.

```swift
let terms = Text("By continuing you agree to the terms…")
    .font(.subheadline)
    .foregroundStyle(.secondary)

ViewThatFits(in: .vertical) {
    terms
    ScrollView { terms }
}
.frame(height: 120)
```

**Note:** The short text on top doesn't scroll or bounce. The long text below falls back to the `ScrollView`.

## On macOS

Adapt a layout to the window's actual width, since Mac windows resize freely.

### Rules

- **Keep every feature available at every size.** A narrow window can show fewer controls at once, but the rest should move into a menu, not disappear.
- **Plan for very wide and very narrow windows.** People resize Mac windows to any shape. Check your layout at the smallest size you allow and at the largest.
- **Change the layout in ways people recognize.** When space runs out, rearrange what's there, like stacking side-by-side items, rather than switching to a different design.

### Pitfalls

- **Size classes don't help on the Mac.** The horizontal size class there is always `.regular`, however narrow the window gets.
- **Keep geometry work light.** Geometry can change on every frame of a scroll or resize. Return a small value, like a `Bool`, so the action runs only when it flips.

### Key APIs

`ViewThatFits(in:)`, `.onGeometryChange(for:of:action:)`, `HStackLayout`, `VStackLayout`, `.frame(minWidth:minHeight:)`, `.defaultSize(width:height:)`

### Variants

#### Labels, then icons, then a menu

`ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal)` shows the first child whose ideal width fits; drag the slider to narrow the space.

```swift
ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
    HStack {
        Button("New Note", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") { }
        Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { }
        Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash") { }
    }
    HStack {
        Button("New Note", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") { }
        Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { }
        Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash") { }
    }
    .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
    Menu("Actions", systemImage: "ellipsis.circle") {
        Button("New Note", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") { }
        Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { }
        Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash") { }
    }
    .fixedSize()
}
```

**Note:** List the children in order of preference, usually widest first. `in: .horizontal` checks only the width, so a child that's taller still counts as fitting.

#### Stack the columns below a width you choose

`.onGeometryChange` turns the width into a `Bool`, and `AnyLayout` switches between `HStackLayout` and `VStackLayout` without losing the state of the views inside.

```swift
@State private var isNarrow = false

let layout = isNarrow
    ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading))
    : AnyLayout(HStackLayout(alignment: .top))

layout {
    Image(systemName: "photo")
        .font(.largeTitle)
        .frame(width: 120, height: 80)
        .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 8))
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Lake Tahoe").font(.headline)
        Text("Clear water and granite peaks.")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
.onGeometryChange(for: Bool.self) { proxy in
    proxy.size.width < 360
} action: { narrow in
    isNarrow = narrow
}
```

**Note:** The transform runs often, so keep it cheap and return the smallest value you need. The action runs only when that value changes.

## Related

`geometry-reader`, `stacks`, `layout-basics`, `stacks-grid`, `split-views`, `window-group`, `windows-layout`


<!-- topic: geometry-reader -->
---
id: geometry-reader
title: GeometryReader
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/geometryreader.md
---

# GeometryReader

Three ways to size a view relative to its container or read its size.

Also called: getBoundingClientRect, ResizeObserver, vw, percentage width, measure size, onLayout, container width, containerRelativeFrame, onGeometryChange.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Reach for `GeometryReader` last.** `containerRelativeFrame` and `onGeometryChange` cover most needs without changing the layout around them.
- **`onGeometryChange` is new but back-deployed.** It's available from iOS 16, so you can use it in most apps today.

## Guide

Where CSS uses `width: 50%` or a `ResizeObserver`, SwiftUI has three tools. Pick the first one that does the job:

```swift
ScrollView(.horizontal) {
    HStack(spacing: 10) {
        ForEach(0..<6, id: \.self) { i in
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
                .fill(.blue.gradient)
                .frame(height: 80)
                .containerRelativeFrame(.horizontal, count: 3, span: 1, spacing: 10)
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The container is the nearest scroll view, list, or window, never the parent stack. Here it's the horizontal `ScrollView`.

## Key APIs

- `.containerRelativeFrame(_:)`: Sizes a view as a share of its container, with `count` and `span`.
- `.onGeometryChange(for:of:action:)`: Reads a size or position into state.
- `GeometryReader { proxy in }`: Fills the offered space and passes its size to the content.
- `proxy.size`: The size the reader was offered.
- `proxy.frame(in: .global)`: A view's position in another coordinate space.

## Variants

### onGeometryChange

`.onGeometryChange` reads the label's width into `@State` as you type, without changing its layout.

```swift
@State private var name = "Hello"
@State private var width: CGFloat = 0

VStack(spacing: 12) {
    Text(name)
        .font(.title.bold())
        .onGeometryChange(for: CGFloat.self) { proxy in
            proxy.size.width
        } action: { newWidth in
            width = newWidth
        }
    Capsule()
        .fill(.tint)
        .frame(width: width, height: 6)
    Text("\(Int(width)) pt wide")
        .font(.caption.monospacedDigit())
    TextField("Text", text: $name)
        .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
}
```

**Important:** Don't feed a measured size back into the same view's size. That can loop forever. Use it to drive other views.

### GeometryReader

A `GeometryReader` fills the offered space and passes its size to the content as `proxy.size`.

```swift
GeometryReader { proxy in
    let size = proxy.size
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("\(Int(size.width)) × \(Int(size.height))")
            .font(.headline.monospacedDigit())
        Capsule()
            .fill(.tint)
            .frame(width: size.width * 0.3, height: 8)
        Text("30% of the width")
            .font(.caption)
    }
}
.frame(height: 120)
.background(.tint.opacity(0.1))
```

**Important:** A `GeometryReader` takes all the space it's offered and puts its content at the top-leading corner. In a `VStack`, it pushes everything else away.

## Related

`view-that-fits`, `layout-basics`, `frame`, `scroll-view`


<!-- topic: safe-area -->
---
id: safe-area
title: Safe Area
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/ignoressafearea(_:edges:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# Safe Area

The part of the screen clear of the Dynamic Island, home indicator, bars, and keyboard.

Also called: notch, dynamic island, env(safe-area-inset-top), viewport-fit cover, full screen, edge to edge, home indicator, keyboard avoidance, insets.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
ZStack {
    LinearGradient(colors: [.blue, .purple], startPoint: .top, endPoint: .bottom)
        .ignoresSafeArea()
    Text("Welcome")
        .font(.largeTitle.bold())
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
}
```

**Note:** Put `.ignoresSafeArea()` on the background view only, so text stays clear of the edges. A `.background(_:)` modifier already reaches the edges without it.

## Rules

- **Keep text and controls inside the safe area.** The Dynamic Island and home indicator cover the screen's edges. Anything people need to read or tap belongs inside.
- **Run backgrounds all the way to the edges.** Colors and images that stop at the safe area leave bands at the top and bottom, so the screen looks unfinished.

## Pitfalls

- **It's like CSS `env(safe-area-inset-*)`, applied for you.** SwiftUI keeps views inside the safe area by default; you opt out instead of opting in.
- **The keyboard is part of the safe area.** SwiftUI moves content up when it appears. Opt out with `.ignoresSafeArea(.keyboard)`.

## Key APIs

- `.ignoresSafeArea()`: Lets a view extend under the bars, island, and home indicator.
- `.ignoresSafeArea(edges: .top)`: Extends past only some edges.
- `.background(_:)`: Fills behind a view and extends to the edges on its own.
- `.safeAreaInset(edge:)`: Pins a bar to an edge and moves content clear of it.
- `.safeAreaPadding(_:_:)`: Grows the safe area, so scroll content still reaches the edge.
- `.ignoresSafeArea(.keyboard)`: Stops the keyboard from pushing content up.

## Variants

### Full-bleed header

Use `.ignoresSafeArea(edges: .top)` on the header art only, so the title stays inside.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
    ZStack(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
        LinearGradient(colors: [.orange, .pink], startPoint: .topLeading, endPoint: .bottomTrailing)
            .ignoresSafeArea(edges: .top)
        Text("Weekend Trip")
            .font(.title.bold())
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .padding()
    }
    .frame(height: 160)
    Text("Saturday, 9:00 AM")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        .padding(.horizontal)
    Spacer()
}
```

### Floating bottom bar

Use `.safeAreaInset(edge: .bottom)` to pin a button, so the last row can scroll above it.

```swift
ScrollView {
    VStack(spacing: 10) {
        ForEach(1...20, id: \.self) { i in
            Text("Message \(i)")
                .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
                .padding()
                .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
        }
    }
    .padding(.horizontal)
}
.safeAreaInset(edge: .bottom) {
    Button("New Message", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") {}
        .buttonStyle(.glassProminent)
        .controlSize(.large)
}
```

**Important:** A plain `.overlay(alignment: .bottom)` would cover the last rows. `safeAreaInset` shrinks the safe area by the bar's height, so nothing is hidden.

### padding vs. safeAreaPadding

Scroll both rows: `.safeAreaPadding` insets the cards but lets them scroll to the edge.

```swift
// Cards get clipped 24pt from the edges
ScrollView(.horizontal) { cards }
    .padding(.horizontal, 24)

// Cards start 24pt in, but scroll to the edges
ScrollView(.horizontal) { cards }
    .safeAreaPadding(.horizontal, 24)
```

**Note:** Plain `.padding` shrinks the scroll view itself, so the top row's cards are cut off at the inset.

## Related

`layout-basics`, `scroll-view`, `padding`, `toolbar`


<!-- topic: list -->
---
id: list
title: List
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/list.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables.md
---

# List

A scrolling column of rows, like the ones in Settings, Mail, and Contacts.

Also called: table, ul, li, rows, UITableView, UICollectionView, feed, map array, for each, v-for.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `List` owns scrolling, row separators, section headers, and system behaviors like swipe actions, selection, and pull to refresh.
- It's the SwiftUI version of `UITableView`, and the backbone of most iPhone screens.
- Use it for rows of text people scan and tap.
- For a grid of images or cards, use a lazy grid inside a `ScrollView`.

## Don't use when

- For editable settings, use Form (`form`).

## Default code

```swift
let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"]

List {
    Section("Favorites") {
        ForEach(fruits, id: \.self) { fruit in
            Label(fruit, systemImage: "leaf")
        }
    }
}
```

**Important:** Each item needs a stable identity. Make your model `Identifiable` or pass `id: \.someKey`; array indexes break animations when rows move.

## Built from

List
├── Section("Header")
│   └── ForEach(items)
│       └── Row view
│           └── .swipeActions
└── Section
    └── Fixed row

## Rules

- **Keep row text short.** Short rows are easy to scan and don't wrap or truncate. Put long text on a detail screen people open from the row.
- **Use a chevron for rows that open a screen.** A `NavigationLink` row adds the chevron for you. Don't use an info button to navigate; it only reveals details about the row.
- **Pick the style that fits the content.** Use `.insetGrouped` for settings-like groups and `.plain` for long feeds like messages, where rows run edge to edge.
- **Let people edit lists they own.** People expect to delete and reorder their own items. Add `.onDelete` and `.onMove` and the system handles the gestures.

## Pitfalls

- **`List` is lazy.** It only builds the rows on screen, so it handles thousands of items without slowing down.
- **Selection on iPhone needs edit mode.** `List(selection:)` with a `Set` shows checkmark circles only while editing; add an `EditButton` to the toolbar.
- **Want rows without the list look?** Use a `ScrollView` with a `LazyVStack` for a feed of custom cards.

## Key APIs

- `List(_:rowContent:)`: One row per item in an `Identifiable` collection.
- `ForEach(_:content:)`: Data rows mixed with fixed rows and sections.
- `Section(_:content:)`: Groups rows under a header, with an optional footer.
- `.listStyle(_:)`: `.insetGrouped`, `.plain`, `.sidebar`, and more.
- `.onDelete(perform:)`: On a `ForEach`: swipe to delete, plus edit mode.
- `List(selection:)`: Binds selected rows to an optional or a `Set`.
- `.refreshable { }`: Pull to refresh, running an `async` action.
- `.listRowSeparator(_:)`: Hides or shows one row's separator.

## Variants

### Rows from data

Pass an `Identifiable` array to `List`, like `items.map(item => <li>…</li>)` on the web.

```swift
struct Message: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
    let sender: String
    let preview: String
}

@State private var messages = [
    Message(sender: "Maya", preview: "Are we still on for lunch tomorrow?"),
    Message(sender: "Leo", preview: "Sent you the photos from the trip"),
]

List(messages) { message in
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text(message.sender)
            .font(.headline)
        Text(message.preview)
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            .lineLimit(1)
    }
}
.listStyle(.plain)
```

### Swipe to delete

Add `.onDelete` to the `ForEach`, and every row gets a swipe-to-delete action for free.

```swift
@State private var fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry", "Kiwi"]

List {
    ForEach(fruits, id: \.self) { fruit in
        Text(fruit)
    }
    .onDelete { offsets in
        fruits.remove(atOffsets: offsets)
    }
}
```

**Important:** `.onDelete` goes on the `ForEach`, not the `List`. For other swipe buttons, use Swipe Actions (`swipe-actions`).

### Empty state

Show `ContentUnavailableView` in an `.overlay` when the data is empty. Tap Add to fill the list.

```swift
@State private var items: [String] = []

List(items, id: \.self) { item in
    Text(item)
}
.overlay {
    if items.isEmpty {
        ContentUnavailableView(
            "No Items",
            systemImage: "tray",
            description: Text("Items you add appear here.")
        )
    }
}
```

### Custom row styling

Put `.listRowBackground`, `.listRowInsets`, and `.listRowSeparatorTint` on each row, not on the list.

```swift
List {
    ForEach(["Low", "Medium", "High"], id: \.self) { level in
        Text(level)
            .listRowBackground(Color.orange.opacity(0.15))
            .listRowInsets(.init(top: 14, leading: 24, bottom: 14, trailing: 24))
            .listRowSeparatorTint(.orange)
    }
}
```

## Related

`form`, `swipe-actions`, `navigation-stack`, `lazy-grids`


<!-- topic: form -->
---
id: form
title: Form
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+, formStyle macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/form.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/entering-data.md
---

# Form

A container that lays out controls as grouped rows, like the Settings app.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Use when

- `Form` is a `List` that restyles the controls inside it for data entry: toggles get a trailing switch, pickers become menu rows, and buttons become tappable rows.
- You get the grouped Settings look without styling anything.
- Use it for settings, sign-up, and edit screens.

## Don't use when

- For rows of content people browse, use List (`list`).

## Default code

```swift
@State private var name = ""
@State private var notifications = true

Form {
    Section("Profile") {
        TextField("Name", text: $name)
        Toggle("Notifications", isOn: $notifications)
    }
    Section("About") {
        LabeledContent("Version", value: "2.1")
    }
}
```

**Note:** On iPhone, a `Form` fills the screen like a `List`. Wrap it in a `NavigationStack` to give it a title.

## Built from

Form
├── Section("Header")
│   ├── TextField
│   ├── Toggle
│   └── Picker
└── Section
    ├── LabeledContent
    └── footer: Text

## Rules

- **Offer choices instead of typing.** Picking from a short list is faster than typing and can't go wrong. Use a `Picker`, `Toggle`, or `Stepper` when the answers are known.
- **Validate as people type.** Show problems right away and keep the Continue button disabled until the required fields are filled, so nobody has to go back and fix things.
- **Explain settings in a section footer.** A sentence under a group tells people what a switch does before they change it. Keep the row labels themselves short.
- **Use `SecureField` for passwords, and never prefill one.** It hides each character as people type. Prefilling a password exposes it to anyone holding the phone.

## Pitfalls

- **A form doesn't submit anything.** Each control writes to its own `@State` as it changes, so there's no `onSubmit` for the whole form. Add a Save button if you need one.
- **Show read-only values with `LabeledContent`.** It puts a label on the left and a value on the right, like “Version 2.1” in Settings.

## Key APIs

`Form { }`, `Section(_:content:)`, `Section { } footer: { }`, `LabeledContent(_:value:)`, `.pickerStyle(_:)`, `.disabled(_:)`

## Variants

### Sign-up form with validation

Keep the submit `Button` disabled with `.disabled(_:)` until the input is valid.

```swift
@State private var email = ""
@State private var agreed = false

Form {
    Section("Account") {
        TextField("Email", text: $email)
            .keyboardType(.emailAddress)
            .textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
        Toggle("I agree to the terms", isOn: $agreed)
    }
    Section {
        Button("Create Account") {
            // Submit
        }
        .disabled(!email.contains("@") || !agreed)
    }
}
```

**Note:** A `Button` in a form is just another row, drawn as tinted text.

## On macOS

Groups labeled controls for settings and data entry, in Mac columns or System Settings rows.

### Default code

```swift
@State private var name = ""
@State private var showsLineNumbers = true

Form {
    TextField("Name", text: $name)
    Toggle("Show line numbers", isOn: $showsLineNumbers)
    LabeledContent("Version", value: "2.4")
}
```

**Note:** On the Mac, a plain `Form` uses `.columns`, not the grouped look of iPhone. Add `.formStyle(.grouped)` when you want rows like System Settings.

### Rules

- **Group related settings into sections.** A few small sections are faster to scan than one long run of rows, and a header tells people what each group is for.
- **Offer as few settings as you can.** Pick good defaults so most people never need to change anything. Every extra option makes the one people want harder to find.
- **Keep options for the current task in its window.** Choices like sorting or showing a column belong next to the content they change, not in a settings form people have to go and open.

### Pitfalls

- **Controls change inside a `Form`.** In a grouped form, a toggle becomes a switch and a picker sits at the trailing edge of its row. Put the same controls in a `VStack` and they keep their plain look.
- **A grouped form scrolls by itself.** It's a scroll view, like `List`. The columns style doesn't scroll, so wrap a long one in a `ScrollView` or split it into panes.

### Key APIs

`.formStyle(.columns)`, `.formStyle(.grouped)`, `LabeledContent { } label: { }`

### Variants

#### A classic Mac columns form

`.formStyle(.columns)` right-aligns each label against its control, and by Mac convention the labels end with a colon.

```swift
@State private var startsWith = "Last session"
@State private var fontSize = 13.0
@State private var opensInTabs = true

Form {
    Picker("Start with:", selection: $startsWith) {
        Text("Last session").tag("Last session")
        Text("New document").tag("New document")
    }
    .pickerStyle(.radioGroup)
    Stepper("Font size: \(Int(fontSize)) pt", value: $fontSize, in: 9...24)
    Toggle("Open documents in tabs", isOn: $opensInTabs)
}
.formStyle(.columns)
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Inline picker, Rows that open other screens, Grouped, like System Settings (macOS), Read-only rows with LabeledContent (macOS), Several checkboxes under one label (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/form.md

## Related

`list`, `toggle`, `picker`, `settings-screen`, `labeled-content`, `group-box`, `settings-scene`


<!-- topic: navigation-stack -->
---
id: navigation-stack
title: NavigationStack
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/navigationstack.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/navigation-and-search.md
---

# NavigationStack

Pushes screens on top of each other with a back button, like drilling into a folder.

## Contents

- Use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Use when

- `NavigationStack` owns a stack of screens and the navigation bar above them.
- Each push slides a new screen in with a Back button, and the stack remembers the way back.
- Use it for drill-down hierarchies like Settings or Mail.
- For a sidebar on iPad, use `NavigationSplitView`.
- For top-level sections, put one stack in each tab of a `TabView`.

## Default code

```swift
NavigationStack {
    List(fruits, id: \.self) { fruit in
        NavigationLink(fruit, value: fruit)
    }
    .navigationTitle("Fruits")
    .navigationDestination(for: String.self) { fruit in
        Text(fruit)
    }
}
```

**Important:** Put `.navigationTitle`, `.toolbar`, and `.navigationDestination` on the views inside the stack, not on the `NavigationStack` itself.

## Built from

NavigationStack
└── Root view (a List)
    ├── NavigationLink(value:)
    ├── .navigationTitle
    ├── .toolbar
    └── .navigationDestination
        └── Destination view

## Rules

- **Keep titles short.** Aim for a word or two, under 15 characters, so the bar has room for buttons. Don't use your app's name as a title; it doesn't tell people where they are.
- **Use a large title at the top of a hierarchy.** It tells people where they are, and it shrinks into the bar as they scroll. Pushed screens usually use `.inline`.
- **Keep the standard Back button.** People know it retraces their steps. Don't replace it with a custom “Back” label or hide it unless the screen offers another way out.
- **Put only the most important actions in the bar.** iPhone has room for a few. Move the rest into a More menu with `Menu` in the toolbar.

## Pitfalls

- **Navigate in code with a path.** Bind the stack to an array: append to push, `removeLast()` to go back, and set it to `[]` to pop to the root. A deep link is just a path.
- **Use one stack per tab, and never nest them.** A `NavigationStack` inside another one leads to double bars and links that don't work.
- **`NavigationView` is deprecated.** Use `NavigationStack`, or `NavigationSplitView` for a sidebar.

## Key APIs

`NavigationStack(path:)`, `NavigationLink(_:value:)`, `.navigationDestination(for:)`, `.navigationDestination(item:)`, `.navigationTitle(_:)`, `.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(_:)`, `.toolbar { }`

## Variants

### Routes with an enum

Model each screen as an enum case, and map them all in one `.navigationDestination`, like a route table.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case profile(String)
    case settings
}

@State private var path: [Route] = []

NavigationStack(path: $path) {
    List {
        NavigationLink("Maya's profile", value: Route.profile("Maya"))
        NavigationLink("Settings", value: Route.settings)
    }
    .navigationTitle("Home")
    .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
        switch route {
        case .profile(let name): Text("Profile of \(name)")
        case .settings: Text("Settings")
        }
    }
}
```

**Important:** Every value type you push needs a matching `.navigationDestination(for:)` inside the stack. Without one, the link does nothing.

### Present a detail from a selection

Use `.navigationDestination(item:)` when a button, not a link, decides where to go.

```swift
@State private var selected: String?

NavigationStack {
    VStack(spacing: 12) {
        Button("Open Report") { selected = "Report" }
        Button("Open Invoice") { selected = "Invoice" }
    }
    .buttonStyle(.bordered)
    .navigationTitle("Documents")
    .navigationDestination(item: $selected) { name in
        Text(name)
            .font(.largeTitle)
    }
}
```

## On macOS

Push views inside a window, with a Back button in the toolbar.

### Rules

- **Use the standard Back button.** People know it from every other app. Use the system's symbol, not a text label that says Back.
- **Give every level a short title.** The title tells people where they are as they drill down. Aim for a word or two.

### Pitfalls

- **A link needs a destination for its type.** `NavigationLink(value:)` does nothing until a `navigationDestination(for:)` for that type is somewhere in the stack.
- **Save the path to restore it.** If every value is `Codable`, `NavigationPath.codable` gives you something to store and decode at the next launch.

### Key APIs

`NavigationStack { }`, `NavigationPath`, `path.removeLast()`

### Variants

#### Usage

```swift
let parks = ["Yosemite", "Zion", "Acadia"]

NavigationStack {
    List(parks, id: \.self) { park in
        NavigationLink(park, value: park)
    }
    .navigationDestination(for: String.self) { park in
        Text(park)
            .navigationTitle(park)
    }
    .navigationTitle("Parks")
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Push with links and destinations (macOS), Control the stack with a path (macOS), Different kinds of values (macOS), In a split view (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/navigationstack.md

## Related

`navigation-split-view`, `list`, `toolbar`, `tab-view`, `state-binding`, `opening-windows`


<!-- topic: navigation-split-view -->
---
id: navigation-split-view
title: NavigationSplitView
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/navigationsplitview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sidebars.md

# NavigationSplitView

A sidebar and detail side by side on iPad that collapses into a stack on iPhone.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Use when

- `NavigationSplitView` owns two or three columns: a sidebar, an optional content list, and a detail.
- On iPad they sit side by side; on iPhone they collapse into one `NavigationStack`, where the sidebar is the first screen and picking a row pushes the detail.
- Use it when your app is organized around a list of sources, like Mail or Notes.

## Don't use when

- For a few top-level sections on iPhone, use TabView (`tab-view`) instead.

## Default code

```swift
@State private var folder: String?

NavigationSplitView {
    List(["Inbox", "Sent"], id: \.self, selection: $folder) { folder in
        Label(folder, systemImage: "folder")
    }
    .navigationTitle("Mail")
} detail: {
    Text(folder ?? "Pick a folder")
}
```

**Note:** Drive the detail with `List(selection:)`; you don't need `NavigationLink`s. On iPhone, picking a row pushes the detail for you.

## Built from

NavigationSplitView
├── sidebar
│   └── List(selection:)
├── content (optional)
│   └── List(selection:)
└── detail
    └── View for the selection

## Rules

- **Give sidebar items familiar symbols.** An SF Symbol beside each label makes the list faster to scan, and it matches the system apps.
- **Keep the sidebar to two levels.** Deeper hierarchies get hard to follow in one column. Add a content column between the sidebar and the detail instead.
- **Show the sidebar by default.** A hidden sidebar is easy to miss. Let people hide it themselves; iPad already supports the edge swipe.

## Pitfalls

- **Test on both iPhone and iPad.** One piece of code gives you two layouts, and an empty detail state only shows up on iPad.
- **Show an empty state in the detail.** On iPad the detail is visible before anything is selected, so give it a `ContentUnavailableView`.

## Key APIs

`NavigationSplitView { } detail: { }`, `content: { }`, `List(_:selection:)`, `columnVisibility:`, `.navigationSplitViewStyle(_:)`, `.navigationSplitViewColumnWidth(_:)`

## Variants

### Sidebar from an enum

Model the sidebar as an enum, bind `List(selection:)` to it, and `switch` in the detail.

```swift
enum Folder: String, CaseIterable, Identifiable {
    case inbox = "Inbox", drafts = "Drafts", sent = "Sent"
    var id: Self { self }
}

@State private var folder: Folder? = .inbox

NavigationSplitView {
    List(Folder.allCases, selection: $folder) { folder in
        Label(folder.rawValue, systemImage: "folder")
    }
    .navigationTitle("Mail")
} detail: {
    switch folder {
    case .inbox: Text("Inbox")
    case .drafts: Text("Drafts")
    case .sent: Text("Sent")
    case nil: ContentUnavailableView("No Folder", systemImage: "folder")
    }
}
```

**Note:** Starting with a selection, like `.inbox`, fills the detail on iPad. On iPhone the sidebar still shows first.

## On macOS

Two or three columns, where a selection in the sidebar fills the detail.

### Rules

- **Keep the selection highlighted.** The highlight in each column shows how it leads to the detail, so people always know where they are.
- **Let people hide the sidebar, but show it at first.** Offer a toolbar button and View menu commands to hide and show it. Hiding it by default makes it hard to discover.
- **Show at most two levels in a sidebar.** For deeper hierarchies, add a content column between the sidebar and the detail.
- **Keep important things away from the sidebar's bottom.** People often move windows so the bottom edge is off screen.

### Pitfalls

- **The Mac always shows the content column.** In a three-column view, visibility settings can hide the sidebar, but the middle column stays.
- **This app is built on one.** The sidebar beside this page is a `NavigationSplitView` sidebar, with its search field at the top.

### Key APIs

`init(sidebar:detail:)`, `init(sidebar:content:detail:)`, `.navigationSplitViewColumnWidth`, `.toolbar(removing: .sidebarToggle)`

### Variants

#### Usage

```swift
@State private var selection: String?
let mailboxes = ["Inbox", "Drafts", "Sent"]

NavigationSplitView {
    List(mailboxes, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { mailbox in
        Text(mailbox)
    }
} detail: {
    Text(selection ?? "Select a mailbox")
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Drill down in the detail, Sidebar and detail (macOS), Three columns (macOS), Hide and show the sidebar (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/navigationsplitview.md

## Related

`navigation-stack`, `list`, `tab-view`, `split-views`, `list-styles`, `outline`, `toolbar`, `search`, `inspector`


<!-- topic: tab-view -->
---
id: tab-view
title: TabView
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/tabview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/tab-bars.md
---

# TabView

Switches between top-level sections with a tab bar, or swipes through pages like a carousel.

Also called: tab bar, tabs, bottom navigation, UITabBarController, carousel, pager, swiper, page control, onboarding pages, bottom nav.

## Contents

- Use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `TabView` owns the app's top-level sections and the tab bar that switches between them.
- Each tab keeps its own state, so people can leave a tab and come back to the same place.
- Use it for three to five main areas, like Home, Search, and Profile.
- With `.tabViewStyle(.page)`, the same view becomes a swipeable carousel.

## Default code

```swift
TabView {
    Tab("Home", systemImage: "house") {
        NavigationStack {
            Text("Home")
                .navigationTitle("Home")
        }
    }
    Tab("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") {
        Text("Profile")
    }
}
```

**Important:** Put a `NavigationStack` inside each tab, not one around the `TabView`, so every tab keeps its own back history.

## Built from

TabView(selection:)
├── Tab("Home")
│   └── NavigationStack
│       └── Root view
├── Tab("Inbox")
│   └── NavigationStack
└── Tab(role: .search)

## Rules

- **Use tabs to navigate, not to act.** A tab switches sections. An action like New Post belongs in a toolbar button, where people expect to find it.
- **Label tabs with one word.** Short labels fit on every iPhone and are quick to read. Pair each with a filled SF Symbol.
- **Keep the tab bar visible.** Hiding it makes people forget where they are. Only a sheet or full-screen cover should cover it.
- **Use five tabs or fewer on iPhone.** Extra tabs end up behind a More tab, where people rarely find them. Offer a sidebar with `.sidebarAdaptable` for bigger apps.
- **Save badges for things that need attention.** A badge on every tab turns into noise. Use one for unread messages, not for marketing.

## Pitfalls

- **Prefer `Tab` over `.tabItem`.** The `Tab` type (iOS 18) supports search tabs, sections, and sidebars. The older `.tabItem` modifier still works but can't do those.
- **The tab bar floats as Liquid Glass.** `.tabBarMinimizeBehavior(.onScrollDown)` shrinks it while people scroll, and `.tabViewBottomAccessory` adds a bar above it, like Music's mini player.

## Key APIs

- `Tab(_:systemImage:content:)`: One tab with a label and an SF Symbol.
- `TabView(selection:)`: Binds the current tab, so you can switch in code.
- `.badge(_:)`: A red count on a tab.
- `Tab(role: .search)`: A separate search tab at the trailing end.
- `TabSection(_:content:)`: Groups tabs in the iPad sidebar.
- `.tabViewStyle(_:)`: `.sidebarAdaptable` for iPad, or `.page` for a carousel.
- `.tabBarMinimizeBehavior(_:)`: Shrinks the tab bar while people scroll.
- `.tabViewBottomAccessory { }`: A bar above the tabs, like a mini player.

## Variants

### A stack in every tab

Give each `Tab` its own `NavigationStack`, so pushing in one tab doesn't affect the others.

```swift
TabView {
    Tab("Inbox", systemImage: "tray") {
        NavigationStack {
            List(["Lunch on Friday?", "Your order shipped"], id: \.self) { subject in
                NavigationLink(subject) { Text(subject) }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Inbox")
        }
    }
    .badge(2)
    Tab("Settings", systemImage: "gear") {
        NavigationStack {
            List {
                NavigationLink("Notifications") { Text("Notifications") }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Settings")
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** Push a message in Inbox, switch to Settings and back: Inbox is still on the message.

### Image carousel

Use `.tabViewStyle(.page)` with a fixed height for a swipeable gallery anywhere on a screen.

```swift
TabView {
    ForEach(["mountain.2.fill", "water.waves", "sun.horizon.fill"], id: \.self) { symbol in
        Image(systemName: symbol)
            .font(.system(size: 56))
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
            .background(.teal.gradient)
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
    }
}
.tabViewStyle(.page)
.indexViewStyle(.page(backgroundDisplayMode: .always))
.frame(height: 200)
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 20))
```

**Note:** `.indexViewStyle(.page(backgroundDisplayMode: .always))` puts a backdrop behind the dots so they show on light images.

### Sidebar on iPad

Use `.tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable)` and `TabSection` to let iPad users turn the tabs into a sidebar.

```swift
TabView {
    Tab("Listen Now", systemImage: "play.circle") {
        Text("Listen Now")
    }
    TabSection("Library") {
        Tab("Artists", systemImage: "music.mic") {
            Text("Artists")
        }
        Tab("Albums", systemImage: "square.stack") {
            Text("Albums")
        }
    }
}
.tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable)
```

## Related

`navigation-stack`, `navigation-split-view`, `onboarding`, `toolbar`


<!-- topic: toolbar -->
---
id: toolbar
title: Toolbar
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/toolbar(content:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toolbars.md
---

# Toolbar

Puts buttons and menus in the bar at the top or bottom of a screen.

## Contents

- Use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Use when

- `.toolbar` fills the bars of the screen it's attached to: the navigation bar at the top and an optional bar at the bottom.
- Each screen brings its own items, and they swap as you push and pop.
- A plain `Button` lands in the trailing spot.
- Wrap it in `ToolbarItem(placement:)` to put it somewhere else.

## Default code

```swift
NavigationStack {
    List(1...20, id: \.self) { Text("Note \($0)") }
        .navigationTitle("Notes")
        .toolbar {
            Button("Add", systemImage: "plus") {
                // Add a note
            }
        }
}
```

**Important:** Put `.toolbar` on a view inside the `NavigationStack`, not on the stack itself, or the items won't show.

## Built from

NavigationStack
└── Screen view
    └── .toolbar
        ├── ToolbarItem
        ├── ToolbarSpacer
        ├── ToolbarItem
        └── ToolbarItem(.bottomBar)

## Rules

- **Use symbols for common actions.** Familiar SF Symbols like share and plus are quicker to recognize than words, and leave room for the title. Keep text for actions like Edit that have no clear symbol.
- **Keep the bar uncluttered.** Show the two or three actions people use most, and move the rest into a More menu built with `Menu`.
- **Mark one primary action.** Put Done or Save in `.confirmationAction`, so it's tinted and sits on the trailing side. More than one makes the focus unclear.
- **Keep the standard Back and Close buttons.** People already know what they do. Don't swap them for a text label that says Back or Close.

## Pitfalls

- **Neighboring buttons share one glass capsule.** `ToolbarSpacer(.fixed)` splits them into separate groups, and `ToolbarSpacer(.flexible)` pushes them apart.
- **Add a second line under the title.** `.navigationSubtitle` (iOS 26) shows a smaller line, like Mail's unread count.

## Key APIs

`.toolbar { }`, `ToolbarItem(placement:)`, `.topBarLeading`, `.topBarTrailing`, `.confirmationAction`, `.cancellationAction`, `.bottomBar`, `ToolbarSpacer(_:placement:)`, `.toolbar(_:for:)`

## Variants

### Save and Cancel in a sheet

Use `.cancellationAction` and `.confirmationAction` to put Cancel and Save where people expect them.

```swift
@State private var showEditor = false

Button("New Event") { showEditor = true }
    .sheet(isPresented: $showEditor) {
        NavigationStack {
            Form {
                TextField("Title", text: .constant(""))
            }
            .navigationTitle("New Event")
            .navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
            .toolbar {
                ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) {
                    Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { showEditor = false }
                }
                ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction) {
                    Button("Add", role: .confirm) { showEditor = false }
                }
            }
        }
    }
```

**Note:** A sheet doesn't get a bar of its own. Wrap its content in a `NavigationStack` to show a title and toolbar.

## On macOS

Commands, controls, and search at the top of a window, placed by what they do.

### Rules

- **Use symbols, not words.** Simple, familiar symbols are quicker to scan and take less space. Text works better only for actions a symbol can't show, like Edit.
- **Title the window after its content, not your app.** A title like the mailbox or document name tells people where they are. The app's name tells them nothing about what's in the window.
- **Put every toolbar command in the menu bar too.** People can hide or customize the toolbar, so it can't be the only home for a command.
- **Keep it to a few groups.** Group items by what they do, and aim for no more than three groups. Too many makes the toolbar feel cluttered.

### Pitfalls

- **Narrow windows move items into an overflow menu.** Choose a few items that matter, so little ends up hidden there.
- **Keep window titles short.** The HIG suggests under 15 characters, so the title leaves room for the toolbar's items.

### Key APIs

`.navigation`, `.principal`, `.primaryAction`, `.toolbar(id:)`, `ToolbarSpacer(.fixed)`, `.navigationSubtitle(_:)`

### Variants

#### Usage

```swift
List(["Lunch on Friday?", "Your receipt"], id: \.self) { subject in
    Text(subject)
}
.navigationTitle("Inbox")
.toolbar {
    Button("New Message", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") { }
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Menu in the toolbar, Placements (macOS), A toolbar people can customize (macOS), Space between groups (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/toolbar(content:).md

## Related

`navigation-stack`, `button`, `menu`, `searchable`, `search`, `navigation-split-view`, `toggle`, `commands`, `toolbars-pattern`


<!-- topic: searchable -->
---
id: searchable
title: Searchable
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/searchable(text:placement:prompt:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/search-fields.md
---

# Searchable

Adds a system search field to a screen and hands you the text to filter with.

Also called: search bar, search box, filter, input type=search, UISearchController, UISearchBar, autocomplete, typeahead, find.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var searchText = ""

let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry", "Kiwi"]

NavigationStack {
    List(fruits.filter { searchText.isEmpty || $0.localizedStandardContains(searchText) }, id: \.self) { fruit in
        Text(fruit)
    }
    .navigationTitle("Fruit")
    .searchable(text: $searchText, prompt: "Search fruit")
}
```

**Important:** `.searchable` only draws the field; you filter the data yourself. It also needs a `NavigationStack` around it to have a bar to live in.

## Rules

- **Say what people can search for.** A specific prompt like “Search recipes” sets expectations. The default “Search” doesn't tell people what's inside.
- **Update results as people type.** Live results feel fast and help people narrow down. Wait for the Search key only when a search is slow, like a network request.
- **Suggest searches before people type.** Recent or popular searches in `.searchSuggestions` save typing and show what's possible.
- **Start with the broadest scope.** Show all results first and let people narrow them with scopes. Use scopes only for a few clear categories.

## Pitfalls

- **On iPhone the field sits at the bottom.** In iOS 26 that's the default, where thumbs reach it. `.navigationBarDrawer` keeps it under the title instead.
- **For app-wide search, use a search tab.** `Tab(role: .search)` in a TabView (`tab-view`) keeps search one tap away from every section.

## Key APIs

- `.searchable(text:prompt:)`: Adds the field and binds its text.
- `placement:`: Where the field goes, like `.navigationBarDrawer`.
- `.searchSuggestions { }`: Rows shown while the field is active.
- `.searchCompletion(_:)`: On a suggestion: fills the field when tapped.
- `.searchScopes(_:scopes:)`: A segmented filter under the field.
- `.onSubmit(of: .search)`: Runs when people tap Search on the keyboard.
- `ContentUnavailableView.search(text:)`: The standard “No Results” view.

## Variants

### No results

Show `ContentUnavailableView.search` in an `.overlay` when nothing matches the search text.

```swift
@State private var searchText = ""

let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry", "Kiwi"]

NavigationStack {
    let results = fruits.filter { searchText.isEmpty || $0.localizedStandardContains(searchText) }
    List(results, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
        .navigationTitle("Fruit")
        .searchable(text: $searchText)
        .overlay {
            if results.isEmpty {
                ContentUnavailableView.search(text: searchText)
            }
        }
}
```

### Search when people tap Search

Use `.onSubmit(of: .search)` when a search is slow, like a network request.

```swift
@State private var searchText = ""
@State private var lastSearch = ""

NavigationStack {
    Text(lastSearch.isEmpty ? "Type, then tap Search" : "Results for “\(lastSearch)”")
        .navigationTitle("Store")
        .searchable(text: $searchText)
        .onSubmit(of: .search) {
            lastSearch = searchText
        }
}
```

**Note:** Without it, `searchText` still changes on every keystroke, so you can also debounce in a `.task(id: searchText)`.

### Search tokens

Use `.searchable(text:tokens:)` for filter capsules in the field, like Mail's “From: Maya”.

```swift
struct Tag: Identifiable, Hashable {
    let id: String
}

@State private var text = ""
@State private var tokens: [Tag] = []

NavigationStack {
    List {
        Text(tokens.isEmpty ? "All photos" : "Photos tagged \(tokens.map(\.id).formatted())")
    }
    .navigationTitle("Photos")
    .searchable(text: $text, tokens: $tokens) { tag in
        Label(tag.id, systemImage: "tag")
    }
    .searchSuggestions {
        ForEach([Tag(id: "Beach"), Tag(id: "Dogs")]) { tag in
            Label(tag.id, systemImage: "tag")
                .searchCompletion(tag)
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** People don't know which tokens exist. Offer them as suggestions with `.searchCompletion(tag)`, as here.

## Related

`list`, `navigation-stack`, `text-field`, `toolbar`


<!-- topic: swipe-actions -->
---
id: swipe-actions
title: Swipe Actions & Editing
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/swipeactions(edge:allowsfullswipe:content:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables.md
---

# Swipe Actions & Editing

Lets people swipe rows for actions, delete and reorder them, and pull to refresh.

Also called: swipe to delete, slide to delete, drag to reorder, sortable, pull to refresh, onDelete, edit mode, UIContextualAction, trailingSwipeActions.

## Default code

```swift
@State private var names = ["Maya", "Leo", "Priya"]

List(names, id: \.self) { name in
    Text(name)
        .swipeActions {
            Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash", role: .destructive) {
                names.removeAll { $0 == name }
            }
        }
}
```

**Important:** Once a row has `.swipeActions`, its `.onDelete` swipe stops showing. Add your own Delete button with `role: .destructive`, as here.

## Rules

- **Make the full swipe the expected action.** A full swipe runs the first button without a second tap. Use it for something people do often and can undo, like Delete in Mail or Archive.
- **Keep swipe actions to a few per side.** One to three buttons stay readable. More get squeezed into narrow, hard-to-tap targets.
- **Offer the same actions somewhere visible.** Swipes are hidden until people try them. Repeat important actions in a context menu (`context-menu`), the toolbar, or the detail screen.
- **Let people reorder and delete their own items.** Lists people build, like playlists or reminders, feel broken without editing. `.onMove` and `.onDelete` add it in two lines.

## Pitfalls

- **These only work in a `List`.** Swipe actions, `.onDelete`, and `.onMove` need list rows. `.refreshable` also works on a `ScrollView`.

## Key APIs

- `.swipeActions(edge:)`: Buttons revealed by swiping a row; `.leading` or `.trailing`.
- `allowsFullSwipe:`: Runs the first button on a full swipe. On by default.
- `Button(role: .destructive)`: A red button that animates the row away.
- `.tint(_:)`: The color of any other swipe button.
- `.onDelete(perform:)`: On a `ForEach`: swipe to delete, plus edit mode.
- `.onMove(perform:)`: On a `ForEach`: drag to reorder in edit mode.
- `EditButton()`: Toggles edit mode from the toolbar.
- `.refreshable { }`: Pull to refresh with an `async` action.

## Variants

### Delete and reorder

Add `.onDelete` and `.onMove` to the `ForEach`, and an `EditButton` to show the controls.

```swift
@State private var reminders = ["Buy milk", "Call Mom", "Book flights"]

NavigationStack {
    List {
        ForEach(reminders, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
            .onDelete { reminders.remove(atOffsets: $0) }
            .onMove { reminders.move(fromOffsets: $0, toOffset: $1) }
    }
    .navigationTitle("Reminders")
    .toolbar { EditButton() }
}
```

**Note:** Drag handles only appear in edit mode. Swipe to delete works either way.

### Pull to refresh

Add `.refreshable` to a `List`; the spinner stays until its `async` closure returns.

```swift
@State private var updated: Date?

List {
    Text(updated.map { "Updated \($0.formatted(date: .omitted, time: .shortened))" } ?? "Pull down to refresh")
}
.refreshable {
    try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1)) // Load new data here
    updated = .now
}
```

## Related

`list`, `context-menu`, `toolbar`


<!-- topic: sheet -->
---
id: sheet
title: Sheet
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/sheet(ispresented:ondismiss:content:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets.md
---

# Sheet

Slides a view up over the current screen for a focused task, at full or partial height.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- On macOS
- Related

## Use when

- A sheet slides a view up over the current screen for a focused task, like composing a message or editing a record.
- It's driven by state: set a `Bool` to `true` to show it, and swiping down sets it back to `false`.

## Don't use when

- Use a push in a NavigationStack (`navigation-stack`) to drill deeper, an Alert (`alert`) for a short question, and `.fullScreenCover` for long or immersive tasks like a camera.

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isPresented = false

Button("Show Details") {
    isPresented = true
}
.sheet(isPresented: $isPresented) {
    Text("Details")
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
}
```

**Important:** Put `.sheet` on a view that stays on screen, like the button. If the view it's attached to disappears, the sheet closes with it.

## Built from

.sheet(isPresented:)
└── NavigationStack
    └── Sheet content
        ├── .toolbar
        │   ├── Cancel
        │   └── Done
        └── .presentationDetents

## Rules

- **Pair Done with Cancel.** Cancel on the leading side lets people leave without saving. A lone Done makes finishing the task feel like the only way out.
- **Use the medium detent for quick content.** A half-height sheet keeps the screen behind it in view, like the share sheet. Use full height for writing, like a new message.
- **Show one sheet at a time.** A sheet over a sheet makes people lose their place. Close the first one before opening another.
- **Let people swipe to dismiss.** People expect it. If there are unsaved changes, block the swipe with `.interactiveDismissDisabled` and ask before discarding.

## Pitfalls

- **On iPad a sheet floats as a card.** `.presentationSizing` (iOS 18) sets its size, like `.form` or `.page`.
- **A sheet's content is a new screen.** It doesn't inherit the parent's navigation bar, so wrap it in a `NavigationStack` for a title and buttons.

## Key APIs

`.sheet(isPresented:)`, `.sheet(item:)`, `@Environment(\.dismiss)`, `.presentationDetents(_:)`, `.presentationDragIndicator(_:)`, `.interactiveDismissDisabled(_:)`, `.fullScreenCover(isPresented:)`

## On macOS

A card attached to its window, for a short task like adding an item.

### Default code

```swift
@State private var isAdding = false

Button("New Event…") { isAdding = true }
    .sheet(isPresented: $isAdding) {
        NewEventForm()
    }

struct NewEventForm: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss
    @State private var title = ""

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .trailing) {
            TextField("Title", text: $title)
            HStack {
                Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { dismiss() }
                    .keyboardShortcut(.cancelAction)
                Button("Add") { dismiss() }
                    .keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)
            }
        }
        .padding()
        .frame(width: 360)
    }
}
```

**Note:** End the button's title with … because it opens a sheet that asks for more. Return and Escape run Add and Cancel through their shortcuts.

### Rules

- **Pair the confirming button with Cancel.** A sheet with only Add or Done suggests finishing is the only way out. Cancel lets people leave without saving.
- **Open at a size that fits the content.** People don't usually resize sheets, so pick a sensible size. Allow resizing when the content benefits from more room.
- **Use a window or panel for long or repeated work.** A sheet suits a quick, self-contained task. For editing at length, open a window. For input people give again and again while watching the result, use a panel.

### Pitfalls

- **A sheet blocks only its own window.** The window behind it dims and waits, but people can still switch to your app's other windows.
- **Call `dismiss` from inside the sheet.** Read `@Environment(\.dismiss)` in the sheet's own view. Read in the view that presents the sheet, it would dismiss that view instead.

### Key APIs

`.presentationSizing(_:)`, `.frame(width:height:)`, `.keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)`

### Variants

#### Edit an item

`.sheet(item:)` shows a sheet for the item you set and clears it when the sheet closes, for “edit this one” tasks.

```swift
@State private var editing: Event?

VStack {
    ForEach(events) { event in
        HStack {
            Text(event.title)
            Spacer()
            Button("Edit…") { editing = event }
        }
    }
}
.sheet(item: $editing) { event in
    EventEditor(event: event)
}
```

#### A sheet people can resize

`.presentationSizing(.fitted)` sizes the sheet to its content, and a minimum and maximum frame let people resize it between them.

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $isShowingNotes) {
    NotesEditor()
        .frame(minWidth: 320, idealWidth: 420, maxWidth: 700,
               minHeight: 200, idealHeight: 280, maxHeight: 600)
        .presentationSizing(.fitted)
}
```

**Note:** On the Mac, a `.fitted` sheet can be resized unless you fix its size with `.fixedSize()` or a fixed frame.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Cancel and Done buttons, Sheet for a tapped item, Small sheet that fits its content. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/sheet(ispresented:ondismiss:content:).md

## Related

`alert`, `popover`, `confirmation-dialog`, `navigation-stack`, `window`, `opening-windows`, `keyboard-shortcuts`


<!-- topic: alert -->
---
id: alert
title: Alert
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/alert(_:ispresented:actions:message:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts.md
---

# Alert

Interrupts with an important message and asks for a quick decision.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isPresented = false

Button("Delete Photo", role: .destructive) {
    isPresented = true
}
.alert("Delete Photo?", isPresented: $isPresented) {
    Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) {}
    Button("Delete", role: .destructive) {
        // Delete the photo
    }
} message: {
    Text("This photo will be deleted from all your devices.")
}
```

**Note:** Roles place the buttons for you: `.cancel` goes in the cancel spot and `.destructive` turns red. You don't order them by hand.

## Rules

- **Name the action on the button.** “Delete” says exactly what will happen. “Yes” or “OK” makes people reread the title to find out.
- **Write a title that says what happened.** “Upload Failed” tells people the problem. “Error” or an error code doesn't help them fix it.
- **Use alerts sparingly.** Each one interrupts. Skip them for actions people can undo, like deleting an email, and for information that isn't actionable.
- **Don't show an alert at launch.** People opened the app to do something. Show problems like a lost connection inline instead.

## Pitfalls

- **Any button closes the alert.** It sets the binding back to `false` for you. With no buttons at all, SwiftUI adds an OK button.
- **Pick the right interruption.** Use an alert for something people must see now, a Confirmation Dialog (`confirmation-dialog`) for a choice of actions, and inline text for anything that can wait.

## Key APIs

`.alert(_:isPresented:actions:message:)`, `.alert(_:isPresented:presenting:)`, `.alert(isPresented:error:)`, `Button(role: .cancel)`, `Button(role: .destructive)`, `TextField` in the actions

## Variants

### Confirm for a specific item

Use `presenting:` to hand the tapped item to the alert's buttons and message.

```swift
@State private var photoToDelete: String?
@State private var showDelete = false

HStack {
    ForEach(["Beach", "Forest"], id: \.self) { photo in
        Button("Delete \(photo)") {
            photoToDelete = photo
            showDelete = true
        }
    }
}
.alert("Delete Photo?", isPresented: $showDelete, presenting: photoToDelete) { photo in
    Button("Delete", role: .destructive) {
        // Delete photo
    }
} message: { photo in
    Text("“\(photo)” will be deleted from all your devices.")
}
```

**Note:** With only a destructive button, the alert adds Cancel for you.

## On macOS

Stop to confirm a risky action or report a problem that needs a decision.

### Default code

```swift
@State private var isConfirming = false

Button("Revert…") { isConfirming = true }
    .alert("Revert to the last saved version?", isPresented: $isConfirming) {
        Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { }
        Button("Revert") { revert() }
    } message: {
        Text("Changes since you last saved will be lost.")
    }
```

**Note:** Give Cancel the `.cancel` role instead of ordering buttons by hand. SwiftUI may reorder buttons by their role and prominence.

### Rules

- **Mark a button destructive only when people didn't choose that action.** If someone chose Empty Trash, the dialog's Empty Trash button does what they asked, so Return should run it. Use `.destructive` for a side effect they might not expect.
- **Save the caution symbol for real danger.** `.dialogSeverity(.critical)` adds it. Used often, it stops meaning anything, so keep it for unexpected data loss, not routine saving or deleting.

### Pitfalls

- **Every button closes the dialog.** SwiftUI sets the binding back to `false` after the button's action runs.
- **A confirmation dialog comes with a way out.** It adds a standard dismiss button; a button with the `.cancel` role takes its place.
- **The Mac puts your app icon in the dialog.** Use `.dialogIcon(_:)` to show a different image.

### Key APIs

`.confirmationDialog(_:isPresented:)`, `.dialogSeverity(.critical)`, `.dialogSuppressionToggle(isSuppressed:)`, `.dialogIcon(_:)`

### Variants

#### Report a problem

`.alert(_:isPresented:presenting:)` builds the alert from a value, like the error you caught, and passes it to the buttons and message.

```swift
@State private var failure: SaveFailure?
@State private var isShowingFailure = false

Button("Save") {
    failure = SaveFailure(documentName: "Trip Notes")
    isShowingFailure = true
}
.alert("Couldn't Save Your Changes", isPresented: $isShowingFailure, presenting: failure) { _ in
    Button("OK") { }
} message: { failure in
    Text("“\(failure.documentName)” is on a disk that's full. Free up space and try again.")
}
```

**Note:** OK fits here: the alert reports a problem and offers no choice, so its one button only acknowledges it.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Show an error, Rename prompt, Let people stop the question (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/alert(_:ispresented:actions:message:).md

## Related

`confirmation-dialog`, `sheet`, `button`, `popover`, `keyboard-shortcuts`


<!-- topic: confirmation-dialog -->
---
id: confirmation-dialog
title: Confirmation Dialog
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/confirmationdialog(_:ispresented:titlevisibility:actions:message:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/action-sheets.md
---

# Confirmation Dialog

Asks people to pick from a few actions, or confirm a destructive one.

Also called: action sheet, ActionSheet, UIAlertController actionSheet, confirm, are you sure, choose an option, bottom menu.

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isPresented = false

Button("Discard Draft", role: .destructive) {
    isPresented = true
}
.confirmationDialog("Discard this draft?", isPresented: $isPresented, titleVisibility: .visible) {
    Button("Discard Draft", role: .destructive) {
        // Discard
    }
    Button("Save Draft") {}
}
```

**Important:** The title is hidden by default on iOS. Pass `titleVisibility: .visible` to show it and the message.

## Rules

- **Use a dialog, not an alert, for choices about an action.** When people close a draft, a dialog offers Delete or Save right where they tapped. An alert is for unexpected news.
- **Make the destructive choice red.** `role: .destructive` makes it stand out, so nobody deletes something by accident.
- **Keep the title to one line, and skip the message if you can.** The button people just tapped already explains most of the context.
- **Offer only a few actions.** A dialog that needs to scroll is slow to read. Use a Menu (`menu`) or a sheet for long lists.

## Pitfalls

- **It replaces `ActionSheet`.** In iOS 26 it appears as a glass popover next to the button that opened it, instead of sliding up from the bottom.
- **You don't need a Cancel button.** Tapping outside dismisses it. If you add a `role: .cancel` button, the system decides where it goes.

## Key APIs

- `.confirmationDialog(_:isPresented:)`: Shows a list of actions while a `Bool` is `true`.
- `titleVisibility:`: `.visible` shows the title, hidden by default on iOS.
- `presenting:`: Passes a value, like the item to delete, to the actions.
- `message: { }`: A short line under the title.
- `Button(role: .destructive)`: Turns the action red.

## Variants

### Confirm deleting a specific item

Use `presenting:` to pass the item into the actions, so the button knows what to delete.

```swift
@State private var fileToDelete: String?
@State private var showDelete = false

Button("Delete Report.pdf", role: .destructive) {
    fileToDelete = "Report.pdf"
    showDelete = true
}
.confirmationDialog("Delete file?", isPresented: $showDelete, titleVisibility: .visible, presenting: fileToDelete) { file in
    Button("Delete \(file)", role: .destructive) {
        // Delete the file
    }
}
```

### Choose between actions

Leave the title hidden, and `.confirmationDialog` reads like a quick list of choices.

```swift
@State private var showOptions = false

Button("Add Photo", systemImage: "photo.badge.plus") {
    showOptions = true
}
.confirmationDialog("Add Photo", isPresented: $showOptions) {
    Button("Take Photo") {}
    Button("Choose from Library") {}
    Button("Browse Files") {}
}
```

## Related

`alert`, `menu`, `sheet`, `context-menu`


<!-- topic: popover -->
---
id: popover
title: Popover
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/popover(ispresented:attachmentanchor:arrowedge:content:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/popovers.md
---

# Popover

Shows extra content in a bubble that points at the button that opened it.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var showTip = false

Button("Info", systemImage: "info.circle") {
    showTip = true
}
.popover(isPresented: $showTip) {
    Text("Prices include tax.")
        .padding()
        .presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover)
}
```

**Important:** On iPhone a popover becomes a sheet by default. To keep the bubble, add `.presentationCompactAdaptation` inside the content, as here.

## Rules

- **Keep popovers small.** A popover is for a tip or a few options. If the content needs scrolling, use a sheet.
- **Don't use a popover for warnings.** People can miss it or tap it away. Use an Alert (`alert`) for anything they must see.
- **Show one popover at a time.** Never open a popover from another popover. Close the first one before showing the next.
- **Save changes when it closes.** Tapping outside closes a popover, often by accident. Keep what people entered unless they tap Cancel.

## Pitfalls

- **The popover hugs its content.** Size it yourself with `.padding` or `.frame(width:)`; long text needs a width to wrap.
- **For a list of commands, use a Menu (`menu`).** A popover is for custom content, like a color grid or a short form.

## Key APIs

`.popover(isPresented:)`, `.popover(item:)`, `.presentationCompactAdaptation(_:)`, `arrowEdge:`

## Variants

### Help next to a field

Put an info `Button` beside a label and keep its explanation in a small `.popover`.

```swift
@State private var showHelp = false

HStack {
    Text("Routing number")
    Button("What's this?", systemImage: "info.circle") {
        showHelp = true
    }
    .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
    .popover(isPresented: $showHelp) {
        Text("The 9-digit number at the bottom left of a check.")
            .padding()
            .frame(width: 240)
            .presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover)
    }
}
```

### Popover on iPad, sheet on iPhone

Leave out the adaptation for bigger content: `.popover` floats on iPad and becomes a sheet on iPhone.

```swift
@State private var showSort = false
@State private var sort = "Date"

Button("Sort", systemImage: "arrow.up.arrow.down") {
    showSort = true
}
.popover(isPresented: $showSort) {
    Form {
        Picker("Sort by", selection: $sort) {
            ForEach(["Date", "Name", "Size"], id: \.self) { Text($0) }
        }
        .pickerStyle(.inline)
    }
    .frame(minWidth: 280, minHeight: 220)
    .presentationDetents([.medium])
}
```

**Note:** `.presentationDetents` only applies when the popover turns into a sheet, so it's safe to add for iPhone.

## On macOS

A small panel that points at its control and closes when people click away.

### Default code

```swift
@State private var isShowingDetails = false

Button("Details", systemImage: "info.circle") {
    isShowingDetails = true
}
.popover(isPresented: $isShowingDetails) {
    EventDetails()
        .padding()
}
```

**Note:** Keep the state the popover edits outside it, in the view that shows it. Then clicking away, which closes the popover, never loses a change.

### Rules

- **Keep it small, with a few related controls.** A popover is for a quick look or change, like an event's time. Make it only as big as its content.
- **Point at the control that opened it.** Aim the arrow straight at it, and avoid covering it or content people need while the popover is open.
- **Show one at a time, and nothing on top.** Close an open popover before showing another. Only an alert should ever appear over one.
- **Don't put a warning in a popover.** People can miss it or close it by accident. Use an alert for anything they must read.

### Pitfalls

- **Clicking outside closes it.** A popover doesn't block the window, so it goes away as soon as people click elsewhere.
- **The Mac respects `arrowEdge`.** Leave it out to let the system pick the side that fits.

### Key APIs

`attachmentAnchor:`, `@Environment(\.dismiss)`

### Variants

#### From a toolbar button

A `.popover` suits a toolbar button with a few options, like filters, that apply as soon as people change them.

```swift
@State private var isShowingFilters = false
@State private var showsUnread = true
@State private var showsFlagged = false

.toolbar {
    Button("Filter", systemImage: "line.3.horizontal.decrease.circle") {
        isShowingFilters = true
    }
    .popover(isPresented: $isShowingFilters, arrowEdge: .bottom) {
        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Toggle("Unread", isOn: $showsUnread)
            Toggle("Flagged", isOn: $showsFlagged)
        }
        .padding()
    }
}
```

**Note:** A real `.toolbar` here would land in this window's own toolbar, so the preview draws one. The button and popover are real.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Close it after a choice (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/popover(ispresented:attachmentanchor:arrowedge:content:).md

## Related

`sheet`, `menu`, `context-menu`, `tooltips`, `toolbar`


<!-- topic: context-menu -->
---
id: context-menu
title: Context Menu
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/contextmenu(menuitems:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/context-menus.md
---

# Context Menu

A menu of actions that appears when people touch and hold a view.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Image(systemName: "photo")
    .font(.largeTitle)
    .contextMenu {
        Button("Copy", systemImage: "doc.on.doc") {}
        Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") {}
        Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash", role: .destructive) {}
    }
```

**Note:** Items are ordinary `Button`s. Group them with `Section`, and nest a `Menu` for a submenu.

## Rules

- **Hide items that don't apply.** A context menu shows only what you can do right now. Dimmed items make it longer without helping.
- **Offer the same actions somewhere visible.** People can't see a context menu until they find it. Every item should also be in a toolbar, a button, or the detail screen.
- **Keep it short, with the most-used items first.** A few relevant actions are quick to scan. Leave rare and advanced commands out.
- **Use one level of submenu at most.** A submenu inside a submenu is hard to navigate. Give a submenu a title that predicts what's inside, like “Move to”.

## Pitfalls

- **It's the web's right-click menu.** People open it by touching and holding on iPhone, or with a secondary click on iPad with a trackpad.
- **On a `List` row, the whole row lifts.** For multiple selected rows, `.contextMenu(forSelectionType:)` builds one menu for all of them.

## Key APIs

`.contextMenu { }`, `.contextMenu { } preview: { }`, `Section { }`, `Menu(_:content:)`, `Button(role: .destructive)`, `.contextMenu(forSelectionType:)`

## Variants

### Context menu on list rows

Add `.contextMenu` to each row for actions on that item. Touch and hold a name to try it.

```swift
@State private var contacts = ["Maya", "Leo", "Priya"]
@State private var favorites: Set<String> = []

List(contacts, id: \.self) { name in
    Label(name, systemImage: favorites.contains(name) ? "star.fill" : "person")
        .contextMenu {
            Button(favorites.contains(name) ? "Unfavorite" : "Favorite", systemImage: "star") {
                if favorites.contains(name) { favorites.remove(name) } else { favorites.insert(name) }
            }
            Button("Remove", systemImage: "trash", role: .destructive) {
                contacts.removeAll { $0 == name }
            }
        }
}
```

**Note:** The menu can read the row's value, so `name` tells each button which contact to change.

## On macOS

A menu of actions for the item people Control-click or right-click.

### Default code

```swift
FileIcon(file)
    .contextMenu {
        Button("Open") { open(file) }
        Button("Rename…") { rename(file) }
        Divider()
        Button("Move to Trash", role: .destructive) {
            trash(file)
        }
    }
```

**Note:** The menu opens where people click, so it needs no button of its own. That also means people can't see it's there: put the same commands in the menu bar.

### Rules

- **Keep it short, with the commands people need here.** A context menu is a shortcut to the likely next step, not a list of everything. Leave rare and advanced commands in the menu bar.
- **Hide items that don't apply. Don't dim them.** Unlike the menu bar, a context menu shows only what works for this item. Cut, Copy, and Paste are the exception: they can appear dimmed.
- **Leave keyboard shortcuts out.** The context menu is already the shortcut. Show the keys in the menu bar, where people learn them.
- **Put every item in the menu bar too.** A context menu is hidden until people go looking. The same commands belong in the menu bar, where everyone can find them.
- **Keep submenus to one level.** One submenu with a clear title can shorten a menu. A submenu inside a submenu is hard to reach.

### Pitfalls

- **Every way to open it works.** Control-click and a secondary click, on a mouse or a trackpad, open the same menu.
- **An item menu needs a container with selection.** `contextMenu(forSelectionType:)` never opens outside a `List` or `Table` that supports selection.

### Key APIs

`primaryAction:`, `Menu(_:)`, `Divider()`

### Variants

#### Menus for the selection in a list

`contextMenu(forSelectionType:)` gives you the rows the menu is for: the clicked or selected ones, or none for empty space.

```swift
@State private var selection = Set<Chapter.ID>()

List(chapters, selection: $selection) { chapter in
    Text(chapter.title)
}
.contextMenu(forSelectionType: Chapter.ID.self) { ids in
    if ids.isEmpty {
        Button("New Chapter") { addChapter() }
    } else if ids.count == 1 {
        Button("Rename…") { rename(ids) }
        Button("Delete", role: .destructive) { delete(ids) }
    } else {
        Button("Merge \(ids.count) Chapters") { merge(ids) }
```
