```swift
        Button("Delete \(ids.count) Chapters", role: .destructive) { delete(ids) }
    }
}
```

**Note:** Clicking empty space gives an empty set, even while rows are selected. Use it for commands like New that don't need an item.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Custom preview, Double-click to open a table row (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/contextmenu(menuitems:).md

## Related

`menu`, `popover`, `swipe-actions`, `confirmation-dialog`, `commands`, `list-styles`, `table`


<!-- topic: modifier-order -->
---
id: modifier-order
title: Modifier Order
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/configuring-views.md
---

# Modifier Order

Each modifier wraps the view before it, so changing the order changes the result.

Also called: chaining, modifier chain, css order, box model, wrapper, decorator, why is my background wrong, padding vs background.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Read a chain top to bottom as "take this, then wrap it in that".** The last modifier is the outermost view.
- **When a background looks wrong, check the order first.** Most surprises come from `padding` or `frame` sitting on the wrong side of `background`.

## Guide

In CSS, `padding` and `background` are properties of one box, so their order doesn't matter. In SwiftUI each modifier is a **new view that wraps the one before it**, and `background` paints whatever size it receives. So it matters whether `padding` comes before it or after.

### Playground

Turn modifiers on and off, and move them up or down. The preview and code follow the order you set.

```swift
Text("Hello")
    .font(.title2.bold())
    .padding(20)
    .background(.orange)
    .clipShape(.capsule)
    .border(.primary, width: 3)
    .frame(width: 240, height: 110)
```

### Why order matters

A modifier doesn't change the view you call it on. It returns a **new view** that contains the old one, so each line adds a layer on the outside, like nesting `<div>`s. Here's the chain above, outermost first:

Each layer only knows the size of the layer directly inside it. A `background` after `padding` sees the padded size and fills it. Before it, the `background` sees only the text, and the padding adds clear space outside.

**Note:** Environment modifiers aren't order-sensitive. `.font(.title).padding()` and `.padding().font(.title)` look the same, because `font` passes its value down to everything inside.

## Key APIs

- `.padding(_:)`: Layout: grows the size that later modifiers see.
- `.frame(width:height:)`: Layout: proposes a new size for everything after it.
- `.background(_:)`: Drawing: fills whatever size it's handed.
- `.clipShape(_:)`: Drawing: cuts off everything before it, shadows included.
- `.font(_:)`: Environment: flows down, so its position rarely matters.

## Variants

### Padding inside or outside the color

Put `padding` before `background` for a filled chip, and after it for space around the chip.

```swift
// In the preview, a dashed line marks the padded area
Text("Padding first")
    .padding()
    .background(.yellow)
    .foregroundStyle(.black)

Text("Background first")
    .background(.yellow)
    .foregroundStyle(.black)
    .padding()
```

### A clipped shadow

Call `clipShape` before `shadow`, or the clip cuts the shadow off with everything else.

```swift
// Shadow is cut off
Color.blue
    .frame(width: 100, height: 70)
    .shadow(radius: 12)
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))

// Shadow shows
Color.blue
    .frame(width: 100, height: 70)
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))
    .shadow(radius: 12)
```

### Frame, then background

Put `background` after `frame` to fill the whole frame, not just the text inside it.

```swift
// In the preview, a dashed line marks the frame
Text("Frame first")
    .frame(width: 140, height: 60)
    .background(.mint)
    .foregroundStyle(.black)

Text("Background first")
    .background(.mint)
    .frame(width: 140, height: 60)
    .foregroundStyle(.black)
```

**Note:** `frame` makes a bigger box but doesn't paint it. The dashed line shows the empty frame.

### Stacking the same modifier

Repeat `padding` and `background` to stack layers, like a double border.

```swift
Text("Layered")
    .padding(12)
    .background(.blue)
    .padding(8)
    .background(.blue.opacity(0.3))
```

## Related

`padding`, `background-overlay`, `frame`, `custom-modifier`


<!-- topic: padding -->
---
id: padding
title: padding
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/padding(_:_:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# padding

Adds space around a view, on every edge or only the edges you pick.

Also called: margin, spacing, inset, gutter, padding-left, EdgeInsets, whitespace, layoutMargins.

## Default code

```swift
Text("Weekly summary")
    .padding()
    .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

**Note:** `.padding()` with no number uses the system default, usually 16pt on iPhone. Prefer it to a hard-coded value so spacing matches the platform.

## Rules

- **Give content room to breathe.** Text pressed against the edge of its card looks cramped and is harder to scan. The default `.padding()` matches the margins people see across iOS.
- **Use space to group related items.** Keep related items close and put more space between groups, so people see the structure without extra dividers.
- **Keep padding consistent across a screen.** Cards and rows with the same insets line up and look like one design. Pick a few values and reuse them.

## Pitfalls

- **SwiftUI has no `margin`.** Padding outside a `.background` acts like a margin, and padding inside it acts like CSS padding. See Modifier Order (`modifier-order`).
- **Use `leading` and `trailing`, not left and right.** They flip automatically in right-to-left languages like Arabic and Hebrew.

## Key APIs

- `.padding()`: The system default amount on every edge.
- `.padding(_:)`: A fixed amount in points on every edge.
- `.padding(_:_:)`: Pick edges, like `.horizontal` or `[.top, .leading]`, and an amount.
- `EdgeInsets`: A different amount on each of the four edges.
- `.contentMargins(_:for:)`: Insets the content of a `ScrollView` or `List`.

## Variants

### Card content

Put `.padding()` before `.background` so the card's color fills the space around its content.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 4) {
    Text("Weekly summary")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("You walked 42 km this week.")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.padding()
.background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

### Pill with different edges

Chain `.padding(.horizontal, _:)` and `.padding(.vertical, _:)` for a wide tag or chip.

```swift
Text("Design")
    .font(.subheadline.weight(.medium))
    .padding(.horizontal, 14)
    .padding(.vertical, 6)
    .background(.blue.opacity(0.15), in: .capsule)
```

### Different amount on each edge

Pass `EdgeInsets` to set all four edges in one call, like CSS `padding: 8px 24px 20px 12px`.

```swift
Text("Custom insets")
    .padding(EdgeInsets(top: 8, leading: 12, bottom: 20, trailing: 24))
    .background(.orange.opacity(0.25))
```

## Related

`modifier-order`, `frame`, `background-overlay`, `spacer-divider`


<!-- topic: frame -->
---
id: frame
title: frame
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/frame(width:height:alignment:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# frame

Sets a view's size, or lets it stretch to fill the space it's offered.

Also called: width, height, size, full width, width: 100%, max-width, min-height, flex-grow, fill, stretch.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Text("Welcome back")
    .font(.headline)
    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
    .padding()
    .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

**Note:** A frame is a new, invisible box around the view, not the view itself. Add a `.background` after it to see how big it is.

## Rules

- **Make every tap target at least 44 × 44 points.** Small icons are easy to miss with a finger. Grow the frame with `minWidth` and `minHeight` instead of the icon.
- **Let text set its own width.** Labels get longer in other languages and at larger text sizes. A fixed width cuts them off, so prefer `maxWidth` or no frame at all.
- **Size by the space you have, not the device.** Use flexible frames and `containerRelativeFrame` so the same layout works on every iPhone and in iPad windows.

## Pitfalls

- **Only flexible views fill a frame.** Shapes, colors, and `resizable()` images grow to fit it. Text and controls keep their natural size and sit inside at `alignment`.
- **Mixing fixed and flexible sizes takes two frames.** A single call can't combine `width:` with `maxHeight:`, so chain `.frame(width: 200).frame(maxHeight: .infinity)`.

## Key APIs

- `.frame(width:height:)`: A fixed size in points. Leave one out to keep it natural.
- `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)`: Stretches to fill the width, like CSS `width: 100%`.
- `.frame(minWidth:minHeight:)`: Never smaller than this, but free to grow.
- `alignment:`: Where the content sits inside a larger frame.
- `.fixedSize()`: Keeps the natural size, even if that means overflowing.
- `.containerRelativeFrame(_:)`: Sizes a view as a fraction of its container.

## Variants

### Full-width button

Put `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` on the label, not the button, so the whole bar fills.

```swift
Button {
    // Continue
} label: {
    Text("Continue")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
}
.buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
.controlSize(.large)
```

### Leading-aligned text without a Spacer

Use `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)` to line text up on the leading edge.

```swift
VStack(spacing: 8) {
    Text("Title")
        .font(.headline)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
    Text("A longer subtitle line")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
}
```

**Note:** A `VStack` centers its children by default. This is often simpler than wrapping each line in an `HStack` with a `Spacer`.

### Square avatar

Give icons and avatars a fixed `.frame(width:height:)` so they line up at one size.

```swift
Image(systemName: "person.fill")
    .font(.system(size: 30))
    .foregroundStyle(.white)
    .frame(width: 64, height: 64)
    .background(.indigo.gradient)
    .clipShape(.circle)
```

**Important:** Clip after the frame. Clipping first cuts the small icon, not the 64-point circle.

### Minimum tap target

Use `minWidth` and `minHeight` to keep a small icon button at least 44 points.

```swift
Button {
    // Close
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "xmark")
        .frame(minWidth: 44, minHeight: 44)
        .contentShape(.rect)
}
```

**Note:** `.contentShape(.rect)` makes the empty part of the frame tappable too. The dashed outline shows the target.

## Related

`layout-basics`, `padding`, `spacer-divider`, `geometry-reader`


<!-- topic: background-overlay -->
---
id: background-overlay
title: background & overlay
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/background(alignment:content:).md
---

# background & overlay

Layers a color, shape, or view behind or on top of a view, sized to match it.

Also called: background-color, bg, z-index, position: absolute, badge, layer, border, ZStack, ::before, ::after.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Label("Inbox", systemImage: "tray.fill")
    .padding()
    .background(.blue.opacity(0.15), in: .capsule)
    .overlay(alignment: .topTrailing) {
        Circle()
            .fill(.red)
            .frame(width: 12, height: 12)
    }
```

**Note:** `.background(_:in:)` fills a shape in one step, without clipping the content the way `.clipShape` would.

## Pitfalls

- **A background or overlay never changes the view's size.** Unlike a `ZStack`, it takes the size of the view it's attached to, so it's ideal for decoration.
- **A color background spreads under the safe area.** When `.background(Color)` touches the screen edge, it extends behind the status bar. Pass `ignoresSafeAreaEdges: []` to stop it.

## Key APIs

- `.background(_:in:)`: Fills a shape behind the view, like `.capsule`.
- `.background { }`: Puts any view behind, sized to match.
- `.overlay(alignment:) { }`: Puts any view on top, pinned to an edge or corner.
- `.overlay { Shape().strokeBorder() }`: Draws an outline that lines up with the fill.
- `.background(.ultraThinMaterial)`: A blurred, translucent backdrop.

## Variants

### Avatar with a status dot

Use `.overlay(alignment:)` to pin a status dot to an avatar's corner.

```swift
Image(systemName: "person.crop.circle.fill")
    .font(.system(size: 64))
    .foregroundStyle(.gray)
    .overlay(alignment: .bottomTrailing) {
        Circle()
            .fill(.green)
            .frame(width: 18, height: 18)
            .padding(3)
            .background(.background, in: .circle)
    }
```

**Note:** The `.background(.background, in: .circle)` behind the dot draws a ring in the page color, so the dot stands out in light and dark.

### Notification badge

Pin a count to a corner with `.overlay(alignment: .topTrailing)`, then nudge it with `.offset`.

```swift
Image(systemName: "envelope.fill")
    .font(.system(size: 30))
    .foregroundStyle(.white)
    .frame(width: 64, height: 64)
    .background(.blue.gradient, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 16))
    .overlay(alignment: .topTrailing) {
        Text("3")
            .font(.callout.bold())
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .frame(width: 26, height: 26)
            .background(.red, in: .circle)
            .offset(x: 8, y: -8)
    }
```

### Caption over an image

Put text in an `.overlay` with a dark gradient behind it, so it stays readable on any photo.

```swift
LinearGradient(colors: [.teal, .indigo], startPoint: .topLeading, endPoint: .bottomTrailing)
    .frame(height: 140)
    .overlay(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
        Text("Big Sur, California")
            .font(.headline)
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .padding()
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
            .background(.linearGradient(colors: [.clear, .black.opacity(0.6)], startPoint: .top, endPoint: .bottom))
    }
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

**Important:** White text straight on a photo disappears on bright areas. Always add a scrim or a material behind it.

### Outline with a stroke overlay

Pair a fill with an `.overlay` of `Capsule().strokeBorder()` for an outlined pill.

```swift
Text("Outlined")
    .padding(.horizontal, 20)
    .padding(.vertical, 10)
    .background(.blue.opacity(0.1), in: .capsule)
    .overlay {
        Capsule()
            .strokeBorder(.blue, lineWidth: 1.5)
    }
```

**Note:** `strokeBorder` draws inside the shape's edge. `stroke` straddles it, so half the line hangs outside the fill.

## Related

`modifier-order`, `clip-shape`, `shapes`, `materials`


<!-- topic: clip-shape -->
---
id: clip-shape
title: clipShape
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/clipshape(_:style:).md
---

# clipShape

Cuts a view to a shape, like rounded corners or a circle, and hides the rest.

Also called: border-radius, rounded corners, cornerRadius, corner radius, mask, overflow: hidden, circle image, clip-path, clipped, squircle.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Image(systemName: "photo.fill")
    .font(.largeTitle)
    .foregroundStyle(.white)
    .frame(width: 160, height: 120)
    .background(.indigo.gradient)
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

**Note:** Set the size with `.frame` first, then clip. The clip uses whatever size the view has at that point in the chain.

## Pitfalls

- **`.cornerRadius(_:)` is deprecated.** Use `.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 12))`, or `.background(color, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))` when you only need a rounded fill.
- **Rounded rectangles use smooth corners.** `.rect(cornerRadius:)` draws Apple's continuous "squircle" curve, the same as app icons, by default.
- **Add a shadow after the clip.** A `.shadow` before `.clipShape` gets cut off along with everything else outside the shape.

## Key APIs

- `.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius:))`: Rounded corners, like CSS `border-radius` with `overflow: hidden`.
- `.clipShape(.circle)`: A circle, for avatars and round buttons.
- `.clipShape(.capsule)`: Fully rounded ends, for pills.
- `.rect(topLeadingRadius:…)`: A different radius on each corner.
- `.clipped()`: Cuts off anything outside the view's frame.
- `.contentShape(_:)`: Sets the tappable area to match the visible shape.

## Variants

### Circular profile photo

Use `.clipShape(.circle)` after a square `.frame` for a round profile photo.

```swift
Image(systemName: "person.fill")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .padding(18)
    .foregroundStyle(.white)
    .frame(width: 88, height: 88)
    .background(.teal.gradient)
    .clipShape(.circle)
```

**Note:** For a real photo, use `.resizable()` and `.scaledToFill()` so it crops to the circle instead of squashing.

### Rounded fill without clipping

Use `.background(_:in:)` when you only need a rounded fill, without clipping anything.

```swift
Text("Rounded background")
    .padding()
    .background(.blue.opacity(0.15), in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

**Note:** Nothing gets cut off, so a badge or shadow can still hang outside the shape.

### Match the tap area

Add `.contentShape(.circle)` so only taps inside the visible circle count.

```swift
Button {
    // Play
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "play.fill")
        .font(.title)
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .frame(width: 72, height: 72)
        .background(.pink)
        .clipShape(.circle)
        .contentShape(.circle)
}
.buttonStyle(.plain)
```

**Important:** Clipping is only visual. Without `contentShape`, taps in the square corners outside the circle still trigger the button.

### Concentric corners

Use `ConcentricRectangle` inside a `.containerShape` so inner corners keep an even gap.

```swift
VStack {
    ConcentricRectangle()
        .fill(.blue.gradient)
        .frame(height: 90)
}
.padding(10)
.background(.fill.tertiary)
.containerShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 32))
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 32))
```

**Note:** `ConcentricRectangle` is new in iOS 26. It subtracts the padding from the outer radius for you.

## Related

`shapes`, `background-overlay`, `shadow`, `modifier-order`


<!-- topic: shadow -->
---
id: shadow
title: shadow
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/shadow(color:radius:x:y:).md
---

# shadow

Draws a soft shadow behind a view to lift it off the background.

Also called: box-shadow, drop shadow, elevation, glow, text-shadow, depth, CALayer shadow.

## Default code

```swift
Text("Balance: $2,480")
    .padding()
    .background {
        RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 16)
            .fill(.background)
            .shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.15), radius: 12, y: 6)
    }
```

**Note:** `x` and `y` move the shadow and `radius` blurs it. There is no spread setting like in CSS.

## Pitfalls

- **The default shadow is strong.** It's black at 33% opacity. Most designs use `.black.opacity(0.1)` to `0.2`.
- **Shadows barely show in dark mode.** iOS shows depth there with a lighter fill or a material instead, so don't rely on a shadow alone.

## Key APIs

- `.shadow(radius:)`: A default gray shadow, blurred by `radius`.
- `.shadow(color:radius:x:y:)`: Sets the color and moves the shadow by `x` and `y`.
- `radius:`: The blur amount, like the blur in CSS `box-shadow`.
- `.background { Shape().shadow() }`: Shadows only the card, not its contents.
- `.shadow(.drop(…))`: A shadow as a fill style, for shapes and text.

## Variants

### Shadow on every child

Put `.shadow` on a background shape so only the card casts one, not each piece of text.

```swift
// Every text gets a shadow
VStack {
    Text("Title").font(.headline)
    Text("Subtitle")
}
.shadow(radius: 4)

// Only the card gets a shadow
VStack {
    Text("Title").font(.headline)
    Text("Subtitle")
}
.padding()
.background {
    RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
        .fill(.background.secondary)
        .shadow(radius: 4)
}
```

**Important:** A shadow on a container with no background is applied to every child separately, so each line of text gets its own shadow.

### Readable text on a busy image

Use a tight, dark `.shadow` to help white text stand out on a bright photo.

```swift
ZStack {
    LinearGradient(colors: [.yellow, .orange, .pink], startPoint: .top, endPoint: .bottom)
        .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 12))
    Text("Golden hour")
        .font(.largeTitle.bold())
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.5), radius: 3, y: 2)
}
.frame(height: 120)
```

### Colored glow

Give `.shadow` the view's own color and no offset, and it reads as a glow.

```swift
Circle()
    .fill(.purple)
    .frame(width: 60, height: 60)
    .shadow(color: .purple.opacity(0.8), radius: 20)
```

## Related

`clip-shape`, `background-overlay`, `visual-effects`, `materials`


<!-- topic: foreground-style -->
---
id: foreground-style
title: foregroundStyle & tint
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/foregroundstyle(_:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/color.md
---

# foregroundStyle & tint

Colors text, symbols, and shapes, and sets the accent color of controls.

Also called: color, text color, font color, foregroundColor, accentColor, brand color, secondary text, muted, gray text, tintColor.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Downloads")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("12 files, 2.4 GB")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Button("Download All") {}
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
.tint(.green)
```

**Note:** `foregroundStyle` is for content like text and icons. `tint` is for controls. Setting `foregroundStyle` on a button doesn't change its fill.

## Rules

- **Save your tint color for things people can tap.** If titles and plain text use the same color as buttons, people can't tell what's interactive.
- **Don't rely on color alone.** Some people can't tell red from green. Pair a status color with a symbol or a word so everyone gets the message.
- **Use semantic styles instead of fixed colors.** `.primary`, `.secondary`, and system colors adjust for dark mode and Increase Contrast. A hard-coded gray or hex value doesn't.

## Pitfalls

- **`.foregroundColor(_:)` is deprecated.** `foregroundStyle` takes any style: a color, a gradient, a material, or a level like `.secondary`.
- **Both modifiers flow down to every child.** Set them once on a container, like CSS `color` inherited by nested elements.
- **`tint` replaces `accentColor`.** Set it once near the root of your app to give every control your brand color.

## Key APIs

- `.foregroundStyle(_:)`: Colors text, symbols, and shapes inside the view.
- `.secondary` / `.tertiary`: Dimmer levels of the current style, for supporting text.
- `.foregroundStyle(_:_:)`: Colors the layers of a multi-layer SF Symbol.
- `.tint(_:)`: The accent color of buttons, toggles, sliders, and links.
- `.tint`: A style that means "the current tint", for your own views.

## Variants

### Hierarchy levels

Use `.secondary`, `.tertiary`, and `.quaternary` for supporting text instead of picking grays.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Primary").foregroundStyle(.primary)
    Text("Secondary").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Text("Tertiary").foregroundStyle(.tertiary)
    Text("Quaternary").foregroundStyle(.quaternary)
}
.font(.title3.weight(.semibold))
```

**Note:** These levels adapt to light mode, dark mode, and Increase Contrast automatically.

### Levels follow the parent style

Set a color once on the container, and `.secondary` inside becomes a dimmer version of it.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 2) {
    Text("Workout complete")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("32 min, 410 kcal")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.foregroundStyle(.green)
```

### Brand color for controls

Set `.tint` on a container to recolor every toggle, slider, and prominent button inside.

```swift
@State private var isOn = true

VStack {
    Toggle("Notifications", isOn: $isOn)
    Button("Save") {}
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
.tint(.orange)
```

### Two-color symbols

Pass two styles to `.foregroundStyle(_:_:)` to color the layers of a multi-layer SF Symbol.

```swift
Image(systemName: "person.crop.circle.badge.plus")
    .font(.system(size: 56))
    .foregroundStyle(.blue, .gray)
```

### Gradient text

Pass a gradient to `.foregroundStyle` for colorful headline text; any `ShapeStyle` works.

```swift
Text("Hello, gradient")
    .font(.largeTitle.bold())
    .foregroundStyle(.linearGradient(colors: [.orange, .pink], startPoint: .leading, endPoint: .trailing))
```

## Related

`system-colors`, `font`, `gradients`, `sf-symbols`


<!-- topic: font -->
---
id: font
title: font
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/font(_:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.md
---

# font

Sets the size, weight, and design of text, and scales it with the user's text size.

Also called: font-size, font-weight, font-family, bold, typography, text size, Dynamic Type, h1, UIFont, monospace.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 2) {
    Text("Trip to Lisbon")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("May 4 – 9 · 3 travelers")
        .font(.subheadline)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

**Important:** `.system(size:)` doesn't grow with Dynamic Type, the text size people pick in Settings. Prefer a text style like `.headline`.

## Rules

- **Show hierarchy with size, weight, and color.** A bold title over secondary detail tells people what to read first. Text that all looks the same makes them read every word.
- **Avoid light weights at small sizes.** Ultralight and Thin strokes get hard to read when text is small. Use Regular or heavier for body and caption text.
- **Use text styles instead of fixed sizes.** Many people change their text size in Settings. Text styles follow that choice, and a hard-coded `.system(size:)` doesn't.
- **Stick to one or two typefaces.** The system font with a rounded or serif accent is plenty. More fonts make a screen look unplanned.

## Pitfalls

- **`.font` flows down to every text inside a container.** The closest one wins, so a child can override it, like CSS `font` inheritance.
- **Adjust a font without replacing it.** `fontWeight`, `fontDesign`, `fontWidth`, and `italic` change the current font, so they combine with a style set further up.

## Key APIs

- `.font(.headline)`: A text style that scales with Dynamic Type.
- `.font(.title.weight(.semibold))`: A text style at a different weight.
- `.fontWeight(_:)` / `.bold()`: Changes the weight of the current font.
- `.fontDesign(_:)`: `.rounded`, `.serif`, or `.monospaced`.
- `.monospacedDigit()`: Equal-width digits, so numbers don't shift.
- `.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)`: A custom font that still scales.

## Variants

### The type scale

Use the built-in text styles, from `.largeTitle` to `.caption2`, like a design system's type ramp.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 4) {
    Text("Large Title").font(.largeTitle)
    Text("Title").font(.title)
    Text("Title 2").font(.title2)
    Text("Title 3").font(.title3)
    Text("Headline").font(.headline)
    Text("Body").font(.body)
    Text("Callout").font(.callout)
    Text("Subheadline").font(.subheadline)
    Text("Footnote").font(.footnote)
    Text("Caption").font(.caption)
    Text("Caption 2").font(.caption2)
}
```

### Numbers that don't jiggle

Add `.monospacedDigit()` so timers and counters don't shift sideways as the digits change.

```swift
@State private var start = Date.now

Text(start, style: .timer)
    .font(.largeTitle.weight(.medium))
    .monospacedDigit()
```

### A custom font that still scales

Use `.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` so a custom font grows with Dynamic Type like a text style.

```swift
Text("Once upon a time")
    .font(.custom("Georgia", size: 24, relativeTo: .title2))
```

**Note:** Fonts you bundle need to be listed in your app's Info.plist under `UIAppFonts` before `.custom` can find them.

### Mixed styles in one line

Write Markdown in a `Text` string literal for inline bold, italic, and code.

```swift
Text("Tap **Save** to keep _all_ your `changes`.")
```

**Important:** Markdown only works on literals. For a `String` variable, use `Text(LocalizedStringKey(value))` or `AttributedString(markdown:)`.

## Related

`typography`, `text`, `foreground-style`, `label`


<!-- topic: visual-effects -->
---
id: visual-effects
title: Visual Effects
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view-graphics-and-rendering.md
---

# Visual Effects

Fade, blur, scale, rotate, move, and desaturate a view without changing its layout.

Also called: opacity, blur, transform, scale, rotate, translate, filter: grayscale, CSS transform, CGAffineTransform, alpha.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isDimmed = false

Image(systemName: "star.fill")
    .font(.largeTitle)
    .opacity(isDimmed ? 0.3 : 1)
    .scaleEffect(isDimmed ? 0.8 : 1)
    .onTapGesture {
        withAnimation { isDimmed.toggle() }
    }
```

**Note:** Like CSS `transform` and `filter`, these change how a view is drawn, not where it sits in the layout. Its neighbors never move.

## Pitfalls

- **Use `offset` for nudges, not layout.** To really move something, change the layout with `padding`, stacks, or `frame(alignment:)`.
- **`opacity(0)` still takes up space.** Remove the view with `if` when it should be gone from the layout.
- **Everything here animates.** Change the value inside `withAnimation` and SwiftUI blends between the old and new values.

## Key APIs

- `.opacity(_:)`: Fades the view, from `0` (invisible) to `1`.
- `.blur(radius:)`: Blurs the view, like CSS `filter: blur()`.
- `.scaleEffect(_:anchor:)`: Grows or shrinks the drawing around an anchor point.
- `.rotationEffect(_:anchor:)`: Rotates the drawing, by default around the center.
- `.offset(x:y:)`: Moves the drawing without moving its layout slot.
- `.grayscale(_:)`: Removes color, from `0` (none) to `1` (full gray).

## Variants

### Press to shrink

Use `.scaleEffect` in a custom `ButtonStyle` so the button shrinks while it's pressed.

```swift
struct PressScaleStyle: ButtonStyle {
    func makeBody(configuration: Configuration) -> some View {
        configuration.label
            .font(.headline)
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .padding(.horizontal, 24)
            .padding(.vertical, 12)
            .background(.blue, in: .capsule)
            .scaleEffect(configuration.isPressed ? 0.92 : 1)
            .opacity(configuration.isPressed ? 0.8 : 1)
            .animation(.snappy, value: configuration.isPressed)
    }
}

Button("Press me") {}
    .buttonStyle(PressScaleStyle())
```

**Note:** `configuration.isPressed` is `true` while a finger is down. Press and hold to see it.

### Tap to reveal

Animate `.blur(radius:)` to hide a spoiler until someone taps it.

```swift
@State private var isRevealed = false

Text("The butler did it.")
    .font(.title3.weight(.semibold))
    .blur(radius: isRevealed ? 0 : 8)
    .onTapGesture {
        withAnimation { isRevealed.toggle() }
    }
```

### Rotating chevron

Animate `.rotationEffect` on a chevron to show that a section is expanded.

```swift
@State private var isExpanded = false

Button {
    withAnimation(.snappy) { isExpanded.toggle() }
} label: {
    HStack {
        Text("Details")
        Spacer()
        Image(systemName: "chevron.right")
            .rotationEffect(.degrees(isExpanded ? 90 : 0))
    }
}
```

### Unavailable item

Combine `.grayscale(1)` and `.opacity(0.5)` to show that an item isn't available.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 24) {
    Label("In stock", systemImage: "bag.fill")
        .font(.title2.bold())
        .foregroundStyle(.orange)
    Label("Sold out", systemImage: "bag.fill")
        .font(.title2.bold())
        .foregroundStyle(.orange)
        .grayscale(1)
        .opacity(0.5)
}
```

**Important:** This only changes the look. For a control people shouldn't use, add `.disabled(true)` so it also ignores taps and VoiceOver reports it as dimmed.

## Related

`modifier-order`, `spring`, `transitions`, `shadow`


<!-- topic: custom-modifier -->
---
id: custom-modifier
title: Custom Modifiers
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/viewmodifier.md
---

# Custom Modifiers

Bundles a set of modifiers under one name, so you can reuse a style everywhere.

Also called: ViewModifier, css class, reusable style, mixin, theme, styled component, helper, extension View, design tokens.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Start with a plain `extension View` function.** Reach for a `ViewModifier` struct only when the style needs its own `@State` or reads `@Environment`.
- **Use a style protocol for controls.** `ButtonStyle`, `ToggleStyle`, and `LabelStyle` also know about pressed and disabled states. See Button (`button`).

## Guide

When the same few modifiers show up on every card, give them a name. It's SwiftUI's version of a CSS class: define the look once, apply it in one line, and change every screen in one place.

These three views share one `.cardStyle()`. Change the style and all three update.

```swift
// 1. Define the style once.
struct CardStyle: ViewModifier {
    func body(content: Content) -> some View {
        content
            .padding(16)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
            .background(.purple.opacity(0.12), in: .rect(cornerRadius: 16))
            .overlay {
                RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 16)
                    .strokeBorder(.purple.opacity(0.4))
            }
            .shadow(color: .purple.opacity(0.3), radius: 10, y: 4)
    }
}

// 2. Give it a dot-syntax name.
extension View {
    func cardStyle() -> some View {
        modifier(CardStyle())
    }
}

// 3. Use it anywhere.
Label("Your order shipped", systemImage: "shippingbox.fill")
    .font(.headline)
    .cardStyle()
```

## Key APIs

- `extension View { func … }`: The simplest reusable style: a function that returns the chain.
- `ViewModifier`: A struct that styles any view, and can hold state.
- `body(content:)`: Where a `ViewModifier` applies its modifiers to `content`.
- `.modifier(_:)`: Applies a `ViewModifier` to a view.
- `ButtonStyle`: A reusable look for buttons, with a pressed state.

## Variants

### Just an extension

Write a function in an `extension View` that returns the chain. Often it's all you need.

```swift
extension View {
    func sectionHeaderStyle() -> some View {
        font(.footnote.weight(.semibold))
            .textCase(.uppercase)
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            .tracking(0.5)
    }
}

Text("Recent activity")
    .sectionHeaderStyle()
```

### A ViewModifier that reads the environment

Use a `ViewModifier` struct when the style reads `@Environment`, like this light and dark card.

```swift
struct AdaptiveCard: ViewModifier {
    @Environment(\.colorScheme) private var colorScheme

    func body(content: Content) -> some View {
        content
            .padding()
            .background(.background.secondary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 16))
            .shadow(color: .black.opacity(colorScheme == .dark ? 0 : 0.15), radius: 8, y: 4)
            .overlay {
                if colorScheme == .dark {
                    RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 16).strokeBorder(.white.opacity(0.15))
                }
            }
    }
}

Text("Adapts to dark mode")
    .modifier(AdaptiveCard())
```

**Note:** `content` stands for whatever view the modifier is applied to. This card uses a shadow in light mode and an outline in dark mode, where shadows are hard to see.

### A modifier with a parameter

Give the modifier properties to pass values in, like this `.loading(_:)` that dims any view.

```swift
struct LoadingOverlay: ViewModifier {
    var isLoading: Bool

    func body(content: Content) -> some View {
        content
            .opacity(isLoading ? 0.4 : 1)
            .disabled(isLoading)
            .overlay {
                if isLoading {
                    ProgressView()
                }
            }
            .animation(.default, value: isLoading)
    }
}

extension View {
    func loading(_ isLoading: Bool) -> some View {
        modifier(LoadingOverlay(isLoading: isLoading))
    }
}

@State private var isLoading = false

Button("Place order") { isLoading.toggle() }
    .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
    .loading(isLoading)
```

**Important:** Avoid a catch-all `.if(condition) { … }` helper. Each branch is a different view to SwiftUI, so flipping it resets state instead of animating. Put the condition in the values, like `opacity(isLoading ? 0.4 : 1)` here.

## Related

`modifier-order`, `background-overlay`, `button`, `environment`


<!-- topic: choosing-wrappers -->
---
id: choosing-wrappers
title: Which Wrapper?
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/model-data.md
---

# Which Wrapper?

Answer two questions to pick the right property wrapper for your data.

Also called: property wrapper, state management, useState vs props, which one, data flow, @StateObject vs @ObservedObject, store, context, cheat sheet.

## Pitfalls

- **Start with the smallest tool.** A plain `let` for read-only input, `@State` for a value the view owns. Reach for an `@Observable` class only when several screens share data.
- **`$` turns a property into a `Binding`.** It works on `@State`, `@Binding`, and `@Bindable` properties, and it's what controls like `Toggle` and `TextField` take.

## Guide

Picking the wrong property wrapper is the most common cause of "why isn't my view updating?" bugs. The right one depends on two things: **who owns the data**, and **who needs to change it**.

### Cheat sheet

**Important:** Give each piece of data one owner. If two views each keep their own `@State` for the same thing, they drift apart. Move it up to their nearest common parent and pass it down.

### Older names you'll see

Tutorials from before iOS 17 use `ObservableObject`. It still works, but new code uses the simpler `@Observable` versions:

## Related

`state`, `binding`, `observable`, `environment`


<!-- topic: state -->
---
id: state
title: @State
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/state.md
---

# @State

Stores a value that one view owns, and redraws the view when it changes.

Also called: useState, setState, local state, state variable, reactive variable, variable, store a value, useRef, stateful.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var count = 0

var body: some View {
    Button("Count: \(count)") {
        count += 1
    }
}
```

**Note:** Unlike React's `useState`, there's no setter function. Assign to the property, and SwiftUI redraws every view that reads it.

## Pitfalls

- **Mark it `private`.** The value belongs to the view that declares it. Children get a plain value to read, or a `$binding` to edit.
- **The view is rebuilt; the state isn't.** SwiftUI recreates view structs all the time, but keeps each `@State` value alive while the view stays on screen.
- **Use it for simple values.** `Bool`, `Int`, `String`, enums, and small structs. For data several screens share, hold an @Observable (`observable`) class in `@State` instead.

## Key APIs

- `@State private var count = 0`: Declares a value this view owns, with its starting value.
- `count += 1`: Write to it directly. The view redraws on its own.
- `$count`: A `Binding` that controls and child views can write to.
- `withAnimation { }`: Animates the views that change because of the write.
- `@State private var model = Model()`: Owns an `@Observable` class, created once.

## Variants

### Show a sheet

A `Bool` in `@State` drives `.sheet(isPresented:)`, the usual way to show and hide something.

```swift
@State private var isShowingDetails = false

Button("Show details") {
    isShowingDetails = true
}
.buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
.sheet(isPresented: $isShowingDetails) {
    VStack(spacing: 12) {
        Text("Order #1042")
            .font(.title2.bold())
        Text("Arriving Thursday")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        Button("Close") {
            isShowingDetails = false
        }
        .buttonStyle(.bordered)
    }
    .presentationDetents([.medium])
}
```

**Note:** You only set it to `true`. When people swipe the sheet down, SwiftUI sets it back to `false` through the binding.

### A struct as state

Group related values in a struct, and bind controls to its fields with `$draft.title`.

```swift
struct Draft {
    var title = ""
    var isUrgent = false
}

@State private var draft = Draft()

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
    TextField("Title", text: $draft.title)
        .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
    Toggle("Urgent", isOn: $draft.isUrgent)
    Text(draft.isUrgent ? "🔥 \(draft.title)" : draft.title)
        .font(.headline)
}
.frame(maxWidth: 280)
```

**Note:** Changing any field counts as a change to the whole struct, so every view that reads `draft` redraws.

### Gotcha: state ignores later inputs

The child copies the parent's number into its own `@State`, so it stops following the parent.

```swift
struct Parent: View {
    @State private var count = 0

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 12) {
            Stepper("Parent: \(count)", value: $count)
            Child(count: count)
        }
    }
}

struct Child: View {
    @State var count: Int // ⚠️ Copied once, then ignored

    var body: some View {
        Text("Child: \(count)")
    }
}
```

**Important:** `@State` uses its starting value only once. To follow a value the parent owns, declare `let count: Int`, or `@Binding var count: Int` if the child also changes it.

## Related

`binding`, `choosing-wrappers`, `view-updates`, `observable`


<!-- topic: binding -->
---
id: binding
title: @Binding
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/binding.md
---

# @Binding

Lets a child view read and write a value its parent owns, so both stay in sync.

Also called: props, two-way binding, v-model, lifting state up, callback, pass state to child, inout, shared value, setter.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
struct WiFiRow: View {
    @Binding var isOn: Bool

    var body: some View {
        Toggle("Wi-Fi", isOn: $isOn)
    }
}

// In the parent, which owns it:
// @State private var isOn = true
// WiFiRow(isOn: $isOn)
```

**Note:** Use `@Binding` only when the child changes the value. If it just shows it, declare a plain `let` and pass the value without `$`.

## Pitfalls

- **A binding stores nothing.** It points at a value someone else owns, usually a parent's `@State`, so there's no copy to keep in sync.
- **It's a prop and its setter in one.** Where React passes `value` and `onChange`, SwiftUI passes a single `$value`.
- **Use `.constant(_:)` in previews.** `Toggle("Wi-Fi", isOn: .constant(true))` makes a binding that never changes, handy in `#Preview`.

## Key APIs

- `@Binding var isOn: Bool`: Declares a value the parent owns and this view can change.
- `$isOn`: Passes a binding to a child or a control.
- `$settings.volume`: A binding to one property of a struct.
- `ForEach($items) { $item in }`: A binding to each element of an array.
- `Binding(get:set:)`: A custom binding that converts or validates on the way.
- `.constant(_:)`: A binding that never changes, for previews.

## Variants

### Bind to a property

Write `$settings.volume` to bind a control to one field of a struct in `@State`.

```swift
struct Settings {
    var volume = 0.5
    var isMuted = false
}

@State private var settings = Settings()

VStack(spacing: 12) {
    Slider(value: $settings.volume)
    Toggle("Mute", isOn: $settings.isMuted)
    Text(settings.isMuted ? "Muted" : "Volume \(Int(settings.volume * 100))%")
        .monospacedDigit()
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.frame(maxWidth: 280)
```

### A binding for each row

Pass `$tasks` to `ForEach`, and each row gets a binding to its own element.

```swift
struct TodoItem: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
    var title: String
    var isDone = false
}

@State private var tasks = [
    TodoItem(title: "Buy milk"),
    TodoItem(title: "Walk the dog", isDone: true),
    TodoItem(title: "Learn SwiftUI"),
]

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 10) {
    Text("\(tasks.filter(\.isDone).count) of \(tasks.count) done")
        .font(.headline)
    ForEach($tasks) { $task in
        Toggle(task.title, isOn: $task.isDone)
    }
}
.frame(maxWidth: 280)
```

**Note:** Writing `{ $task in }` gives you both names: `task` to read, and `$task` to pass to a control.

### A custom binding

Use `Binding(get:set:)` when a control's value is derived, like a Mute toggle backed by `volume == 0`.

```swift
@State private var volume = 0.6

var body: some View {
    let isMuted = Binding {
        volume == 0
    } set: { muted in
        volume = muted ? 0 : 0.6
    }

    VStack(spacing: 12) {
        Toggle("Mute", isOn: isMuted)
        Slider(value: $volume)
    }
    .frame(maxWidth: 280)
}
```

## Related

`state`, `observable`, `choosing-wrappers`, `toggle`


<!-- topic: observable -->
---
id: observable
title: @Observable
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/managing-model-data-in-your-app.md
---

# @Observable

Turns a class into a shared model that views watch and redraw from automatically.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Every stored property is tracked.** There's no `@Published` or `objectWillChange`. Mark a property `@ObservationIgnored` to leave it out.
- **Pass models down as plain properties.** Add `@Bindable` only when a child needs `$model.property` for a control like `TextField`.
- **Inject environment models near the root.** Reading `@Environment(Model.self)` when no ancestor called `.environment(model)` crashes the app.

## Guide

`@State` works for a value one view owns. When several views need the same data, put it in a class marked `@Observable`. It's like a store in React: views read from it, and SwiftUI redraws each one when what it read changes.

### Coming from ObservableObject?

Tutorials written before iOS 17 use `ObservableObject`. Here's how each piece maps to the new way:

## Key APIs

`@Observable class Model`, `@State private var model = Model()`, `@Bindable var model: Model`, `.environment(model)`, `@Environment(Model.self)`, `@ObservationIgnored`

## Variants

### A model, its owner, and two views

The screen owns the model in `@State`, the card reads it, and the editor binds to it with `@Bindable`.

```swift
@Observable
class Profile {
    var name = "Taylor"
    var likes = 12
}

struct ProfileScreen: View {
    @State private var profile = Profile()

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            ProfileCard(profile: profile)
            ProfileEditor(profile: profile)
        }
    }
}

struct ProfileCard: View {
    let profile: Profile

    var body: some View {
        HStack {
            Text(profile.name)
                .font(.title3.bold())
            Spacer()
            Button("\(profile.likes)", systemImage: "heart.fill") {
                profile.likes += 1
            }
            .tint(.pink)
        }
    }
}

struct ProfileEditor: View {
    @Bindable var profile: Profile

    var body: some View {
        TextField("Name", text: $profile.name)
            .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
    }
}
```

**Important:** Create the model with `@State private var`, not `let profile = Profile()`. Views are recreated constantly, and a plain property would make a fresh, empty model each time.

## On macOS

One model class that every window, sidebar, and inspector reads and updates.

### Pitfalls

- **Views update only for what their `body` reads.** A view that shows a title redraws when the title changes, not when some other property of the same model does.
- **A missing model is a crash.** Reading `@Environment(Model.self)` when no view above put one there stops the app. Declare the property as `Model?` where it may be missing.
- **Replaces `ObservableObject` for new code.** No `@Published`, `@StateObject`, or `@EnvironmentObject`: use `@State`, `@Bindable`, and `@Environment(Model.self)`.

### Key APIs

`@Bindable var model`

### Variants

#### Create it once, share it with every scene

Own the model with `@State` in your `App`, then pass it to each scene with `.environment(_:)`. Every window and Settings get the same instance.

```swift
@Observable
class ReadingList {
    var articles: [Article] = []
    var showsUnreadCount = true

    var unreadCount: Int {
        articles.filter { !$0.isRead }.count
    }
}

struct Article: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
    var title: String
    var isRead = false
}

@main
struct ReaderApp: App {
    @State private var readingList = ReadingList()

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        .environment(readingList)

        Settings {
            SettingsView()
        }
        .environment(readingList)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Change the setting in the small window and the toolbar of the other one follows. They read the same model.

#### Edit it with @Bindable

Declare the view's model `@Bindable` to get bindings like `$article.title` for controls, such as the fields in an inspector.

```swift
@Observable
class EditableArticle {
    var title = "Designing for the Mac"
    var author = "Sam Lee"
    var isRead = false
}

struct ArticleInspector: View {
    @Bindable var article: EditableArticle

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Title", text: $article.title)
            TextField("Author", text: $article.author)
            Toggle("Read", isOn: $article.isRead)
        }
    }
}
```

#### Read it from the environment

Deep in the view tree, read the model with `@Environment(ReadingList.self)`. For bindings, wrap it in a local `@Bindable` inside `body`.

```swift
struct UnreadSettings: View {
    @Environment(ReadingList.self) private var readingList

    var body: some View {
        @Bindable var readingList = readingList
        Form {
            Toggle("Show unread count", isOn: $readingList.showsUnreadCount)
            LabeledContent("Unread", value: readingList.unreadCount, format: .number)
        }
    }
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Views only watch what they read, Share a model through the environment, Leave a property out with @ObservationIgnored (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/managing-model-data-in-your-app.md

## Related

`state`, `environment`, `view-updates`, `choosing-wrappers`, `state-binding`, `window-group`, `settings-scene`, `inspector`


<!-- topic: environment -->
---
id: environment
title: @Environment
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environment.md
---

# @Environment

Reads values the system or an ancestor passes down, like dark mode or the locale.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@Environment(\.colorScheme) private var colorScheme

var body: some View {
    Text(colorScheme == .dark ? "Good night" : "Good morning")
}
```

**Note:** It works like React's `useContext`: any view reads what an ancestor or the system set, without props through every layer.

## Pitfalls

- **Values flow down, never up.** `.environment(\.key, value)` changes a value for that view and everything inside it, not for parents or siblings. `.font()`, `.tint()`, and `.disabled()` work the same way.
- **Mark environment properties `private`.** The view reads them itself; nobody passes them in.
- **A missing model crashes.** `@Environment(Model.self)` stops the app if no ancestor called `.environment(model)`. Declare it as `Model?` when it might be absent. See @Observable (`observable`).

## Key APIs

`@Environment(\.colorScheme)`, `.environment(\.key, value)`, `@Entry var name = default`, `.environment(model)`, `@Environment(Model.self)`

## Variants

### Close a sheet with dismiss

Read `dismiss` inside a sheet to close it, without a binding from the parent.

```swift
struct ContentView: View {
    @State private var isShowingSheet = false

    var body: some View {
        Button("Open sheet") { isShowingSheet = true }
            .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
            .sheet(isPresented: $isShowingSheet) {
                SheetContent()
            }
    }
}

struct SheetContent: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            Text("All set!")
                .font(.title2.bold())
            Button("Done") { dismiss() }
                .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        }
        .presentationDetents([.height(200)])
    }
}
```

**Note:** Some environment values are actions you call like functions, such as `dismiss()` and `openURL(url)`.

## On macOS

Values that flow down from a window to every view inside it, from control size to actions.

### Pitfalls

- **It only flows down.** A value you set applies to that view and the views inside it. Parents and siblings never see it.
- **Prefer the dedicated modifier.** Write `.controlSize(.small)` rather than `.environment(\.controlSize, .small)`, and give your own values a modifier too.
- **Actions live here too.** `openWindow`, `dismissWindow`, and `openSettings` are values you call like functions.

### Key APIs

`@Environment(\.controlSize)`, `\.openWindow`, `\.openSettings`, `\.appearsActive`, `\.dismissWindow`

### Variants

#### Open another window

Read `openWindow` and call it with the ID of a `Window` or `WindowGroup` in your app. This one opens a real window.

```swift
@main
struct ReaderApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        Window("Activity", id: "activity") {
            ActivityView()
        }
    }
}

struct ShowActivityButton: View {
    @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

    var body: some View {
        Button("Show Activity") {
            openWindow(id: "activity")
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** A `Window` also gets an item in the Window menu, so people can reopen it without your button.

#### Open Settings from your own button

Call `openSettings` to show your Settings window, for example from an empty state. This one opens this app's Settings.

```swift
struct AccountsEmptyState: View {
    @Environment(\.openSettings) private var openSettings

    var body: some View {
        ContentUnavailableView {
            Label("No Accounts", systemImage: "person.crop.circle")
        } actions: {
            Button("Add an Account…") {
                openSettings()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

#### Look inactive when the window isn't key

Read `appearsActive` in custom views and drop the accent color when it's false. Click another window to see this badge turn gray.

```swift
struct LiveBadge: View {
    @Environment(\.appearsActive) private var appearsActive

    var body: some View {
        Label("Live", systemImage: "dot.radiowaves.left.and.right")
            .font(.callout.weight(.semibold))
            .padding(.horizontal, 10)
            .padding(.vertical, 4)
            .foregroundStyle(appearsActive ? .white : .secondary)
            .background(appearsActive ? Color.accentColor : Color.secondary.opacity(0.2), in: .capsule)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Selection in lists and tables turns gray on its own. Views and styles you draw yourself need to check `appearsActive`.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Your own value with @Entry, Respect Reduce Motion, Your own value with @Entry (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environment.md

## Related

`observable`, `choosing-wrappers`, `binding`, `sheet`, `state-binding`, `opening-windows`, `settings-scene`, `button`


<!-- topic: lifecycle -->
---
id: lifecycle
title: View Lifecycle
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/onappear(perform:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/loading.md
---

# View Lifecycle

Run code when a view appears, load data with task, and react to changes with onChange.

Also called: useEffect, componentDidMount, viewDidLoad, viewWillAppear, mounted, watch, fetch on load, debounce, lifecycle hooks, onDisappear.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var quote = "Loading…"

var body: some View {
    Text(quote)
        .task {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1)) // Pretend to load
            quote = "Less, but better."
        }
}
```

**Note:** `.task` is `useEffect` without the cleanup function. SwiftUI cancels the work for you when the view goes away.

## Rules

- **Show something right away.** A blank screen looks broken. Show the layout with placeholder content, then fill it in when `.task` finishes.
- **Keep the screen usable while it loads.** Load in `.task` so people can still scroll, search, or go back. Don't cover the whole screen with a spinner that blocks every tap.
- **Show progress for longer waits.** Use `ProgressView()` when you can't tell how long it will take, and `ProgressView(value:)` when you can.

## Pitfalls

- **`onAppear` can run many times.** It fires each time the view comes back on screen, such as after switching tabs or navigating back. It isn't a constructor.
- **Keep side effects out of `init` and `body`.** SwiftUI calls them far more often than the view appears, so start work from `.task`, `.onChange`, or a button.

## Key APIs

- `.task { }`: Runs `async` work on appear; cancelled when the view goes away.
- `.task(id:) { }`: Cancels and restarts the work whenever `id` changes.
- `.onAppear { }`: Runs code each time the view appears.
- `.onDisappear { }`: Runs code when the view leaves the screen.
- `.onChange(of:initial:)`: Runs code when a value changes, with old and new values.
- `.refreshable { }`: Adds pull to refresh to a `List` or `ScrollView`.

## Variants

### Load data when a view appears

Show a placeholder, then fill it in from `.task(id:)` so a Reload button can restart it.

```swift
@State private var quote: String?
@State private var reloadID = 0

func loadQuote() async -> String {
    try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1)) // Pretend network call
    return ["Stay hungry.", "Ship it.", "Less, but better."].randomElement()!
}

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    if let quote {
        Text(quote)
            .font(.title3.bold())
    } else {
        ProgressView()
    }
    Button("Reload") { reloadID += 1 }
}
.frame(height: 100)
.task(id: reloadID) {
    quote = nil
    quote = await loadQuote()
}
```

**Note:** Changing the `id` cancels the running task and starts a new one, so a reload never races an older load.

### Search as you type

Use `.task(id: query)` to cancel the previous search each time the text changes.

```swift
@State private var query = ""
@State private var results: [String] = []
let fruits = ["Apple", "Apricot", "Banana", "Blueberry", "Cherry", "Grape", "Mango", "Peach"]

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 10) {
    TextField("Search fruit", text: $query)
        .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
        .autocorrectionDisabled()
    Text(results.isEmpty ? "No matches" : results.joined(separator: ", "))
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.frame(maxWidth: 280)
.task(id: query) {
    do {
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(400)) // Debounce
    } catch {
        return // Cancelled: the user kept typing
    }
    results = fruits.filter { query.isEmpty || $0.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains(query) }
}
```

**Note:** Sleeping first debounces the search: it runs only once typing pauses. A cancelled sleep throws, which ends the old task.

### Keep related values in sync

Use `.onChange(of:)` to update one value when another changes, like Airplane Mode turning Wi-Fi off.

```swift
@State private var isAirplaneMode = false
@State private var isWiFiOn = true

VStack(spacing: 12) {
    Toggle("Airplane Mode", systemImage: "airplane", isOn: $isAirplaneMode)
    Toggle("Wi-Fi", systemImage: "wifi", isOn: $isWiFiOn)
}
.frame(maxWidth: 280)
.onChange(of: isAirplaneMode) { _, isOn in
    if isOn {
        withAnimation { isWiFiOn = false }
    }
}
```

**Important:** `onChange` doesn't run for the starting value. Pass `initial: true` if it should also run when the view appears.

## Related

`state`, `view-updates`, `searchable`, `progress-view`


<!-- topic: view-updates -->
---
id: view-updates
title: How Views Update
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/model-data.md
---

# How Views Update

See which views run their body again when state changes, and why the rest don't.

Also called: re-render, rerender, render cycle, virtual DOM, reconciliation, diffing, view not updating, refresh, setNeedsDisplay, performance.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Variants
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Running `body` isn't redrawing pixels.** SwiftUI compares the result with what's on screen and only touches what's different, much like React's reconciliation.
- **Small views keep updates small.** A child's `body` reruns only when its inputs or the state it reads change, so split big views into parts.

## Guide

A SwiftUI view is a lightweight description, not a thing on screen. When state changes, SwiftUI calls `body` again on the views that depend on it, compares the new description with the old one, and updates only what's different.

**Important:** Keep `body` fast and free of side effects: no network calls and no changing state. SwiftUI may call it at any time, so start work from a button, `.task`, or `.onChange`.

### Debugging updates

When a view updates more than you expect, add `let _ = Self._printChanges()` as the first line of its `body`. Xcode's console then prints what caused each update, such as `Parent: _count changed.`

## Variants

### Values flow down

Each box flashes yellow and counts when its `body` runs; a child reruns only when its input changes.

```swift
struct Parent: View {
    @State private var count = 0
    @State private var name = "Taylor"

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            HStack {
                Button("count + 1") { count += 1 }
                Button("Rename") { name = name == "Taylor" ? "Sam" : "Taylor" }
            }
            CountView(count: count)
            NameView(name: name)
            Badge()
        }
    }
}

struct CountView: View {
    let count: Int
    var body: some View { Text("count = \(count)") }
}

struct NameView: View {
    let name: String
    var body: some View { Text("name = \(name)") }
}

struct Badge: View {
    var body: some View { Image(systemName: "star.fill") }
}
```

**Note:** The parent reads both values, so it reruns every time. `Badge` takes no inputs, so it never does.

### @Observable tracks what you read

Move the values into an `@Observable` model, and only the view that reads a changed property reruns.

```swift
@Observable
class Model {
    var count = 0
    var name = "Taylor"
}

struct Parent: View {
    @State private var model = Model()

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            HStack {
                Button("count + 1") { model.count += 1 }
                Button("Rename") { model.name = model.name == "Taylor" ? "Sam" : "Taylor" }
            }
            CountView(model: model) // Reads model.count
            NameView(model: model)  // Reads model.name
        }
    }
}

struct CountView: View {
    let model: Model
    var body: some View { Text("count = \(model.count)") }
}

struct NameView: View {
    let model: Model
    var body: some View { Text("name = \(model.name)") }
}
```

**Note:** The parent passes the model along but never reads `count` or `name` in `body`, so now even the parent stays still.

## Related

`state`, `observable`, `choosing-wrappers`, `lifecycle`


<!-- topic: animation-curves -->
---
id: animation-curves
title: Animation Curves
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/animation.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# Animation Curves

Animate any state change, and pick a curve for how it speeds up and slows down.

Also called: easing, ease-in-out, transition-timing-function, cubic-bezier, CSS transition, timing function, UIView.animate, duration, delay, withAnimation.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isExpanded = false

RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
    .fill(.blue)
    .frame(height: isExpanded ? 200 : 80)
    .onTapGesture {
        withAnimation(.easeInOut(duration: 0.3)) {
            isExpanded.toggle()
        }
    }
```

**Important:** Always pass `value:` to `.animation(_:value:)`. The old version without it is deprecated and animates changes you didn't mean to.

## Rules

- **Keep feedback animations short.** A quick response feels light and tells people their tap worked. A slow one makes them wait for the interface to catch up.
- **Animate with a purpose.** Motion should explain what changed or where something went. Decoration that moves for its own sake distracts, and can make some people feel unwell.
- **Make motion optional.** Check Reduce Motion and swap big movement for a fade or no animation, so nothing important is shown only through motion.
- **Don't animate actions people repeat all the time.** System controls already have subtle motion. Extra animation on something tapped dozens of times a day gets tiresome fast.

## Pitfalls

- **You animate state, not views.** Change a value inside `withAnimation`, and every view that reads it moves from the old look to the new one.
- **`withAnimation` versus `.animation(_:value:)`.** `withAnimation` animates everything the change touches. The modifier animates only its own view, and only when `value` changes.
- **The default is a spring.** Since iOS 17, `withAnimation { }` with no argument uses a smooth spring, not ease-in-out. Pass `.easeInOut(duration:)` when you need an exact duration.

## Key APIs

- `withAnimation(_:_:)`: Animates every view the state change affects.
- `.animation(_:value:)`: Animates only this view, when `value` changes.
- `.easeInOut(duration:)`: Slow start and end. Also `.easeIn`, `.easeOut`, and `.linear`.
- `.delay(_:)`: Waits before the animation starts.
- `.repeatForever(autoreverses:)`: Loops the animation until the view goes away.
- `withAnimation(_:_:completion:)`: Runs code when the animation finishes (iOS 17+).
- `\.accessibilityReduceMotion`: True when the person turned on Reduce Motion.

## Variants

### Curves side by side

Give each view its own `.animation(_:value:)` curve; only the curve differs between these four dots.

```swift
@State private var isMoved = false

let curves: [(String, Animation)] = [
    ("linear", .linear(duration: 1)),
    ("easeIn", .easeIn(duration: 1)),
    ("easeOut", .easeOut(duration: 1)),
    ("easeInOut", .easeInOut(duration: 1)),
]

VStack {
    ForEach(curves, id: \.0) { name, animation in
        Circle()
            .frame(width: 28, height: 28)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: isMoved ? .trailing : .leading)
            .animation(animation, value: isMoved)
    }
    Button("Race") { isMoved.toggle() }
}
```

**Note:** Ease-out (fast start, gentle stop) feels the most responsive for things appearing on screen. Linear looks mechanical, so save it for spinners and progress.

### Repeat forever

Add `.repeatForever(autoreverses: true)` and flip the state in `.onAppear` for an endless pulse.

```swift
@State private var isPulsing = false

Circle()
    .fill(.red)
    .frame(width: 16, height: 16)
    .scaleEffect(isPulsing ? 1.4 : 1)
    .opacity(isPulsing ? 0.4 : 1)
    .animation(.easeInOut(duration: 0.8).repeatForever(autoreverses: true), value: isPulsing)
    .onAppear { isPulsing = true }
```

**Note:** A repeating animation never ends on its own. Keep it for live status like recording, and skip it when Reduce Motion is on.

### Run code when it finishes

Pass a `completion:` closure to `withAnimation` to chain a next step or clean up afterward.

```swift
@State private var isExpanded = false
@State private var status = "Ready"

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
        .fill(.teal)
        .frame(width: isExpanded ? 220 : 80, height: 44)
    Text(status)
    Button("Animate") {
        status = "Animating…"
        withAnimation(.easeOut(duration: 0.6)) {
            isExpanded.toggle()
        } completion: {
            status = "Done!"
        }
    }
}
```

### Respect Reduce Motion

Read `\.accessibilityReduceMotion` and pass `nil` to `withAnimation` to skip the movement.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
@State private var isExpanded = false

RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
    .fill(.indigo)
    .frame(width: isExpanded ? 220 : 80, height: 44)
    .onTapGesture {
        withAnimation(reduceMotion ? nil : .easeOut(duration: 0.4)) {
            isExpanded.toggle()
        }
    }
```

**Note:** Turn it on in Settings > Accessibility > Motion to test. A short fade is often a better fallback than no animation at all.

## Related

`spring`, `transitions`, `phase-animator`, `content-transition`


<!-- topic: spring -->
---
id: spring
title: Spring
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/spring.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# Spring

A natural, physics-based animation set by how long it takes and how much it bounces.

Also called: bounce, easing, physics, react-spring, damping, stiffness, usingSpringWithDamping, animation curve, snappy.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isLiked = false

Image(systemName: isLiked ? "heart.fill" : "heart")
    .font(.largeTitle)
    .foregroundStyle(.pink)
    .scaleEffect(isLiked ? 1.2 : 1)
    .onTapGesture {
        withAnimation(.spring(duration: 0.4, bounce: 0.5)) {
            isLiked.toggle()
        }
    }
```

**Note:** `bounce` runs from `0` (no overshoot) to just under `1`. Negative values make the spring slower and heavier, with no overshoot.

## Rules

- **Keep the bounce small in everyday UI.** A little overshoot feels lively and confirms the change. A lot of it looks cartoonish and slows people down.
- **Make motion match the gesture.** A card dragged down should settle back down, and a view that slid in from the bottom should leave the same way. Motion that contradicts the gesture disorients people.
- **Never make people wait for an animation.** Keep the interface usable while things move. Springs pick up from wherever they are when interrupted, so you rarely need to block input.

## Pitfalls

- **`duration` and `bounce` replace stiffness and damping.** If you know react-spring or UIKit's damping ratio, think "how long" and "how springy" instead; SwiftUI converts for you.
- **Springs are the default.** `withAnimation { }` with no argument already uses a smooth spring, so reach for a preset before tuning numbers.

## Key APIs

- `.spring(duration:bounce:)`: A spring with your own settle time and bounce.
- `.smooth`: No overshoot. A calm default for most changes.
- `.snappy`: A little overshoot. Quick and responsive.
- `.bouncy`: The most overshoot. Playful moments only.
- `.bouncy(duration:extraBounce:)`: Tunes a preset without leaving it.
- `.interactiveSpring()`: A fast spring for views that track a finger.
- `Spring.settlingDuration`: How long a spring really takes to come to rest.

## Variants

### The presets, side by side

Use the `.smooth`, `.snappy`, and `.bouncy` presets; they take the same time and differ only in overshoot.

```swift
@State private var isMoved = false

VStack {
    Circle().frame(width: 28, height: 28)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: isMoved ? .trailing : .leading)
        .animation(.smooth, value: isMoved)
    Circle().frame(width: 28, height: 28)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: isMoved ? .trailing : .leading)
        .animation(.snappy, value: isMoved)
    Circle().frame(width: 28, height: 28)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: isMoved ? .trailing : .leading)
        .animation(.bouncy, value: isMoved)
    Button("Play") { isMoved.toggle() }
}
```

**Note:** Start with `.smooth` for layout changes and `.snappy` for taps. Save `.bouncy` for playful moments like a like or a reward.

### Drag and snap back

Track a `DragGesture` directly, then let `.spring(duration:bounce:)` carry the card home on release.

```swift
@State private var offset = CGSize.zero

RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 20)
    .fill(.indigo.gradient)
    .frame(width: 120, height: 120)
    .offset(offset)
    .gesture(
        DragGesture()
            .onChanged { offset = $0.translation }
            .onEnded { _ in
                withAnimation(.spring(duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.4)) {
                    offset = .zero
                }
            }
    )
```

**Note:** Springs keep their momentum when interrupted. Grab the card while it's still moving and it follows your finger without a jump.

### Springy press effect

Scale a custom `ButtonStyle` on `isPressed`, and let `.animation(_:value:)` spring it back on release.

```swift
struct SquishyButtonStyle: ButtonStyle {
    func makeBody(configuration: Configuration) -> some View {
        configuration.label
            .padding(.horizontal, 24)
            .padding(.vertical, 14)
            .background(.pink.gradient, in: .capsule)
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .scaleEffect(configuration.isPressed ? 0.88 : 1)
            .animation(.bouncy(duration: 0.3, extraBounce: 0.2), value: configuration.isPressed)
    }
}

Button("Hold me") {}
    .buttonStyle(SquishyButtonStyle())
```

## Related

`animation-curves`, `transitions`, `keyframe-animator`, `haptics`


<!-- topic: transitions -->
---
id: transitions
title: Transitions
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/anytransition.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# Transitions

Control how a view animates in when it's added and out when it's removed.

Also called: enter animation, exit animation, fade in, slide in, AnimatePresence, v-if transition, show hide, appear, insertion, removal.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isShown = false

VStack {
    Button("Show Details") {
        withAnimation { isShown.toggle() }
    }
    if isShown {
        Text("Arrives Thursday")
            .transition(.scale.combined(with: .opacity))
    }
}
```

**Important:** A transition runs only when a view is added or removed, as in `if isShown { }`, and only when that change is animated. Changing a view's properties is a normal animation.

## Rules

- **Leave the way you came in.** A banner that drops from the top should go back up. Leaving in a new direction breaks the sense of where it lives.
- **Keep transitions quick and subtle.** A short fade or slide shows what changed without making people watch it. Save big entrances for rare moments.
- **Fall back to a fade with Reduce Motion.** Sliding and scaling can be uncomfortable for some people. When `accessibilityReduceMotion` is on, use `.opacity` instead.

## Pitfalls

- **Like `AnimatePresence`, built in.** On the web you keep an element mounted until its exit animation ends. In SwiftUI, removing it inside an animated change is enough.
- **The default is `.opacity`.** A view inside an animated `if` fades in and out even without a `.transition` modifier.

## Key APIs

- `.transition(_:)`: How this view enters and leaves.
- `.opacity`, `.scale`, `.slide`: Fade, grow from the center, or slide across.
- `.move(edge:)`: Slides in from an edge and out the same way.
- `.push(from:)`: Pushes in from one edge while the old view leaves the other.
- `.combined(with:)`: Runs two transitions at once, like move and fade.
- `.asymmetric(insertion:removal:)`: Different transitions for entering and leaving.
- `.blurReplace`: Blurs and fades, good for swapping content (iOS 17+).

## Variants

### Expandable details

Combine `.move(edge: .top)` with `.opacity` so extra details unfold beneath a row.

```swift
@State private var isExpanded = false

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
    Button {
        withAnimation(.snappy) { isExpanded.toggle() }
    } label: {
        HStack {
            Text("Shipping details").font(.headline)
            Spacer()
            Image(systemName: "chevron.down")
                .rotationEffect(.degrees(isExpanded ? 180 : 0))
        }
    }
    .buttonStyle(.plain)

    if isExpanded {
        Text("Arrives Thursday. Free returns within 30 days.")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            .transition(.move(edge: .top).combined(with: .opacity))
    }
}
.padding()
.background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 16))
.clipped()
```

**Note:** Moving views can draw outside their container. `.clipped()` on the container hides them until they're inside it.

### Toast from the top
