Use `.asymmetric(insertion:removal:)` so the toast drops in from the top and shrinks away when it leaves.

```swift
@State private var showsToast = false

VStack {
    if showsToast {
        Label("Saved to Photos", systemImage: "checkmark.circle.fill")
            .padding(.horizontal, 16)
            .padding(.vertical, 10)
            .background(.regularMaterial, in: .capsule)
            .transition(.asymmetric(
                insertion: .move(edge: .top).combined(with: .opacity),
                removal: .scale(scale: 0.8).combined(with: .opacity)
            ))
    }
    Spacer()
    Button("Save") {
        withAnimation(.bouncy) { showsToast = true }
        Task {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1.5))
            withAnimation(.smooth) { showsToast = false }
        }
    }
}
.frame(height: 150)
```

### Swap content with .push

Use `.push(from:)` with a new `.id` per step, so the old step leaves as the next pushes in.

```swift
@State private var step = 1

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    Text("Step \(step)")
        .font(.largeTitle.bold())
        .id(step)
        .transition(.push(from: .trailing))
    Button("Next") {
        withAnimation(.smooth) { step = step % 3 + 1 }
    }
}
.clipped()
```

**Important:** Without `.id(step)`, SwiftUI keeps the same `Text` and only changes its string, so no transition runs.

## Related

`animation-curves`, `matched-geometry`, `content-transition`, `spring`


<!-- topic: matched-geometry -->
---
id: matched-geometry
title: Matched Geometry
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/matchedgeometryeffect(id:in:properties:anchor:issource:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# Matched Geometry

Morph one view into another, like a sliding tab highlight or a card growing full screen.

Also called: hero animation, shared element transition, FLIP, layoutId, framer motion layout, morph, zoom transition, magic move, namespace.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Morph only things people see as the same object.** A thumbnail growing into its detail explains where the detail came from. Morphing unrelated views into each other just confuses.
- **Let people go back the way they came.** A screen that zoomed out of a tile should shrink back into it. The zoom transition does this, including swipe to dismiss.
- **Keep it quick.** A hero animation people see every time they open an item should feel instant. Use a short spring like `.snappy`.

## Pitfalls

- **Both views need the same `id` and the same `@Namespace`.** Declare the namespace once in the parent, and pass it to child views as a `Namespace.ID`.
- **It only links frames.** Each view still fades in or out with its own transition while its frame moves, so add `.transition(.identity)` if you see a cross-fade you don't want.

## Key APIs

- `@Namespace`: A scope for ids, declared once in the parent view.
- `.matchedGeometryEffect(id:in:)`: Links this view's frame to others with the same id.
- `isSource:`: Pass `false` on copies that should follow, not lead.
- `.matchedTransitionSource(id:in:)`: Marks the tile a new screen zooms out of (iOS 18+).
- `.navigationTransition(.zoom(sourceID:in:))`: Zooms a pushed screen or sheet from its source.

## Variants

### Sliding tab indicator

Draw one `.matchedGeometryEffect(id:in:)` highlight behind the selected tab, and it slides between tabs.

```swift
@State private var selected = "Music"
@Namespace private var tabs

HStack(spacing: 4) {
    ForEach(["Music", "Podcasts", "Books"], id: \.self) { tab in
        Text(tab)
            .font(.subheadline.weight(.semibold))
            .foregroundStyle(selected == tab ? .white : .primary)
            .padding(.horizontal, 14)
            .padding(.vertical, 8)
            .background {
                if selected == tab {
                    Capsule()
                        .fill(.indigo)
                        .matchedGeometryEffect(id: "highlight", in: tabs)
                }
            }
            .onTapGesture {
                withAnimation(.snappy) { selected = tab }
            }
    }
}
.padding(4)
.background(.fill.tertiary, in: .capsule)
```

**Important:** The change must happen inside `withAnimation`. Without it, the highlight jumps to the new tab.

### Card that expands

Give each shared piece its own `matchedGeometryEffect` id, so the art and title travel between layouts.

```swift
@State private var isExpanded = false
@Namespace private var card

VStack {
    if isExpanded {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 20)
                .fill(.orange.gradient)
                .matchedGeometryEffect(id: "art", in: card)
                .frame(height: 160)
            Text("Sunset Drive")
                .font(.title2.bold())
                .matchedGeometryEffect(id: "title", in: card)
            Text("A playlist for golden hour.")
                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
    } else {
        HStack(spacing: 12) {
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 10)
                .fill(.orange.gradient)
                .matchedGeometryEffect(id: "art", in: card)
                .frame(width: 56, height: 56)
            Text("Sunset Drive")
                .font(.headline)
                .matchedGeometryEffect(id: "title", in: card)
            Spacer()
        }
    }
}
.onTapGesture {
    withAnimation(.spring(duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2)) {
        isExpanded.toggle()
    }
}
```

**Important:** Each id can be on screen only once. If both versions show at the same time, give one `isSource: false`, or SwiftUI warns and the result is unpredictable.

### Zoom transition

Pair `.matchedTransitionSource(id:in:)` on the tile with `.navigationTransition(.zoom(sourceID:in:))` on the new screen.

```swift
struct Album: Identifiable {
    let id: Int
    let name: String
    let color: Color
}

@Namespace private var zoom
@State private var selected: Album?
let albums = [
    Album(id: 0, name: "Pink", color: .pink),
    Album(id: 1, name: "Orange", color: .orange),
    Album(id: 2, name: "Teal", color: .teal),
    Album(id: 3, name: "Indigo", color: .indigo),
]

LazyVGrid(columns: [GridItem(), GridItem()], spacing: 12) {
    ForEach(albums) { album in
        Button {
            selected = album
        } label: {
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 16)
                .fill(album.color.gradient)
                .frame(height: 100)
        }
        .matchedTransitionSource(id: album.id, in: zoom)
    }
}
.fullScreenCover(item: $selected) { album in
    Rectangle()
        .fill(album.color.gradient)
        .ignoresSafeArea()
        .overlay {
            Button("Close") { selected = nil }
                .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        }
        .navigationTransition(.zoom(sourceID: album.id, in: zoom))
}
```

**Note:** The same two modifiers work for a `NavigationLink` push and a `.sheet`. Put `.navigationTransition` on the destination's root view.

## Related

`transitions`, `navigation-stack`, `spring`, `sheet`


<!-- topic: phase-animator -->
---
id: phase-animator
title: PhaseAnimator
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/phaseanimator.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# PhaseAnimator

Steps a view through a list of states, either in a loop or each time a value changes.

Also called: loop animation, multi-step animation, sequence, CSS animation, animation-iteration-count, infinite, pulse, shake, attention.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var count = 0

Button("Add to Cart", systemImage: "cart") {
    count += 1
}
.buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
.phaseAnimator([1.0, 1.2], trigger: count) { content, scale in
    content.scaleEffect(scale)
}
```

**Note:** Leave out `trigger:` and the phases loop forever. With a trigger, they play once each time the value changes, then return to the first phase.

## Rules

- **Loop only what's truly ongoing.** One pulsing indicator says "this is live." When several things move at once, nothing stands out and the screen feels restless.
- **Don't rely on motion alone.** A shake or bounce is a hint. Pair it with text, like an error message, so people who miss the motion still get the point.
- **Keep feedback short.** A triggered animation should finish in well under a second, so people can keep going without waiting.

## Pitfalls

- **Phases are whole states.** Use numbers for one property, or an `enum` with computed properties when several change together.
- **Phases or keyframes?** Use `PhaseAnimator` when each step is a state. Use KeyframeAnimator (`keyframe-animator`) when properties need their own exact timing, like CSS `@keyframes`.

## Key APIs

- `.phaseAnimator(_:content:animation:)`: Loops through the phases forever.
- `.phaseAnimator(_:trigger:content:animation:)`: Plays the phases once each time `trigger` changes.
- `content:`: Gets the view and current phase; apply modifiers here.
- `animation:`: Picks the animation into each phase.
- `PhaseAnimator`: The same thing as a view, wrapping its content.

## Variants

### Shake on error

Pass the attempt count as `trigger:` to shake the field each time sign-in fails.

```swift
@State private var attempts = 0

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    SecureField("Password", text: .constant("1234"))
        .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
        .frame(width: 220)
        .phaseAnimator([0.0, -12, 12, -8, 8, 0], trigger: attempts) { content, offset in
            content.offset(x: offset)
        } animation: { _ in
            .linear(duration: 0.06)
        }
    Button("Sign In") { attempts += 1 }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
```

**Note:** A shake alone is easy to miss. Show an error message too, and skip the shake when Reduce Motion is on.

### Steps as an enum

Describe each step as an `enum` case when scale and rotation change together.

```swift
enum LikePhase: CaseIterable {
    case idle, grow, settle

    var scale: Double {
        switch self {
        case .idle: 1
        case .grow: 1.4
        case .settle: 1.1
        }
    }
    var angle: Double { self == .grow ? -12 : 0 }
}

@State private var likes = 0

Button {
    likes += 1
} label: {
    Label("\(likes)", systemImage: "hand.thumbsup.fill")
}
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
.phaseAnimator(LikePhase.allCases, trigger: likes) { content, phase in
    content
        .scaleEffect(phase.scale)
        .rotationEffect(.degrees(phase.angle))
} animation: { phase in
    phase == .grow ? .snappy(duration: 0.15) : .bouncy
}
```

**Note:** The `animation:` closure gets the phase it's animating to, so the quick grow and the bouncy settle each get their own curve.

### Loading dots

Without a `trigger:`, `.phaseAnimator` loops on its own, so three delayed dots need no state.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 8) {
    ForEach(0..<3) { index in
        Circle()
            .frame(width: 12, height: 12)
            .phaseAnimator([0.3, 1]) { content, phase in
                content.opacity(phase).scaleEffect(phase)
            } animation: { _ in
                .easeInOut(duration: 0.5).delay(Double(index) * 0.15)
            }
    }
}
.foregroundStyle(.secondary)
```

**Note:** For a standard spinner, use `ProgressView`. Custom loaders are best kept for branded moments.

## Related

`keyframe-animator`, `animation-curves`, `symbol-effects`, `spring`


<!-- topic: keyframe-animator -->
---
id: keyframe-animator
title: KeyframeAnimator
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/keyframeanimator.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# KeyframeAnimator

Animates several properties on their own timelines, like a jump that squashes, spins, and lands.

Also called: @keyframes, CSS keyframes, timeline, CAKeyframeAnimation, choreography, squash and stretch, multi-property animation, lottie.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var rings = 0

Image(systemName: "bell.fill")
    .font(.largeTitle)
    .onTapGesture { rings += 1 }
    .keyframeAnimator(initialValue: 0.0, trigger: rings) { content, angle in
        content.rotationEffect(.degrees(angle), anchor: .top)
    } keyframes: { _ in
        KeyframeTrack {
            CubicKeyframe(20, duration: 0.1)
            CubicKeyframe(-15, duration: 0.15)
            SpringKeyframe(0, duration: 0.3)
        }
    }
```

**Note:** To animate several properties, use a struct as `initialValue` and add one `KeyframeTrack(\.property)` per property, as in the demo's code.

## Rules

- **Rest between loops.** A looping animation with a pause reads as a gentle reminder. Without one it feels frantic and pulls attention from everything else.
- **Save choreography for special moments.** A multi-step animation suits a reward or a first launch. On something people do all day, it slows them down.
- **Keep it optional.** When Reduce Motion is on, skip the keyframes or show the end state, and make sure the meaning comes through without them.

## Pitfalls

- **Like CSS `@keyframes`, but per property.** Each `KeyframeTrack` animates one property of your value struct on its own timeline, and all tracks run at the same time.
- **Make the tracks the same length.** Add up each track's durations to the same total, so every property finishes together.

## Key APIs

- `.keyframeAnimator(initialValue:trigger:)`: Plays the keyframes once each time `trigger` changes.
- `repeating: true`: Loops the keyframes while the view is on screen.
- `KeyframeTrack(_:)`: One property's timeline, picked by key path.
- `CubicKeyframe`: Moves smoothly to the value.
- `SpringKeyframe`: Springs to the value, with physics.
- `LinearKeyframe`: Moves at a constant speed.
- `MoveKeyframe`: Jumps to the value instantly.

## Variants

### Shake on a wrong passcode

Animate one `KeyframeTrack` on the x offset, and end with a `SpringKeyframe` to settle in the center.

```swift
@State private var attempts = 0

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    HStack(spacing: 14) {
        ForEach(0..<4) { _ in
            Circle().frame(width: 14, height: 14)
        }
    }
    .foregroundStyle(.red)
    .keyframeAnimator(initialValue: 0.0, trigger: attempts) { content, x in
        content.offset(x: x)
    } keyframes: { _ in
        KeyframeTrack {
            CubicKeyframe(-16, duration: 0.07)
            CubicKeyframe(14, duration: 0.07)
            CubicKeyframe(-10, duration: 0.07)
            CubicKeyframe(6, duration: 0.07)
            SpringKeyframe(0, duration: 0.2)
        }
    }
    Button("Try passcode") { attempts += 1 }
}
```

**Note:** Keyframe values only change how the view draws, not its layout, so the shaking dots don't push other views around.

### Ringing bell

Pass `repeating: true` to loop the keyframes, and end with a still `LinearKeyframe` as a pause.

```swift
Image(systemName: "bell.fill")
    .font(.system(size: 48))
    .foregroundStyle(.orange)
    .keyframeAnimator(initialValue: 0.0, repeating: true) { content, degrees in
        content.rotationEffect(.degrees(degrees), anchor: .top)
    } keyframes: { _ in
        KeyframeTrack {
            CubicKeyframe(20, duration: 0.1)
            CubicKeyframe(-18, duration: 0.15)
            CubicKeyframe(12, duration: 0.15)
            CubicKeyframe(-6, duration: 0.15)
            CubicKeyframe(0, duration: 0.1)
            LinearKeyframe(0, duration: 1)
        }
    }
```

## Related

`phase-animator`, `spring`, `animation-curves`


<!-- topic: symbol-effects -->
---
id: symbol-effects
title: Symbol Effects
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/symboleffect(_:options:value:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sf-symbols.md
---

# Symbol Effects

Built-in SF Symbol animations, like bounce, pulse, and wiggle, with one modifier.

Also called: icon animation, animated icon, bounce, pulse, wiggle, spinner icon, lottie, font awesome animation, sfsymbols.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var unread = 0

Button {
    unread += 1
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "bell.fill")
        .symbolEffect(.bounce, value: unread)
}
```

**Note:** Pass `value:` to play the effect once per change, or `isActive:` to keep it running while a flag is true.

## Rules

- **Animate one symbol at a time.** A single moving symbol draws the eye to what changed. When several animate together, they compete and the screen feels busy.
- **Pick the effect that matches the meaning.** People read `.bounce` as "something just happened" and `.pulse` or `.variableColor` as "still working." Using one for the other sends the wrong signal.
- **Fit the effect to your app's tone.** A playful wiggle suits a game or a social app. A finance or health app usually calls for quieter effects.

## Pitfalls

- **One modifier covers a whole group.** `.symbolEffect` animates every symbol inside the view, so you can put it on a `Label`, a button, or a stack.
- **Newer effects need newer iOS.** `.wiggle`, `.breathe`, and `.rotate` need iOS 18, and `.drawOn` and `.drawOff` need iOS 26.

## Key APIs

- `.symbolEffect(_:value:)`: Plays the effect once each time `value` changes.
- `.symbolEffect(_:isActive:)`: Runs the effect continuously while `isActive` is true.
- `.bounce`, `.wiggle`: A quick nudge: something happened, or look here.
- `.pulse`, `.breathe`: A steady throb for ongoing activity.
- `.variableColor.iterative`: Lights the symbol's layers one by one.
- `.contentTransition(.symbolEffect(.replace))`: Animates a change of symbol name.
- `.transition(.symbolEffect(.drawOn))`: Draws a symbol in along its strokes (iOS 26).

## Variants

### Notification badge

Pass the unread count to `.symbolEffect(.bounce, value:)` so the bell bounces on each new notification.

```swift
@State private var unread = 0

Button {
    unread += 1
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "bell.badge.fill")
        .symbolRenderingMode(.palette)
        .foregroundStyle(.red, .primary)
        .font(.largeTitle)
        .symbolEffect(.bounce, value: unread)
}
.buttonStyle(.plain)
```

### Play / pause button

Change the symbol name and add `.contentTransition(.symbolEffect(.replace))` to animate the swap.

```swift
@State private var isPlaying = false

Button {
    isPlaying.toggle()
} label: {
    Image(systemName: isPlaying ? "pause.fill" : "play.fill")
        .font(.largeTitle)
        .contentTransition(.symbolEffect(.replace))
        .frame(width: 72, height: 72)
}
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
.buttonBorderShape(.circle)
```

**Note:** Related symbols, like `bell` and `bell.slash`, morph with Magic Replace. Unrelated ones, like play and pause, scale down and up instead.

### Loading indicator

Use `.symbolEffect(_:isActive:)` to animate a symbol while work runs, and stop when it's done.

```swift
@State private var isSyncing = true

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
    Label("Syncing…", systemImage: "arrow.triangle.2.circlepath.icloud")
        .symbolEffect(.pulse, isActive: isSyncing)
    Label("Searching", systemImage: "wifi")
        .symbolEffect(.variableColor.iterative, isActive: isSyncing)
}
.font(.title3)
```

**Note:** Set `isActive` back to `false` when the work finishes. The symbol finishes its current cycle and settles.

### Draw on and off

Use `.transition(.symbolEffect(.drawOn))` to trace a symbol along its strokes as it appears.

```swift
@State private var isShown = true

VStack(spacing: 20) {
    ZStack {
        if isShown {
            Image(systemName: "signature")
                .font(.system(size: 64))
                .transition(.symbolEffect(.drawOn))
        }
    }
    .frame(height: 80)

    Button(isShown ? "Erase" : "Sign") {
        withAnimation { isShown.toggle() }
    }
    .buttonStyle(.bordered)
}
```

**Note:** Drawing needs iOS 26 and a symbol that supports it. Check in the SF Symbols app; other symbols fall back to a fade.

## Related

`sf-symbols`, `content-transition`, `phase-animator`, `image`


<!-- topic: content-transition -->
---
id: content-transition
title: Content Transitions
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/contenttransition.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# Content Transitions

Animate content changing in place, like digits rolling on a counter or one icon becoming another.

Also called: counter animation, number ticker, rolling digits, odometer, animate text change, count up, icon swap, crossfade.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var count = 0

VStack {
    Text("\(count)")
        .font(.largeTitle.bold())
        .contentTransition(.numericText(value: Double(count)))
        .animation(.snappy, value: count)
    Button("Add") { count += 1 }
}
```

**Important:** A content transition plays only when the change is animated. Wrap it in `withAnimation`, or add `.animation(_:value:)` as above.

## Rules

- **Keep changing numbers from shifting.** Proportional digits change width as the value changes, so nearby text jumps around. Monospaced digits keep everything still.
- **Animate values people are watching.** A rolling price or score confirms a change they made. For text they're reading, a quiet crossfade or no animation is easier on the eyes.
- **Keep it quick.** A number should settle in a fraction of a second, so people can read the new value right away.

## Pitfalls

- **Same view, new content.** A content transition animates what's drawn inside one view. To animate a view being added or removed, use Transitions (`transitions`).
- **Like a CSS number ticker, without the library.** On the web you'd reach for a counter package; here one modifier on `Text` does it.

## Key APIs

- `.contentTransition(_:)`: How this view's content animates when it changes.
- `.numericText(value:)`: Rolls digits, up or down depending on `value`.
- `.numericText(countsDown:)`: Rolls digits down when there's no value to compare.
- `.interpolate`: Blends weight, size, and color between the two states.
- `.opacity`: A plain crossfade between old and new content.
- `.identity`: No animation; the content just changes.
- `.symbolEffect(.replace)`: Swaps one SF Symbol for another.

## Variants

### Price that rolls

Use `.numericText(value:)` on formatted currency too; each digit rolls on its own.

```swift
@State private var quantity = 1
let price = 4.99

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    Text(Double(quantity) * price, format: .currency(code: "USD"))
        .font(.largeTitle.bold())
        .contentTransition(.numericText(value: Double(quantity)))
        .animation(.snappy, value: quantity)
    Stepper("Quantity: \(quantity)", value: $quantity, in: 1...20)
        .frame(width: 220)
}
```

**Note:** `value:` tells SwiftUI whether the number went up or down, so the digits roll in the right direction.

### Countdown timer

Redraw with a `TimelineView` each second, and use `.numericText(countsDown: true)` to roll digits down.

```swift
@State private var end = Date.now.addingTimeInterval(90)

TimelineView(.periodic(from: .now, by: 1)) { context in
    let seconds = max(0, Int(end.timeIntervalSince(context.date)))
    Text(String(format: "%d:%02d", seconds / 60, seconds % 60))
        .font(.system(size: 56, weight: .semibold, design: .monospaced))
        .contentTransition(.numericText(countsDown: true))
        .animation(.default, value: seconds)
}
```

### Follow button

Use `.interpolate` to morph a button's label and style in one animated update.

```swift
@State private var isFollowing = false

Button {
    withAnimation(.snappy) { isFollowing.toggle() }
} label: {
    Label(isFollowing ? "Following" : "Follow",
          systemImage: isFollowing ? "checkmark" : "plus")
        .contentTransition(.interpolate)
}
.buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
.tint(isFollowing ? .gray : .blue)
```

## Related

`symbol-effects`, `transitions`, `text`, `animation-curves`


<!-- topic: haptics -->
---
id: haptics
title: Haptics
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, watchOS 10.0+, visionOS 26.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/sensoryfeedback.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-haptics.md
---

# Haptics

Play a tap, buzz, or click on the device when something happens.

Also called: vibrate, vibration, taptic, navigator.vibrate, UIImpactFeedbackGenerator, UINotificationFeedbackGenerator, feedback, buzz, rumble.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var saveCount = 0

Button("Save") {
    saveCount += 1
}
.buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
.sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger: saveCount)
```

**Important:** Haptics only play on a real iPhone or Apple Watch. The Simulator and iPad stay silent, so test on a device. The demo shows a visual pulse instead.

## Rules

- **Pair every haptic with something people can see.** Many people never feel haptics: iPad has none, and anyone can turn them off. The screen should tell the same story.
- **Use each type for what it means.** People learn that `.success` means done and `.error` means failed. Playing them for anything else muddles the signal.
- **Use haptics sparingly.** A haptic on every tap gets tiresome. Toggles, pickers, and pull to refresh already play their own, so don't add another on top.

## Pitfalls

- **You change state; SwiftUI plays the haptic.** Unlike `navigator.vibrate()`, you don't call anything. The feedback plays whenever its `trigger` value changes.
- **Some types only play on other devices.** `.start` and `.stop` play only on Apple Watch, `.increase` and `.decrease` on Apple Watch and Vision Pro, and `.levelChange` on a Mac.

## Key APIs

- `.sensoryFeedback(_:trigger:)`: Plays feedback each time `trigger` changes.
- `.sensoryFeedback(_:trigger:condition:)`: Plays only when your closure returns `true`.
- `.sensoryFeedback(trigger:_:)`: Picks the feedback, or `nil`, from the old and new values.
- `.success`, `.warning`, `.error`: The outcome of a task.
- `.selection`: A light tick as a value changes.
- `.impact(weight:)`: A bump, from `.light` to `.heavy`.
- `.alignment`: A crisp tick when something snaps into place.

## Variants

### Success or error from one trigger

Use `.sensoryFeedback(trigger:_:)` to pick `.success`, `.error`, or `nil` from the new value.

```swift
enum SaveResult { case none, saved, failed }
@State private var result = SaveResult.none

HStack {
    Button("Save") { result = .saved }
    Button("Fail", role: .destructive) { result = .failed }
}
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
.sensoryFeedback(trigger: result) { _, newValue in
    switch newValue {
    case .saved: .success
    case .failed: .error
    case .none: nil
    }
}
```

### Ticks on a custom control

Play `.selection`, the light tick of a picker wheel, each time a custom rating changes.

```swift
@State private var rating = 3

HStack {
    ForEach(1...5, id: \.self) { star in
        Image(systemName: star <= rating ? "star.fill" : "star")
            .foregroundStyle(.yellow)
            .onTapGesture { rating = star }
    }
}
.font(.title)
.sensoryFeedback(.selection, trigger: rating)
```

**Note:** System pickers, toggles, and sliders already play their own haptics. Add `.selection` only to controls you build yourself.

### Snap into alignment

Drag the circle across the guide; `.alignment` ticks the moment it snaps to the center.

```swift
@State private var offset: CGFloat = -90
@State private var dragStart: CGFloat?
private var isCentered: Bool { abs(offset) < 12 }

ZStack {
    Capsule()
        .fill(isCentered ? Color.indigo : Color.secondary.opacity(0.4))
        .frame(width: 3, height: 90)
    Circle()
        .fill(.indigo.gradient)
        .frame(width: 56, height: 56)
        .offset(x: isCentered ? 0 : offset)
        .animation(.snappy, value: isCentered)
        .gesture(
            DragGesture()
                .onChanged { drag in
                    let start = dragStart ?? offset
                    dragStart = start
                    offset = min(max(start + drag.translation.width, -110), 110)
                }
                .onEnded { _ in dragStart = nil }
        )
}
.sensoryFeedback(.alignment, trigger: isCentered) { _, centered in centered }
```

**Note:** The `condition:` closure returns `true` only when the circle snaps in, so nothing plays as it leaves the guide.

## Related

`button`, `toggle`, `picker`, `symbol-effects`


<!-- topic: system-colors -->
---
id: system-colors
title: System Colors
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/color.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/color.md
---

# System Colors

Colors that adapt to light mode, dark mode, and accessibility settings for you.

Also called: palette, theme, dark mode, css variables, design tokens, UIColor, label color, background color, colour, hex.

## Rules

- **Use semantic colors instead of fixed ones.** `.white` and `.black` never change, so a card that looks right in light mode glows in dark mode.
- **Don't rely on color alone.** Some people can't tell red from green. Pair color with a symbol or a word so the meaning survives.
- **Use each semantic color for its job.** Don't use `separator` for text or `secondaryLabel` as a fill. Each one is tuned for its role, and borrowed colors break in other modes.
- **Save the accent color for things people can tap.** If plain text uses the same color as buttons, people can't tell what's interactive.

## Pitfalls

- **Semantic colors describe a job, not a value.** `Color(.label)` and `Color(.systemBackground)` flip in dark mode on their own, like CSS custom properties under `prefers-color-scheme`.
- **Put custom colors in the asset catalog.** Add a Color Set with Any and Dark appearances, then use it as `Color("Brand")`. The `AccentColor` set there tints the whole app.

## Guide

Each swatch shows one color in **light** mode (left) and **dark** mode (right). You write one name and iOS picks the value. Tap a swatch to copy its code.

### Text

For text and symbols, from most to least important.

### Backgrounds and fills

Layer these from back to front. In dark mode the higher layers get *lighter*, so cards still stand out.

### Standard colors

For accents and meaning. Write them as `.red` or `Color.red`.

**Note:** Standard colors shift slightly in dark mode and again with Increase Contrast. Use the name, never a hex value copied from a screenshot.

## Key APIs

- `Color(.systemBackground)`: Any UIKit semantic color, wrapped for SwiftUI.
- `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`: Text levels, from `.primary` down to `.quaternary`.
- `.background(.background)`: The screen's own background, as a style.
- `Color.red`: A standard color, tuned for light and dark mode.
- `.tint(_:)`: The accent color for controls inside a view.
- `Color("Brand")`: A custom color from the asset catalog.
- `@Environment(\.colorScheme)`: Reads whether the view is `.light` or `.dark`.

## Variants

### Text levels with hierarchical styles

Ask `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)` for a level instead of naming a label color; SwiftUI picks the shade.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Primary").foregroundStyle(.primary)
    Text("Secondary").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Text("Tertiary").foregroundStyle(.tertiary)
    Text("Quaternary").foregroundStyle(.quaternary)
}
.font(.title3.bold())
```

**Note:** On a material (`materials`), these levels turn vibrant and blend with the blur. A fixed color like `.gray` doesn't.

### Brand color with tint

Set `.tint(_:)` on a container to recolor every button, toggle, and link inside it.

```swift
@State private var isOn = true

VStack(spacing: 16) {
    Toggle("Notifications", isOn: $isOn)
    Button("Continue") {}
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
    Link("Privacy Policy", destination: URL(string: "https://example.com")!)
}
.tint(.orange)
```

**Note:** To change the accent color for the whole app, set the `AccentColor` in the asset catalog instead.

## Related

`foreground-style`, `gradients`, `materials`, `typography`


<!-- topic: typography -->
---
id: typography
title: Typography
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/font.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Typography

Apple's built-in text styles, which resize automatically when people change their text size.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules

- **Use text styles, not fixed point sizes.** Many people raise their text size. A fixed size ignores that setting and stays small.
- **Avoid light weights for small text.** Ultralight, Thin, and Light strokes are hard to see at small sizes. Use Regular or heavier.
- **Let layouts grow with the text.** Allow text to wrap instead of truncating, and stack side-by-side items at accessibility sizes.
- **Use few typefaces.** One family with a few styles and weights shows hierarchy clearly. Mixing many fonts makes a screen feel unplanned.

## Pitfalls

- **Text styles are your type scale.** They work like `h1` and `body` in a CSS reset, but they also follow the person's text size setting, like `rem`.
- **Test big sizes without changing Settings.** Add `.dynamicTypeSize(.accessibility3)` to a preview, or use the Variants button in Xcode's canvas.

## Guide

iOS has eleven **text styles**. Pick one by its *role*, like a title, the body, or a caption, and iOS sets the size, weight, and line spacing. Drag the slider to see each one grow with the person's text size setting.

**Important:** `.font(.system(size: 17))` is a fixed size, like `px` in CSS, and ignores the text size setting. Use a text style, or `.system(.body)`, so it scales like `rem`.

### Weight, design, and width

Start from a text style, then adjust it. Every combination still scales with Dynamic Type. Widths only exist for the default San Francisco design, so they have no effect on `.serif` or `.rounded`.

```swift
Text("Hello, SwiftUI")
    .font(.largeTitle)
    .fontWeight(.bold)
    .fontDesign(.rounded)
```

## Key APIs

`.font(.body)`, `.fontWeight(_:)`, `.fontDesign(_:)`, `.font(.custom(_:size:relativeTo:))`, `@ScaledMetric`, `.monospacedDigit()`, `@Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize)`

## Variants

### Custom font that still scales

Pass `relativeTo:` to `.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` so your font grows with that text style.

```swift
Text("The quick brown fox")
    .font(.custom("Georgia", size: 20, relativeTo: .title3))
```

**Note:** A bundled font also needs its file listed under `UIAppFonts` in Info.plist. Georgia ships with iOS.

### Stack items at large sizes

Check `isAccessibilitySize` on the `dynamicTypeSize` environment value, and switch a row to a column.

```swift
@Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var typeSize

let layout = typeSize.isAccessibilitySize
    ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading))
    : AnyLayout(HStackLayout())

layout {
    Text("Delivery")
    Spacer(minLength: 0)
    Text("Friday, 9–11 AM")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

**Note:** Accessibility sizes can make text more than three times larger. Avoid fixed heights so rows can grow.

## On macOS

Mac text is smaller than iPhone text: 13 points by default, and 10 at the smallest.

### Rules

- **Keep text at 10 points or larger.** 13 points is the Mac's default size, and 10 is the smallest Apple recommends. Footnote and caption styles are already 10 points.
- **Avoid light weights.** Ultralight, Thin, and Light are hard to read, especially at small sizes. Stay with Regular, Medium, Semibold, or Bold.
- **Show hierarchy with size, weight, and color.** A heading in `.headline` over body text in `.secondary` gray reads at a glance. Use the built-in styles so your levels match other Mac apps.
- **Use as few typefaces as you can.** Mixing several fonts muddies the hierarchy and makes an app look unfinished. The system font in a few styles covers most apps.
- **Give long text room between lines.** Loose leading helps people keep their place across wide paragraphs. Tighten it only for one or two lines in a cramped row, never for three or more.

### Pitfalls

- **Custom fonts follow the same sizes.** Keep body text at 13 points and the smallest text at 10, and go larger if the font is thin.

### Key APIs

`.font(.headline)`, `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`, `.font(.body.monospaced())`, `.font(.body.leading(.loose))`

### Variants

#### Build a hierarchy from text styles

Use `.headline` for the title, the default `.body` for the main line, and `.subheadline` in `.secondary` for details.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 2) {
    Text("Weekly Planning")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("Agenda for Monday's meeting")
    Text("Today, 9:41 AM")
        .font(.subheadline)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

#### Emphasize with weight

Use `.fontWeight(.semibold)` to stress a word or a total without adding another size to the window.

```swift
HStack {
    Text("Total")
    Spacer()
    Text("$128.40")
        .fontWeight(.semibold)
}
.frame(width: 220)
```

#### Keep changing numbers still

Add `.monospacedDigit()` to a clock or a column of numbers, so the digits don't shift as the value changes.

```swift
TimelineView(.periodic(from: .now, by: 1)) { context in
    Text(context.date, format: .dateTime.hour().minute().second())
        .font(.title.monospacedDigit())
}
```

#### Monospaced text for code

`Font.monospaced()` switches a text style to SF Mono, for code, file paths, and anything people compare column by column.

```swift
Text("~/Library/Containers/")
    .font(.body.monospaced())
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Scale your own numbers, Numbers that don't jump, Loose leading for long passages (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/font.md

## Related

`font`, `text`, `system-colors`, `sf-symbols`, `text-label`, `writing`, `contrast-transparency`


<!-- topic: materials -->
---
id: materials
title: Materials
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+, macOS 12.0+, visionOS 1.0+, macOS 26.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/material.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Materials

Frosted, blurred backgrounds that let the content behind them show through.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Now Playing")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("Midnight City")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.padding()
.background(.regularMaterial, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

**Note:** A material blurs whatever is behind the view, so it only shows over an image or color. On a plain background it looks like a gray fill.

## Rules

- **Use vibrant text styles on materials.** `.secondary` and `.tertiary` pick up the colors behind the blur and stay readable. A fixed `.gray` looks flat and muddy.
- **Use thicker materials behind text.** Thin materials keep more of the background visible, which helps people keep their place. Thicker ones give text and fine details more contrast.
- **Keep materials in the content layer.** Use them for cards, captions, and overlays. Floating controls and bars get Liquid Glass instead.
- **Pick a material for its purpose, not its color.** Its tint changes with the mode and accessibility settings, so don't count on a particular shade.

## Pitfalls

- **A material is a `ShapeStyle`.** Use it anywhere a color goes: `.background(.thinMaterial)`, `.fill`, or `.presentationBackground` on a sheet.
- **It's CSS `backdrop-filter: blur()` with extras.** It also adapts to light and dark mode and adds a tint so text stays readable.
- **For controls and bars, use Liquid Glass (`liquid-glass`).** Since iOS 26, materials are for backgrounds inside your content.

## Key APIs

`.background(.regularMaterial)`, `.background(_:in:)`, `.ultraThinMaterial`, `.ultraThickMaterial`, `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`, `.presentationBackground(_:)`

## Variants

### Caption over a photo

Put `.ultraThinMaterial` behind a caption so it stays readable on any image, light or dark.

```swift
Image("photo")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .frame(height: 220)
    .overlay(alignment: .bottom) {
        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Text("Photo of the Day").font(.headline)
            Text("Readable on any image").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
        .padding()
        .background(.ultraThinMaterial)
    }
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 20))
```

### Floating badge

Use `.background(.thinMaterial, in: .capsule)` for counts, tags, and status that sit above content.

```swift
Label("3 new", systemImage: "bell.fill")
    .font(.subheadline.weight(.semibold))
    .padding(.horizontal, 14)
    .padding(.vertical, 8)
    .background(.thinMaterial, in: .capsule)
```

## On macOS

Liquid Glass for controls that float above content, standard materials within it.

### Rules

- **Keep Liquid Glass out of the content.** Glass marks the layer of controls and navigation that floats above your content. Glass cards and backgrounds inside the content blur that line; use a standard material there instead.
- **Use glass sparingly on your own controls.** Glass draws attention to what's beneath it. Save it for the few custom controls that matter most, like the playback controls over a video.
- **Use clear glass only over rich media.** The clear variant lets photos and video show through. Over bright content, add a dark layer at about 35% opacity behind it so labels stay readable.
- **Use vibrant colors on materials.** Hierarchical styles like `.secondary` blend with a material for contrast. A fixed color, like `.gray`, turns that blending off.

### Pitfalls

- **Standard components already use Liquid Glass.** Toolbars, sidebars, and system controls pick it up on their own in macOS 26. Reach for `.glassEffect` only for your own controls.
- **A material blurs your app, not the desktop.** SwiftUI's materials blur the content inside your window, not what's behind it on screen.

### Key APIs

`.glassEffect(_:in:)`, `GlassEffectContainer`, `.buttonStyle(.glass)`, `.buttonStyle(.glassProminent)`, `.glassEffect(.clear)`, `\.accessibilityReduceTransparency`

### Variants

#### Glass buttons over media

Use `.buttonStyle(.glass)` for controls that float over a photo or video, and wrap them in a `GlassEffectContainer`.

```swift
ZStack(alignment: .bottom) {
    Image("photo")
        .resizable()
        .scaledToFill()
    GlassEffectContainer {
        HStack {
            Button("Previous", systemImage: "backward.fill") { }
            Button("Play", systemImage: "play.fill") { }
            Button("Next", systemImage: "forward.fill") { }
        }
        .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
        .buttonStyle(.glass)
    }
    .padding()
}
.frame(width: 360, height: 200)
.clipped()
```

#### Clear glass with a dimming layer

Use `.glassEffect(.clear)` over bright media, with a dark layer behind it so the label stays readable.

```swift
ZStack {
    Image("photo")
        .resizable()
        .scaledToFill()
    Color.black.opacity(0.35)
    Label("Lisbon", systemImage: "mappin")
        .font(.title3)
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .padding(.horizontal, 16)
        .padding(.vertical, 10)
        .glassEffect(.clear)
}
.frame(width: 360, height: 200)
.clipped()
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Progress overlay, A material in the content (macOS), Respect Reduce Transparency (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/material.md

## Related

`liquid-glass`, `background-overlay`, `system-colors`, `visual-effects`, `color`, `dark-mode`, `contrast-transparency`, `toolbar`, `navigation-split-view`


<!-- topic: shapes -->
---
id: shapes
title: Shapes
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/shape.md
---

# Shapes

Rectangles, circles, capsules, and your own paths, ready to fill, stroke, or clip with.

Also called: border-radius, rounded corners, circle, svg, path, pill, div, canvas, draw, UIBezierPath.

## Contents

- Default code
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 24)
    .fill(.blue)
    .frame(width: 240, height: 180)
```

**Note:** A shape fills all the space it's offered, like a `div` at 100% width and height. Give it a size with `.frame`.

## Pitfalls

- **Use shape shorthands wherever a shape is expected.** `.rect(cornerRadius: 12)`, `.capsule`, and `.circle` work in `.clipShape`, `.background(_:in:)`, and `.contentShape`.
- **Corners are continuous by default.** Rounded rectangles use Apple's smooth corner curve, which looks softer than CSS `border-radius`.

## Key APIs

- `RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius:)`: A rectangle with rounded corners.
- `Circle()`, `Capsule()`: A circle, and a pill with fully round ends.
- `.fill(_:)`: Paints the inside with a color or gradient.
- `.strokeBorder(_:lineWidth:)`: Draws an outline inside the edge.
- `.clipShape(_:)`: Cuts any view to a shape.
- `.background(_:in:)`: Puts a shape-filled background behind a view.
- `.trim(from:to:)`: Draws only part of the outline, for rings.
- `Shape`: Your own shape: return a `Path` from `path(in:)`.

## Variants

### Shapes as backgrounds and clips

Usually a shape styles another view, through `.background(_:in:)`, `.clipShape`, or `.overlay`.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 12) {
    Text("Tag")
        .padding(.horizontal, 12)
        .padding(.vertical, 6)
        .background(.blue.opacity(0.15), in: .capsule)

    Image(systemName: "person.fill")
        .font(.title)
        .frame(width: 56, height: 56)
        .background(.orange.gradient)
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .clipShape(.circle)

    Text("Card")
        .padding()
        .overlay {
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
                .strokeBorder(.secondary, lineWidth: 1)
        }
}
```

**Important:** Use `.strokeBorder` for borders. `.stroke` centers the line on the edge, so half of it spills outside and can get clipped.

### Progress ring with trim

Use `.trim(from:to:)` to draw only part of a circle's outline, like a progress ring.

```swift
@State private var progress = 0.65

ZStack {
    Circle()
        .stroke(.fill.tertiary, lineWidth: 14)
    Circle()
        .trim(from: 0, to: progress)
        .stroke(.green, style: StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 14, lineCap: .round))
        .rotationEffect(.degrees(-90))
    Text(progress, format: .percent.precision(.fractionLength(0)))
        .font(.title2.bold())
}
.frame(width: 120, height: 120)
```

### Concentric corners

`ConcentricRectangle` takes its corner radius from its container, so nested corners line up.

```swift
VStack {
    Text("Inner content")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
        .background(.blue.opacity(0.2), in: ConcentricRectangle())
}
.padding(10)
.frame(width: 240, height: 140)
.background(.fill.tertiary)
.containerShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 32))
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 32))
```

**Note:** `ConcentricRectangle` is new in iOS 26. Use it for buttons and cards inside sheets and other rounded containers.

## Related

`clip-shape`, `gradients`, `background-overlay`, `frame`


<!-- topic: gradients -->
---
id: gradients
title: Gradients
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/gradient.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/color.md
---

# Gradients

Smooth blends between colors: in a line, outward from a point, around a circle, or across a mesh.

Also called: linear-gradient, radial-gradient, conic-gradient, background-image, mesh, fade, ombre, CAGradientLayer.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 24)
    .fill(
        LinearGradient(
            colors: [.orange, .pink, .purple],
            startPoint: .topLeading,
            endPoint: .bottomTrailing
        )
    )
    .frame(height: 220)
```

## Rules

- **Keep text readable on gradients.** Check contrast at the lightest part of the gradient, not the middle. Add a dark fade or pick deeper colors where text sits.
- **Check gradients in dark mode.** System colors shift between modes, and a gradient that glows on white can feel harsh on black.
- **Don't use a gradient as the only signal.** A green-to-red bar needs a number or a label too, since some people can't tell those colors apart.

## Pitfalls

- **Gradients are `ShapeStyle`s, like colors.** Pass one to `.fill`, `.background`, or `.foregroundStyle` to paint shapes, views, or text.
- **They map to CSS.** `LinearGradient` is `linear-gradient`, `RadialGradient` is `radial-gradient`, and `AngularGradient` is `conic-gradient`.
- **`MeshGradient` needs iOS 18.** It blends a grid of colors; animate its points with `TimelineView` for a living background.

## Key APIs

- `Color.blue.gradient`: A subtle gradient the system tunes for you.
- `LinearGradient`: Blends colors along a line between two points.
- `RadialGradient`: Blends outward from a center point.
- `AngularGradient`: Blends around a center, like a color wheel.
- `MeshGradient`: Blends a grid of colors (iOS 18).
- `Gradient.Stop(color:location:)`: Places a color at an exact spot, from 0 to 1.

## Variants

### Fade for readable text

Lay a clear-to-black `LinearGradient` over a photo so white text reads on any image.

```swift
Image("photo")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .frame(height: 220)
    .overlay {
        LinearGradient(colors: [.clear, .black.opacity(0.7)],
                       startPoint: .center, endPoint: .bottom)
    }
    .overlay(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
        Text("Weekend Getaways")
            .font(.title2.bold())
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .padding()
    }
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 20))
```

**Note:** Designers call this a scrim. Start it near the middle so the top of the photo stays bright.

### Icon tile with the shorthand

Use `Color.pink.gradient` for a quick, subtle gradient, like the icons in Settings.

```swift
let icons: [(String, Color)] = [("heart.fill", .pink), ("bell.fill", .red), ("gearshape.fill", .gray)]

HStack(spacing: 16) {
    ForEach(icons, id: \.0) { symbol, color in
        Image(systemName: symbol)
            .font(.title2)
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .frame(width: 56, height: 56)
            .background(color.gradient, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 14))
    }
}
```

### Gradient text

Pass a gradient to `.foregroundStyle` to paint text and SF Symbols.

```swift
Text("Hello, gradients")
    .font(.largeTitle.bold())
    .foregroundStyle(
        LinearGradient(colors: [.orange, .pink, .purple],
                       startPoint: .leading, endPoint: .trailing)
    )
```

### Hard stops

Put two `Gradient.Stop`s at the same location to get a sharp edge instead of a blend.

```swift
Capsule()
    .fill(LinearGradient(
        stops: [
            .init(color: .green, location: 0),
            .init(color: .green, location: 0.6),
            .init(color: .gray.opacity(0.3), location: 0.6),
            .init(color: .gray.opacity(0.3), location: 1),
        ],
        startPoint: .leading, endPoint: .trailing
    ))
    .frame(height: 16)
```

## Related

`system-colors`, `shapes`, `foreground-style`, `materials`


<!-- topic: sf-symbols -->
---
id: sf-symbols
title: SF Symbols
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/image/init(systemname:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sf-symbols.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# SF Symbols

Thousands of built-in icons that match the system font and scale with text.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Image(systemName: "heart.fill")
    .font(.title)
    .foregroundStyle(.pink)

Label("Favorites", systemImage: "heart.fill")
```

**Important:** Size a symbol with `.font`, not `.resizable()` and `.frame`. That keeps it aligned with text and at the right weight.

## Rules

- **Let symbols match the text beside them.** Symbols come in the same weights as San Francisco. Set the size and weight with `.font` so the icon and its label look like one piece.
- **Use variable color for change, not depth.** A variable value shows a level that changes over time, like signal or volume. To give a symbol depth, use `.hierarchical` instead.
- **Use a symbol for its usual meaning.** People know `trash` means delete and `square.and.arrow.up` means share. Reusing them for something else confuses people.
- **Check the rendering mode at small sizes.** Fine layers in `.multicolor` or `.palette` can blur together in a toolbar. Use `.monochrome` if details get lost.

## Pitfalls

- **Find names in the SF Symbols app.** It's free for Mac and shows each symbol's minimum iOS version. An unknown name draws nothing and logs a warning.
- **To animate a symbol, see Symbol Effects (`symbol-effects`).** Bounce, pulse, and replace work on any symbol.

## Key APIs

`Image(systemName:)`, `Label(_:systemImage:)`, `.font(_:)`, `.imageScale(_:)`, `.symbolRenderingMode(_:)`, `.symbolVariant(_:)`, `Image(systemName:variableValue:)`

## Variants

### Symbols next to text

Use `Label` to pair a symbol with text, or put an `Image` right inside a `Text`.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
    Label("Settings", systemImage: "gearshape.fill")
    Label("Downloads", systemImage: "arrow.down.circle")
        .font(.title2.bold())
    Text("Rated \(Image(systemName: "star.fill")) 4.8")
        .foregroundStyle(.orange)
}
```

**Note:** An `Image` inside `Text` flows and wraps like a word, which suits ratings and inline hints.

### Variants

`.symbolVariant` switches every symbol inside a view to its filled, circled, or slashed version.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 24) {
    Image(systemName: "bell")
    Image(systemName: "bell").symbolVariant(.fill)
    Image(systemName: "bell").symbolVariant(.circle)
    Image(systemName: "bell").symbolVariant(.slash)
}
.font(.largeTitle)
```

**Note:** Tab bars apply `.fill` for you, so give a `Tab` the outline name and iOS picks the right one.

## On macOS

Icons drawn to match the system font, for toolbars, sidebars, and menus.

### Rules

- **Let the symbol match the text.** Each symbol weight matches a weight of the system font. Leave the weight to the font, so a symbol and its label look like one piece.
- **Use plain symbols in the toolbar.** Toolbar items already get a shape and hover and selection states from the system. Symbols with a circle or square around them add a second border.
- **In a menu, give every item in a group an icon or none.** Icons help people find common actions faster, but a group where only some items have one looks unbalanced. Skip the icon if no symbol clearly fits.
- **Use the standard symbol for a common action.** Share is `square.and.arrow.up`, Delete is `trash`, and Search is `magnifyingglass` everywhere on the Mac. A different symbol for the same action makes people stop and think.
- **Check the rendering mode at the size you use.** Fine layers that look good large can blur together small or on a busy background. Try another mode if the details get lost.

### Pitfalls

- **Check which system version a symbol needs.** New symbols and features each year don't exist on older releases. The SF Symbols app shows each symbol's availability.
- **Symbols aren't for app icons or logos.** Apple's terms for SF Symbols don't allow them, or look-alikes, in app icons, logos, or other trademarks.

### Key APIs

`.symbolVariant(.fill)`, `.symbolEffect(_:value:)`

### Variants

#### A symbol with its label

Use `Label` so SwiftUI can show the symbol, the title, or both, as a sidebar, toolbar, or menu expects.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
    Label("Downloads", systemImage: "arrow.down.circle")
    Label("Shared", systemImage: "person.2")
    Label("Trash", systemImage: "trash")
}
```

#### Adjust emphasis with the scale

`.imageScale(_:)` makes a symbol smaller or larger than its text without changing the weight they share.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 24) {
    Label("Small", systemImage: "bell")
        .imageScale(.small)
    Label("Medium", systemImage: "bell")
        .imageScale(.medium)
    Label("Large", systemImage: "bell")
        .imageScale(.large)
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Add depth with a rendering mode (macOS), Show a level with variable color (macOS), Confirm an action with an animation (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/image/init(systemname:).md

## Related

`image`, `label`, `symbol-effects`, `typography`, `image-symbols`, `toolbar`, `menu`, `app-icons`, `motion`


<!-- topic: charts -->
---
id: charts
title: Swift Charts
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/charts.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/charts.md
---

# Swift Charts

Bar, line, area, point, and pie charts built from your data in a few lines.

Also called: graph, chart.js, recharts, d3, plot, pie chart, donut, bar chart, line graph, visualization.

## Contents

- Use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `Chart` comes from the Swift Charts framework.
- You loop over your data like `ForEach` and describe each value as a *mark*, such as a bar, line, or point.
- The chart draws the axes, scales, and legend for you.
- Use it for real data, like sales or steps over time.
- For a single value against a range, use `Gauge` or `ProgressView` instead.

## Default code

```swift
Chart(sales) { sale in
    BarMark(
        x: .value("Month", sale.month),
        y: .value("Sales", sale.amount)
    )
}
.frame(height: 240)
```

**Important:** Add `import Charts` at the top of the file. Your data needs to be `Identifiable`, or pass `id:` like in `ForEach`.

## Built from

Chart(sales)
├── BarMark, LineMark, …
│   └── .foregroundStyle(by:)
├── RuleMark
├── .chartYScale(domain:)
└── .chartXSelection(value:)

## Rules

- **Start bar charts at zero.** People compare bar heights. Cutting off the bottom makes small differences look huge.
- **Say what the chart shows.** A short title with the main takeaway helps everyone, and VoiceOver users most of all, before they read the details.
- **Don't hide key numbers behind a touch.** Touching to inspect is a bonus. Show the most important value, like today's total, without any interaction.
- **Make charts accessible.** Give every `.value` a clear name, and add `.accessibilityLabel` to marks when the default reading isn't enough.

## Pitfalls

- **Axes, gridlines, and the legend are automatic.** Change them only when you need to, with `.chartXAxis`, `.chartYAxis`, and `.chartLegend`.
- **Pie and donut charts need iOS 17.** Use `SectorMark` with `innerRadius: .ratio(0.6)` for a donut.

## Key APIs

- `Chart(_:content:)`: Loops over your data and draws marks.
- `BarMark(x:y:)`: A bar for each value. Swap x and y for horizontal bars.
- `LineMark(x:y:)`: Connects values with a line, for trends over time.
- `.value(_:_:)`: Names a value for the axis and VoiceOver.
- `.foregroundStyle(by:)`: Splits data into colored series, with a legend.
- `RuleMark(y:)`: A reference line, like a goal or average.
- `.chartYScale(domain:)`: Sets the axis range, like `0...100`.
- `.chartXSelection(value:)`: Binds the value under the finger (iOS 17).

## Variants

### Trend over time

Plot a `Date` on the x-axis with `LineMark`, and pass `unit: .day` so values snap to days.

```swift
struct DaySteps: Identifiable {
    let date: Date
    let count: Int
    var id: Date { date }
}

Chart(steps) { day in
    LineMark(
        x: .value("Day", day.date, unit: .day),
        y: .value("Steps", day.count)
    )
    .interpolationMethod(.catmullRom)
    .symbol(.circle)
}
.frame(height: 200)
```

**Note:** Without `unit:`, dates plot as exact moments, and axis labels may show times instead of days.

### Highlight a value with a rule

Add a `RuleMark` to draw a reference line, like a goal or average, across the bars.

```swift
Chart {
    ForEach(sales) { sale in
        BarMark(
            x: .value("Month", sale.month),
            y: .value("Sales", sale.amount)
        )
        .foregroundStyle(sale.amount >= 50 ? Color.green : Color.gray.opacity(0.5))
    }
    RuleMark(y: .value("Goal", 50))
        .lineStyle(StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 2, dash: [5, 4]))
        .annotation(position: .top, alignment: .leading) {
            Text("Goal").font(.caption.bold())
        }
}
.frame(height: 200)
```

### Touch to inspect

`.chartXSelection(value:)` binds the value under the finger. Touch and drag across the bars.

```swift
@State private var selectedMonth: String?

Chart(sales) { sale in
    BarMark(
        x: .value("Month", sale.month),
        y: .value("Sales", sale.amount)
    )
    .foregroundStyle(selectedMonth == nil || selectedMonth == sale.month
                     ? Color.blue : Color.blue.opacity(0.3))
}
.chartXSelection(value: $selectedMonth)
.frame(height: 200)
```

**Note:** The binding goes back to `nil` when the finger lifts. Selection needs iOS 17.

### Sparkline

Hide both axes with `.chartXAxis(.hidden)` for a tiny trend line in a row or stat card.

```swift
HStack {
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Revenue").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        Text("$74k").font(.title.bold())
    }
    Chart(sales) { sale in
        AreaMark(x: .value("Month", sale.month), y: .value("Sales", sale.amount))
            .foregroundStyle(.green.opacity(0.2).gradient)
        LineMark(x: .value("Month", sale.month), y: .value("Sales", sale.amount))
            .foregroundStyle(.green)
    }
    .chartXAxis(.hidden)
    .chartYAxis(.hidden)
    .frame(width: 120, height: 50)
}
```

## Related

`gradients`, `system-colors`, `gauge`, `progress-view`


<!-- topic: map -->
---
id: map
title: Map
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/mapkit/map.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/maps.md
---

# Map

An interactive Apple Map with markers, custom pins, styles, and a camera you control.

Also called: google maps, mapbox, leaflet, location, pin, marker, MKMapView, satellite, directions, geo.

## Contents

- Use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `Map` shows an interactive Apple Map.
- You put content inside it, like `Marker`, `Annotation`, and `MapPolyline`, and a camera position binding controls what part of the world it shows.
- It comes from MapKit and works like a SwiftUI view: size it with `.frame`, style it with `.mapStyle`, and add controls with `.mapControls`.

## Default code

```swift
@State private var position: MapCameraPosition = .automatic

let bridge = CLLocationCoordinate2D(latitude: 37.8199, longitude: -122.4783)

Map(position: $position) {
    Marker("Golden Gate Bridge", systemImage: "road.lanes", coordinate: bridge)
        .tint(.orange)
}
.mapStyle(.standard(elevation: .realistic))
```

**Important:** Add `import MapKit`. Older tutorials use `Map(coordinateRegion:)`, which is deprecated since iOS 17.

## Built from

Map(position: $position)
├── Marker / Annotation
├── MapPolyline
├── .mapStyle(.standard)
└── .mapControls
    └── MapCompass()

## Rules

- **Keep maps interactive.** People expect to pan and zoom any map. If a small map can't move, open a full map when they tap it.
- **Mute the map when your pins matter most.** The muted style drops the saturation, so your markers and overlays stand out.
- **Tint markers to match your app.** Use `.tint` and a symbol that fits the place, so pins feel part of your design and are easy to tell apart.
- **Don't cover the Apple logo and legal link for long.** They sit in the map's corner. Leave padding around them, and keep cards and controls from hiding them all the time.

## Pitfalls

- **Showing the person's location needs permission.** Add `NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription` to Info.plist, ask with `CLLocationManager`, then add `UserAnnotation()` to the map.
- **No API key needed.** Map tiles load over the network, so the map stays blank until they arrive.

## Key APIs

- `Map(position:selection:)`: A map with a camera binding and optional selection.
- `MapCameraPosition`: What the map shows: `.automatic`, `.region`, `.camera`, or `.item`.
- `Marker(_:systemImage:coordinate:)`: The standard balloon pin.
- `Annotation(_:coordinate:)`: Any SwiftUI view, pinned to a spot.
- `MapPolyline(coordinates:)`: A line through coordinates, like a route.
- `.mapStyle(_:)`: `.standard`, `.imagery` (satellite), or `.hybrid`.
- `.mapControls { }`: Compass, scale, and location buttons.
- `UserAnnotation()`: The person's location, once they allow it.

## Variants

### Selectable markers

Pass a `selection` binding and `.tag` each marker. Tapping a pin selects and enlarges it.

```swift
struct Landmark: Identifiable {
    let name: String
    let coordinate: CLLocationCoordinate2D
    var id: String { name }
}

let landmarks = [
    Landmark(name: "Eiffel Tower", coordinate: .init(latitude: 48.8584, longitude: 2.2945)),
    Landmark(name: "Louvre", coordinate: .init(latitude: 48.8606, longitude: 2.3376)),
    Landmark(name: "Notre-Dame", coordinate: .init(latitude: 48.8530, longitude: 2.3499)),
]

@State private var selection: String?
@State private var position: MapCameraPosition = .camera(
    MapCamera(centerCoordinate: .init(latitude: 48.857, longitude: 2.322), distance: 9000)
)

VStack {
    Map(position: $position, selection: $selection) {
        ForEach(landmarks) { landmark in
            Marker(landmark.name, coordinate: landmark.coordinate)
                .tag(landmark.name)
        }
    }
    .frame(height: 260)
    Text(selection ?? "Tap a pin")
        .font(.headline)
}
```

### Draw a route

`MapPolyline` connects coordinates with a line, like a walking route between two flags.

```swift
let route = [
    CLLocationCoordinate2D(latitude: 37.8199, longitude: -122.4783),
    CLLocationCoordinate2D(latitude: 37.8060, longitude: -122.4660),
    CLLocationCoordinate2D(latitude: 37.8029, longitude: -122.4484),
    CLLocationCoordinate2D(latitude: 37.8080, longitude: -122.4177),
]

Map {
    MapPolyline(coordinates: route)
        .stroke(.blue, style: StrokeStyle(lineWidth: 5, lineCap: .round, lineJoin: .round))
    Marker("Start", systemImage: "flag.fill", coordinate: route[0])
        .tint(.green)
    Marker("End", systemImage: "flag.checkered", coordinate: route[route.count - 1])
        .tint(.red)
}
.frame(height: 240)
```

**Note:** For real driving directions, get a route from `MKDirections` and pass `MapPolyline(route.polyline)`.

### A small, non-interactive map

Pass `interactionModes: []` for an address preview, so the page scrolls past the map.

```swift
let cafe = CLLocationCoordinate2D(latitude: 48.8606, longitude: 2.3376)

Map(initialPosition: .camera(MapCamera(centerCoordinate: cafe, distance: 1200)),
    interactionModes: []) {
    Marker("Café", systemImage: "cup.and.saucer.fill", coordinate: cafe)
        .tint(.brown)
}
.frame(height: 140)
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 16))
```

**Note:** People still expect a map to respond. Open a full map, or Apple Maps, when they tap it.

## Related

`sheet`, `safe-area`, `sf-symbols`, `charts`


<!-- topic: login-form -->
---
id: login-form
title: Login Screen
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 26.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/signinwithapplebutton.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sign-in-with-apple.md
---

# Login Screen

An email and password sign-in screen with AutoFill, focus handling, and Sign in with Apple.

## Rules

- **Make Sign in with Apple as big as your other sign-in buttons.** It saves people from typing a password, so it deserves equal weight. A smaller button reads as an afterthought.
- **Let people look around before you ask them to sign in.** A sign-in wall on first launch makes many people quit. Ask when an account unlocks something they want, and say what it is.
- **Use a secure field for the password, and never prefill it.** Hidden characters protect people in public places. An empty field means they authenticate themselves, by typing or with a saved password.

## Pitfalls

- **Set `.textContentType` on both fields.** With `.emailAddress` and `.password`, iOS offers saved passwords and AutoFill, the biggest usability win on a login screen.
- **Add the Sign in with Apple capability to your app target.** Without it, `SignInWithAppleButton` still draws, but every request fails.
- **Put the form in a `ScrollView`.** The keyboard covers half of a small phone, and scrolling keeps every field and button reachable.

**Note:** The fields are a TextField (`text-field`) and a SecureField (`secure-field`) that swap when you tap the eye. @FocusState (`focus-state`) plus `.onSubmit` moves to the password on Return, like `tabindex` on the web.

**Note:** **Sign In** is a Button (`button`) that stays disabled until the form is valid and shows a ProgressView (`progress-view`) while it works, so nobody taps twice. Sign in with Apple is the real `SignInWithAppleButton` from AuthenticationServices.

**Note:** **Why iOS 26?** Only the Liquid Glass (`liquid-glass`) button styles need it. Change `.glassProminent` to `.borderedProminent` and `.glass` to `.bordered`, and the screen runs on iOS 17.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Code. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/signinwithapplebutton.md

## Related

`text-field`, `secure-field`, `focus-state`, `button`


<!-- topic: settings-screen -->
---
id: settings-screen
title: Settings Screen
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/form.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/settings.md
---

# Settings Screen

A grouped settings form with toggles, a picker, a drill-down row, and sign-out confirmation.

## Rules

- **Keep row titles short and explain in the footer.** Short titles scan quickly down the screen, and one footer sentence gives the detail without wrapping every row.
- **Pick defaults that suit most people.** Every setting is a decision someone has to make. Good defaults let most people use the app without ever opening Settings.
- **Offer few settings, and keep task options on the task's screen.** A long settings list is hard to search. Controls like sort order or filters belong on the screen they change, where people can see the result.
- **Put Sign Out in its own section at the bottom.** Keeping it apart from everyday rows prevents accidental taps, and a `confirmationDialog` gives people a second chance.

## Pitfalls

- **Save preferences with `@AppStorage`.** Swap each `@State` for `@AppStorage("key")` and the choice survives relaunches, much like `localStorage` on the web.
- **Use `.pickerStyle(.navigationLink)` for long lists.** A `Picker` in a `Form` opens a menu by default; the navigation-link style pushes a full list instead.

**Note:** The screen is one Form (`form`) in a NavigationStack (`navigation-stack`), which gives it the Settings app look. Each row type, from Toggle (`toggle`) and Picker (`picker`) to `NavigationLink` and `LabeledContent`, styles itself to match.

**Note:** The colored icons are a Label (`label`) with a custom icon: an SF Symbol on a rounded, gradient square. Sign Out asks first with a confirmation dialog (`confirmation-dialog`).

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Code. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/form.md

## Related

`form`, `toggle`, `picker`, `confirmation-dialog`


<!-- topic: inbox-list -->
---
id: inbox-list
title: Inbox List
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/swipeactions(edge:allowsfullswipe:content:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables.md
---

# Inbox List

A mail-style list with unread dots, swipe actions, a filter menu, and search.

## Rules

- **Keep row text short, and let the detail view hold the rest.** Rows of the same height are quick to scan. Cap the preview with `.lineLimit(2)` and show the full message when the row opens.
- **Put gentle swipe actions on the leading edge.** Mark as Read on the left and Archive or Delete on the right is the layout people know from Mail, so destructive actions are never a stray swipe away.
- **Use the plain list style for a feed.** Edge-to-edge rows suit a long run of similar items like messages. Save the grouped, inset style for settings-like content.

## Pitfalls

- **A destructive swipe doesn't delete your data.** `Button(role: .destructive)` turns red and slides the row away on a full swipe, but you still remove the item from your array.
- **Make your model `Identifiable`.** With a stable `id`, SwiftUI animates inserts and deletes instead of redrawing the whole list.

**Note:** A plain List (`list`) of `NavigationLink` rows inside a NavigationStack (`navigation-stack`). Each row has its own swipe actions (`swipe-actions`), one set per edge, not one set on the `List`.

**Note:** .searchable (`searchable`) adds the search field, and a Menu (`menu`) in the `toolbar` holds the Unread Only toggle. Both filter the array `ForEach` shows, and `ContentUnavailableView.search` appears when nothing matches.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Code. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/swipeactions(edge:allowsfullswipe:content:).md

## Related

`list`, `swipe-actions`, `searchable`, `navigation-stack`


<!-- topic: empty-state -->
---
id: empty-state
title: Empty States
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/contentunavailableview.md
---

# Empty States

What to show when a screen has no content, no search results, or an error.

Also called: empty view, no results, zero state, placeholder, blank slate, no data, error screen, 404, ContentUnavailableView.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Variants
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Use `ContentUnavailableView` instead of building your own.** It replaces the hand-made icon, title, and subtitle stack, with the right fonts, colors, spacing, and Dynamic Type.
- **Say why it's empty and offer one next step.** A short reason plus one action, like Browse or Try Again, beats a blank screen. Don't put anything there people need later, since it disappears once content arrives.

**Note:** One `ContentUnavailableView` sits in an `.overlay` on a List (`list`). When the list is empty it shows the first-run message with a Button (`button`); when search (`searchable`) finds nothing it switches to `ContentUnavailableView.search`.

**Important:** Overlay the empty state on the `List` instead of swapping the list out. Otherwise the search field and toolbar disappear along with it.

## Variants

### Code

```swift
import SwiftUI

struct FavoritesScreen: View {
    @State private var favorites: [String] = []
    @State private var searchText = ""

    private let recipes = [
        "Lemon Herb Chicken", "Miso Ramen", "Shakshuka",
        "Margherita Pizza", "Thai Green Curry", "Banana Bread",
    ]

    private var results: [String] {
        searchText.isEmpty ? favorites : favorites.filter { $0.localizedStandardContains(searchText) }
    }

    var body: some View {
        List {
            ForEach(results, id: \.self) { recipe in
                Label(recipe, systemImage: "heart.fill")
                    .symbolRenderingMode(.multicolor)
            }
            .onDelete { offsets in
                let removed = offsets.map { results[$0] }
                favorites.removeAll { removed.contains($0) }
            }
        }
        .navigationTitle("Favorites")
        .searchable(text: $searchText, prompt: "Search favorites")
        .overlay {
            if favorites.isEmpty {
                ContentUnavailableView {
                    Label("No Favorites Yet", systemImage: "heart")
                } description: {
                    Text("Tap the heart on any recipe to save it here for later.")
                } actions: {
                    Button("Browse Recipes") {
                        withAnimation { favorites = recipes }
                    }
                    .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
                }
            } else if results.isEmpty {
                ContentUnavailableView.search(text: searchText)
            }
        }
        .toolbar {
            if !favorites.isEmpty {
                Button("Clear") {
                    withAnimation { favorites = [] }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

#Preview {
    NavigationStack {
        FavoritesScreen()
    }
}
```

### Simple

Give `ContentUnavailableView` a title, a `systemImage`, and a one-line `description` of what goes here.

```swift
ContentUnavailableView(
    "No Photos",
    systemImage: "photo.on.rectangle",
    description: Text("Photos you take will appear here.")
)
```

### No search results

Pass the search text to `.search(text:)` and it writes the “No Results for …” message for you.

```swift
@State private var searchText = "zebra"

ContentUnavailableView.search(text: searchText)
```

### Error with a retry

Use the closure form with `actions:` to add a button, such as Try Again after an error.

```swift
ContentUnavailableView {
    Label("You're Offline", systemImage: "wifi.slash")
} description: {
    Text("Check your connection and try again.")
} actions: {
    Button("Try Again") {
        // reload
    }
    .buttonStyle(.bordered)
}
```

## Related

`list`, `searchable`, `sf-symbols`, `button`


<!-- topic: onboarding -->
---
id: onboarding
title: Onboarding
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 26.0+, macOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/pagetabviewstyle.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/onboarding.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Onboarding

A paged welcome flow with Continue and Skip buttons that ends with Get Started.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules
