- **Keep it short, and always let people skip.** Three or four pages is plenty. People who would rather explore on their own should get into the app in one tap.
- **Teach by doing, not by reading.** People remember a feature they tried better than a slide that described it. Consider tips shown in context, with `TipKit`, instead of more pages.
- **Ask for permissions when the reason is clear.** If the app can't work without, say, notifications, ask during onboarding and explain why. Otherwise wait until people first use the feature.

## Pitfalls

- **Show onboarding only once.** Save completion with `@AppStorage("hasOnboarded")` and skip the flow when it's `true`. The demo uses `@State` so you can replay it.
- **Keep the page dots visible on light backgrounds.** `.indexViewStyle(.page(backgroundDisplayMode: .always))` draws a capsule behind them.

**Note:** The pager is a TabView (`tab-view`) with `.tabViewStyle(.page)`. Each page has a `.tag`, and Continue changes the bound `selection` inside `withAnimation` so it slides like a swipe.

**Note:** Each page's symbol bounces in with a symbol effect (`symbol-effects`), and the finished state fades in with a transition (`transitions`). Continue is a Button (`button`) whose title changes on the last page.

**Note:** **Why iOS 26?** Only `.buttonStyle(.glassProminent)` needs it. Change it to `.borderedProminent` and the screen runs on iOS 17.

## On macOS

Open straight into the app, and teach in context instead of up front.

### Rules

- **Open straight into the app.** People want to start right away. Skip the splash screen, or keep it brief enough to take in at a glance.
- **Teach by doing.** People remember what they try more than what they read. Let them safely perform the task you're teaching.
- **Prefer tips in context to one long tour.** A tip next to the feature, when it's relevant, is easier to absorb than a list of everything up front.
- **Make a tutorial optional, and easy to find later.** If people skip it, don't show it on every launch. Put it somewhere like the Help menu.
- **Put off setup.** Start with sensible defaults. Ask for permission when someone first uses the feature that needs it, and for ratings after they've used the app a while.
- **Leave legal text to the App Store.** The store shows agreements and disclaimers before people download. Don't open the app with them.

### Pitfalls

- **The Mac doesn't use launch screens.** iPhone and iPad apps show one while they start. A Mac app just opens its windows, so make that fast.
- **Tips are for features people haven't found.** Apple's TipKit docs say to use them sparingly, not to walk people through the app or to advertise.

### Key APIs

`.defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)`, `.restorationBehavior(.disabled)`, `ContentUnavailableView`, `TipView`, `Tips.configure()`

### Variants

#### A welcome window when nothing is restored

A `Window` with `.defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)` opens at launch when there are no document windows to bring back.

```swift
@main
struct ScribbleApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        DocumentGroup(newDocument: NoteDocument()) { file in
            NoteEditor(document: file.$document)
        }

        Window("Welcome to Scribble", id: "welcome") {
            WelcomeView()
        }
        .defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)
        .restorationBehavior(.disabled)
    }
}
```

**Note:** `.restorationBehavior(.disabled)` keeps the welcome window from reopening on its own along with people's documents.

#### An empty state that shows the way

Use `ContentUnavailableView` for the first, empty window: say what goes here and offer the first step.

```swift
ContentUnavailableView {
    Label("No Notes Yet", systemImage: "note.text")
} description: {
    Text("Notes you write appear here.")
} actions: {
    Button("New Note") { }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
```

#### A tip beside the feature

Define a `Tip`, configure TipKit once at launch, and place a `TipView` next to what it explains.

```swift
import TipKit

struct PinTip: Tip {
    var title: Text { Text("Pin important notes") }
    var message: Text? { Text("Pinned notes stay at the top of the list.") }
    var image: Image? { Image(systemName: "pin") }
}

@main
struct NotesApp: App {
    init() {
        try? Tips.configure()
    }

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { NotesView() }
    }
}

struct NotesView: View {
    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            TipView(PinTip(), arrowEdge: .bottom)
            Button("Pin", systemImage: "pin") { }
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The preview draws the tip. This catalog doesn't set up TipKit, so a real `TipView` wouldn't appear here.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Code. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/pagetabviewstyle.md

## Related

`tab-view`, `symbol-effects`, `button`, `transitions`, `welcome-window`, `empty-states`, `windows-tabs`, `settings-pattern`, `privacy-permissions`


<!-- topic: profile -->
---
id: profile
title: Profile Screen
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 26.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/lazyvgrid.md
---

# Profile Screen

A social profile with an avatar, stats, Follow and Message buttons, and a photo grid.

## Pitfalls

- **`AsyncImage` doesn't cache.** Photos can download again when they scroll back into view. That's fine for a demo; real apps usually add a caching image loader.
- **Roll numbers with `.contentTransition(.numericText(value:))`.** Change the count inside `withAnimation` and the digits roll like an odometer.

**Note:** The photos are AsyncImage (`async-image`) views with placeholders, laid out in a three-column LazyVGrid (`lazy-grids`) under a segmented Picker (`picker`).

**Important:** Square tiles need a trick. Put `Color.clear.aspectRatio(1, contentMode: .fit)` in each cell, draw the image in an `.overlay`, then `.clipped()`, or wide photos stretch the grid.

**Note:** The follower count uses a numeric content transition (`content-transition`). The toolbar Menu (`menu`) holds a ShareLink (`share-link`) and a destructive Block action.

**Note:** **Why iOS 26?** Only the Liquid Glass button styles need it. Change `.glassProminent` to `.borderedProminent` and `.glass` to `.bordered`, and the screen runs on iOS 17.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Code. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/lazyvgrid.md

## Related

`lazy-grids`, `async-image`, `picker`, `content-transition`


<!-- topic: detail-screen -->
---
id: detail-screen
title: Detail Screen
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 26.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/glasseffect(_:in:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toolbars.md
---

# Detail Screen

A listing page with a full-bleed hero, a glass toolbar, and a floating Reserve bar.

## Rules

- **Keep the toolbar to a few actions.** Each extra button makes the others harder to find and tap. Move rarely used actions into a More menu.
- **Use plain system symbols for toolbar buttons.** Familiar symbols like `heart` and `square.and.arrow.up` read at a glance, and the glass already gives each one a container, so skip the outlined `.circle` versions.
- **Use the standard Back button.** People know what the system chevron does. A custom back button or a text label that says Back makes them stop and check.

## Pitfalls

- **`.safeAreaInset(edge: .bottom)` pins a bar and makes room for it.** The scroll content ends above the bar instead of hiding behind it, like a fixed footer plus matching padding on the web.
- **Use `.glassEffect()` only on floating controls.** Keep it off the content itself; glass layered on glass looks muddy.

**Note:** The hero is an AsyncImage (`async-image`) that runs under the navigation bar thanks to `.ignoresSafeArea(edges: .top)` (see safe area (`safe-area`)). In iOS 26 the bar is transparent and its buttons float on Liquid Glass (`liquid-glass`).

**Note:** The heart and share buttons sit in the `toolbar`, and `ToolbarSpacer(.fixed)` splits them into separate glass groups.

**Note:** The price bar is a `.safeAreaInset` with `.glassEffect`. **Reserve** presents a `sheet` with a DatePicker (`date-picker`) and a Stepper (`stepper`) at a medium detent.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Code. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/glasseffect(_:in:).md

## Related

`liquid-glass`, `toolbar`, `sheet`, `async-image`


<!-- topic: dark-mode -->
---
id: dark-mode
title: Dark Mode
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/supporting-dark-mode-in-your-interface.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/dark-mode.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Dark Mode

Use colors that adapt, so your app looks right in light and dark.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules

- **Use colors that adapt.** System styles like `.primary` and `.secondary` switch with the appearance. A fixed value like `.black` stays black, even on a black background.
- **Follow the system setting.** Skip an in-app Light / Dark switch. People already chose in Settings, and an app that ignores it can look broken.
- **Let sheets and popovers lift.** In dark mode, iOS gives views in front a slightly lighter, elevated background. Use the system backgrounds so a sheet separates from the screen behind it.
- **Tone down bright images.** A photo with a white background glows on a dark screen. Darken it slightly in dark mode.
- **Check contrast in both modes.** Text needs at least 4.5:1 contrast with its background, and Apple suggests aiming for 7:1 with custom colors in small text. A gray that works on white often fails on black.

## Pitfalls

- **Dark isn't light turned upside down.** Apple's dark palette uses dimmer backgrounds and brighter foregrounds, and many colors aren't simple inversions. Pick each dark value on purpose.
- **Leave people's own colors alone.** If someone picks a color for their content, like ink in a drawing, keep it in both modes. Adaptive colors are for your app's chrome.

## Guide

Many people run their iPhone in dark mode, and some let it switch automatically through the day, even while your app is open. If you build with **system colors and styles**, most of your app adapts for free. The work is in the colors, images, and backgrounds you pick yourself.

### Test both appearances

Check every screen in light and dark before you ship:

```swift
#Preview("Light") { ContentView() }
#Preview("Dark") {
    ContentView()
        .preferredColorScheme(.dark)
}
```

## Key APIs

`.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`, `Color("Brand")`, `\.colorScheme`, `.preferredColorScheme(_:)`, `\.colorSchemeContrast`

## Variants

### Use semantic styles

Use `.primary`, `.secondary`, and the system backgrounds instead of fixed colors, and dark mode comes for free.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 12) {
    Image(systemName: "figure.run")
        .foregroundStyle(.tint)
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Morning Run")
            .foregroundStyle(.primary)
        Text("5.2 km")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
.padding()
.background(Color(.secondarySystemBackground),
            in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

### Add your own color with a dark variant

Add a Color Set to your asset catalog with a light and a dark value, then use it by name.

```swift
// Brand: a Color Set with a Dark variant
Text("Pro")
    .font(.caption.bold())
    .padding(.horizontal, 10)
    .padding(.vertical, 4)
    .foregroundStyle(.white)
    .background(Color("Brand"), in: .capsule)
```

**Note:** The color switches on its own: no `if` in your view. Pick a brighter dark value so it still stands out on a dark background.

## On macOS

Build from colors that adapt, so your app looks right in light, dark, and Auto.

### Rules

- **Check contrast in both appearances.** Text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and Apple suggests 7:1 for custom colors in small text. A gray that works on white often fails on a dark gray.
- **Let system views draw text.** Text fields and text views adjust for the appearance and for vibrancy on their own. Drawing text yourself means doing that work too.
- **Stay dark only when content calls for it.** A viewer for photos or video can stay dark so the interface recedes. Everything else should follow the person's choice.

### Pitfalls

- **Dark isn't light turned inside out.** The dark palette uses dimmer backgrounds and brighter foregrounds, and many colors aren't simple inversions. Pick each dark value on purpose.
- **Appearance can change while your app runs.** With Auto, the Mac switches during the day. Read colors when you draw, never once at launch.

### Key APIs

`.fill.tertiary`

### Variants

#### Use semantic styles

Use `.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tint`, and translucent fills instead of fixed colors, and Dark Mode comes for free.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 10) {
    Image(systemName: "airplane")
        .foregroundStyle(.tint)
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Flight to Lisbon")
        Text("Gate B12 · 9:40 AM")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
.padding(10)
.background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 8))
```

#### Your own color, with a dark variant

Add a Color Set to the asset catalog with an Any and a Dark value, then use it by name.

```swift
// Brand: a Color Set with a Dark Appearance variant
Text("Pro")
    .font(.caption.bold())
    .padding(.horizontal, 10)
    .padding(.vertical, 4)
    .foregroundStyle(.white)
    .background(Color("Brand"), in: .capsule)
```

**Note:** The color switches on its own: no `if` in your view. Pick a brighter dark value so it still stands out on a dark window.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Adjust an image for dark mode, Keep a media screen dark, Keep a media window dark (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/supporting-dark-mode-in-your-interface.md

## Related

`system-colors`, `materials`, `color-and-contrast`, `sf-symbols`, `foreground-style`, `image`, `color`, `contrast-transparency`, `settings-pattern`


<!-- topic: layout-adaptivity -->
---
id: layout-adaptivity
title: Layout & Adaptivity
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environmentvalues/horizontalsizeclass.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Layout & Adaptivity

Build layouts that fit any screen, window size, orientation, and text size.

Also called: responsive, responsive design, media query, breakpoint, @media, container query, size class, horizontalSizeClass, compact, regular.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Decide by available space, not by device.** Size classes and `ViewThatFits` describe the room you really have. Checking for iPad or landscape breaks as soon as a window gets resized.
- **Keep every feature at every size.** A narrow window can show fewer buttons, but the actions should move into a menu, not disappear.
- **Keep content inside the safe area.** The Dynamic Island, the Home indicator, and bars cover the screen's edges. Let backgrounds run edge to edge, but keep text and controls inside.
- **Make room for larger text.** With big Dynamic Type sizes, side-by-side text runs out of room. Stack it vertically instead of cutting it off.
- **Test the extremes first.** Check the smallest and largest layouts, then other languages and text sizes. Problems show up at the edges.

## Pitfalls

- **Full-screen-only iPad apps are going away.** As of iPadOS 26, the `UIRequiresFullScreen` key is deprecated. Starting in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, apps built with the iOS 27 SDK generally can't use it to opt out of resizing.
- **Size classes can change while your app runs.** Rotating, resizing a window, or opening another app beside yours can flip them, so never read them once and cache the result.

## Guide

Your app never gets one fixed screen. It runs on phones of different sizes, in portrait and landscape, and in iPad windows that people resize at will. Like responsive design on the web, you describe how the layout **adapts**, and SwiftUI does the measuring. The difference: you react to the space you're given, not to the device.

### Size classes

iOS sums up the space in each direction as one of two **size classes**: `compact` (narrow or short) or `regular` (wide or tall). They're the closest thing to a media query breakpoint, and built-in views like `NavigationSplitView` already use them.

**Note:** The device, its orientation, and iPad multitasking all set the size class. Read it, but don't try to guess it from the device.

## Key APIs

- `\.horizontalSizeClass`: `.compact` when narrow, `.regular` when wide.
- `ViewThatFits`: Shows the first child that fits.
- `AnyLayout`: Switches stack direction without losing state.
- `GridItem(.adaptive)`: As many columns as fit.
- `.containerRelativeFrame(_:)`: Sizes a view relative to its container.
- `.onGeometryChange(for:)`: Reacts to a view's real size.

## Variants

### Switch layouts with the size class

Read `horizontalSizeClass` and use `AnyLayout` to stack vertically when compact and side by side when regular.

```swift
@Environment(\.horizontalSizeClass) private var sizeClass

let layout = sizeClass == .regular
    ? AnyLayout(HStackLayout(spacing: 12))
    : AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8))
layout {
    Image(systemName: "photo")
        .font(.title)
        .frame(width: 80, height: 56)
        .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 8))
    Text("Trip to Lisbon")
        .font(.headline)
}
```

**Note:** `AnyLayout` keeps the children's state when it switches, unlike an `if` that swaps an `HStack` for a `VStack`.

### Show the version that fits

List options from largest to smallest in `ViewThatFits`, and SwiftUI shows the first one with room.

```swift
ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
    HStack {
        Button("Reply", systemImage: "arrowshape.turn.up.left") {}
        Button("Forward", systemImage: "arrowshape.turn.up.right") {}
    }
    HStack {
        Button("Reply", systemImage: "arrowshape.turn.up.left") {}
        Button("Forward", systemImage: "arrowshape.turn.up.right") {}
    }
    .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
}
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
```

**Note:** Both versions keep the same actions. The narrow one just drops the words.

### Let a grid pick its columns

Use an adaptive `GridItem` to fit as many columns as the width allows, with no size checks.

```swift
LazyVGrid(columns: [GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 70))]) {
    ForEach(0..<6) { index in
        RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 10)
            .fill(.blue.gradient)
            .frame(height: 50)
            .overlay { Text("\(index + 1)").foregroundStyle(.white) }
    }
}
```

### Size cards to the screen

Use `.containerRelativeFrame` to make each card a share of the scroll view's width, on any screen.

```swift
ScrollView(.horizontal) {
    HStack(spacing: 12) {
        ForEach(0..<5) { index in
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
                .fill(.orange.gradient)
                .frame(height: 90)
                .containerRelativeFrame(.horizontal, count: 2, spacing: 12)
        }
    }
}
.contentMargins(.horizontal, 16)
```

**Note:** With `count: 2`, two cards fill the width on iPhone and on a wide iPad window alike. Raise the count for regular widths if you want more.

## Related

`safe-area`, `view-that-fits`, `stacks`, `grid`, `lazy-grids`, `navigation-split-view`, `dynamic-type`, `geometry-reader`


<!-- topic: motion -->
---
id: motion
title: Motion
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/animation.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Motion

Animate to explain what changed, keep it short, and know when to skip it.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules

- **Animate with a purpose.** Motion should explain what changed or confirm an action. Motion that's only decoration distracts people and can make some feel unwell.
- **Don't let motion carry the message alone.** Not everyone sees or wants animation. Pair it with text, a symbol, or a haptic so the meaning survives without it.
- **Keep feedback brief.** Short, precise motion feels light and often tells people more than a big show. Tie it closely to the action that caused it.
- **Go easy on things people do often.** Standard controls already animate. A custom effect on an action people repeat all day soon feels slow.
- **Never make people wait for an animation.** Let people keep tapping while things move. SwiftUI animations can be interrupted, so don't block input until one finishes.

## Pitfalls

- **Springs are the default.** Since iOS 17, `withAnimation` without an argument uses a spring, not ease-in-out.
- **A spring can be interrupted.** If someone taps again mid-animation, SwiftUI heads to the new target and keeps the current speed, so nothing jumps.

## Guide

Good motion answers a question: where did that come from, did my tap work, what changed? iOS animates its own controls, so most of your work is choosing **when** to animate your own views, picking a short **spring**, and having a plan for people who turn on **Reduce Motion**.

### Tune a spring

Apple's advice is to set the **duration** first for the pace, then add **bounce** for character.

## Key APIs

`withAnimation(_:_:)`, `.animation(_:value:)`, `.spring(duration:bounce:)`, `.smooth` `.snappy` `.bouncy`, `.transition(_:)`, `\.accessibilityReduceMotion`, `.sensoryFeedback(_:trigger:)`

## Variants

### Animate a change people made

Wrap the state change in `withAnimation` so the new content slides in instead of popping.

```swift
@State private var showDetails = false

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Button(showDetails ? "Hide Details" : "Show Details") {
        withAnimation(.snappy) {
            showDetails.toggle()
        }
    }
    if showDetails {
        Text("Ships in 2–3 days")
            .transition(.move(edge: .top).combined(with: .opacity))
    }
}
```

### Offer a fade when Reduce Motion is on

Read `accessibilityReduceMotion` and swap movement for a cross-fade.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
@State private var isShowing = false

VStack {
    Button("Toggle Banner") {
        withAnimation { isShowing.toggle() }
    }
    if isShowing {
        Text("Back online")
            .padding()
            .background(.green.opacity(0.2), in: .capsule)
            .transition(reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .bottom))
    }
}
```

**Note:** Reduce Motion doesn't mean no animation. Fades and color changes are fine; big moves, zooms, and spins are what to drop.

## On macOS

Animate to explain a change, keep it brief, and tone it down for Reduce Motion.

### Rules

- **Keep feedback short and precise.** A quick animation tied exactly to what someone did reads instantly. A long or showy one gets in the way.
- **Match the motion to the action.** If a panel slides down to appear, it should slide back up to leave, not off to the side. Motion that contradicts the action disorients.
- **Don't rely on motion alone.** Some people turn motion down or miss it. Say what happened in another way too, like a label or a changed state.
- **Tone it down for Reduce Motion.** Cut automatic and repeating animations, zooming, and scaling. Swap slides for fades, tighten springs so they don't bounce, and don't animate blurs or depth.

### Pitfalls

- **Many system components already animate.** Use them as they are, and add your own motion only to custom views, following the same rules.
- **Test with Reduce Motion on.** Turn it on in the Mac's Accessibility settings and walk through your app: anything that still zooms, slides, or bounces on its own needs a quieter version.

### Key APIs

`.contentTransition(.numericText())`, `.symbolEffect(_:value:)`

### Variants

#### Animate a change people made

Wrap the state change in `withAnimation(.snappy)` so a new row eases in where it lands.

```swift
@State private var stops = ["Alfama", "Belém"]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    ForEach(stops, id: \.self) { stop in
        Label(stop, systemImage: "mappin")
    }
    Button("Add Stop") {
        withAnimation(.snappy) {
            stops.append("Stop \(stops.count + 1)")
        }
    }
}
```

#### Fade instead of slide for Reduce Motion

Read `accessibilityReduceMotion` and pick an `.opacity` transition when it's on.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
@State private var showsBanner = false

VStack {
    Button(showsBanner ? "Hide Banner" : "Show Banner") {
        withAnimation { showsBanner.toggle() }
    }
    if showsBanner {
        Text("Your trip is saved.")
            .padding(10)
            .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 8))
            .transition(reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .top).combined(with: .opacity))
    }
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Confirm with a symbol and a haptic, Let numbers roll (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/animation.md

## Related

`spring`, `animation-curves`, `transitions`, `reduce-motion`, `symbol-effects`, `haptics`, `matched-geometry`, `phase-animator`, `animation`, `sf-symbols`, `materials`


<!-- topic: app-icons -->
---
id: app-icons
title: App Icons
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 26.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/creating-your-app-icon-using-icon-composer.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/app-icons.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# App Icons

Design one layered icon that the system turns into every appearance and size.

Also called: app icon, icon, favicon, Icon Composer, .icon file, AppIcon, home screen icon, dark icon, tinted icon, clear icon.

## Rules

- **Build around one simple idea.** Pick a single shape that captures your app. Fine details turn to mush at small sizes and under the system's highlights and shadows.
- **Leave the words out.** Your app's name already sits under the icon, and text in the icon can't be read at small sizes or translated. A single letter is fine if it's part of your brand.
- **Hand over square, flat layers.** The system rounds the corners and adds highlights, shadows, and depth. Pre-rounded corners or baked-in effects clash with them and can leave jagged edges.
- **Keep the same features in every appearance.** Dark, clear, and tinted versions should be recognizably the same icon. Swapping elements makes your app hard to find when people change their Home Screen.
- **Draw it; don't photograph it.** Photos, screenshots, and copies of standard controls lose detail when small and split badly into layers. Make an illustration of the idea instead.

## Pitfalls

- **Older iOS versions are covered.** When your app supports releases before the Liquid Glass icon style, Xcode builds matching images for them from the same Icon Composer file at build time.
- **The `.icon` file replaces the asset catalog icon.** Once it's in your project, Xcode uses it instead of an `AppIcon` image set. Keep the asset catalog only if you want the old artwork on older releases.

## Guide

Since iOS 26, app icons are made of **layers** that the system renders in Liquid Glass, with highlights and depth that react to light and movement. You design one icon in **Icon Composer**, and iOS produces every size and every Home Screen appearance from that single file.

### How an icon is built

**Note:** Group your layers into at most four groups. Each group becomes a level of depth, and you can tune its glass effects together.

## Key APIs

- Icon Composer: Apple's tool for layered icons. Ships with Xcode.
- `AppIcon.icon`: The file you add to your Xcode project.
- `supportsAlternateIcons`: Whether the app can switch icons.
- `setAlternateIconName(_:)`: Switches to an alternate icon. UIKit only.

## Variants

### Let people pick an alternate icon

Call `setAlternateIconName` from a settings screen. SwiftUI has no equivalent, so this one is UIKit.

```swift
Button("Use Night Icon") {
    Task {
        guard UIApplication.shared.supportsAlternateIcons else { return }
        try? await UIApplication.shared.setAlternateIconName("NightIcon")
    }
}
```

**Important:** Each alternate icon needs its own dark, clear, and tinted versions, and App Review checks it like your main icon. List the extra icons in the target's Alternate App Icon Sets build setting.

## On macOS

A square, layered icon that the Mac rounds and finishes in Liquid Glass.

### Rules

- **Keep it simple.** Pick one idea that captures your app and draw it with a few bold shapes. Fine details get busy under the system's highlights and disappear at small sizes.
- **Leave out words.** Text in an icon isn't accessible or localized, and it's often too small to read. Add it only when it's essential to your brand; the app's name usually appears nearby.
- **Let the system add the effects.** The Mac adds highlights, shadows, refraction, and translucency that respond to the environment. Baked-in shadows, bevels, and glows fight with them and stay static.
- **Prefer illustrations to photos and screenshots.** Photos are full of detail that falls apart at small sizes and across appearances. Draw a simple picture of what matters instead, and don't copy your app's interface.
- **Keep it recognizable in every appearance.** People can switch their icons to dark, clear, or tinted. Keep the same shapes in each one, so your app is still easy to find.
- **Don't draw Apple hardware.** Apple's products are copyrighted, so don't reproduce a Mac, iPhone, or other device in your icon.

### Pitfalls

- **One Icon Composer file covers every size.** The system scales your icon down for small places, so you don't export a set of sizes anymore.
- **SF Symbols can't be part of your icon.** Apple's terms for SF Symbols don't allow them, or look-alikes, in app icons and logos. Draw your own shapes.

## Related

`liquid-glass`, `dark-mode`, `sf-symbols`, `materials`, `color`, `mac-screenshots`


<!-- topic: writing -->
---
id: writing
title: Writing
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/writing.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Writing

Short, specific words for buttons, alerts, errors, and empty screens.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules

- **Label buttons with verbs.** Say what happens when people tap. Clever or cute labels make them stop and think.
- **Name the action in alert buttons.** "OK" can mean "go ahead" or "got it". Use the verb, and always call the way out "Cancel".
- **Say how to fix an error.** Show the message next to the problem, don't blame, and skip "Oops". Tell people what will work.
- **Skip "we".** It's unclear who "we" is, especially in an error. Describe what happened instead.
- **Give empty screens a next step.** An empty list is a chance to explain what goes there and offer the button that fills it.
- **Write for the device.** On iPhone and iPad, people tap, not click. Use the gestures and words that match what's in their hand.

## Pitfalls

- **Keep a word list.** Write down what you call things ("Library" or "Collection"? "Remove" or "Delete"?) and use the same word everywhere.
- **Read it out loud.** If a sentence sounds stiff or long when spoken, cut it down. Fewer words are almost always clearer.

## Guide

The words in your app are part of the interface. A clear button label saves a tap on the wrong thing, and a good error message saves a support email. Pick a **voice** that fits your app, then adjust the **tone** to the moment: calm for a failed payment, warm for a finished goal.

### Capitalization

Pick title case or sentence case for each kind of text, and stick to it. For buttons and alerts, Apple uses these rules:

## Key APIs

`.alert(_:isPresented:actions:)`, `Button(_:role:action:)`, `ContentUnavailableView`, `TextField(_:text:prompt:)`, `Section { } footer: { }`

## Variants

### A clear alert

Give `.alert` a specific title, a short message only if it helps, and buttons named after their action.

```swift
@State private var isConfirming = false

Button("Delete Photos", role: .destructive) {
    isConfirming = true
}
.alert("Delete 3 Photos?", isPresented: $isConfirming) {
    Button("Delete", role: .destructive) { }
    Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { }
} message: {
    Text("This can't be undone.")
}
```

**Note:** Skip alerts for things people can undo, like deleting one email. Save them for actions that can't be reversed.

### An error next to the field

Show the format in the `prompt`, and put any error right under the field with what to do next.

```swift
@State private var email = "maya@"

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 6) {
    TextField("Email", text: $email, prompt: Text("name@example.com"))
        .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
    Label("Enter the full address, like name@example.com.", systemImage: "exclamationmark.circle")
        .font(.footnote)
        .foregroundStyle(.red)
}
```

## On macOS

Menu and button names people recognize: verbs, title case, and an ellipsis when more is needed.

### Rules

- **Add an ellipsis when a command needs more input.** The … tells people a window or panel will ask for something before the command finishes, like a file name for Export. Use the ellipsis character, not three periods.
- **Use title case in menus.** Capitalize every word except articles, coordinating conjunctions, and short prepositions, and always capitalize the last word: Bring All to Front.
- **Start actions with a verb.** A button or menu item that does something should say what it does. Plain beats clever.
- **Let a toggled item say what it will do.** Instead of two items, one item can switch between Show Map and Hide Map. For an attribute that's on, like a text style, a checkmark works better.
- **Write errors that help.** Show the message next to the problem, don't blame anyone, and say how to fix it. Skip “Oops” and avoid “we”: it's never clear who that is.
- **Describe the Mac's own actions.** People click, double-click, and press keys on a Mac. Saying tap, or describing a gesture the Mac doesn't have, sounds like an app from another device.

### Pitfalls

- **Pick a capitalization style and stick to it.** Menus use title case on the Mac. For other text, like headings and alerts, choose title or sentence case per kind of element and use it everywhere.
- **Say window, not scene.** People see windows. Scene, view, and other words from your code don't belong in the interface.

### Key APIs

`Button("Export…")`, `CommandGroup(after:)`, `CommandMenu(_:)`, `.keyboardShortcut(_:modifiers:)`, `.help(_:)`, `String(localized:)`

### Variants

#### Name menu commands the Mac way

Give each command a verb in title case, and end it with … when it opens a panel or window to ask for more.

```swift
.commands {
    CommandGroup(after: .newItem) {
        Button("Duplicate Trip") { }
            .keyboardShortcut("s", modifiers: [.shift, .command])
        Button("Export Itinerary…") { }
            .keyboardShortcut("e", modifiers: [.shift, .command])
    }
}
```

**Note:** Menu bar menus belong to the app, not a page, so the preview draws this one. See Commands (`commands`) for adding them.

#### A label that follows the state

Switch the title with the state, so the item always says what clicking it will do.

```swift
@State private var showsMap = true

Button(showsMap ? "Hide Map" : "Show Map") {
    showsMap.toggle()
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: An empty state with a way forward, A setting that explains itself, An error next to the field (macOS), A button that opens more (macOS).

## Related

`alert`, `confirmation-dialog`, `empty-state`, `text-field`, `button`, `voiceover`, `commands`, `menu-bar-conventions`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `empty-states`


<!-- topic: accessibility -->
---
id: accessibility
title: Accessibility
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view-accessibility.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Accessibility

What to support from day one so everyone can use your app.

Also called: a11y, accessible, screen reader, aria, WCAG, inclusive design, disability, assistive technology, Accessibility Nutrition Labels.

## Rules

- **Make controls at least 44 × 44 points.** Small targets are hard to hit, especially with limited dexterity. Grow the tappable area with padding or a frame, even if the icon stays small.
- **Leave room between controls.** Spacing matters as much as size. About 12 points around controls with a background, and about 24 around plain icons, keeps people from tapping the wrong one.
- **Offer a button for every gesture.** If a swipe deletes or a long press opens options, give people another way to do it too, such as a visible button or menu.
- **Don't hide things on a timer.** Messages that dismiss themselves can vanish before someone using VoiceOver or reading slowly gets to them. Let people close them.

## Pitfalls

- **Accessibility Inspector finds problems for you.** It ships with Xcode and highlights missing labels, small targets, and low contrast while your app runs.
- **As of October 2026, Accessibility Nutrition Labels are voluntary.** You declare in App Store Connect which features your app supports, and they show on your product page. Apple says they'll become required for new apps and updates over time, without a date yet.

## Guide

People use iPhone in many ways: listening with **VoiceOver**, reading at a much larger text size, with motion turned down, or without telling certain colors apart. SwiftUI's standard controls handle a lot of this for you. Your work is mostly in the custom parts: icon-only buttons, fixed sizes, your own animations, and color choices.

```swift
struct DeliveryCard: View {
    @Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var typeSize
    @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
    @State private var bounce = false

    var body: some View {
        let layout = typeSize.isAccessibilitySize
            ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading))
            : AnyLayout(HStackLayout())
        layout {
            Image(systemName: "box.truck.fill")
                .font(.title2)
                .offset(y: bounce && !reduceMotion ? -4 : 0)
                .accessibilityHidden(true)
            VStack(alignment: .leading) {
                Text("Order 1042").font(.headline)
                Label("Out for delivery", systemImage: "shippingbox.circle.fill")
                    .font(.subheadline)
                Text("Arrives today by 6 PM")
                    .font(.subheadline)
                    .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            }
        }
        .accessibilityElement(children: .combine)
        .onAppear {
            withAnimation(.easeInOut.repeatForever()) { bounce = true }
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The switches here only change this preview. Your app reads the real settings from the environment, as in the code above.

### Start here

Check these off as you build. Each one links to a page that shows how.

- **Label every icon-only button**: Give it a short name VoiceOver can read, like “Share”. (`voiceover`)
- **Hide decorative images**: Use `Image(decorative:)` or `.accessibilityHidden(true)`. (`voiceover`)
- **Use text styles, not fixed sizes**: `.font(.body)` grows with the person's text size. (`dynamic-type`)
- **Check the largest text sizes**: Text should wrap, not overlap or cut off. (`dynamic-type`)
- **Swap big motion for fades**: Do it when Reduce Motion is on, and add Pause to anything that loops. (`reduce-motion`)
- **Meet 4.5:1 contrast for text**: In light and dark mode. (`color-and-contrast`)
- **Never rely on color alone**: Add an icon, shape, or word to every status. (`color-and-contrast`)
- **Make targets at least 44 × 44 pt**: Add padding around small icons. (`button`)
- **Tell the App Store what you support**: Accessibility Nutrition Labels in App Store Connect. (`accessibility-labels`)

## Key APIs

- `.accessibilityLabel(_:)`: What VoiceOver says for a view.
- `.font(.body)`: A text style that grows with Dynamic Type.
- `\.accessibilityReduceMotion`: True when people turn on Reduce Motion.
- `\.colorSchemeContrast`: `.increased` when Increase Contrast is on.
- `\.dynamicTypeSize`: The text size people picked in Settings.

## Related

`voiceover`, `dynamic-type`, `reduce-motion`, `color-and-contrast`, `accessibility-labels`, `typography`


<!-- topic: voiceover -->
---
id: voiceover
title: VoiceOver
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view-accessibility.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# VoiceOver

Labels, traits, and grouping that tell the screen reader what each view is.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules

- **Label every icon-only button.** Without a label, VoiceOver has nothing useful to say, and people can't tell what the button does.
- **Leave the control type out of the label.** VoiceOver already says “Button” from the trait. Writing it in the label makes it say it twice.
- **Make labels make sense on their own.** People often jump between controls without hearing what's around them. “Remove AirPods” works out of context; three buttons all called “Delete” don't.
- **Hide images that are only decoration.** Skipping them saves people time. Describe images that carry meaning, but only what the image adds beyond nearby text.
- **Mark headings.** VoiceOver users can jump from heading to heading with the rotor, the way sighted people skim. Use the `.isHeader` trait on section titles.
- **Keep hints short and about the result.** A hint like “Saves the recipe” says what happens. Skip the gesture (“Double-tap to…”), which VoiceOver already explains.

## Pitfalls

- **Standard controls are labeled for you.** `Button`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, and `TextField` take their label and value from what they show. Add modifiers where a view has no text.
- **Voice Control uses the same labels.** People say a control's name to tap it, so a missing label also breaks voice commands.
- **Listen to it.** Turn on VoiceOver on a device, or open Accessibility Inspector in Xcode, and swipe through each screen.

## Guide

VoiceOver reads the screen aloud, one element at a time, as people swipe. For each element it speaks a **label** (what it is called), a **value** (its current state), its **traits** (button, heading, selected), and, after a pause, an optional **hint**. Your job is to fill those in where SwiftUI can't guess them.

### Hear it

```swift
Button {
    // Share
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "square.and.arrow.up")
}
```

**Note:** This is a close approximation. The exact wording and pauses depend on the device, the language, and the person's VoiceOver settings.

## Key APIs

`.accessibilityLabel(_:)`, `.accessibilityValue(_:)`, `.accessibilityHint(_:)`, `.accessibilityAddTraits(_:)`, `.accessibilityElement(children:)`, `.accessibilityHidden(true)`, `.accessibilityAction(named:_:)`

## Variants

### Label an icon-only button

Use `Label` with `.labelStyle(.iconOnly)`: the icon shows, and the title becomes the VoiceOver label.

```swift
Button {
    // Share the recipe
} label: {
    Label("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up")
        .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
}
```

**Note:** For a plain `Image` label, add `.accessibilityLabel("Share")` to the button instead.

### Read a row as one stop

`.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)` merges the texts inside, so people hear the whole row in one swipe.

```swift
HStack {
    Image(systemName: "fork.knife")
        .accessibilityHidden(true)
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Lemon Pasta")
        Text("25 min")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)
```

**Important:** Don't combine a row that holds several buttons. Each one needs its own stop, or a named action.

## On macOS

Labels, grouping, and rotors that let the screen reader describe your windows.

### Rules

- **Label every key element.** VoiceOver speaks labels people never see. An icon-only button with no label tells them nothing about what it does.
- **Describe images that carry meaning, and hide the rest.** Describe only what the image adds to nearby text. Skipping decoration saves people time.
- **Give windows clear titles and sections real headings.** The title is the first thing VoiceOver reports. Headings let people skim a window the way sighted people scan it.
- **Say how things belong together.** Closeness and alignment show sighted people that a photo and caption go together. Group them so VoiceOver reads them together too.
- **Announce changes people can't see.** When content appears, moves, or finishes loading somewhere else, tell assistive tools, so people's picture of the window stays right.

### Pitfalls

- **Standard controls describe themselves.** `Button`, `Toggle`, `TextField`, and `Picker` take their label and value from what they show. Add modifiers where a view has no text, or where SwiftUI can't guess.
- **Toolbar titles still count.** Hiding a window's title with `.toolbar(removing: .title)` is a visual change; assistive tools still get the title.

### Key APIs

`.accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader)`, `.accessibilityRotor(_:entries:entryLabel:)`

### Variants

#### Label an icon-only button

Use a `Label` with `.labelStyle(.iconOnly)`: the icon shows, and the title becomes what VoiceOver reads.

```swift
Button {
    // Share the note
} label: {
    Label("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up")
        .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
}
```

**Note:** With a plain `Image` as the label, add `.accessibilityLabel("Share")` to the button instead.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Describe a custom control, Name your gestures, Mark section headings, Read a row as one element (macOS), Offer hover-only buttons as actions (macOS), Add a rotor for what people look for (macOS), Announce a change (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view-accessibility.md

## Related

`accessibility`, `button`, `label`, `image`, `dynamic-type`, `keyboard-access`, `contrast-transparency`, `image-symbols`, `toolbar`


<!-- topic: dynamic-type -->
---
id: dynamic-type
title: Dynamic Type
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/dynamictypesize.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Dynamic Type

Let text grow to the size people choose, and keep layouts readable when it does.

Also called: larger text, text size, font scaling, rem, zoom, responsive text, accessibility sizes, ScaledMetric, UIContentSizeCategory, preferredFont.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Let text wrap instead of cutting it off.** At large sizes, a one-line limit hides most of the text. Let it take as many lines as it needs, especially in scrolling content.
- **Stack side-by-side items at large sizes.** A label and a value on one line crowd each other when text is huge. Put the value under the label instead.
- **Grow meaningful icons with the text.** An icon that carries meaning should stay as easy to see as the words next to it. SF Symbols scale with the font automatically.
- **Keep the most important things at the top.** When text grows, the layout gets longer. Keep the order the same so people don't lose track of the main content.
- **Support at least 200 percent.** Apple asks for text that can reach about twice its default size. On iPhone, the accessibility sizes go past 200 percent at `accessibility3` and past 300 percent at `accessibility5`.

## Pitfalls

- **There are 12 sizes.** Seven standard ones, from `xSmall` to `xxxLarge`, plus five accessibility sizes, `accessibility1` to `accessibility5`. The default is `large`, where `.body` is 17 points.
- **Try it in Settings.** Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text, with Larger Accessibility Sizes turned on, unlocks the five biggest sizes.

## Guide

**Dynamic Type** is the text size people pick in Settings. It works like `rem` on the web: text set with a text style, such as `.font(.body)`, scales with it. There are 12 sizes, and the largest makes text more than three times its default size, so your layouts need room to grow.

```swift
@Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var typeSize

let layout = typeSize.isAccessibilitySize
    ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading))
    : AnyLayout(HStackLayout(alignment: .firstTextBaseline))

layout {
    Text("Maya Chen")
        .font(.headline)
    Spacer(minLength: 0)
    Text("9:41 AM")
        .font(.subheadline)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
Text("Are we still on for lunch tomorrow?")
    .font(.subheadline)
```

**Important:** `.font(.system(size: 17))` is a fixed size, like `px`, and never grows. Use a text style, or `@ScaledMetric` for your own numbers.

## Key APIs

- `.font(.body)`: A text style. All of them scale.
- `@ScaledMetric`: Scales your own numbers, like an icon size.
- `\.dynamicTypeSize`: The current size, to adapt a layout.
- `.isAccessibilitySize`: True for the five largest sizes.
- `ViewThatFits`: Picks the first layout that fits.
- `.dynamicTypeSize(_:)`: Sets or limits the size for a view.
- `.accessibilityShowsLargeContentViewer()`: A big popup for items that must stay small.

## Variants

### Scale your own sizes

`@ScaledMetric` grows a number, like an avatar size or padding, in step with a text style.

```swift
@ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .body) private var avatar = 40.0

HStack {
    Circle()
        .fill(.blue.gradient)
        .frame(width: avatar, height: avatar)
    Text("Maya Chen")
}
```

### Switch layout at accessibility sizes

Read `dynamicTypeSize` and check `.isAccessibilitySize` to turn a row into a column.

```swift
@Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var typeSize

let layout = typeSize.isAccessibilitySize
    ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading))
    : AnyLayout(HStackLayout())

layout {
    Text("Pickup")
    Spacer(minLength: 0)
    Text("Today, 4:30 PM")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

**Note:** `AnyLayout` swaps the container without rebuilding the views inside, so their state survives the switch.

### Let SwiftUI pick the layout

`ViewThatFits` tries each child in order and shows the first that fits, here buttons side by side, then stacked.

```swift
ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
    HStack {
        Button("Not Now") {}
            .buttonStyle(.bordered)
        Button("Turn On Notifications") {}
            .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
    }
    VStack {
        Button("Turn On Notifications") {}
            .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        Button("Not Now") {}
            .buttonStyle(.bordered)
    }
}
```

### Items that must stay small

For chrome that can't grow, like a custom tab bar, add `.accessibilityShowsLargeContentViewer()`: a long press shows a big version.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 32) {
    Label("Home", systemImage: "house")
    Label("Library", systemImage: "books.vertical")
}
.labelStyle(.iconOnly)
.dynamicTypeSize(...DynamicTypeSize.xxxLarge)
.accessibilityShowsLargeContentViewer()
```

**Important:** Use this only for small, repeated chrome. Never cap the size of body text or the main content.

### Preview a big size

Put `.dynamicTypeSize(_:)` on a preview to check a large size without changing Settings.

```swift
#Preview {
    ContentView()
        .dynamicTypeSize(.accessibility3)
}
```

## Related

`typography`, `font`, `view-that-fits`, `accessibility`, `sf-symbols`


<!-- topic: reduce-motion -->
---
id: reduce-motion
title: Reduce Motion
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environmentvalues/accessibilityreducemotion.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Reduce Motion

Swap big movement for fades when people ask for less motion.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules

- **Replace motion with a fade, don't just delete it.** If an animation shows where something went, like an item landing in a cart, keep that meaning with a dissolve, highlight, or color change.
- **Cut zooming, spinning, and depth effects.** Parallax, big scale changes, spins, and animated blur cause the most discomfort. Turn them off or replace them when the setting is on.
- **Let people pause anything that moves on its own.** Carousels, looping backgrounds, and autoplaying video should stop with Reduce Motion, or at least have a visible pause button.
- **Don't make people wait for an animation.** Keep feedback short, and let people act before it finishes, especially for something they'll see many times.
- **Never use motion as the only signal.** Some people turn motion down or don't notice it. Pair it with text, a color or shape change, or a haptic.

## Pitfalls

- **It's `prefers-reduced-motion` for SwiftUI.** Read it from the environment, and SwiftUI updates the view when the setting changes.
- **Focus on your own animations.** Apple's standard components can adjust their motion for accessibility settings themselves. Custom transitions and springs are up to you.

## Guide

**Reduce Motion** is a setting for people who get dizzy, nauseous, or distracted by movement on screen. When it's on, turn off motion that's only decoration, and replace motion that carries meaning with something calmer, like a fade. Don't strip every animation: an app with no transitions at all can be more confusing.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion

// The item flies into the cart, or fades out.
.transition(reduceMotion
    ? .opacity
    : .scale(scale: 0.2, anchor: .topTrailing).combined(with: .opacity))

// The cart bounces, or gets a soft highlight.
withAnimation(reduceMotion ? .easeInOut : .bouncy) {
    inCart = true
}
```

### What to change

When the setting is on, check every custom animation:

## Key APIs

`\.accessibilityReduceMotion`, `.transition(.opacity)`, `withAnimation(_:_:)`, `.animation(_:value:)`, `\.accessibilityPlayAnimatedImages`

## Variants

### Swap a slide for a fade

Read `accessibilityReduceMotion` from the environment and pick the transition with it.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
@State private var showsBanner = false

VStack {
    if showsBanner {
        Text("Saved to Favorites")
            .padding()
            .background(.green.opacity(0.2), in: .capsule)
            .transition(reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .top))
    }
    Button("Save") {
        withAnimation { showsBanner.toggle() }
    }
}
```

**Note:** On this device, Reduce Motion is off, so the preview shows the slide.

## On macOS

Trade sliding, zooming, and bouncing for fades when people ask for less motion.

### Rules

- **Fade instead of moving.** Swap slides along any axis for a dissolve. If the motion showed where something went, keep that meaning with a highlight or a badge.
- **Drop zooms, depth, and blur.** Scaling, animating layers toward or away from the viewer, and animating into or out of a blur cause the most discomfort. Turn them off with the setting.
- **Tighten springs.** Less bounce means less movement to follow. A smooth curve that settles without overshooting works well.
- **Let people stop anything that moves on its own.** Stop carousels and looping backgrounds with Reduce Motion, and give them a visible pause button either way.
- **Skip motion on things people do all the time.** Standard controls already have subtle animations. Extra animation on a frequent action makes people wait every time.

### Pitfalls

- **It's `prefers-reduced-motion` for SwiftUI.** Read it from the environment, and the view updates when the setting changes.
- **Focus on your own animations.** Standard components can adjust their motion themselves. Custom transitions, springs, and anything that moves on its own are up to you.

### Variants

#### Swap a slide for a fade

Read `accessibilityReduceMotion` from the environment and pick the transition with it.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
@State private var showsBanner = false

VStack {
    if showsBanner {
        Text("Saved to Library")
            .padding(8)
            .background(.green.opacity(0.2), in: .capsule)
            .transition(reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .top))
    }
    Button("Save") {
        withAnimation { showsBanner.toggle() }
    }
}
```

**Note:** Reduce Motion is off on this Mac, so the preview slides.

#### Calm a spring

Pass a smooth curve to `withAnimation` instead of a bouncy spring, so things settle without overshooting.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
@State private var isExpanded = false

RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
    .fill(.blue.gradient)
    .frame(width: isExpanded ? 220 : 110, height: 60)
    .onTapGesture {
        withAnimation(reduceMotion ? .easeInOut : .bouncy(extraBounce: 0.3)) {
            isExpanded.toggle()
        }
    }
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Calm a spring, Stop autoplay, Stop autoplay (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environmentvalues/accessibilityreducemotion.md

## Related

`transitions`, `spring`, `animation-curves`, `accessibility`, `symbol-effects`, `motion`, `animation`, `contrast-transparency`, `keyboard-access`

id: color-and-contrast
title: Color & Contrast
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+

# Color & Contrast

Readable contrast, Increase Contrast support, and never using color as the only signal.

Also called: contrast ratio, WCAG, AA, 4.5:1, color blind, colour blind, colorblind, high contrast, prefers-contrast, Increase Contrast.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Never use color as the only signal.** Some people can't tell red from green. Add a shape, icon, or word so the meaning survives without color.
- **Give text at least 4.5:1 contrast.** Light text on a light fill washes out, especially outdoors or for people with low vision.
- **Check dark mode separately.** Contrast that passes in light mode can fail in dark mode. Dim gray on black is a common miss.
- **Prefer system colors.** Colors like `.primary`, `.secondary`, and `.blue` already have versions for dark mode and Increase Contrast. Custom colors need each version from you.

## Pitfalls

- **The ratio runs from 1:1 to 21:1.** It compares the relative brightness of two colors. Don't round it up: 4.49:1 doesn't pass 4.5:1.
- **Test in grayscale.** Turn on the Grayscale color filter in the Accessibility settings. It isn't what color-blind people see, but if you can't use your app in gray, something relies on color alone.

## Guide

Three things make color work for everyone: enough **contrast** between text and its background, support for the **Increase Contrast** setting, and never using **color alone** to say something. System colors and styles help with the first two, so most of the work is in your own colors.

### Minimum contrast

Accessibility Inspector checks your colors against these WCAG AA ratios:

**Note:** For icons, borders, and other parts of a control that aren't text, 3:1 is the common minimum.

## Key APIs

- `\.colorSchemeContrast`: `.increased` when Increase Contrast is on.
- `\.accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor`: True when people ask for shapes, not just color.
- `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`: System styles adapt to contrast and dark mode.
- `Label(_:systemImage:)`: Text plus an icon, an easy second cue.

## Variants

### Respond to Increase Contrast

Read `colorSchemeContrast` and strengthen custom colors and borders when it's `.increased`.

```swift
@Environment(\.colorSchemeContrast) private var contrast

Text("Beta")
    .font(.caption.bold())
    .padding(.horizontal, 10)
    .padding(.vertical, 4)
    .foregroundStyle(contrast == .increased ? .white : .purple)
    .background(.purple.opacity(contrast == .increased ? 1 : 0.15), in: .capsule)
```

**Note:** If you only need different colors, add a High Contrast variant to the color in your asset catalog instead. It switches on its own.

### Give every status a shape

Pair each color with its own symbol in a `Label`, and keep the text in the primary color.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Label {
        Text("Paid")
    } icon: {
        Image(systemName: "checkmark.circle.fill")
            .foregroundStyle(.green)
    }
    Label {
        Text("Failed")
    } icon: {
        Image(systemName: "xmark.octagon.fill")
            .foregroundStyle(.red)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Colored text is often too light to read. Tint the icon and leave the words in `.primary`.

### Explain errors in words

A red border alone is easy to miss. Add a message with an icon under the field.

```swift
@State private var email = "maya@"

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 6) {
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .padding(10)
        .overlay {
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 8)
                .strokeBorder(.red)
        }
    Label("Enter a full email address.", systemImage: "exclamationmark.circle.fill")
        .font(.footnote)
        .foregroundStyle(.red)
}
```

### Add shapes when people ask

When `accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor` is true, swap color-only marks for symbols.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor) private var noColorOnly

HStack {
    Image(systemName: noColorOnly ? "checkmark.circle.fill" : "circle.fill")
        .foregroundStyle(.green)
    Text("Available")
}
```

**Important:** Treat this as a fallback. Apple's guidance is to design without color-only cues from the start.

## Related

`system-colors`, `accessibility`, `foreground-style`, `label`


<!-- topic: launching -->

id: launching
title: Launching
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+

hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/launching.md
reviewed: October 2026
