# Launching

Open fast, look like your first screen, and pick up where people left off.

Also called: launch screen, splash screen, LaunchScreen.storyboard, UILaunchScreen, app startup, app launch, cold start, startup time, state restoration, restore state.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Make the launch screen match your first screen.** Use the same background and bars, without the content. It makes the app feel ready at once, with no flash when your real screen appears.
- **Leave out text and logos.** The launch screen can't be localized, and it isn't a branding spot. Show a logo only if it's a fixed part of your first screen.
- **Launch instantly; no splash delays.** People want to start right away. If you need a splash, show it as the first step of `onboarding`, not as a timer on every launch.
- **Restore where people left off.** Reopen the same tab, screen, and scroll position, so nobody has to retrace their steps.
- **Don't greet people with an alert or a prompt.** Show problems, like being offline, inside the screen, and ask for permissions (`requesting-permission`) when a feature needs them.

## Pitfalls

- **The launch screen isn't SwiftUI.** It's an Info.plist entry or a storyboard that the system draws before any of your code runs, so it can't animate or show live data.
- **Slow launches get killed.** On iOS, the system's watchdog ends an app that takes too long to launch. Move work out of `init` and into `.task`.
- **Every app needs one.** As of iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, Apple's technote TN3192 says a launch screen is required for App Store submission.
- **`@SceneStorage` is for small UI state.** Keep model data and anything sensitive out of it. It's also gone if people close the window or remove it from the app switcher.

## Guide

Launching runs from the tap on your icon until your first screen is ready. iOS shows your launch screen instantly, then swaps in your first screen. The goal is for that swap to go unnoticed: a launch screen that looks like the app, a first screen that shows up fast, and the same place people left.

## Key APIs

- `UILaunchScreen`: Info.plist launch screen: color, image, bars.
- `UILaunchStoryboardName`: A storyboard launch screen instead.
- `@SceneStorage`: Restores small UI state per window.
- `.task { }`: Starts loading after the first frame.
- `@Environment(\.scenePhase)`: Tells you when the app goes inactive.

## Variants

### A launch screen in Info.plist

Add a `UILaunchScreen` dictionary with your background color and the bars your first screen has.

```xml
<!-- Info.plist -->
<key>UILaunchScreen</key>
<dict>
    <key>UIColorName</key>
    <string>LaunchBackground</string>
    <key>UINavigationBar</key>
    <dict/>
    <key>UITabBar</key>
    <dict/>
</dict>
```

**Note:** `UIColorName` names a color in your asset catalog. Leave it out and the system uses the standard background, which follows light and dark mode.

### Restore the last tab

Use `@SceneStorage` instead of `@State` for the selected tab, and SwiftUI brings it back on the next launch.

```swift
@SceneStorage("selectedTab") private var selectedTab = "today"

TabView(selection: $selectedTab) {
    Tab("Today", systemImage: "sun.max", value: "today") {
        Text("Today")
    }
    Tab("Library", systemImage: "books.vertical", value: "library") {
        Text("Library")
    }
}
```

### Show the screen, then load

Draw the first screen right away and start slow work in `.task`, with placeholders (`loading`) while it runs.

```swift
struct ExpensesScreen: View {
    @State private var expenses: [String] = []
    @State private var isLoading = true

    var body: some View {
        List(isLoading ? ["Placeholder row", "Placeholder row"] : expenses, id: \.self) {
            Text($0)
        }
        .redacted(reason: isLoading ? .placeholder : [])
        .task {
            // Not in init: the screen is already on display.
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1))
            expenses = ["Lunch", "Train ticket"]
            isLoading = false
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`onboarding`, `loading`, `requesting-permission`, `tab-view`, `lifecycle`


<!-- topic: loading -->
---
id: loading
title: Loading
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/redacted(reason:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/loading.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Loading

Show something right away, then swap in the content, an empty state, or an error.

Also called: loading state, skeleton, skeleton screen, shimmer, spinner, activity indicator, placeholder, Suspense, useEffect fetch, fetch data.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Show something right away.** A blank screen looks broken. Draw the layout with placeholders and fill it in as data arrives.
- **Say how long, and what's happening.** When you know the size of the work, use a bar instead of a spinner, and label it with what's happening. A plain “Loading” tells people nothing.
- **Let people keep going while they wait.** Load in the background and keep the rest of the app usable. If stopping is safe, offer a Cancel button.
- **Keep progress moving, and stay on one style.** A frozen bar reads as a frozen app, so explain any stall. Don't morph a spinner into a bar; they're different shapes.

## Pitfalls

- **It's a skeleton screen, built in.** `.redacted(reason: .placeholder)` turns your real layout into gray shapes, so you don't build a second, fake version of the screen.
- **`.task` is `useEffect` with cleanup for free.** It starts before the view appears and SwiftUI cancels it when the view goes away.
- **Refresh on your own, too.** Pull to refresh with `.refreshable` is welcome, but people expect content to update without having to ask every time.

## Guide

Every screen that fetches data has four states: loading, loaded, empty, and failed. Plan all four up front. Show the layout right away with placeholders, then swap in the content, an empty message, or an error with a way to try again.

Tap **Reload** to watch the screen load, or pick a state to see each one.

```swift
enum LoadState<Value> {
    case loading
    case loaded(Value)
    case failed(Error)
}

struct OrdersView: View {
    @State private var state: LoadState<[String]> = .loading

    var body: some View {
        Group {
            switch state {
            case .loading:
                List(0..<4, id: \.self) { _ in
                    Text("Placeholder order")
                }
                .redacted(reason: .placeholder)
            case .loaded(let orders) where orders.isEmpty:
                ContentUnavailableView(
                    "No Orders",
                    systemImage: "bag",
                    description: Text("Orders you place appear here.")
                )
            case .loaded(let orders):
                List(orders, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
            case .failed:
                ContentUnavailableView {
                    Label("Couldn't Load Orders", systemImage: "wifi.exclamationmark")
                } description: {
                    Text("Check your connection and try again.")
                } actions: {
                    Button("Try Again") { Task { await load() } }
                }
            }
        }
        .task { await load() }
    }

    func load() async {
        state = .loading
        do {
            state = .loaded(try await fetchOrders())
        } catch {
            // If the view went away, there's nothing to show.
            if !Task.isCancelled { state = .failed(error) }
        }
    }

    func fetchOrders() async throws -> [String] {
        try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1))
        return ["Coffee beans", "Oat milk"]
    }
}
```

**Important:** SwiftUI cancels `.task` when the view disappears, and a fetch that respects cancellation then throws. Check `Task.isCancelled` before you show an error, or people see “Couldn't load” for a screen they just left.

## Key APIs

- `.task { }`: Runs async work as the view appears.
- `.task(id:) { }`: Cancels and restarts the work when `id` changes.
- `.redacted(reason: .placeholder)`: Draws views as gray placeholders.
- `ProgressView(value:total:)`: A bar that fills as work completes.
- `ProgressView()`: A spinner, for work of unknown length.
- `ContentUnavailableView`: Empty and error states with an action.
- `.refreshable { }`: Adds pull to refresh to a `List`.

## Variants

### Placeholders

Add `.redacted(reason: .placeholder)` to real rows with sample data to get a skeleton of the screen.

```swift
@State private var isLoading = true

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
    Label("Coffee beans, 1 kg", systemImage: "bag")
    Label("Oat milk, 6 pack", systemImage: "bag")
    Label("Paper filters", systemImage: "bag")
}
.redacted(reason: isLoading ? .placeholder : [])

Toggle("Loading", isOn: $isLoading)
```

### Progress you can measure

Use `ProgressView(value:total:)` with a label when you know how much work is left.

```swift
@State private var done = 0

ProgressView(value: Double(done), total: 12) {
    Text("Downloading photos")
} currentValueLabel: {
    Text("\(done) of 12")
}
.task {
    while done < 12 {
        do { try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(0.4)) } catch { return }
        done += 1
    }
}
```

**Note:** Pace the bar evenly. Jumping to 90% and then sitting there for minutes feels like the app is stuck.

## Related

`progress-view`, `empty-state`, `async-image`, `lifecycle`, `launching`, `feedback`


<!-- topic: feedback -->
---
id: feedback
title: Feedback
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/sensoryfeedback(_:trigger:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/feedback.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Feedback

Tell people what happened, with an interruption that matches how much it matters.

Also called: toast, snackbar, banner, flash message, error message, success message, validation message, status message, notification, inline error.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Match the interruption to the importance.** Status and minor problems belong in the screen, near what they describe. Save alerts for things people must act on.
- **Say what happened and what to do next.** A specific title and a way forward help people recover. “Error” or a code number helps no one.
- **Don't rely on color alone.** Add a symbol and a short message to the red, so the problem is clear to everyone.
- **Don't warn about what people expect.** Deleting an email is what someone asked for, so it needs no alert, especially if they can undo (`undo-redo`). Warn only before loss that's unexpected and can't be undone.
- **Confirm only what matters.** People assume things worked. Confirm big moments, like a payment, and always tell people when something failed and why.
- **Use haptics for their meaning, alongside the visuals.** `.success` means success everywhere. A haptic backs up what's on screen; it's never the only signal. See Haptics (`haptics`).

## Pitfalls

- **Toasts are up to you.** For a web-style toast or snackbar, show a small banner with `.safeAreaInset`, or put the status in the toolbar.
- **Feedback has to reach everyone.** Pair color with words or a symbol, so it still works with the sound off, eyes elsewhere, or VoiceOver on.

## Guide

Feedback tells people the status of something, whether an action worked, or that something needs their attention. The rule of thumb: the more it matters, the more it may interrupt. Most feedback should be quiet and sit right next to what it's about.

## Key APIs

- `.sensoryFeedback(_:trigger:)`: Plays a haptic when a value changes.
- `.alert(_:isPresented:)`: Interrupts for critical, actionable news.
- `.safeAreaInset(edge:)`: Pins a banner above or below content.
- `ToolbarItem(placement: .status)`: Quiet status text in the toolbar.
- `ContentUnavailableView`: A whole screen that couldn't load.

## Variants

### Inline validation

Check a field when people leave it, and show the problem right under it with a symbol and words.

```swift
@State private var email = ""
@FocusState private var isEditing: Bool

var isValid: Bool {
    email.contains("@") && email.contains(".")
}

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 6) {
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .keyboardType(.emailAddress)
        .textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
        .focused($isEditing)
        .padding(10)
        .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 10))
    if !isEditing && !email.isEmpty && !isValid {
        Label("Enter a complete email address.", systemImage: "exclamationmark.circle")
            .font(.footnote)
            .foregroundStyle(.red)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Waiting until people leave the field avoids flagging an address they're still typing. See Entering Data (`entering-data`).

### Success you can feel

Swap the button's label when a big task finishes, and add `.sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger:)` to back it up.

```swift
@State private var isPaid = false

Button {
    isPaid = true
} label: {
    Label(isPaid ? "Paid" : "Pay $24.00",
          systemImage: isPaid ? "checkmark.circle.fill" : "creditcard")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
}
.buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
.tint(isPaid ? .green : .accentColor)
.disabled(isPaid)
.sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger: isPaid)
```

### Banner for a problem that doesn't block

Pin a short message with `.safeAreaInset(edge: .top)` and keep showing what you have.

```swift
@State private var isOffline = true

List(["Groceries", "Errands", "Work"], id: \.self) { list in
    Text(list)
}
.safeAreaInset(edge: .top) {
    if isOffline {
        Label("You're offline. Showing saved lists.", systemImage: "wifi.slash")
            .font(.subheadline)
            .padding(10)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
            .background(.yellow.opacity(0.25))
    }
}
```

### Alert for what can't wait

Use `.alert` when people must decide something now. Name the problem and give a specific way out.

```swift
@State private var saveFailed = false

Button("Save Draft") { saveFailed = true }
    .alert("Couldn't Save Draft", isPresented: $saveFailed) {
        Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { }
        Button("Try Again") { }
    } message: {
        Text("The server didn't respond. Your text is still here.")
    }
```

**Note:** Button titles say what happens, like Try Again or Delete. Use “OK” only in alerts that just inform. See Alert (`alert`).

### Status in the toolbar

Put ongoing status, like the last sync time, in a `ToolbarItem(placement: .status)` where people can check it.

```swift
List(["Inbox", "Sent", "Archive"], id: \.self) { box in
    Text(box)
}
.navigationTitle("Mail")
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .status) {
        VStack {
            Text("Updated Just Now").font(.caption)
            Text("3 Unread").font(.caption2).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`haptics`, `alert`, `confirmation-dialog`, `text-field`, `entering-data`, `undo-redo`


<!-- topic: entering-data -->
---
id: entering-data
title: Entering Data
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/keyboardtype(_:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/entering-data.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Entering Data

Ask for less, show the right keyboard, and catch mistakes while people type.

Also called: form input, input type, inputmode, autocomplete, keyboard type, <input type="email">, autofill, one-time code, form validation, return key.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Offer choices instead of typing.** Picking from a short list is faster and can't be misspelled. Use a Picker (`picker`) or DatePicker (`date-picker`) when the answers are known.
- **Make clear what goes in each field.** Give each field a label and a sample value in the prompt, like `name@example.com`, so people know the format.
- **Check values as soon as people enter them.** Point out a problem next to the field right away, not in a list after they tap Submit. Keep Continue disabled until the required fields are filled in.
- **Get it from the system when you can.** Don't ask for what iOS already knows. Content types let people AutoFill names, addresses, passwords, and one-time codes.
- **Hide secrets, and never prefill a password.** Use a SecureField (`secure-field`) for passwords, and let people type it or use AutoFill, Face ID, or a passkey.

## Pitfalls

- **`.keyboardType` is HTML's `inputmode`, and `.textContentType` is `autocomplete`.** The first picks the keys; the second tells iOS what the field is, so it can offer AutoFill.
- **Validate the value, not the keys.** A keyboard type only picks which keys show first. People can still paste anything, so check what arrives.

## Guide

Typing on a phone is slow and easy to get wrong. Ask only for what you can't get another way, offer choices instead of blank fields, and tell iOS what each field is for. It then shows the right keyboard and can fill the value in for people.

## Key APIs

- `.keyboardType(.emailAddress)`: Picks the keys: email, numbers, phone.
- `.textContentType(_:)`: Says what the field is, for AutoFill.
- `.textInputAutocapitalization`: `.never` turns off the automatic shift key.
- `.autocorrectionDisabled()`: Stops autocorrect on names and codes.
- `.submitLabel(.next)`: Changes the Return key's title.
- `.onSubmit { }`: Runs when people tap Return.
- `TextField(_:value:format:)`: Edits a number, date, or currency.

## Variants

### The right keyboard for each field

Pair `.keyboardType` with `.textContentType` so people get the right keys and AutoFill. Tap a field to see its keyboard.

```swift
@State private var email = ""
@State private var phone = ""
@State private var code = ""

Form {
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .keyboardType(.emailAddress)
        .textContentType(.emailAddress)
        .textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
        .autocorrectionDisabled()
    TextField("Phone", text: $phone)
        .keyboardType(.phonePad)
        .textContentType(.telephoneNumber)
    TextField("Code", text: $code)
        .keyboardType(.numberPad)
        .textContentType(.oneTimeCode)
}
```

**Important:** Turn off capitalization and autocorrect for emails, usernames, and codes. Otherwise iOS “fixes” them as people type.

### Choose instead of type

Use a `DatePicker` or `Picker` when the answers are known. There's nothing to misspell.

```swift
@State private var date = Date.now
@State private var guests = 2

Form {
    DatePicker("Date", selection: $date, displayedComponents: .date)
    Picker("Guests", selection: $guests) {
        ForEach(1...8, id: \.self) { Text("\($0)") }
    }
}
```

### Return moves to the next field

Set `.submitLabel(.next)` and move focus (`focus-state`) in `.onSubmit`, so people never reach for the screen.

```swift
enum Field { case name, email }
@State private var name = ""
@State private var email = ""
@FocusState private var focus: Field?

Form {
    TextField("Name", text: $name)
        .textContentType(.name)
        .focused($focus, equals: .name)
        .submitLabel(.next)
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .textContentType(.emailAddress)
        .keyboardType(.emailAddress)
        .focused($focus, equals: .email)
        .submitLabel(.done)
}
.onSubmit {
    focus = focus == .name ? .email : nil
}
```

### Numbers and money

Give `TextField` a `value` and a `format` and it accepts and shows numbers, here as currency.

```swift
@State private var amount = 12.5

TextField("Amount", value: $amount, format: .currency(code: "USD"))
    .keyboardType(.decimalPad)
```

**Note:** If people type something the format can't read, the bound value stays as it was.

### Continue only when ready

Show problems next to the field, and disable Continue until the required values are valid.

```swift
@State private var email = ""
@State private var agreed = false

var isValid: Bool {
    email.contains("@") && email.contains(".") && agreed
}

Form {
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .keyboardType(.emailAddress)
        .textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
    Toggle("I agree to the terms", isOn: $agreed)
    Button("Continue") { }
        .disabled(!isValid)
}
```

## Related

`form`, `text-field`, `secure-field`, `focus-state`, `picker`, `date-picker`, `login-form`, `feedback`


<!-- topic: modality -->
---
id: modality
title: Modality
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/fullscreencover(ispresented:ondismiss:content:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Modality

When to use a sheet, full-screen cover, alert, or popover, and how people get out.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Always give an obvious way out.** People look for buttons at the top of a sheet, and expect to swipe it down. If there's a Done button, pair it with Cancel so finishing isn't the only exit.
- **Ask before throwing away work.** If closing would lose what people typed, whether by button or by swipe, ask first and offer to keep editing or discard.
- **Keep it short, and name the task.** A modal is a quick detour. A clear title, like “New Event”, helps people remember why they're there; a deep hierarchy inside makes them forget.
- **Show one at a time.** Close a sheet before you open another. Only an alert may appear on top of a modal, and never two alerts at once.
- **Use popovers on iPad, sheets on iPhone.** A popover is for a few options in a wide layout. On iPhone, SwiftUI shows a popover as a sheet, which is usually what you want.

## Pitfalls

- **Push for drill-down, present for a side task.** Use a NavigationStack (`navigation-stack`) push to go deeper into content, and a modal to step aside for a moment, like opening a `<dialog>` on the web.
- **`dismiss` closes whatever presented the view.** Read `@Environment(\.dismiss)` inside the sheet or cover, not in the view that opened it.

## Guide

A modal view takes people out of what they were doing until they finish or close it. That focus is useful for a short task or a critical choice, and annoying for anything else. Present modally only when it clearly helps, and always make the way out obvious.

## Key APIs

`.sheet(isPresented:)`, `.fullScreenCover(isPresented:)`, `.popover(isPresented:)`, `.confirmationDialog(...)`, `@Environment(\.dismiss)`, `.interactiveDismissDisabled()`, `Button(role: .confirm)`

## Variants

### Sheet with Cancel and Done

Put Cancel on the leading side and Done on the trailing side, using the `.cancellationAction` and `.confirmationAction` placements.

```swift
struct NewEventSheet: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss
    @State private var title = ""

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            Form {
                TextField("Title", text: $title)
            }
            .navigationTitle("New Event")
            .navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
            .toolbar {
                ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) {
                    Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { dismiss() }
                }
                ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction) {
                    Button("Done", role: .confirm) { dismiss() }
                        .disabled(title.isEmpty)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

// In the presenting view:
// .sheet(isPresented: $isAdding) { NewEventSheet() }
```

### Protect unsaved changes

Block the swipe with `.interactiveDismissDisabled`, and ask with a `.confirmationDialog` before Cancel throws away text.

```swift
struct NoteSheet: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss
    @State private var text = ""
    @State private var confirmDiscard = false

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            TextEditor(text: $text)
                .navigationTitle("New Note")
                .navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
                .toolbar {
                    ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) {
                        Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) {
                            if text.isEmpty { dismiss() } else { confirmDiscard = true }
                        }
                        .confirmationDialog("Discard this note?", isPresented: $confirmDiscard) {
                            Button("Discard Note", role: .destructive) { dismiss() }
                            Button("Keep Editing", role: .cancel) { }
                        }
                    }
                    ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction) {
                        Button("Save", role: .confirm) { dismiss() }
                    }
                }
        }
        .interactiveDismissDisabled(!text.isEmpty)
    }
}
```

### Full-screen cover

Use `.fullScreenCover` for immersive content. It can't be swiped away, so add a clear close button.

```swift
@State private var isViewing = false

Button("View Photo") { isViewing = true }
    .fullScreenCover(isPresented: $isViewing) {
        NavigationStack {
            Image(systemName: "photo")
                .font(.system(size: 120))
                .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
                .toolbar {
                    Button("Close", systemImage: "xmark", role: .close) {
                        isViewing = false
                    }
                }
        }
    }
```

### Popover that adapts

A `.popover` points at its button on iPad and turns into a sheet on iPhone, so one modifier fits both.

```swift
@State private var showsFilters = false

Button("Filters", systemImage: "line.3.horizontal.decrease") {
    showsFilters = true
}
.popover(isPresented: $showsFilters) {
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Toggle("Unread Only", isOn: .constant(true))
        Toggle("With Attachments", isOn: .constant(false))
    }
    .padding()
    .frame(minWidth: 260)
    .presentationDetents([.medium])
}
```

**Note:** Adding `.presentationCompactAdaptation` with `.popover` keeps a real popover on iPhone, but small screens are usually better served by the sheet.

## Related

`sheet`, `alert`, `popover`, `confirmation-dialog`, `feedback`, `navigation-stack`


<!-- topic: undo-redo -->
---
id: undo-redo
title: Undo and Redo
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS, macOS]
availability: iOS 13.0+, macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environmentvalues/undomanager.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/undo-and-redo.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Undo and Redo

Let people take back what they did, instead of asking “Are you sure?” first.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- On macOS
- Related

## Rules

- **Offer undo instead of asking first.** For everyday deletes, just do it and let people undo. A confirmation every time slows people down, and they soon tap through it without reading.
- **Say what will be undone.** On iPhone, shaking shows an alert titled “Undo” plus your action name. One or two words, like “Delete Bread”, tell people exactly what comes back.
- **Show what changed.** If the undone change is off screen, scroll to it or highlight it. Otherwise people think nothing happened and undo again.
- **Let people undo many times.** Don't cap the history without a reason. People expect to step back through everything since they opened or saved their work.
- **Keep the system gestures, and add buttons only if needed.** Don't reuse shake or the three-finger swipe for anything else. If you add Undo and Redo buttons, put them in the toolbar with the standard symbols.

## Pitfalls

- **Register undo for your own changes.** Deleting or moving rows can't be undone unless you register it. Text fields manage typing themselves, so try shake to undo in yours to confirm it behaves as you expect.
- **`undoManager` can be `nil`.** It is where undo isn't supported, so call it with `?.` and skip registering.
- **Still confirm what can't be undone.** For a rare, permanent action, like deleting an account, a confirmation dialog (`confirmation-dialog`) is still the right call.

## Guide

Undo lets people try things without fear. People shake their iPhone, swipe with three fingers, or press ⌘Z on an iPad keyboard. SwiftUI hands you the window's `UndoManager`, and you tell it how to reverse each change.

Delete a few items, then tap **Undo** and **Redo**. The button shows the name you set with `setActionName`.

```swift
@MainActor @Observable
final class Groceries {
    var items = ["Apples", "Bread", "Coffee", "Eggs"]

    func remove(_ item: String, undoManager: UndoManager?) {
        guard let index = items.firstIndex(of: item) else { return }
        items.remove(at: index)
        undoManager?.registerUndo(withTarget: self) { list in
            list.insert(item, at: index, undoManager: undoManager)
        }
        undoManager?.setActionName("Delete \(item)")
    }

    func insert(_ item: String, at index: Int, undoManager: UndoManager?) {
        items.insert(item, at: index)
        // Registering here is what makes Redo work.
        undoManager?.registerUndo(withTarget: self) { list in
            list.remove(item, undoManager: undoManager)
        }
        undoManager?.setActionName("Delete \(item)")
    }
}

struct GroceryList: View {
    @State private var groceries = Groceries()
    @Environment(\.undoManager) private var undoManager

    var body: some View {
        List {
            ForEach(groceries.items, id: \.self) { item in
                Text(item)
            }
            .onDelete { offsets in
                for item in offsets.map({ groceries.items[$0] }) {
                    groceries.remove(item, undoManager: undoManager)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**Important:** `registerUndo` needs a class to call back, so keep the data in an `@Observable` class, not in `@State` structs. Register the reverse step inside the undo handler, too, or Redo stays grayed out.

## Key APIs

`@Environment(\.undoManager)`, `registerUndo(withTarget:handler:)`, `setActionName(_:)`, `undo()` and `redo()`, `canUndo` and `canRedo`, `beginUndoGrouping()`, `removeAllActions(withTarget:)`

## On macOS

Let people take back any change with ⌘Z, and tell them what they're undoing.

### Rules

- **Keep Undo and Redo at the top of the Edit menu.** Mac users look for them there, and press ⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z without looking.
- **Don't limit undo without reason.** People expect to undo everything since they opened or saved the document.
- **Undo a burst of small changes as one.** Dragging a slider makes many tiny changes. Record one undo for the whole drag, so one ⌘Z puts it back.
- **Add undo buttons only when you must.** The Edit menu and ⌘Z are where people go. If your app needs buttons too, put them in the toolbar with the standard symbols.

### Pitfalls

- **The window brings the undo manager.** Read `\.undoManager` from the environment. It's `nil` where undo isn't supported, so skip registering then.
- **Undo registers redo for you.** When an undo runs code that registers its own undo, that becomes the redo. Write each change as a method that registers its opposite.

### Key APIs

`undoMenuItemTitle`, `canUndo` / `canRedo`

More variants, left out to keep this file short: One undo for a whole drag (macOS), Undo and redo buttons, when you need them (macOS). Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environmentvalues/undomanager.md

## Related

`confirmation-dialog`, `alert`, `list`, `swipe-actions`, `toolbar`, `feedback`, `menu-bar-conventions`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `commands`, `document-editor`


<!-- topic: requesting-permission -->
---
id: requesting-permission
title: Requesting Permission
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/requesting-access-to-protected-resources.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Requesting Permission

Ask for access when a feature needs it, say why, and handle “no” gracefully.

Also called: permission prompt, permissions, authorization, purpose string, usage description, Info.plist, NSCameraUsageDescription, camera permission, location permission, pre-permission.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Ask when people use the feature, not at launch.** A prompt makes sense right after someone taps Scan Receipt. On first launch it's a mystery, unless the app can't work at all without it.
- **Write a purpose string that says exactly why.** The system prompt shows your sentence under its title. Make it one specific, complete sentence about what people get.
- **Give an explanation screen one button: Continue.** If you explain before the prompt, the only button should open it. A button called Allow, or a way to skip, steers people, and the HIG calls that manipulative.
- **Have a plan for “Don't Allow”.** Keep the rest of the app working and offer another way, like typing an address when location is off. As of 2026, App Review Guideline 5.1.1(iv) asks for this.
- **Ask only for what the feature needs.** Don't require the microphone to post a photo. As of 2026, Guideline 5.1.1(iv) forbids pushing people into access a feature doesn't need.

## Pitfalls

- **A missing purpose string is a crash and a rejection.** Without the Info.plist key, the access attempt fails and may crash, and App Review rejects the build. That includes APIs used by SDKs you add.
- **You usually get one prompt.** After people answer, the system remembers and doesn't ask again. Only Settings can change it, and people can change it there at any time.
- **Sometimes a picker beats a permission.** As of 2026, Guideline 5.1.1(iii) asks you to use a system picker or share sheet, like `PhotosPicker`, instead of full access to Photos or Contacts where you can.

## Guide

iOS guards the camera, microphone, location, photos, contacts, and more. The first time your app reaches for one, the system asks people with an alert that shows your own explanation, called a purpose string. Ask at the moment it makes sense, and design for both answers.

Tap **Scan Receipt** and answer the prompt, which is simulated here. Then try **Reset** and say no.

```swift
import AVFoundation
import SwiftUI

struct ScanReceiptButton: View {
    @State private var status = AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus(for: .video)
    @Environment(\.openURL) private var openURL

    var body: some View {
        switch status {
        case .authorized:
            Text("Camera ready") // Show your scanner here.
        case .denied, .restricted:
            ContentUnavailableView {
                Label("Camera Access Is Off", systemImage: "video.slash")
            } description: {
                Text("Turn on Camera in Settings to scan receipts, or add a photo instead.")
            } actions: {
                Button("Open Settings") {
                    if let url = URL(string: UIApplication.openSettingsURLString) {
                        openURL(url)
                    }
                }
            }
        default:
            Button("Scan Receipt", systemImage: "camera") {
                Task {
                    _ = await AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .video)
                    status = AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus(for: .video)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**Important:** Check the status every time the feature opens, not once at launch. People can turn access off in Settings whenever they like.

## Key APIs

`NSCameraUsageDescription`, `authorizationStatus(for:)`, `requestAccess(for:)`, `openSettingsURLString`, `LocationButton`, `PhotosPicker`

## Variants

### The purpose string

Add the usage description key for each resource to Info.plist. The system shows it in the prompt.

```xml
<!-- Info.plist -->
<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>Scan receipts to add expenses automatically.</string>
```

**Note:** In Xcode you can also add it in the target's Info tab, or as the `INFOPLIST_KEY_NSCameraUsageDescription` build setting. Localize it like any other text.

### An explanation screen, if you need one

When the context doesn't explain itself, show one screen with a single Continue button that opens the prompt.

```swift
VStack(spacing: 16) {
    Image(systemName: "doc.viewfinder")
        .font(.system(size: 56))
        .foregroundStyle(.tint)
    Text("Scan Receipts")
        .font(.title2.bold())
    Text("Point your camera at a receipt and Expenses fills in the amount and date for you.")
        .multilineTextAlignment(.center)
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Button("Continue") {
        Task { await AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .video) }
    }
    .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
.padding()
```

**Important:** Don't add Not Now, Close, or Cancel, and don't title the button Allow. As of 2026, the HIG says either one can feel manipulative, and App Review rejects misleading pre-prompt screens for tracking.

### Send people to Settings

When access is off, explain what it's for and open your app's Settings page with `openSettingsURLString`.

```swift
@Environment(\.openURL) private var openURL

Button("Open Settings") {
    if let url = URL(string: UIApplication.openSettingsURLString) {
        openURL(url)
    }
}
```

## Related

`onboarding`, `launching`, `alert`, `entering-data`, `privacy-details`


<!-- topic: submission-checklist -->
---
id: submission-checklist
title: Submission Checklist
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Submission Checklist

Everything to check before you tap Submit for Review, in one list.

Also called: pre-submit, before you submit, launch checklist, app store checklist, preflight, ready to ship, submit for review, Guideline 2.1, Guideline 2.3, Guideline 4.2.

## Pitfalls

- **Your checkmarks stay on this device.** Come back before every submission and tap Reset when you start the next version.
- **Updates get reviewed too.** Every new version goes through App Review, so run the list again for updates, not only for your first release.

## Guide

App Review checks your app, its App Store listing, and the information you give reviewers. This list collects the common missteps Apple says slow down review or cause a rejection. Tick each item off, and tap **Read** for the details.

**Important:** As of 2026, Apple says over 40% of unresolved review issues fall under guideline 2.1, App Completeness: crashes, placeholder content, broken links, and missing review information.

### The app

- **Test on a real device**: Fix crashes and bugs on the latest iOS. Reviewers use real devices and real networks. (`testflight`)
- **Try it on iPad**: iPhone apps can run on iPad in compatibility mode, so make sure nothing breaks there.
- **Remove placeholder content**: No lorem ipsum, test images, or empty “coming soon” screens. (`states-check`)
- **Handle empty, loading, and error states**: No blank screens or raw error codes. (`states-check`)
- **Check that every link works**: Including your support and privacy policy links.
- **Make it more than a website**: A repackaged website or a collection of links fails guideline 4.2. (`native-not-web`)
- **Test Dark Mode and the largest text**: Every screen should stay readable in both. (`appearance-check`)
- **Include a launch screen**: As of iOS 27, Apple's TN3192 says it's required for App Store submission. (`launching`)

### Accounts, privacy, and payments

- **Let people delete their account**: Required in the app if people can create an account there. Guideline 5.1.1(v). (`delete-account`)
- **Offer an equivalent login option**: If you use a third-party or social login. Guideline 4.8. (`sign-in-with-apple`)
- **Link your privacy policy**: In the app and in App Store Connect. Guideline 5.1.1(i). (`privacy-details`)
- **Explain every permission request**: Each purpose string says clearly why you need the data. Guideline 5.1.1(ii). (`requesting-permission`)
- **Sell digital content with In-App Purchase**: Not license keys or your own checkout. Guideline 3.1.1. (`paywall`)

### App Store Connect

- **Make the listing match the app**: Description, screenshots, and previews show what the app really does. Guideline 2.3. (`rejection-guide`)
- **Add a support URL with real contact details**: People and App Review need a way to reach you.
- **Answer the privacy questions accurately**: Your privacy information is metadata too. Guideline 2.3. (`privacy-details`)
- **Build with the required SDK**: As of April 28, 2026, uploads must use Xcode 26 or later and the iOS 26 SDK. (`releasing`)

### Review information

- **Add a working demo account**: If the app has a login. The credentials must not expire. (`app-review`)
- **Write clear review notes**: Explain non-obvious features, hardware, and in-app purchases. (`app-review`)
- **Keep your backend running**: Servers must be live and reachable during review. (`app-review`)
- **Check your contact details**: A name, email, and phone number App Review can use. (`app-review`)
- **Pick a release option**: Manual, automatic, or automatic after a date. (`releasing`)

## Related

`rejection-guide`, `app-review`, `testflight`, `releasing`

# Common Rejections

The guidelines apps break most often, what each means, and how to fix it.

Also called: rejected, rejection, app store rejection, why was my app rejected, app review guidelines, guideline numbers, metadata rejected, Guideline 2.1, Guideline 2.3, Guideline 2.3.3.

## Pitfalls

- **The rejection message names the guideline.** Start with that number, fix everything it lists, and reply in App Store Connect if anything is unclear.
- **The guidelines change.** Apple calls them a living document. As of October 2026, the latest update is dated June 8, 2026.

## Guide

Every rejection message cites one or more numbered App Review Guidelines. A few numbers come up again and again. Find yours below, then fix the cause, not just the symptom.

### How often apps are rejected

In 2025, Apple reviewed **9,100,620** app submissions and rejected **2,093,244** of them. Performance problems, the section that includes 2.1, led by far:

**Note:** One submission can break several guidelines, so the sections add up to more than the total. The Design section covers copycats, minimum functionality, and spam.

### The usual suspects

Tap a guideline to see what it means and how to fix it.

## Related

`submission-checklist`, `app-review`, `native-not-web`, `states-check`


<!-- topic: native-not-web -->
---
id: native-not-web
title: Native, Not Web
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Native, Not Web

What makes an app feel like a website in a frame, and how to fix it.

Also called: web wrapper, webview, WKWebView, website in an app, wrapped website, PWA, hybrid app, hamburger menu, breadcrumbs, app-like.

## Rules

- **Put top-level sections in a tab bar.** People expect to switch sections from the bottom of the screen with one tap. A hamburger menu hides them behind an extra step.
- **Use the system navigation bar.** People expect a Back button at the top and a swipe from the edge to go back. `NavigationStack` gives you both; a web header doesn't.
- **Use system controls, not web form inputs.** A `Toggle` and a `Picker` look and behave the way they do in every other app, so nobody has to learn your version.
- **Format content for iPhone.** Apple names web content that isn't formatted for iOS as a reason apps fail. Use readable rows, not a desktop page squeezed down.

## Pitfalls

- **Use what iPhone already offers.** The HIG points to features like widgets, Siri shortcuts, Face ID sign-in, and swiping back as what makes an app feel at home.
- **Ask what the app adds.** If it offers nothing beyond what your website shows in Safari, expect App Review to ask the same question under 4.2.

## Guide

### What Apple requires

Guideline **4.2, Minimum Functionality**, asks for features, content, and interface that go beyond a repackaged website. Apps that are mostly marketing, web clippings, content aggregators, or a collection of links don't qualify (4.2.2). Guideline **4.0** sets a minimum bar for clean, easy-to-use design.

### Why

People already have Safari. They download an app because it does more, and because it works like the rest of their iPhone: tabs at the bottom, swipe to go back, system controls, Dark Mode, and their chosen text size.

## Key APIs

- `TabView` + `Tab`: Top-level sections in a bottom tab bar.
- `NavigationStack`: Push and pop screens, with back swipe.
- `NavigationLink`: A row or button that pushes a screen.
- `Toggle`: A system on/off switch.
- `Picker`: A choice from a list, instead of a select.
- `.swipeActions`: Row actions people reveal by swiping.
- `.refreshable`: Pull to refresh on a list.

## Variants

### Sections in a tab bar

Use `TabView` with one `Tab` per section, and give each tab its own `NavigationStack`.

```swift
TabView {
    Tab("Shop", systemImage: "bag") {
        NavigationStack {
            List(products) { product in
                NavigationLink(product.name) {
                    ProductView(product: product)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Shop")
        }
    }
    Tab("Orders", systemImage: "shippingbox") {
        NavigationStack {
            OrdersView()
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** Each tab keeps its own navigation history, so switching tabs and coming back returns people to where they were.

### System controls in a form

Use `Form` with `Toggle` and `Picker` instead of drawing web-style checkboxes and select boxes.

```swift
@State private var emailMe = true
@State private var size = "Medium"

Form {
    Toggle("Email Me Updates", isOn: $emailMe)
    Picker("Size", selection: $size) {
        ForEach(["Small", "Medium", "Large"], id: \.self) {
            Text($0)
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`tab-view`, `navigation-stack`, `form`, `toggle`, `picker`, `appearance-check`, `rejection-guide`


<!-- topic: appearance-check -->
---
id: appearance-check
title: Dark Mode & Large Text
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/dynamictypesize.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/dark-mode.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Dark Mode & Large Text

Before you submit, check every screen in Dark Mode and at the largest text size.

Also called: dark mode, dark theme, prefers-color-scheme, light mode, dynamic type, font scaling, rem, text size, larger text, accessibility sizes.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Follow the system appearance.** People set light or dark for the whole phone. An app-only appearance setting means more work for them, and an app that ignores the setting looks broken.
- **Keep contrast high in both modes.** The HIG asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and suggests 7:1 for custom colors, especially in small text. System label colors are a safe start.
- **Don't cut text off at large sizes.** At the largest sizes, show as much text as at the default size. Stack items vertically instead of truncating them.

## Pitfalls

- **Test on a device too.** Turn on Larger Accessibility Sizes in Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text, then drag the slider to the end.
- **Increase Contrast changes things again.** The HIG suggests checking Dark Mode with Increase Contrast and Reduce Transparency on, separately and together.

## Guide

People pick Dark Mode and their text size once, for the whole phone, and expect every app to follow. Bugs here are easy to miss, because you probably develop in light mode at the default size. Make these two checks part of every submission.

Switch the screen below between broken and fixed, then turn on Dark Mode and the largest text.

**Important:** Hard-coded `Color.black` text disappears in Dark Mode, and `.system(size:)` fonts stay the same size when people pick larger text (try AX5 above). Both look fine until someone changes a setting.

### Before you submit

- **All text is readable in Dark Mode**: No dark text on a dark background. (`dark-mode`)
- **Images and icons show up on dark backgrounds**: Check logos and illustrations with transparent edges.
- **Text grows at the largest sizes**: Every label uses a text style, not a fixed point size. (`dynamic-type`)
- **Nothing important is cut off**: Rows stack, and buttons stay on screen and tappable.
- **The app follows the system setting**: No separate light/dark switch that overrides it.

## Key APIs

- `.dynamicTypeSize(_:)`: Sets or limits the text size for a view.
- `\.dynamicTypeSize`: Reads the person's current text size.
- `.isAccessibilitySize`: True for the five largest sizes.
- `.preferredColorScheme(_:)`: Forces light or dark, for previews.
- `\.colorScheme`: Reads whether the view is light or dark.
- `ViewThatFits`: Picks the first layout that fits.

## Variants

### Preview both in Xcode

Add a second `#Preview` with `.preferredColorScheme(.dark)` and a large `.dynamicTypeSize` to see both while you work.

```swift
#Preview("Light") {
    OrderSummary()
}

#Preview("Dark, largest text") {
    OrderSummary()
        .preferredColorScheme(.dark)
        .dynamicTypeSize(.accessibility3)
}
```

### Colors that adapt

Use `.primary`, `.secondary`, and `.fill` styles instead of fixed colors. They switch automatically between light and dark.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Deliver to")
    Text("12 Harbour St")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.padding()
.background(.fill.tertiary,
            in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

### A row that stacks when text is large

Wrap a row in `ViewThatFits`. It uses the side-by-side layout when it fits, and the stacked one when it doesn't.

```swift
ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
    HStack {
        Text("Deliver to")
        Spacer()
        Text("12 Harbour St")
    }
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Deliver to")
        Text("12 Harbour St")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
```

**Note:** For bigger changes, read `@Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize)` and check `.isAccessibilitySize` to switch layouts yourself.

## Related

`dark-mode`, `dynamic-type`, `system-colors`, `typography`, `view-that-fits`, `states-check`


<!-- topic: states-check -->
---
id: states-check
title: Empty, Loading & Error
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/contentunavailableview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/loading.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Empty, Loading & Error

Give every screen an empty, loading, and error state, and ship no placeholders.

Also called: empty state, loading state, error state, skeleton, skeleton screen, spinner, placeholder, lorem ipsum, zero state, offline.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Never ship placeholder content.** Apple rejects apps with placeholder text or images under guideline 2.1. Search your project for “lorem” and “TODO” before you submit.
- **Show something right away.** The HIG warns that a blank screen looks like a broken app. Show a skeleton or a spinner while content loads.
- **Say what went wrong and what to do next.** An error should explain the problem in plain words and offer a way out, like Try Again.

## Pitfalls

- **Test with no network.** Turn on Airplane Mode and open every screen. Reviewers use real networks, and yours won't always be fast.
- **Test as a brand-new user.** A fresh account has no data, so every list starts empty. That's the first thing a reviewer with a demo account may see.

## Guide

### What Apple requires

Guideline **2.1, App Completeness**, says to submit a final version: no placeholder text, empty websites, or other temporary content, and nothing that crashes or shows obvious technical problems. As of 2026, Apple says this guideline is behind over 40% of unresolved review issues.

### Why

Real data is messy. Lists are empty on day one, networks drop, and servers fail. A screen that only handles the happy path shows a blank page or a spinner forever, and people assume the app is broken.

One screen, four states. Tap through them, or let it cycle.

### Before you submit

- **No placeholder text or images**: Search for “lorem”, “TODO”, and test images.
- **Every list has an empty state**: Explain what goes there and how to add the first item. (`empty-state`)
- **Every load shows progress**: A skeleton or spinner, never a blank screen. (`progress-view`)
- **Every error explains itself**: Plain words and a way to try again.
- **The app works offline, or says why it can't**: Open every screen in Airplane Mode.
- **Every link and button goes somewhere**: No dead links or “coming soon” screens.

## Key APIs

- `ContentUnavailableView`: Empty, no-results, and error screens.
- `.search(text:)`: A ready-made “No Results” view.
- `ProgressView`: A spinner or progress bar.
- `.redacted(reason:)`: Turns content into a skeleton.
- `.task { }`: Starts loading when the view appears.
- `.refreshable { }`: Pull to refresh to try again.

## Variants

### Model the states

Keep the screen's state in one `enum` and `switch` over it, so the compiler makes you handle every case.

```swift
enum LoadState {
    case loading
    case loaded([String])
    case failed
}

@State private var state = LoadState.loading

var body: some View {
    switch state {
    case .loading:
        ProgressView()
    case .loaded(let names) where names.isEmpty:
        ContentUnavailableView("No Friends Yet",
            systemImage: "person.2",
            description: Text("Invite someone to get started."))
    case .loaded(let names):
        List(names, id: \.self) { Text($0) }
    case .failed:
        ContentUnavailableView("Couldn't Load Friends",
            systemImage: "wifi.slash")
    }
}
```

**Note:** Start loading in `.task { }` on the view. It starts before the view appears, and SwiftUI cancels it if the view goes away first.

### A skeleton while loading

Add `.redacted(reason: .placeholder)` to sample rows so people see the layout before the data arrives.

```swift
List(sampleNames, id: \.self) { name in
    Label(name, systemImage: "person.crop.circle")
}
.redacted(reason: isLoading ? .placeholder : [])
```

**Important:** Redacted sample rows are fine while loading. Make sure they never stay on screen as the final content.

## Related

`empty-state`, `progress-view`, `async-image`, `submission-checklist`, `rejection-guide`


<!-- topic: testflight -->
---
id: testflight
title: TestFlight
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/test-a-beta-version/testflight-overview/
reviewed: October 2026
---

# TestFlight

Share beta builds with your team and up to 10,000 outside testers.

Also called: beta, beta testing, beta testers, staging, preview build, internal testers, external testers, public link, build expired, TestFlight App Review.

## Rules

- **Use TestFlight for betas, not the App Store.** Guideline 2.2 says demos, betas, and trial versions don't belong on the App Store. A TestFlight build should still be meant for public release and follow the guidelines.
- **Don't pay testers.** Guideline 2.2 doesn't allow giving TestFlight builds in exchange for any compensation, including as a reward for crowdfunding.
- **Tell testers what to test.** The What to Test notes appear in the TestFlight app. Specific requests get specific feedback.

## Pitfalls

- **Testers get up to 30 devices.** Each tester can install your beta on up to 30 of their devices.
- **Rating prompts don't show in TestFlight.** `requestReview` has no effect in TestFlight builds, so test it in development instead.
- **Review has a daily limit.** As of 2026, you can submit up to six builds for TestFlight App Review in 24 hours.

## Guide

TestFlight is Apple's beta testing service. You upload a build to App Store Connect, add testers, and they install it with the free TestFlight app and send feedback with screenshots. It's also the easiest way to test on the real devices App Review will use.

### Internal vs. external testers

**Note:** To create an external group, you first need an internal group. Builds you upload as TestFlight Internal Only can only go to internal groups.

### Builds expire after 90 days

Each build can be tested for up to 90 days. Upload a new build before then to keep testing. Pick an upload date to estimate when a build expires:

**Important:** If you don't expire a build yourself, testers can keep using it after the same version goes live on the App Store, until the 90 days are up.

## Related

`app-review`, `releasing`, `submission-checklist`


<!-- topic: app-review -->
---
id: app-review
title: App Review
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/
reviewed: October 2026
---

# App Review

What reviewers need from you, how long review takes, and what to do if you're rejected.

Also called: submit for review, review notes, demo account, test account, reviewer, review time, how long does review take, rejected, resolution center, appeal.

## Rules

- **Write review notes a stranger can follow.** The reviewer has never seen your app. Tell them where things are and how to reach features that need setup.
- **Appeal with specifics, not feelings.** Name the guideline, then explain point by point how the app meets it. Apple's own example of an incomplete appeal just asks them to take another look.

## Pitfalls

- **Book a call if you're unsure.** App Review offers 30-minute video appointments to talk through the guidelines before you submit.
- **Already on the store? Bug fixes aren't held up.** If a bug fix update is rejected for an unrelated issue, Apple may let it through and have you fix the issue next time, unless it's a legal or safety problem.

## Guide

App Review checks every new app and every update before it reaches the App Store. Your job is to make that check easy: a finished build, a way in, and notes that explain anything that isn't obvious.

### What reviewers need

Fill in the **App Review Information** section of your version in App Store Connect. Customers never see it.

**Important:** Use a demo account that won't expire, and keep your servers running during review. If sign-in also needs a code, put it in the notes, or review may wait for a call.

In the notes, Apple asks for your app's concept and audience, what changed in an update, the devices and iOS versions you tested, and any external services it relies on. For auto-renewable subscriptions, include an account with an expired subscription so the reviewer can see the whole purchase flow.

### How long it takes

As of 2026, Apple says it aims to review at least half of submissions within 24 hours and 90% within 48 hours. Apps with regulated content, new capabilities, or missing documents take longer. Tap a status to see what it means:

**Note:** Facing a critical bug or a dated event? You can request an expedited review after you submit. Save it for real emergencies.

### Appealing

Appeal when you believe the app follows the guidelines, the reviewer misunderstood it, or you were treated unfairly. Reply to the rejection first. Then send **one** appeal per rejected app that covers every cited guideline.

**Important:** Resubmitting starts a new review and closes your appeal. Don't do both.

## Related

`submission-checklist`, `rejection-guide`, `testflight`, `releasing`


<!-- topic: releasing -->
---
id: releasing
title: Releasing
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-your-apps-availability/select-an-app-store-version-release-option/
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Releasing

Choose when an approved version goes live, roll updates out slowly, and number builds right.

Also called: release, launch, go live, publish, deploy, phased release, staged rollout, gradual rollout, version number, build number.

## Rules

- **Ask for ratings after people succeed, not at launch.** The HIG suggests asking after someone completes a task or level. On first launch they haven't formed an opinion yet.

## Pitfalls

- **You can't roll back.** If a release has a problem, fix it in a new version and submit that. App Store Connect has no way to go back to the previous one.
- **Use the required SDK.** As of April 28, 2026, apps uploaded to App Store Connect must be built with Xcode 26 or later and the iOS 26 SDK.
- **Updates need What's New text.** It's required for every version after the first, up to 4,000 characters. Guideline 2.3.12 asks you to list significant changes there.

## Guide

Approval doesn't have to mean going live. In App Store Connect, each version has a release option, and updates can roll out to a few people at a time.

### When it goes live

Set this in the **App Store Version Release** section of the version before you submit. Pick an option to see what happens after approval:

**Note:** If a version sits in Pending Developer Release for more than 30 days, Apple emails you a reminder.

### Phased release for updates

For an update, you can turn on **phased release**. Over 7 days, the update goes to a growing random share of people who have automatic updates on. Drag through the week:

**Important:** Anyone can still download the update from the App Store by hand during the rollout. Phased release only slows automatic updates.

You can pause for up to 30 days in total if you spot a problem, and release to everyone at any time.

### Version and build numbers

Every upload has two numbers. The **version** is what people see on the App Store, written as three numbers like `1.2.0`. Its Info.plist key is `CFBundleShortVersionString`. The **build**, `CFBundleVersion`, identifies each upload. Increase the build every time you upload, and the version for each release.

### After launch

Then keep an eye on ratings and reviews in App Store Connect. You can post one public response per review; it can take up to 24 hours to appear.

## Key APIs

- `CFBundleShortVersionString`: The version people see, like 1.2.0.
- `CFBundleVersion`: The build string; unique per upload.
- `\.requestReview`: Asks StoreKit to show a rating prompt.

## Variants

### Show the version in Settings

Read both numbers from `Bundle.main` so people and your support team can tell which build they have.

```swift
let info = Bundle.main.infoDictionary
let version = info?["CFBundleShortVersionString"] as? String ?? "?"
let build = info?["CFBundleVersion"] as? String ?? "?"

Section {
    LabeledContent("Version", value: "\(version) (\(build))")
}
```

### Ask for a rating at the right moment

Read `requestReview` from the environment and call it after someone succeeds. StoreKit decides whether the prompt actually appears.

```swift
import StoreKit

@Environment(\.requestReview) private var requestReview
@State private var finishedTrips = 0

Button("Finish Trip") {
    finishedTrips += 1
}
.onChange(of: finishedTrips) { _, count in
    if count == 3 {
        requestReview()
    }
}
```

**Note:** As of 2026, StoreKit shows the prompt at most three times in 365 days to someone who hasn't rated the app on that device. The preview only shows when the call would happen.

## Related

`app-review`, `testflight`, `submission-checklist`


<!-- topic: sign-in-with-apple -->
---
id: sign-in-with-apple
title: Sign in with Apple
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 14.0+, macOS 11.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/signinwithapplebutton.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sign-in-with-apple.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Sign in with Apple

Apple's sign-in button, and when App Review expects you to offer it.

Also called: Guideline 4.8, login services, apple login, login with apple, continue with apple, social login, OAuth, SSO, single sign-on, ASAuthorizationAppleIDButton.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
SignInWithAppleButton(.signIn) { request in
    request.requestedScopes = [.fullName, .email]
} onCompletion: { result in
    switch result {
    case .success(let authorization):
        print(authorization.credential)
    case .failure(let error):
        print(error.localizedDescription)
    }
}
.signInWithAppleButtonStyle(.black)
.frame(height: 50)
```

**Important:** Add the **Sign in with Apple** capability to your target in Xcode's Signing & Capabilities tab. Without it the button still draws, but every request fails.

## Rules

- **Make it as big as your other sign-in buttons.** The HIG asks for a Sign in with Apple button no smaller than the others, visible without scrolling.
- **Pick the style that contrasts with the background.** Use `.black` on light backgrounds and `.white` on dark ones. `.whiteOutline` is for white backgrounds where plain white would vanish.
- **Ask people to sign in only when it's worth it.** Let people look around first, and say what an account gets them. Forcing sign-in on launch makes people leave.
- **Don't ask for a password or a “real” email afterwards.** Not needing a password is the point. If someone chose Hide My Email, respect the relay address instead of asking for their personal one.
- **Keep the button at least 140 × 30 points.** As of 2026, the HIG lists 140 pt wide and 30 pt tall as the minimum, with a margin of a tenth of the button's height around it.

## Pitfalls

- **Show which sign-in people used.** A line like “Using Sign in with Apple” in your account screen helps people remember how they signed up.
- **Revoke tokens when an account is deleted.** Apple's account deletion guidance asks apps that use Sign in with Apple to revoke the user's tokens with the Sign in with Apple REST API. See Delete Account (`delete-account`).

**Note:** You don't need a second option if your app uses only your own accounts (email and password, passkeys), or if people must sign in with an existing school, work, or government ID, or to the third-party service whose content the app shows, like a mail client.

## Key APIs

- `SignInWithAppleButton`: The system button. Takes a label, a request closure, and a completion closure.
- `.signInWithAppleButtonStyle(_:)`: `.black`, `.white`, or `.whiteOutline`.
- `.signIn`, `.signUp`, `.continue`: The three button titles.
- `requestedScopes`: Ask for `.fullName` and `.email`, or nothing.
- `ASAuthorizationAppleIDCredential`: The result: `user`, `email`, `fullName`, tokens.
- `getCredentialState(forUserID:)`: Checks if the Apple sign-in is still valid.

## Variants

### Next to other sign-in buttons

Give `SignInWithAppleButton` the same frame as your other providers, and put it where nobody has to scroll.

```swift
@Environment(\.colorScheme) private var colorScheme

VStack(spacing: 12) {
    SignInWithAppleButton(.continue) { request in
        request.requestedScopes = [.fullName, .email]
    } onCompletion: { result in
        // Handle the result
    }
    .signInWithAppleButtonStyle(colorScheme == .dark ? .white : .black)
    .frame(height: 50)

    Button {
        // Your Google sign-in
    } label: {
        Text("Continue with Google")
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
    }
    .buttonStyle(.bordered)
    .controlSize(.extraLarge)
}
```

**Important:** If Google or Facebook is your only login, App Review rejects the app under Guideline 4.8 until you add an equivalent option.

### Read the credential

On success, the credential is an `ASAuthorizationAppleIDCredential`. Its `user` id is stable, so key your account on it.

```swift
SignInWithAppleButton(.signIn) { request in
    request.requestedScopes = [.fullName, .email]
} onCompletion: { result in
    guard case .success(let authorization) = result,
          let credential = authorization.credential
            as? ASAuthorizationAppleIDCredential
    else { return }

    let userID = credential.user        // Always there
    let email = credential.email        // First time only
    let name = credential.fullName      // First time only
    // Send these to your server and save them now.
}
```

**Important:** The credential carries the name and email only the first time someone signs in. Store them right away: later sign-ins leave out the name, and the email comes only inside the identity token.

## Related

`login-form`, `delete-account`, `button`, `settings-screen`


<!-- topic: delete-account -->
---
id: delete-account
title: Delete Account
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/managing-accounts.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Delete Account

If people can create an account in your app, they must be able to delete it there too.

Also called: Guideline 5.1.1(v), 5.1.1(v), account deletion, delete my account, remove account, close account, deactivate account, right to be forgotten, GDPR, CCPA.

## Contents

- Rules
- Guide
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Put it where people look: account settings.** Apple asks for a deletion option that's easy to find, typically in your account settings. Don't bury it in the privacy policy or terms.
- **Delete the account, not just deactivate it.** You can offer a pause too, but deactivating or disabling alone doesn't meet the rule.
- **Don't send people to support.** Unless your app is in a highly regulated field like banking or health, you can't require a call, an email, or a chat. Asking for a code sent to their email or phone is fine.
- **Link straight to the web deletion page.** If deletion finishes on your website, link to that exact page, not your home page. Apple rejects flows that make deletion unnecessarily hard.
- **Say how long it takes, and confirm when it's done.** Manual deletion that takes a while is allowed, as long as people know what to expect and hear back at the end.

## Guide

### What Apple requires

As of 2026, App Review Guideline **5.1.1(v)** says that if your app supports account creation, people must be able to **start deleting their account from inside the app**. Deleting means removing the account and its personal data, except what you're legally required to keep.

**Note:** This includes accounts your app creates automatically, like guest accounts, and accounts people create through a link to your website. Supporting deletion only where the law requires it (GDPR, CCPA) isn't enough: it has to work for everyone.

### Why

People shared personal data with you to make the account. Letting them take it back, without hunting or emailing anyone, keeps that trust.

A complete flow: a row in Settings, a screen that says what happens, one confirmation, and a result. Tap **Delete Account** to walk through it.

### What to say

Keep each message short and specific:

• **What goes:** the account and everything in it, including posts and photos other people can see.

• **What stays:** anything the law makes you keep, and why.

• **Subscriptions:** billing continues through Apple until people cancel.

• **When:** how long it takes, and that you'll confirm when it's done.

**Note:** You may offer to schedule deletion for when a subscription ends, as long as people can also delete right away.

### Before you submit

- **Deletion starts inside the app**: Usually a Delete Account row in account settings. (`settings-screen`)
- **It deletes, not deactivates**: The account and the personal data you don't have to keep.
- **No call, email, or chat needed**: Only highly regulated apps (5.1.1(ix)) may use a support flow.
- **Web flows get a direct link**: To the deletion page itself, not your home page or policy.
- **Shared content goes too**: Posts, photos, and reviews other people can see.
- **Subscriptions are explained**: Billing continues through Apple until people cancel. (`paywall`)
- **People know when it's done**: Say how long it takes, then confirm.
- **Sign in with Apple tokens are revoked**: With the Sign in with Apple REST API. (`sign-in-with-apple`)

## Variants

### The Settings row

Put a `NavigationLink` to the deletion screen in its own section at the bottom of your account settings.

```swift
Form {
    Section("Account") {
        LabeledContent("Email", value: "maya@example.com")
        Button("Sign Out") { signOut() }
    }
    Section {
        NavigationLink("Delete Account") {
            DeleteAccountView()
        }
        .foregroundStyle(.red)
    }
}
.navigationTitle("Account")
```

### The deletion screen

Say what gets deleted, handle subscriptions, then confirm once with `.confirmationDialog`.

```swift
import StoreKit

struct DeleteAccountView: View {
    @State private var isConfirming = false
    @State private var showsSubscriptions = false

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Section {
                Text("This permanently deletes your account, recipes, and comments.")
            }
            Section {
                Button("Manage Subscription") {
                    showsSubscriptions = true
                }
            } footer: {
                Text("Billing for Pro continues through Apple until you cancel it.")
            }
            Section {
                Button("Delete Account", role: .destructive) {
                    isConfirming = true
                }
                .confirmationDialog("Delete your account?", isPresented: $isConfirming, titleVisibility: .visible) {
                    Button("Delete Account", role: .destructive) {
                        Task { await deleteAccount() }
                    }
                } message: {
                    Text("This can't be undone.")
                }
            }
        }
        .navigationTitle("Delete Account")
        .manageSubscriptionsSheet(isPresented: $showsSubscriptions)
    }
}
```

**Important:** Deleting the account doesn't cancel an App Store subscription. Apple asks you to tell people that billing continues through Apple and to have them cancel first; `manageSubscriptionsSheet` opens the system screen for that.

## Related

`settings-screen`, `confirmation-dialog`, `sign-in-with-apple`, `paywall`


<!-- topic: paywall -->
---
id: paywall
title: Paywall
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 17.0+, macOS 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit/subscriptionstoreview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/apple-in-app-purchase.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Paywall

Sell digital features with StoreKit's ready-made store views, and show what Apple requires.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Show the full price people will be billed.** The HIG asks for the total billing amount on every option. A monthly breakdown can sit next to it, not instead of it.
- **Say what happens when a free trial ends.** People need to know they'll be charged automatically, how much, and when.
- **Give existing customers a way back in.** The sign-up screen needs a way for current subscribers to sign in or restore purchases, plus links to your terms and privacy policy.
- **Use Apple's purchase sheet as it is.** The system confirms every purchase to prevent accidents. Don't copy it or change it.
- **Don't pitch a subscription to someone who has one.** They may think it lapsed. Check their status first, and make canceling easy to find in your settings.

## Pitfalls

- **Products load only when StoreKit can find them.** In Xcode, add a StoreKit configuration file and pick it in the scheme to test without App Store Connect.
- **Physical goods can't use In-App Purchase.** In-App Purchase is for digital content and features. Goods and services used outside the app, like groceries or tickets, need another payment method, such as Apple Pay or card entry (Guideline 3.1.3(e)).

## Guide

### What Apple requires

As of 2026, the App Review Guidelines say:

• **3.1.1:** to unlock features or content in your app, use In-App Purchase, not license keys, QR codes, or crypto. Purchases that can be restored need a way to restore them.

• **3.1.2:** an auto-renewable subscription must give ongoing value, last at least seven days, and work on all of the person's devices. Before asking people to subscribe, say clearly what they get for the price.

• **2.1(b):** your in-app purchases must be complete, visible to the reviewer, and working when you submit.

**Note:** There are exceptions for linking to other ways to pay, such as on the United States storefront and for “reader” apps. See Guidelines 3.1.1(a) and 3.1.3 before you rely on one.

### Why

People should know exactly what they'll pay and for how long before they tap Subscribe, and get back what they bought on a new phone.

### Before you submit

- **Digital unlocks use In-App Purchase**: Guideline 3.1.1, unless an exception applies.
- **Restore Purchases is easy to find**: On the paywall, and ideally in settings too.
- **Every option shows its price and length**: The total amount billed, localized by StoreKit.
- **Trials say what's charged after**: How long, then how much, billed automatically.
- **Terms and privacy links are there**: On the paywall and in your App Store metadata.
- **Purchases are ready for review**: Complete, visible, and working (2.1(b)).
- **Tested with StoreKit Testing**: Buy, cancel, and restore in Xcode first.
- **Account deletion covers billing**: Tell people their subscription continues until they cancel. (`delete-account`)

## Key APIs

`SubscriptionStoreView`, `ProductView(id:)`, `StoreView(ids:)`, `.storeButton(_:for:)`, `AppStore.sync()`, `.subscriptionStatusTask`, `.currentEntitlementTask`

## Variants

### A subscription paywall

`SubscriptionStoreView` loads a subscription group and draws the options, prices, buy button, and policy links for you.

```swift
import StoreKit

SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: "21482041") {
    VStack(spacing: 8) {
        Image(systemName: "fork.knife.circle.fill")
            .font(.system(size: 56))
            .foregroundStyle(.tint)
        Text("Recipes Pro")
            .font(.largeTitle.bold())
        Text("Unlimited recipes, meal plans, and shopping lists.")
            .multilineTextAlignment(.center)
    }
    .padding()
}
.storeButton(.visible, for: .restorePurchases)
.subscriptionStoreControlStyle(.picker)
```

**Note:** This catalog has no products to load, so the preview is a static drawing of a paywall like the one the code makes. The code is real StoreKit; run it with a StoreKit configuration file.

### One product

Use `ProductView(id:)` for a single purchase, like a lifetime unlock. Pick `.productViewStyle(.large)` for a hero card.

```swift
ProductView(id: "com.example.recipes.lifetime") {
    Image(systemName: "infinity.circle.fill")
        .font(.largeTitle)
        .foregroundStyle(.tint)
}
.productViewStyle(.compact)
```

### A small store

`StoreView(ids:)` lists several products, such as tips or packs, and adds columns when there's room.

```swift
StoreView(ids: [
    "com.example.recipes.tip.small",
    "com.example.recipes.tip.large",
])
.storeButton(.visible, for: .restorePurchases)
```

### Your own Restore button

In a custom paywall, call `AppStore.sync()` from a Restore Purchases button.

