```swift
Button("Restore Purchases") {
    Task {
        try? await AppStore.sync()
    }
}
```

**Important:** Call `sync()` only when someone taps the button: it asks them to sign in to the App Store. StoreKit already keeps purchases up to date on its own, including after a reinstall.

### Unlock Pro when subscribed

`.subscriptionStatusTask(for:)` runs whenever the subscription status changes, so the app unlocks or locks right away.

```swift
@State private var isPro = false

Text(isPro ? "Pro" : "Free")
    .subscriptionStatusTask(for: "21482041") { taskState in
        if let statuses = taskState.value {
            isPro = statuses.contains { $0.state == .subscribed }
        }
    }
```

**Note:** For a one-time purchase, use `.currentEntitlementTask(for:)` with the product ID instead.

## Related

`delete-account`, `request-review`, `onboarding`, `settings-screen`


<!-- topic: request-review -->
---
id: request-review
title: Asking for Reviews
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
availability: iOS 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, visionOS 1.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/storekit/requestreviewaction.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/ratings-and-reviews.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Asking for Reviews

Ask for an App Store rating with the system prompt, at a good moment, and never for a reward.

Also called: Guideline 5.6.1, Guideline 3.2.2(x), requestReview, RequestReviewAction, SKStoreReviewController, rate this app, rate us, app rating, review prompt, star rating.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Ask after people finish something.** Right after a completed task, people have an opinion. On first launch or during onboarding they don't, and may rate you lower.
- **Use the system prompt, not your own.** Guideline 5.6.1 says to use Apple's API and disallows custom review prompts, so don't build your own “Rate us” alert.
- **Never trade rewards for reviews.** Don't lock features behind a rating or pay for one. A plain Write a Review row in Settings is fine.
- **Don't interrupt a task.** Wait for a natural pause, like the end of a level, not the middle of checkout.
- **Space requests out.** The HIG suggests at least a week or two between requests, and asking again only after people use the app more.

## Pitfalls

- **In Xcode it always shows; in TestFlight it never does.** Development builds show the prompt on every call so you can test it. TestFlight builds ignore the call.
- **People can turn these prompts off.** A setting stops review requests from every app, so your call may do nothing at all.

## Guide

### What Apple requires

As of 2026, the App Review Guidelines say:

• **5.6.1:** ask for reviews with Apple's API. Custom review prompts aren't allowed.

• **3.2.2(x):** never make people rate or review your app to use a feature or see content.

• **Section 3:** manipulating reviews with paid, incentivized, filtered, or fake feedback can get you removed from the Developer Program.

### Why

Ratings help people choose apps only if they're honest. The system prompt lets people rate in one tap without leaving your app, and it limits how often anyone is asked.

### How often it shows

You only *request* a review. As of 2026, the system decides whether to show it:

• At most **three times in 365 days** for someone who hasn't rated your app on that device.

• After they've rated, only for a **new version**, and only when more than 365 days have passed.

**Important:** Because the prompt may not appear, don't call it from a button like “Rate This App”. That button would do nothing most of the time. Link to the App Store instead.

### Before you submit

- **Only the system prompt**: No homemade “Rate us” alert (5.6.1).
- **Nothing is locked behind a rating**: Features and content work without one (3.2.2(x)).
- **No rewards for reviews**: No coins, unlocks, or discounts for rating.
- **Asked after a success, not at launch**: And never in the middle of a task.
- **No requestReview on a button tap**: Use a Write a Review link instead.
- **Asked at most once per version**: Store the version you last asked in.

## Key APIs

- `@Environment(\.requestReview)`: Gets the review action.
- `requestReview()`: Asks the system to show the prompt, if it allows it.
- `action=write-review`: Add to your product page URL to open the review form.
- `@AppStorage`: Remember counts and the last version you asked in.

## Variants

### Ask after a completed task

Read `requestReview` from the environment, count finished tasks, and ask once per version after a short pause.

```swift
@Environment(\.requestReview) private var requestReview
@AppStorage("finishedWorkouts") private var finishedWorkouts = 0
@AppStorage("lastVersionAsked") private var lastVersionAsked = ""

func workoutFinished() {
    finishedWorkouts += 1
    let version = Bundle.main.object(forInfoDictionaryKey: "CFBundleShortVersionString") as? String ?? ""
    guard finishedWorkouts >= 3, version != lastVersionAsked else { return }
    lastVersionAsked = version
    Task {
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(2))
        requestReview()
    }
}
```

### A Write a Review link

For a button people can always tap, open your product page with `action=write-review` added to the URL.

```swift
// Your App Store product page, plus ?action=write-review
Link("Write a Review", destination: URL(string: "https://apps.apple.com/app/id1234567890?action=write-review")!)
```

## Related

`delete-account`, `paywall`, `settings-screen`, `alert`


<!-- topic: screenshots -->
---
id: screenshots
title: Screenshots
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-information/screenshot-specifications/
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Screenshots

The screenshot sizes App Store Connect requires, and how to make clean ones.

Also called: app store screenshots, screenshot sizes, screenshot dimensions, marketing screenshots, store listing, product page, app preview, preview video, promo video, status bar.

## Rules

- **Show the app in use.** Guideline 2.3.3 says screenshots must show your app working, not just a title card, a login screen, or a splash screen.
- **Leave out prices and other platforms.** Guideline 2.3.7 keeps prices out of screenshots, and 2.3.10 keeps out the names and icons of other mobile platforms.
- **Use a clean status bar.** A low battery or a random time pulls attention from your app. Override the Simulator's status bar before you shoot.
- **Use made-up people and data.** Guideline 2.3.9 asks for fictional account details, never a real person's, and you need the rights to every image you show.
- **Keep it suitable for everyone.** Guideline 2.3.8 says screenshots and previews must fit a 4+ rating, even when your app is rated higher.

## Pitfalls

- **The first screenshots do the most work.** When there's no app preview, the first one to three screenshots show in App Store search results, so lead with what your app is for.
- **Consider one Dark Mode screenshot.** If your app supports it, showing it helps. That's our suggestion, not an Apple rule.
- **Upload them per language if your UI is translated.** Screenshots are localizable, so each language can show your app in that language.

## Guide

Every version you submit needs screenshots in App Store Connect. Guideline 2.3.3 says they must show your app in use. They're the first thing people judge your app by, so it pays to make them clean and clear.

### What you must upload

- iPhone (required): At least one screenshot for iPhone with Dynamic Island, medium display: **1206 × 2622** or **1179 × 2556** px in portrait.
- iPad (if your app runs on iPad): At least one for the 13-inch iPad display: **2064 × 2752** or **2048 × 2732** px in portrait.
- How many: 1 to 10 per display size.
- Format: PNG or JPEG, with no transparency.

**Note:** As of October 2026. If your UI is the same across sizes, upload only these and App Store Connect scales them down for smaller iPhones and iPads.

**Note:** Apple's spec page also says screenshots for iPhone Duo become required in April 2027 for apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later.

### Which simulator to use

Take screenshots on a simulator in the required display class. Its screenshots come out at the right pixel size, so you don't need to resize them.

### Clean screenshots from the Simulator

`simctl` comes with Xcode. Boot your simulator, run your app with sample data, then run these in Terminal:

```swift
# A clean status bar: fixed time, full signal and battery
xcrun simctl status_bar booted override --time 9:41 \
  --batteryState charged --batteryLevel 100 \
  --cellularBars 4 --wifiBars 3

# Save a full-size PNG
xcrun simctl io booted screenshot home.png

# Put the status bar back
xcrun simctl status_bar booted clear
```

**Note:** `booted` means the simulator that's running. With several running, pass a device ID from `xcrun simctl list` instead.

### App previews

App previews are optional videos that play before your screenshots. You can add up to three per display size and language. Each one runs 15 to 30 seconds and is up to 500 MB.

Guideline 2.3.4 says a preview may only use screen recordings of your app. You can add narration and text overlays to explain what's happening.

```swift
# Record as H.264. Press Control-C to stop.
xcrun simctl io booted recordVideo \
  --codec=h264 preview.mov
```

**Important:** `recordVideo` saves HEVC by default, and App Store Connect expects H.264 or ProRes 422 (HQ). Pass `--codec=h264`, and trim the video to 15 to 30 seconds before you upload.

## Related

`submission-checklist`, `dark-mode`, `privacy-details`, `store-forms`, `rejection-guide`


<!-- topic: privacy-details -->
---
id: privacy-details
title: Privacy Details
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/privacy-manifest-files.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Privacy Details

Tell Apple what data your app collects, and why it uses certain APIs.

Also called: privacy nutrition label, privacy label, app privacy, data collection, privacy manifest, PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, xcprivacy, required reason API, NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes, UserDefaults.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Make the privacy policy easy to find.** Guideline 5.1.1(i) wants a link in App Store Connect and inside the app. A row in Settings is the usual place.
- **Ask only for data you need.** Guideline 5.1.1(iii) and the HIG both say to collect only what a feature needs. Prefer a system picker over full access to Photos or Contacts.
- **Get permission before you share data, including with AI.** Guideline 5.1.2(i) says to disclose where personal data goes, including third-party AI services, and get explicit permission first.
- **Don't lock features behind a permission.** Under 5.1.2(i), you can't require people to allow notifications, location, or tracking to use your app.

## Pitfalls

- **You can change your answers without an update.** Edit App Privacy whenever your data use changes; it isn't tied to a build.
- **Purpose strings count too.** Guideline 5.1.1(ii) says each permission prompt must explain clearly and completely how you use the data.

## Guide

Apple needs three privacy pieces before your app ships: a **privacy policy** link (Guideline 5.1.1(i)), **App Privacy answers** in App Store Connect, which become the privacy label on your product page, and a **privacy manifest** if your code or SDKs use certain APIs.

People read the label before they download, and the manifest stops apps from quietly fingerprinting devices.

### The privacy label

You answer questions about each type of data you or your SDKs collect. **Collect** means sending data off the device and keeping it longer than it takes to handle the request. Data that never leaves the device doesn't count.

**Important:** SDKs count as yours. If an analytics or ad SDK collects data, you declare it, even if you never look at that data.

### Fill it in

1. In App Store Connect, open your app and choose **App Privacy** in the sidebar.
2. Click **Get Started** and say whether you or your partners collect data.
3. Pick every data type you collect, then answer how each one is used, whether it's linked to the person, and whether it's used for tracking.
4. Next to **Privacy Policy**, click Edit and enter your policy's URL.
5. Click **Publish**. The label appears on your product page.

### The privacy manifest

`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` is a property list in your app target. In Xcode, choose File > New File and pick **App Privacy**. It lists the data you collect, your tracking domains, and any **required reason APIs** you call, with a code for why.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes</key>
    <array>
        <dict>
            <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPIType</key>
            <string>NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults</string>
            <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypeReasons</key>
            <array>
                <string>CA92.1</string>
            </array>
        </dict>
    </array>
</dict>
</plist>
```

**Important:** `@AppStorage` reads and writes `UserDefaults`, so almost every SwiftUI app needs this entry. `CA92.1` means only your app reads and writes the values. Since May 1, 2024, App Store Connect doesn't accept uploads that use these APIs without a declared reason.

### Required reason APIs

These are the five categories, with the reason most apps use. Pick the code that matches what your app actually does; Apple's docs list the rest.

- User defaults: `CA92.1`: your own app's settings. Use `1C8F.1` for an App Group.
- File timestamps: `C617.1`: files in your app's container.
- System boot time: `35F9.1`: measuring time between events.
- Disk space: `E174.1`: checking for room before writing.
- Active keyboards: `54BD.1`: adapting your UI to the keyboard.

### Third-party SDKs

Each SDK reports its own data use and required reason APIs in its own manifest; it can't rely on yours. Xcode combines all the manifests into one report to help you fill in the label.

**Note:** Apple keeps a list of commonly used SDKs, such as Firebase modules, Alamofire, and SDWebImage. A new app, or an update that adds one, must include that SDK's manifest, and a signature if you add it as a binary.

### Before you submit

- **Privacy policy URL in App Store Connect**: It's required for every app.
- **Privacy policy link in the app**: Somewhere easy to find, like Settings. (`settings-screen`)
- **App Privacy answers published**: Include data your SDKs collect.
- **Privacy manifest in your target**: `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, with a reason for each required reason API.
- **SDK manifests included**: Update SDKs on Apple's list to versions that ship one.
- **A clear purpose string for each permission**: Say what you use the data for. (`requesting-permission`)

## Key APIs

`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, `NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes`, `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes`, `NSPrivacyTracking`, `Link`

## Variants

### Privacy policy row

Use `Link` in your settings screen; it opens the policy in Safari.

```swift
Form {
    Section("About") {
        Link("Privacy Policy", destination: URL(string: "https://example.com/privacy")!)
    }
}
```

## Related

`settings-screen`, `requesting-permission`, `store-forms`, `submission-checklist`, `rejection-guide`


<!-- topic: accessibility-labels -->
---
id: accessibility-labels
title: Accessibility Labels
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/overview-of-accessibility-nutrition-labels
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Accessibility Labels

Accessibility Nutrition Labels show which accessibility features your app supports.

Also called: accessibility label, accessibility nutrition label, App Accessibility, a11y, VoiceOver, Voice Control, Larger Text, Dynamic Type, Dark Interface, Differentiate Without Color.

## Rules

- **Claim a feature only if every common task works.** Apple's rule is that people can finish all the app's common tasks with that feature alone. App Review can ask you to fix misleading labels.
- **Don't rely on color alone.** To claim Differentiate Without Color Alone, pair color with a shape, symbol, or text.
- **Let text grow without cutting it off.** Larger Text means text reaches at least 200% without overlapping or heavy truncation. System Zoom doesn't count.
- **Keep a dark interface dark.** For Dark Interface, every common task has to stay dark. A sudden white screen can hurt someone with light sensitivity.

## Pitfalls

- **Answer per device.** Support can differ between iPhone and iPad, so App Store Connect asks for each one, and you should test on each.
- **Add an accessibility URL.** An optional link on your product page can explain settings, caption languages, or areas that aren't supported yet.
- **Re-check with every update.** Apple asks you to keep the labels accurate as your app changes.

## Guide

Accessibility Nutrition Labels are a section on your App Store product page that lists the accessibility features your app supports, like VoiceOver and Larger Text. People see them on iOS 26 and later, and can even search for them, as in “VoiceOver note taking apps”.

**Note:** As of October 2026 the labels are voluntary. Apple says they'll become required for new apps and updates over time. If you don't answer, your page says you haven't indicated support yet.

### The nine features

Turn on the features your app supports to build a sample of the section. Apple suggests evaluating them in this order, starting with VoiceOver.

### How to evaluate your app

1. List your app's **common tasks**: its main features, plus first launch, login, purchases, and settings.
2. Turn on one feature, starting with VoiceOver, and learn to use it well.
3. Try every common task with only that feature, on each device you support.
4. Claim the feature only if all of them work. Note the gaps and fix them next release.

**Important:** Zoom and Hover Text don't count as Larger Text support. They work in every app already, so your own text has to grow, through Dynamic Type or an in-app size setting.

### Add them in App Store Connect

1. Open your app and choose **App Accessibility** in the sidebar, then **Get Started**.
2. Pick a device, say whether you support any features, and select them.
3. Click **Publish**. You can only publish for devices with a live version, and changes can take 24 hours to show.

## Key APIs

- `.accessibilityLabel(_:)`: What VoiceOver reads for a view.
- `.font(.body)`: Text styles scale with Larger Text.
- `\.dynamicTypeSize`: The person's text size.
- `\.accessibilityReduceMotion`: Reduce Motion is on.

## Variants

### Label icon-only buttons

Use `.accessibilityLabel(_:)` so VoiceOver and Voice Control have a name to read and say.

```swift
Button {
    isFavorite.toggle()
} label: {
    Image(systemName: isFavorite ? "heart.fill" : "heart")
}
.accessibilityLabel("Favorite")
```

### Stack rows at large text sizes

Read `dynamicTypeSize` and stack the row at accessibility sizes, shown second here, so text never overlaps.

```swift
@Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var size

var body: some View {
    let layout = size.isAccessibilitySize
        ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading))
        : AnyLayout(HStackLayout())
    layout {
        Text("Delivery")
        Spacer()
        Text("Tomorrow, 9–11 AM")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
```

## Related

`accessibility`, `voiceover`, `dynamic-type`, `color-and-contrast`, `reduce-motion`, `dark-mode`


<!-- topic: store-forms -->
---
id: store-forms
title: Other Required Forms
platforms: [iOS, iPadOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-information/app-information/
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Other Required Forms

Age rating, encryption, EU trader status, content rights, and the Xcode you need.

Also called: age rating, age rating questionnaire, parental controls, Made for Kids, export compliance, encryption, ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption, Digital Services Act, DSA, trader status.

## Rules

- **Answer the age questions honestly.** Guideline 2.3.6 warns that a wrong rating surprises customers and can draw attention from regulators.
- **Rate for what people can reach, not just what you made.** An in-app browser that can open any website makes the app 16+ on its own, and a social media feature makes it at least 13+.
- **Only show content you have the rights to.** Guideline 5.2.1 says not to use trademarks, copyrighted work, or patented ideas without permission.

## Pitfalls

- **Most of these live in App Information.** Open your app in App Store Connect and choose App Information under General in the sidebar.
- **Requirements change every year.** Check Apple's Upcoming Requirements page before you plan a release.

## Guide

Besides screenshots and privacy, App Store Connect asks a few more questions before you can submit. Each takes minutes, but a missing answer blocks your upload or keeps your app out of a region.

### Age rating

Answer the age rating questionnaire under **App Information**. It asks about in-app controls, capabilities like web access and chat, and how often mature content appears. Apple works out the rating from your answers.

As of 2026 the ratings are **4+**, **9+**, **13+**, **16+**, and **18+**. They show on devices running iOS 26 and later, and since January 31, 2026, you must answer the updated questions to submit updates. Some regions, like Australia, Brazil, and Korea, add their own.

**Important:** If people can browse to any website inside your app, that alone makes it 16+. Many apps add an in-app browser without realizing it.

**Note:** Choose **Made for Kids** only if your rating is 4+ or 9+. You can't undo it once App Review approves the app, and every update has to follow the Kids category rules.

### Encryption

Every upload goes to a server in the U.S., so U.S. export rules apply to any encryption in your app. Add this key to your Info.plist to answer the question once instead of on every upload:

```xml
<key>ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption</key>
<false/>
```

Use `false` if your app, and every library in it, uses no encryption or only exempt encryption. HTTPS through `URLSession` is usually exempt. Use `true` for your own encryption, then upload documents in App Store Connect and add the code Apple sends you as `ITSEncryptionExportComplianceCode`.

**Note:** Exempt encryption can still mean paperwork: you might need to send a year-end self-classification report to the U.S. government.

### EU trader status

The EU's Digital Services Act requires developers with apps on the EU App Store to declare whether they're a **trader**. Traders have their address, phone number, and email shown on their product page in the EU. Since February 17, 2025, apps without a trader status have been removed from the EU App Store until one is provided.

You decide whether you're a trader; Apple can't decide for you. Things that point to yes:

- Revenue: The app is paid, has in-app purchases, or shows ads.
- Promotion: You advertise or sell products or services through it.
- Tax: You're registered for VAT.
- Profession: You build it as part of your business or job.

**Note:** A hobbyist with no plan to make money may not be a trader. If you're unsure, ask a lawyer. The Account Holder or an Admin declares it under Business, on the Agreements tab.

### Content rights

In **App Information**, you say whether your app contains, shows, or accesses third-party content. If it does, you need the rights to that content in every country where you sell the app.

### Build with the current Xcode

- Xcode and SDK: Since April 28, 2026, uploads must be built with **Xcode 26** or later and the **iOS 26 SDK**.
- Minimum iOS: Since September 9, 2026, iPhone and iPad apps must target **iOS 13** or later.

### Before you submit

- **Age rating questionnaire answered**: Under App Information. Answer for the content people can reach.
- **Encryption answered in Info.plist**: Set `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` so uploads skip the question.
- **EU trader status declared**: Under Business > Agreements, if your app is on the EU App Store.
- **Content rights answered**: And the rights to any third-party content you show.
- **Built with Xcode 26 or later**: App Store Connect won't accept builds from older versions.
- **Privacy label and policy done**: Every app needs both, plus a manifest if it uses required reason APIs. (`privacy-details`)
- **Screenshots uploaded**: iPhone, plus 13-inch iPad if you support iPad. (`screenshots`)

## Related

`privacy-details`, `screenshots`, `accessibility-labels`, `submission-checklist`, `releasing`


<!-- topic: gauge-progress -->
---
id: gauge-progress
title: Gauge & ProgressView
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/progressview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/progress-indicators.md
---

# Gauge & ProgressView

Progress bars and spinners for work under way, and gauges for a level in a range.

Also called: progress bar, spinner, activity indicator, loading, NSProgressIndicator, <progress>, <meter>, level indicator, NSLevelIndicator, capacity.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var progress = 0.6

ProgressView(value: progress) {
    Text("Exporting photos…")
}
```

**Note:** The default total is `1.0`, so `value` is a fraction. Pass `total:` to count in your own units, like files or bytes.

## Rules

- **Show how far along it is whenever you can.** A determinate bar lets people decide whether to wait or come back later. Switch an indeterminate bar to a determinate one as soon as you know the total.
- **Keep it moving, and keep it honest.** A stalled indicator looks like a frozen app. Advance at an even pace instead of racing to 90% and crawling through the rest.
- **Don't label a spinner.** A spinner usually appears right after people start something, so they know what it's for. It's small enough for a background task or a spot next to a control.
- **Let people stop long tasks.** Add a Cancel button when stopping has no bad side effects. If it would lose work, ask before you stop.
- **Don't switch between a spinner and a bar.** They're different shapes and sizes, so swapping one for the other mid-task looks jumpy. Pick one and keep it.

## Pitfalls

- **A value makes it determinate.** `ProgressView(value:)` fills a bar; `ProgressView()` with no value animates without an end.
- **Gauge is for a level, not a task.** Use it for things like storage or battery that sit somewhere in a range, and `ProgressView` for work that finishes.
- **Progress over a time span updates itself.** `ProgressView(timerInterval:)` fills as the clock moves through a date range.

## Key APIs

- `ProgressView()`: Indeterminate: a spinner by default.
- `ProgressView(value:total:)`: Determinate: a bar that fills.
- `.progressViewStyle(.linear)`: A bar, even when indeterminate.
- `.progressViewStyle(.circular)`: A spinner or a filling circle.
- `Gauge(value:in:label:)`: A value within a range.
- `.gaugeStyle(.linearCapacity)`: A bar filled up to the value.
- `.gaugeStyle(.accessoryCircular)`: A small ring with a marker.
- `.controlSize(.small)`: A smaller spinner for tight spots.

## Variants

### A task people can cancel

Show the count in `currentValueLabel` and put a Cancel button beside the bar, so people can stop a long copy.

```swift
@State private var copied = 0.0

HStack {
    ProgressView(value: copied, total: 120) {
        Text("Copying photos")
    } currentValueLabel: {
        Text("\(Int(copied)) of 120")
    }
    Button("Cancel") {
        cancelCopy()
    }
}
```

### An indeterminate bar

Without a value, `.linear` draws a bar that animates without an end, which the Mac offers alongside the spinner.

```swift
ProgressView {
    Text("Preparing export")
}
.progressViewStyle(.linear)
```

### A small spinner for background work

`.controlSize(.small)` makes the spinner fit next to a button or in a toolbar while something loads in the background.

```swift
@State private var isChecking = false

HStack(spacing: 8) {
    Button("Check for Updates") {
        isChecking = true
    }
    .disabled(isChecking)
    if isChecking {
        ProgressView()
            .controlSize(.small)
    }
}
```

### A capacity gauge

`.linearCapacity` fills a bar up to the value, and `minimumValueLabel` and `maximumValueLabel` show the ends of the range.

```swift
Gauge(value: 0.72) {
    Text("Storage")
} currentValueLabel: {
    Text("72%")
} minimumValueLabel: {
    Text("0")
} maximumValueLabel: {
    Text("1 TB")
}
.gaugeStyle(.linearCapacity)
.tint(.orange)
```

**Note:** Write labels for the value and both ends even when a style hides some of them: VoiceOver reads them.

### A small circular gauge

`.accessoryCircular` draws a ring with a marker at the value, and a gradient tint shows what high and low mean.

```swift
Gauge(value: 0.35) {
    Text("CPU")
} currentValueLabel: {
    Text("35")
}
.gaugeStyle(.accessoryCircular)
.tint(Gradient(colors: [.green, .yellow, .red]))
```

## Related

`slider`, `labeled-content`, `toolbar`, `button`


<!-- topic: control-group -->
---
id: control-group
title: ControlGroup
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 12.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/controlgroup.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toolbars.md
---

# ControlGroup

Related buttons joined into one control, in a toolbar or in content.

Also called: button group, segmented buttons, NSSegmentedControl momentary, back forward, zoom in out, toolbar group, btn-group, controlGroupStyle.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
ControlGroup("Zoom", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") {
    Button("Zoom Out", systemImage: "minus.magnifyingglass") {
        zoomOut()
    }
    Button("Zoom In", systemImage: "plus.magnifyingglass") {
        zoomIn()
    }
}
.labelStyle(.iconOnly)
```

**Note:** Like a `.btn-group` of buttons on the web. Each button keeps its own action; the group only changes how they're drawn.

## Rules

- **Group toolbar items by what they do.** Put commands that work together side by side, like zooming out and in. Navigation and critical actions such as Done get their own familiar spots.
- **Keep the number of groups small.** Too many groups make a toolbar look cluttered and hard to scan. Aim for three at most.
- **Use a group for actions and a picker for a choice.** Don't mix buttons that act with segments that stay selected. For one choice among several, use a segmented Picker (`picker`).

## Pitfalls

- **The label matters in a toolbar.** When a toolbar runs out of room, the group moves into the overflow menu under its label, so give it one.
- **Each button keeps its own title.** Use `Button(_:systemImage:action:)` with `.labelStyle(.iconOnly)`, and VoiceOver still reads each title.

## Key APIs

- `ControlGroup { … }`: Groups the buttons inside it.
- `ControlGroup(_:systemImage:content:)`: With a label for menus and overflow.
- `.controlGroupStyle(.navigation)`: For back and forward buttons.
- `.controlGroupStyle(.menu)`: Shows the buttons as a menu.
- `.controlGroupStyle(.palette)`: Shows the content as a palette.
- `.labelStyle(.iconOnly)`: Symbols only, titles kept for VoiceOver.

## Variants

### Back and forward in a toolbar

Use `.controlGroupStyle(.navigation)` for back and forward, in the toolbar's `.navigation` placement.

```swift
@State private var page = 3

Text("Page \(page)")
    .navigationTitle("Page \(page) of 5")
    .toolbar {
        ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation) {
            ControlGroup("Navigation", systemImage: "arrow.left.arrow.right") {
                Button("Back", systemImage: "chevron.left") { page -= 1 }
                    .disabled(page == 1)
                Button("Forward", systemImage: "chevron.right") { page += 1 }
                    .disabled(page == 5)
            }
            .controlGroupStyle(.navigation)
        }
    }
```

**Note:** A real `.toolbar` here would land in this window's toolbar, so the preview draws one. Open the sample to see the real thing.

### Zoom controls under a view

In content, a group keeps paired actions together, such as zooming out and in below an image.

```swift
@State private var zoom = 100

VStack {
    Image(systemName: "photo")
        .font(.system(size: 48 * Double(zoom) / 100))
    ControlGroup {
        Button("Zoom Out", systemImage: "minus") { zoom -= 25 }
        Button("Actual Size") { zoom = 100 }
        Button("Zoom In", systemImage: "plus") { zoom += 25 }
    }
    .fixedSize()
}
```

### A group as a menu

`.controlGroupStyle(.menu)` folds the buttons into a menu under the group's label, for actions people need now and then.

```swift
ControlGroup("Arrange", systemImage: "square.3.layers.3d") {
    Button("Bring to Front") { bringToFront() }
    Button("Send to Back") { sendToBack() }
}
.controlGroupStyle(.menu)
```

## Related

`button`, `picker`, `menu`, `toolbar`, `toolbars-pattern`


<!-- topic: labeled-content -->
---
id: labeled-content
title: LabeledContent
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/labeledcontent.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/labels.md
---

# LabeledContent

A label and a value in one row that lines up with the rest of a form.

Also called: label value, key value, info row, property row, <dl>, definition list, get info, detail row, form row, inspector row.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Form {
    LabeledContent("Version", value: "2.4 (118)")
    LabeledContent("Size", value: 18_400_000, format: .byteCount(style: .file))
}
.formStyle(.grouped)
```

**Note:** Like a `<dt>` and `<dd>` pair, but the layout comes from the container: a `Form`'s style decides where the label goes.

## Rules

- **Show read-only details as text.** A text value is for reading and copying, not editing. When people should change the value, put a text field or another control in the value instead.
- **Let people copy useful details.** Values like an error code, an address, or a version number are worth pasting elsewhere. Pass them as a string or with `format:`, and SwiftUI makes them selectable where it can.
- **Show importance with the system's label colors.** Primary for the main text and secondary for supporting text keep the hierarchy clear in light and dark, as a grouped form does.

## Pitfalls

- **Text values are selectable where possible.** SwiftUI makes a text value selectable, so people can copy a serial number or a path.
- **It's a label for anything.** Any view can be the value: a field and a stepper, a group of checkboxes, or a custom view.

## Key APIs

- `LabeledContent(_:value:)`: A read-only text value.
- `LabeledContent(_:value:format:)`: A value with a format style.
- `LabeledContent(_:content:)`: Any view as the value.
- `LabeledContent(content:label:)`: Any view as the label too.
- `.labelsHidden()`: Hides the label on screen.
- `.labeledContentStyle(_:)`: Your own layout for every row inside.

## Variants

### Details in an inspector

Pass `format:` to show numbers, sizes, and dates the way the person's region writes them.

```swift
let created = Date.now

Form {
    Section("Information") {
        LabeledContent("Kind", value: "JPEG image")
        LabeledContent("Size", value: 2_480_000, format: .byteCount(style: .file))
        LabeledContent("Created", value: created, format: .dateTime.day().month().year())
    }
}
.formStyle(.grouped)
```

### A control as the value

Give any view a label that lines up with the other rows, like a field with a stepper beside it.

```swift
@State private var copies = 1

Form {
    LabeledContent("Copies:") {
        HStack(spacing: 4) {
            TextField("Copies", value: $copies, format: .number)
                .frame(width: 44)
            Stepper("Copies", value: $copies, in: 1...99)
        }
        .labelsHidden()
    }
    Picker("Paper size:", selection: .constant("A4")) {
        Text("A4").tag("A4")
        Text("US Letter").tag("US Letter")
    }
}
```

### Checkboxes under one label

In a grouped form, toggles inside `LabeledContent` become checkboxes stacked under one label, instead of switches.

```swift
@State private var refreshesStatus = true
@State private var fetchesServer = false
@State private var addsFiles = true

Form {
    LabeledContent("Source Control") {
        Toggle("Refresh status automatically", isOn: $refreshesStatus)
        Toggle("Fetch server status", isOn: $fetchesServer)
        Toggle("Add and remove files", isOn: $addsFiles)
    }
}
.formStyle(.grouped)
```

### A label with a subtitle

Give the label two `Text` views: the first is the title, the second a line of detail under it.

```swift
Form {
    LabeledContent {
        Text("4.2 GB")
    } label: {
        Text("Cache")
        Text("Downloaded previews and thumbnails")
    }
}
.formStyle(.grouped)
```

## Related

`form`, `inspector`, `toggle`, `stepper`, `text-label`


<!-- topic: focus-keyboard -->
---
id: focus-keyboard
title: Focus & Keyboard Navigation
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 12.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/focus.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/focus-and-selection.md
---

# Focus & Keyboard Navigation

Decide which view gets typed keys, and let people move around with Tab.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Use the system's focus ring.** People know what it means at a glance, and it's tuned for the Mac. Draw your own focus look only when you really need one.
- **Don't move focus on your own.** People track where they are by where focus is. Change it only in response to something they do.
- **Make content focusable, and let the system handle controls.** Fields, lists, and your custom content should take focus. Full Keyboard Access already lets people reach buttons, toggles, and sliders.
- **Ring fields, highlight rows.** A focus ring suits text and search fields. In a list or collection, highlight the whole row or item instead.

## Pitfalls

- **Custom views take focus.** Built with the macOS 14 SDK or later, a `.focusable()` view can get focus even with keyboard navigation off. Pass `interactions: .activate` for a button-like view that should wait for it.
- **Return `.ignored` to pass a key on.** `.handled` stops the key at your view; `.ignored` lets views further up still get it.

## Guide

Keyboard focus decides which view gets the keys people press. On the Mac, people type into the focused field and press Tab to move to the next one. A focused text field shows a focus ring.

SwiftUI handles the common cases: text fields take focus when clicked, and Tab moves through them in reading order. Use `@FocusState` when you need to read or move focus yourself.

### Keys people use

- Tab and ⇧Tab: Move to the next or previous control.
- ⌃Tab and ⌃⇧Tab: Move to the next or previous group of controls, or to the next table when Tab moves between cells.
- Esc: Cancel the current action.
- Full Keyboard Access: With it on, people can reach every control with the keyboard. It's in the Accessibility section of System Settings.

## Key APIs

`@FocusState`, `.focused(_:equals:)`, `.defaultFocus(_:_:)`, `.focusable()`, `.onKeyPress(_:action:)`, `.focusEffectDisabled()`, `.focusSection()`

## Variants

### Move focus to what needs fixing

Bind each field to a case with `.focused(_:equals:)`. Setting the `@FocusState` moves focus there, here to the first empty field.

```swift
enum Field: Hashable {
    case name, email
}

@State private var name = ""
@State private var email = ""
@FocusState private var focusedField: Field?

Form {
    TextField("Name", text: $name)
        .focused($focusedField, equals: .name)
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .focused($focusedField, equals: .email)
    Button("Join") {
        if name.isEmpty {
            focusedField = .name
        } else if email.isEmpty {
            focusedField = .email
        } else {
            focusedField = nil
        }
    }
}
.frame(width: 300)
```

**Important:** Give each field its own value. If two views share one, setting it focuses the first, and SwiftUI warns you at runtime.

### Start focus in the right place

`.defaultFocus` picks where focus goes when the window opens. In a reply, that's the message, not the To field.

```swift
enum ReplyField: Hashable {
    case to, subject, message
}

@State private var to = "sam@example.com"
@State private var subject = "Re: Saturday"
@State private var message = ""
@FocusState private var focus: ReplyField?

VStack {
    Form {
        TextField("To", text: $to)
            .focused($focus, equals: .to)
        TextField("Subject", text: $subject)
            .focused($focus, equals: .subject)
    }
    TextEditor(text: $message)
        .font(.body)
        .focused($focus, equals: .message)
}
.defaultFocus($focus, .message)
```

**Note:** Default focus applies when a window first appears, so open the sample as a window to try it.

### Keys for a custom view

Make a view `.focusable()`, then handle keys with `.onKeyPress`. Click the stars, then press ← or →.

```swift
@State private var rating = 3
@FocusState private var isFocused: Bool

HStack {
    ForEach(1...5, id: \.self) { star in
        Image(systemName: star <= rating ? "star.fill" : "star")
    }
}
.foregroundStyle(.orange)
.padding(6)
.focusable()
.focused($isFocused)
.onTapGesture { isFocused = true }
.onKeyPress(.leftArrow) {
    rating = max(1, rating - 1)
    return .handled
}
.onKeyPress(.rightArrow) {
    rating = min(5, rating + 1)
    return .handled
}
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Your own focus look, Tab down a column first. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/focus.md

## Related

`text-field`, `secure-field`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `keyboard-access`, `form`


<!-- topic: text-label -->
---
id: text-label
title: Text & Label
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/text.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/labels.md
---

# Text & Label

Shows read-only text, and pairs a short title with an icon in a label.

Also called: label, string, <p>, <span>, NSTextField, font, text style, bold, markdown, AttributedString.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Quarterly Report")
        .font(.headline)
    Text("Updated today")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Label("Shared with 3 people", systemImage: "person.2")
}
```

**Note:** `Text` is like a `<span>`: it takes only the space it needs and wraps when its width is limited.

## Rules

- **Rank text with the label colors.** Primary for the main information, secondary for supporting details, tertiary for something unavailable. People see what matters first.
- **Avoid light weights, especially in small text.** Ultralight, Thin, and Light are hard to read at small sizes. Regular, Medium, Semibold, and Bold hold up.
- **Let people copy useful text.** Error messages, serial numbers, and addresses are often needed somewhere else. Make them selectable.
- **Prefer the system font and its text styles.** Text styles give you a consistent hierarchy of sizes and weights. Keep the number of typefaces small, even in a custom design.

## Pitfalls

- **Text styles have fixed sizes on the Mac.** `.body` is 13 points and `.largeTitle` is 26. The Mac doesn't support Dynamic Type.
- **A container can choose how a `Label` looks.** On the Mac, a toolbar shows only a label's icon unless you set `.labelStyle(.titleAndIcon)`.

## Key APIs

- `Text(_:)`: Read-only text, one or more lines.
- `.font(_:)`: A text style such as `.headline` or `.caption`.
- `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`: Ranks text with the system's label colors.
- `.textSelection(.enabled)`: Lets people select and copy the text.
- `.lineLimit(_:)`: Caps the lines; the rest is truncated.
- `.truncationMode(_:)`: Where the ellipsis goes: `.head`, `.middle`, `.tail`.
- `Label(_:systemImage:)`: A title with an SF Symbol.
- `.labelStyle(_:)`: `.titleAndIcon`, `.titleOnly`, or `.iconOnly`.

## Variants

### Text people can copy

Add `.textSelection(.enabled)` to details people need elsewhere. They drag to select, then copy with ⌘C.

```swift
Grid(alignment: .leading) {
    GridRow {
        Text("Serial Number").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        Text("C02XK1JHJG5J")
    }
    GridRow {
        Text("IP Address").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        Text("192.168.1.24")
    }
}
.textSelection(.enabled)
```

**Note:** Put `.textSelection` on a container to make every `Text` inside it selectable. Buttons don't support selection.

### Dates, sizes, and percentages

Pass a value and a `format:` instead of building strings. The output follows the person's language and region.

```swift
let modified = Date.now

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text(modified, format: .dateTime.month().day().year())
    Text(Int64(2_400_000), format: .byteCount(style: .file))
    Text(0.42, format: .percent)
}
```

### A long path in a short space

Use `.lineLimit(1)` with `.truncationMode(.middle)` so both ends of a path stay visible, and `.help` to show all of it on hover.

```swift
let path = "/Users/jo/Documents/Projects/Catalog/Exports/final-v3.pdf"

Text(path)
    .lineLimit(1)
    .truncationMode(.middle)
    .help(path)
    .frame(width: 240)
```

### Bold and italic inside a sentence

Make an `AttributedString` from Markdown to style part of a sentence. Attributes in the string win over modifiers on the `Text`.

```swift
let note = try! AttributedString(markdown: "Your trial ends **Friday**. Export your work _before then_.")

Text(note)
    .font(.title3)
```

### Label styles

A `Label` pairs a title with an icon. `.labelStyle` shows both, only the title, or only the icon.

```swift
HStack(spacing: 32) {
    Label("Rain", systemImage: "cloud.rain")
        .labelStyle(.titleAndIcon)
    Label("Rain", systemImage: "cloud.rain")
        .labelStyle(.titleOnly)
    Label("Rain", systemImage: "cloud.rain")
        .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
}
```

### A label with your own icon

Use `Label { } icon: { }` to put any view in the icon spot, like a person's initials.

```swift
Label {
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Jordan Lee")
        Text("Designer")
            .font(.subheadline)
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
} icon: {
    Circle()
        .fill(.teal)
        .frame(width: 32, height: 32)
        .overlay(Text("JL").font(.caption.bold()).foregroundStyle(.white))
}
```

## Related

`image-symbols`, `typography`, `labeled-content`, `text-field`, `writing`


<!-- topic: image-symbols -->
---
id: image-symbols
title: Image & SF Symbols
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/image.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sf-symbols.md
---

# Image & SF Symbols

Show pictures from your app, and thousands of system symbols that match your text.

Also called: <img>, icon, icons, NSImage, NSImageView, SF Symbols, systemName, symbol, rendering mode, hierarchical.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
Label("Downloads", systemImage: "arrow.down.circle")

Image(systemName: "cloud.sun.rain.fill")
    .symbolRenderingMode(.multicolor)
    .font(.largeTitle)
```

**Note:** Size a symbol with `.font`, like text. It scales with the font and lines up with text on the same line.

## Rules

- **Size symbols with the font, not a frame.** A symbol matches the weight and size of the text beside it. Use `.imageScale` to give it more or less emphasis.
- **Check the rendering mode where it's used.** Size and background change how well people can see a symbol's details. Try another mode if a symbol is hard to read.
- **Use variable color for change, not depth.** It suits values that change, like volume or signal strength. To show depth, use the hierarchical mode instead.
- **Animate symbols with a purpose.** Each effect says something, like a bounce for “this happened.” Too many animations distract people from their work.
- **Make a clickable image a button.** On the Mac, an image people click should be a `Button` with an image, not an image with a tap gesture.

## Pitfalls

- **Image modifiers come first.** `.resizable()` returns an `Image`, so call it before view modifiers like `.frame` or `.padding`.
- **Symbols depend on the OS version.** A symbol or effect added in a given year isn't there on older systems. The SF Symbols app shows each one's availability.

## Key APIs

- `Image(systemName:)`: An SF Symbol by name.
- `Image(_:)`: An image from your asset catalog.
- `.resizable()`: Lets an image grow or shrink to its frame.
- `.symbolRenderingMode(_:)`: `.hierarchical`, `.palette`, or `.multicolor`.
- `Image(systemName:variableValue:)`: Fills a symbol's layers by a 0–1 value.
- `.imageScale(_:)`: A symbol's size next to its text.
- `.symbolEffect(_:value:)`: Plays an effect when a value changes.
- `Image(decorative:)`: An image VoiceOver skips.

## Variants

### Symbols next to text

A symbol takes its size from the font. `.imageScale` makes it smaller or larger than the text without changing the text.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
    Label("Small", systemImage: "heart.fill")
        .imageScale(.small)
    Label("Medium", systemImage: "heart.fill")
        .imageScale(.medium)
    Label("Large", systemImage: "heart.fill")
        .imageScale(.large)
}
.foregroundStyle(.pink)
```

### A level with a variable value

Pass `variableValue:` from 0 to 1 and the symbol fills its layers to match, like a volume indicator.

```swift
@State private var volume = 0.5

HStack {
    Image(systemName: "speaker.wave.3.fill", variableValue: volume)
        .frame(width: 24)
    Slider(value: $volume)
        .frame(width: 180)
}
.font(.title2)
```

### Effects that answer a click

Bounce a symbol each time a value changes with `.symbolEffect(.bounce, value:)`, and swap symbols with a `.replace` transition.

```swift
@State private var alerts = 0
@State private var isMuted = false

HStack(spacing: 24) {
    Button("Ring", systemImage: "bell") { alerts += 1 }
        .symbolEffect(.bounce, value: alerts)
    Button(isMuted ? "Unmute" : "Mute", systemImage: isMuted ? "speaker.slash" : "speaker.wave.2") {
        isMuted.toggle()
    }
    .contentTransition(.symbolEffect(.replace))
}
```

### Show that work is ongoing

Use an effect that repeats, like `.pulse`, with `isActive:` so it stops when the work does.

```swift
@State private var isSyncing = true

VStack(spacing: 12) {
    Image(systemName: "arrow.triangle.2.circlepath.icloud")
        .font(.largeTitle)
        .symbolEffect(.pulse, isActive: isSyncing)
    Toggle("Syncing", isOn: $isSyncing)
}
```

### A photo from your asset catalog

Call `.resizable()`, then `.scaledToFill()` and a frame, and clip the overflow so the photo fills the space.

```swift
Image("photo")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .frame(width: 260, height: 150)
    .clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

**Note:** For the Mac, give bitmaps @1x and @2x versions, or use PDF or SVG for flat artwork that needs to scale.

## Related

`sf-symbols`, `text-label`, `async-image`, `app-icons`, `color`


<!-- topic: stacks-grid -->
---
id: stacks-grid
title: Stacks & Grid
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+, Grid macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/layout-fundamentals.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
---

# Stacks & Grid

Line views up in rows, columns, layers, and tables that grow with the window.

Also called: HStack, VStack, ZStack, Grid, GridRow, Spacer, flexbox, flex, css grid, row.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 12) {
    Image(systemName: "doc.text")
        .font(.title)
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Quarterly Report")
            .font(.headline)
        Text("Edited yesterday")
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Stacks nest: an `HStack` of an icon and a `VStack` of two lines is the most common row on the Mac, like `display: flex` inside `display: flex`.

## Rules

- **Line up labels and fields so the eye can scan down them.** People read aligned items as related. A `Grid` with a trailing-aligned label column keeps every field starting at the same edge.
- **Put the most important things at the top leading corner.** People usually read a window from top to bottom and from the leading side, so that's where they look first.
- **Group related items so people can see what belongs together.** Extra space between groups often says it on its own. A container shape or a separator line can make the grouping clearer.
- **Keep important controls away from the bottom of the window.** People often drag a Mac window partly below the bottom of the screen, which hides whatever sits along its lower edge.

## Pitfalls

- **A stack is only as big as its content until something flexible is inside.** Add a `Spacer` or `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` and it takes all the width the window offers.
- **`Grid` lays out every cell up front.** That's how it lines up columns. For hundreds of cells inside a `ScrollView`, use `LazyVGrid` instead.

## Key APIs

- `HStack(alignment:spacing:)`: Lays views out left to right.
- `VStack(alignment:spacing:)`: Lays views out top to bottom.
- `ZStack(alignment:)`: Layers views on top of each other.
- `Spacer()`: Flexible space that pushes its neighbors apart.
- `Grid` and `GridRow`: Rows whose cells line up in columns.
- `.gridColumnAlignment(_:)`: Aligns one whole grid column.
- `.gridCellColumns(_:)`: Lets a cell span several columns.
- `.layoutPriority(_:)`: Decides which view shrinks last.

## Variants

### Push items apart with Spacer

A `Spacer` grows to fill the row, so the count stays left and the button stays right at any width; drag the slider to resize.

```swift
HStack {
    Text("12 items")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Spacer()
    Button("Add Item", systemImage: "plus") { }
}
.padding(.horizontal)
```

### Labels and fields in a Grid

In a `Grid`, `.gridColumnAlignment(.trailing)` right-aligns the label column, and `.gridCellColumns(2)` lets the checkbox span the field and button columns.

```swift
@State private var name = "Ada Lovelace"
@State private var asksFirst = true

Grid(alignment: .leadingFirstTextBaseline) {
    GridRow {
        Text("Name:")
            .gridColumnAlignment(.trailing)
        TextField("Name", text: $name)
            .labelsHidden()
        Button("Reset") { }
    }
    GridRow {
        Text("Save to:")
        Text("Downloads")
        Button("Choose…") { }
    }
    GridRow {
        Color.clear
            .gridCellUnsizedAxes([.horizontal, .vertical])
        Toggle("Ask before saving", isOn: $asksFirst)
            .gridCellColumns(2)
    }
}
```

### Choose what shrinks first

When the window gets narrow, `.layoutPriority(1)` keeps the file name whole and lets the folder path truncate instead.

```swift
HStack {
    Text("Budget 2027.numbers")
        .bold()
        .layoutPriority(1)
    Text("~/Documents/Finance/Planning")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.lineLimit(1)
```

**Note:** Every view starts at priority 0, and siblings share the space evenly. A higher priority gets its space before the others.

### A caption over a photo with ZStack

`ZStack(alignment: .bottomLeading)` draws later views on top and pins them to the corner you choose.

```swift
ZStack(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
    Image("photo")
        .resizable()
        .scaledToFill()
    Text("Lake Tahoe")
        .font(.headline)
        .foregroundStyle(.white)
        .padding(8)
        .background(.black.opacity(0.5), in: .rect(cornerRadius: 6))
        .padding(10)
}
.frame(width: 300, height: 180)
.clipShape(.rect(cornerRadius: 12))
```

## Related

`form`, `view-that-fits`, `windows-layout`


<!-- topic: group-box -->
---
id: group-box
title: GroupBox & DisclosureGroup
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+, DisclosureGroup macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/groupbox.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/boxes.md
---

# GroupBox & DisclosureGroup

Box related controls together, and tuck advanced ones under a disclosure triangle.

Also called: GroupBox, DisclosureGroup, box, NSBox, fieldset, <fieldset>, <details>, <summary>, disclosure triangle, expand.

## Contents

- Use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `GroupBox` draws a rounded background around related content, with an optional title above it.
- `DisclosureGroup` shows a label with a triangle that hides or shows its content.
- Use a box to set a few controls apart inside a larger window, and a disclosure group to keep advanced options out of the way until someone asks for them.

## Default code

```swift
@State private var includesMetadata = true

GroupBox("Export") {
    DisclosureGroup("Advanced Options") {
        Toggle("Include metadata", isOn: $includesMetadata)
    }
}
```

## Built from

GroupBox("Export")
└── VStack
    ├── Picker("Format")
    └── DisclosureGroup
        ├── Toggle
        └── Toggle

## Rules

- **Show subgroups with space, not boxes inside boxes.** Every box adds a border. Nest them and the window starts to feel busy and cramped; padding and alignment can do the same job.
- **Name a disclosure triangle after what it reveals.** A label like “Advanced Options” tells people what they'll find before they open it. “More” makes them click to find out.
- **Keep a box small next to the window around it.** A box that fills most of the window stops looking like a group and just crowds everything else.
- **Title a box with a short phrase in sentence case.** Skip ending punctuation, except in a settings pane, where Mac box titles end with a colon.
- **Leave the everyday controls outside the triangle.** Put what most people need where they can see it, and hide only the advanced options.

## Pitfalls

- **On the Mac, a box's title sits above the box.** Pass a string or a `Label`; the box sets its content apart from the window around it.
- **For a tree of data, don't nest disclosure groups by hand.** `List(children:)` and `OutlineGroup` build the triangles for you; see Outline lists (`outline`).

## Key APIs

- `GroupBox(_:content:)`: A box with a text title.
- `GroupBox { } label: { }`: A box with any title view, like a `Label`.
- `DisclosureGroup(_:content:)`: Content behind a disclosure triangle.
- `DisclosureGroup(_:isExpanded:)`: Lets you open or close it from code.
- `.disclosureGroupStyle(_:)`: Replaces the triangle with your own look.

## Variants

### Titled boxes in a settings pane

Two small `GroupBox`es split a settings pane into topics, each titled with a colon, as Mac settings panes do.

```swift
@State private var opensLastWindow = true
@State private var checksUpdates = true
@State private var syncsBookmarks = true
@State private var syncsHistory = false

VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
    GroupBox("At startup:") {
        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Toggle("Reopen last window", isOn: $opensLastWindow)
            Toggle("Check for updates", isOn: $checksUpdates)
        }
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
    }
    GroupBox("Sync:") {
        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Toggle("Bookmarks", isOn: $syncsBookmarks)
            Toggle("History", isOn: $syncsHistory)
        }
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
    }
}
.frame(width: 280)
```

### A box with an icon and a summary

Pass a `Label` as the box's title when a symbol helps people find it at a glance.

```swift
GroupBox {
    VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 6) {
        ProgressView(value: 0.62)
        Text("310 GB of 500 GB used")
            .font(.callout)
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
} label: {
    Label("Storage", systemImage: "internaldrive")
}
.frame(width: 280)
```

### Advanced options in a form

Inside a grouped `Form`, a `DisclosureGroup` becomes a row that opens to more rows, below the setting most people need.

```swift
@State private var quality = 0.8
@State private var keepsOriginal = true
@State private var stripsLocation = false

Form {
    Slider(value: $quality, in: 0...1) {
        Text("Quality")
    }
    DisclosureGroup("Advanced Options") {
        Toggle("Keep original", isOn: $keepsOriginal)
        Toggle("Remove location", isOn: $stripsLocation)
    }
}
.formStyle(.grouped)
```

### Open the way people left it

Bind `isExpanded` to `@AppStorage` so a disclosure group stays open or closed the next time the window opens.

```swift
@AppStorage("showsDetails") private var showsDetails = false

DisclosureGroup("Details", isExpanded: $showsDetails) {
    LabeledContent("Created", value: "March 3, 2026")
    LabeledContent("Size", value: "2.4 MB")
}
.frame(width: 260)
```

## Related

`form`, `outline`, `stacks-grid`


<!-- topic: split-views -->
---
id: split-views
title: Split views
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/hsplitview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views.md
---

# Split views

Panes people resize by dragging the divider between them, side by side or stacked.

Also called: HSplitView, VSplitView, split view, NSSplitView, NSSplitViewController, pane, panes, divider, resizable panel, splitter.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `HSplitView` puts its children side by side and `VSplitView` stacks them, each with a divider people drag to resize the panes.
- Nest one in the other for an editor with a file list on the left and a console underneath.
- It brings the sidebar look and the toolbar's sidebar button.

## Don't use when

- For sidebar navigation, with a list that picks what the detail shows, use NavigationSplitView (`navigation-split-view`) instead.

## Built from

HSplitView
├── FileList
└── VSplitView
    ├── Editor
    └── Console

## Rules

- **Give every pane a minimum and maximum size.** If a pane can shrink to nothing, its divider seems to disappear and people can't find it to drag back. A `minWidth` keeps it in reach.
- **Let people hide a pane, and give them more than one way back.** Someone editing may want the console gone. Offer a toolbar button and a menu command with a keyboard shortcut to show it again.
- **Keep the selection highlighted in each pane.** When a choice in one pane decides what the next one shows, a lasting highlight tells people how they got there.
- **Consider drag and drop between panes.** Panes show different levels of your content at once, so dragging an item to another pane is a natural way to move it.

## Pitfalls

- **`HSplitView` and `VSplitView` are Mac only.** If you share the view with another platform, give it another layout there.
- **They add nothing to the toolbar.** Unlike `NavigationSplitView`, there's no sidebar button. If a pane can hide, add your own toolbar button and menu command for it.

**Note:** Put a `minWidth` on each pane. Without one, people can drag a divider until the pane next to it is gone.

## Key APIs

- `HSplitView { }`: Side-by-side panes with draggable dividers.
- `VSplitView { }`: Stacked panes with draggable dividers.
- `.frame(minWidth:idealWidth:maxWidth:)`: Limits how far a pane resizes.
- `NavigationSplitView`: Sidebar and detail columns for navigation.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@State private var text = ""

HSplitView {
    List(["README.md", "App.swift"], id: \.self) { Text($0) }
        .frame(minWidth: 150, idealWidth: 200, maxWidth: 320)
    TextEditor(text: $text)
        .frame(minWidth: 300)
}
```

### A list beside an editor

`HSplitView` puts a divider between its children that people drag, and each pane's minimum and maximum width stops it.

```swift
HSplitView {
    List(["README.md", "App.swift", "Model.swift"], id: \.self) {
        Text($0)
    }
    .frame(minWidth: 120, idealWidth: 160, maxWidth: 240)
    Text("App.swift")
        .frame(minWidth: 200, maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
}
```

### An editor over a console

`VSplitView` stacks its children with a horizontal divider, so people choose how much room the console gets.

```swift
VSplitView {
    Text("App.swift")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 80, maxHeight: .infinity)
    Text("Build succeeded")
        .font(.callout.monospaced())
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 50, maxHeight: .infinity, alignment: .topLeading)
        .padding(8)
}
```

### A pane people can hide

Leave a pane out with `if` and toggle it from a toolbar button, plus a matching menu command so people have another way back.

```swift
@State private var showsConsole = true

VSplitView {
    Text("App.swift")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 80, maxHeight: .infinity)
    if showsConsole {
        Text("Build succeeded")
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 50, maxHeight: .infinity)
    }
}
.toolbar {
    Toggle("Console", systemImage: "rectangle.bottomthird.inset.filled", isOn: $showsConsole)
}
```

**Note:** A real `.toolbar` here would land in this window's own toolbar, so the preview draws one. The panes demo window has the real thing.

## Related

`navigation-split-view`, `inspector`, `stacks-grid`, `windows-layout`


<!-- topic: list-styles -->
---
id: list-styles
title: List styles
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+, Collapsible sections macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/liststyle.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables.md
---

# List styles

Sidebar, inset, and bordered lists, with rows people click to select, one or many.

Also called: List, listStyle, sidebar, inset, bordered, plain, NSTableView, source list, alternatingRowBackgrounds, zebra stripes.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- A `List` shows rows in one column and handles selection and scrolling for you.
- Its style decides the look: `.sidebar` for the source list on the leading edge of a window, `.inset` for content with rounded selection, and `.bordered` for a boxed list inside a form or settings pane.

## Don't use when

- For several columns of data, use a Table (`table`).
- For a hierarchy, see Outline lists (`outline`).

## Default code

```swift
@State private var selection: String?
private let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"]

List(fruits, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { fruit in
    Text(fruit)
}
```

**Note:** `selection:` takes an optional for one row at a time, or a `Set` for several. Without it, rows don't highlight when clicked.

## Rules

- **Keep row text short.** Rows are for scanning. Show a title, and put the long text in a detail view people open from the row.
- **Keep the selected row highlighted when it drives a detail view.** A lasting highlight shows people where they are. A list of options can instead flash the row and show a checkmark.
- **Show at most two levels in a sidebar.** Deeper hierarchies are hard to follow there. Add a content column between the sidebar and the detail instead.
- **Let the sidebar's icons follow the accent color.** People pick an accent color for every app. Save fixed colors for the few icons that need to stand out.

## Pitfalls

- **Selection on the Mac needs no edit mode.** Bind `selection:` to a `Set` and people can select several rows right away, with no Edit button.
- **Sidebar section headers can collapse.** In the `.sidebar` style, people can hide a section from its header.

## Key APIs

- `List(_:selection:rowContent:)`: Rows from data, optionally selectable.
- `.listStyle(.sidebar)`: A source list with collapsible sections.
- `.listStyle(.inset)`: Content rows with inset selection.
- `.listStyle(.bordered)`: A boxed list for forms and panes.
- `.alternatingRowBackgrounds()`: Stripes every other row.
- `.onDeleteCommand(perform:)`: Runs on the Delete key or Delete command.
- `.contextMenu(forSelectionType:)`: A menu and double-click for selected rows.

## Variants

### A sidebar with collapsible sections

`.listStyle(.sidebar)` gives the source list look, `Section(isExpanded:)` lets people fold a section, and `.badge` shows a count.

```swift
@State private var selection: String? = "Inbox"
@State private var showsFavorites = true
@State private var showsTags = true

List(selection: $selection) {
    Section("Favorites", isExpanded: $showsFavorites) {
        Label("Inbox", systemImage: "tray")
            .badge(12)
            .tag("Inbox")
        Label("Flagged", systemImage: "flag")
            .tag("Flagged")
    }
    Section("Tags", isExpanded: $showsTags) {
        Label("Work", systemImage: "tag")
            .tag("Work")
        Label("Family", systemImage: "tag")
            .tag("Family")
    }
}
.listStyle(.sidebar)
.frame(width: 220, height: 240)
```

### A bordered list with add and remove buttons

Use `.listStyle(.bordered)` for a short list in a settings pane, with `+` and `−` buttons below and `.onDeleteCommand` for the Delete key.

```swift
struct BlockedSenders: View {
    @State private var blocked = ["spam@example.com", "deals@example.net"]
    @State private var selection: String?

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 0) {
            List(blocked, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { Text($0) }
                .listStyle(.bordered)
                .alternatingRowBackgrounds()
                .onDeleteCommand { removeSelected() }
            HStack(spacing: 0) {
                Button("Add", systemImage: "plus") {
                    blocked.append("new@example.com")
                }
                Button("Remove", systemImage: "minus") { removeSelected() }
                    .disabled(selection == nil)
            }
            .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
            .buttonStyle(.borderless)
            .padding(4)
        }
        .frame(width: 280, height: 180)
    }

    private func removeSelected() {
        blocked.removeAll { $0 == selection }
        selection = nil
    }
}
```

### Select several, and double-click to open

Bind `selection:` to a `Set` for multiple selection, and `.contextMenu(forSelectionType:)` adds a menu plus a `primaryAction` for double-click.

```swift
@State private var notes = ["Groceries", "Packing list", "Book ideas"]
@State private var selection: Set<String> = []
@Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

List(notes, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { note in
    Text(note)
}
.contextMenu(forSelectionType: String.self) { items in
    Button("Open") { }
    Button("Delete", role: .destructive) {
        notes.removeAll { items.contains($0) }
    }
} primaryAction: { items in
    for item in items {
        openWindow(value: item)
    }
}
```

**Note:** On the Mac, a single click selects a row and a double click runs the primary action. Opening a window this way needs a `WindowGroup(for: String.self)` scene in your app.

## Related

`table`, `outline`, `navigation-split-view`, `context-menu`


<!-- topic: table -->
---
id: table
title: Table
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 12.0+, Column customization macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/table.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables.md
---

# Table

Rows of data in columns that people sort, resize, and select, like Finder's list view.

Also called: TableColumn, NSTableView, data grid, spreadsheet, <table>, columns, sort, sortOrder, KeyPathComparator, SortComparator.

## Contents

- Use when
- Don't use when
- Default code
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `Table` shows a collection as rows, with one `TableColumn` per property.
- People can click a column header to sort, drag column edges to resize, and select one row or many.
- Use it when each item has several values worth comparing side by side.

## Don't use when

- For one value per row, a List (`list-styles`) is simpler.

## Default code

```swift
struct FileRow: Identifiable {
    let name: String
    let kind: String
    let size: Int64
    var id: String { name }

    static let samples = [
        FileRow(name: "Report.pdf", kind: "PDF document", size: 1_250_000),
        FileRow(name: "Notes.txt", kind: "Plain text", size: 4_000),
    ]
}

@State private var selection = Set<FileRow.ID>()

Table(FileRow.samples, selection: $selection) {
    TableColumn("Name", value: \.name)
    TableColumn("Kind", value: \.kind)
}
```

**Note:** Each row needs a stable `id`: selection stores ids, not rows. The other snippets on this page reuse this `FileRow`.

## Built from

Table(files, selection:, sortOrder:)
├── TableColumn("Name", value: \.name)
├── TableColumn("Kind", value: \.kind)
└── TableColumn("Size", value: \.size)

## Rules

- **Let people sort by clicking a column header.** Clicking the header of the column that's already sorted should sort it again in the opposite direction.
- **Let people resize columns.** Values vary in width. Resizing lets people read clipped text or focus on the columns they care about.
- **Consider striped rows in a wide table.** Alternating row colors help the eye follow one row across many columns.
- **Name columns with short nouns, without punctuation.** Headings like “Name” and “Date Modified” say what's below them. Skip trailing colons.
- **Use an outline for data that nests.** If rows contain other rows, like folders and files, show them with disclosure triangles in an `outline`.

## Pitfalls

- **Sorting is your job.** The table shows which column is sorted and in which direction, but you sort the data yourself when `sortOrder` changes.
- **A `Table` scrolls on its own.** Don't wrap it in a `ScrollView`; give it a frame, or let the window size it.

## Key APIs

- `Table(_:selection:sortOrder:)`: Rows from data, selectable and sortable.
- `TableColumn(_:value:)`: A column that shows and sorts by a key path.
- `KeyPathComparator(_:)`: Describes one sort: a key path and order.
- `.width(min:ideal:max:)`: Limits how wide a column can get.
- `.contextMenu(forSelectionType:)`: A menu and double-click for selected rows.
- `.customizationID(_:)`: Lets people hide and reorder a column.
- `.tableStyle(_:)`: `.inset` or `.bordered`.
- `.alternatingRowBackgrounds()`: Stripes every other row.

## Variants

### Right-click and double-click selected rows

`.contextMenu(forSelectionType:)` builds a menu for the rows people clicked, and `primaryAction` runs when they double-click.

```swift
@State private var files = FileRow.samples
@State private var selection = Set<FileRow.ID>()

Table(files, selection: $selection) {
    TableColumn("Name", value: \.name)
    TableColumn("Kind", value: \.kind)
}
.contextMenu(forSelectionType: FileRow.ID.self) { ids in
    if ids.isEmpty {
        Button("New File") { }
    } else {
        Button("Open") { }
        Button("Move to Trash", role: .destructive) {
            files.removeAll { ids.contains($0.id) }
        }
    }
} primaryAction: { ids in
    // Open each double-clicked file.
}
```

**Note:** Right-clicking empty space gives the menu an empty set, even when rows are selected. That's where “New File” goes.

### Columns people can hide and reorder

Give each column a `.customizationID` and pass a `TableColumnCustomization`, stored with `@SceneStorage` so the layout comes back with the window.

```swift
@SceneStorage("FilesTable") private var columns = TableColumnCustomization<FileRow>()

Table(FileRow.samples, columnCustomization: $columns) {
    TableColumn("Name", value: \.name)
        .customizationID("name")
    TableColumn("Kind", value: \.kind)
        .customizationID("kind")
    TableColumn("Size") { file in
        Text(file.size, format: .byteCount(style: .file))
    }
    .customizationID("size")
}
```

**Note:** A column without a customization ID can't be hidden or moved. You can also hide one from code: `columns[visibility: "size"] = .hidden`.

### Columns with sensible widths

`.width(min:ideal:max:)` sets how far people can resize a column, and a fixed `.width(_:)` suits short values like a size.

```swift
Table(FileRow.samples) {
    TableColumn("Name", value: \.name)
        .width(min: 120, ideal: 180)
    TableColumn("Kind", value: \.kind)
        .width(min: 80, max: 160)
    TableColumn("Size") { file in
        Text(file.size, format: .byteCount(style: .file))
            .monospacedDigit()
    }
    .width(70)
}
```

## Related

`list-styles`, `outline`, `context-menu`, `inspector`


<!-- topic: outline -->
---
id: outline
title: Outline lists
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+, Outline Table macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/outlinegroup.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/outline-views.md
---

# Outline lists

Folders inside folders: rows with disclosure triangles that open to show their children.

Also called: OutlineGroup, outline view, NSOutlineView, tree, tree view, hierarchy, nested list, children, List children, disclosure triangle.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- Give a `List` tree-shaped data and a key path to each item's children, and it draws a disclosure triangle on every row that has some.
- People open and close branches, like folders in Finder's list view.
- Use `List(_:children:)` for a whole outline, `OutlineGroup` to put a tree inside one section of a list, and `Table(_:children:)` when each row also needs columns.

## Built from

List(files, children: \.children)
└── Label(file.name)
    └── (children, when expanded)

## Rules

- **Show the hierarchy in the first column only.** Indent and put triangles in the first column. The other columns hold details about each item, like its size or date.
- **Use a table when nothing nests.** Triangles on data that has no children only add clutter. A flat collection belongs in a `table` or list.
- **Remember what people expanded.** If someone opened three folders to reach a file, show it that way next time instead of making them dig again.
- **Give every column of a multicolumn outline a heading.** Use short nouns without punctuation, so people know what each value is.
- **Consider a search field for a long outline.** When the outline is the main part of the window, a search field in the toolbar helps people find a value fast.

## Pitfalls
