- **`children` decides which rows get a triangle.** A row whose children are `nil` is a leaf. An empty array still shows a triangle, like an empty folder.
- **Branches start closed.** Every branch `OutlineGroup` builds begins collapsed. To reopen what people had open last time, track expansion yourself, as in the last example.

**Important:** `children` must be optional. Leaves return `nil`; returning `[]` for them shows a triangle that opens to nothing.

## Key APIs

- `List(_:children:rowContent:)`: A whole list built from a tree.
- `OutlineGroup(_:children:)`: A tree inside a list or section.
- `Table(_:children:columns:)`: An outline with columns, like Finder.
- `DisclosureGroup(isExpanded:)`: One branch whose state you control.
- `DisclosureTableRow`: A table row that opens to more rows.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
struct FileNode: Identifiable {
    let name: String
    var children: [FileNode]? = nil
    var id: String { name }
}

let files = [
    FileNode(name: "Documents", children: [
        FileNode(name: "Report.pdf"),
    ]),
    FileNode(name: "Notes.txt"),
]

List(files, children: \.children) { file in
    Label(file.name, systemImage: file.children == nil ? "doc" : "folder")
}
```

### A file tree with List(children:)

Pass the tree and the key path to each item's children, and add `selection:` so people can click a row at any depth.

```swift
@State private var selection: FileNode.ID?

List(FileNode.samples, children: \.children, selection: $selection) { file in
    Label(file.name, systemImage: file.symbol)
}
.frame(width: 280, height: 220)
```

**Note:** The examples on this page use the `FileNode` from Usage, plus a `symbol` name, a `totalSize`, and some `samples`.

### A tree inside one sidebar section

`OutlineGroup` builds the same triangles inside a `Section`, so a sidebar can mix flat rows with a tree.

```swift
@State private var selection: FileNode.ID?

List(selection: $selection) {
    Section("Favorites") {
        Label("Recents", systemImage: "clock")
        Label("Shared", systemImage: "person.2")
    }
    Section("Locations") {
        OutlineGroup(FileNode.samples, children: \.children) { file in
            Label(file.name, systemImage: file.symbol)
        }
    }
}
.listStyle(.sidebar)
.frame(width: 240, height: 260)
```

### Finder-style: an outline with columns

`Table(_:children:)` puts the tree in the first column and details in the others, like Finder's list view.

```swift
@State private var selection = Set<FileNode.ID>()

Table(FileNode.samples, children: \.children, selection: $selection) {
    TableColumn("Name") { file in
        Label(file.name, systemImage: file.symbol)
    }
    TableColumn("Size") { file in
        Text(file.totalSize, format: .byteCount(style: .file))
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
    .width(90)
}
.frame(width: 420, height: 220)
```

### Expansion you keep track of

Build the tree from `DisclosureGroup(isExpanded:)` rows and keep the open ids in a `Set` you can save, to reopen the outline as people left it.

```swift
struct FileTree: View {
    let nodes: [FileNode]
    @Binding var expanded: Set<FileNode.ID>

    var body: some View {
        ForEach(nodes) { node in
            if let children = node.children {
                DisclosureGroup(isExpanded: Binding {
                    expanded.contains(node.id)
                } set: { isOpen in
                    if isOpen { expanded.insert(node.id) } else { expanded.remove(node.id) }
                }) {
                    FileTree(nodes: children, expanded: $expanded)
                } label: {
                    Label(node.name, systemImage: node.symbol)
                }
            } else {
                Label(node.name, systemImage: node.symbol)
            }
        }
    }
}

@State private var expanded: Set<FileNode.ID> = ["Documents"]

List {
    FileTree(nodes: FileNode.samples, expanded: $expanded)
}
```

## Related

`list-styles`, `table`, `group-box`


<!-- topic: inspector -->
---
id: inspector
title: Inspector
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/inspector(ispresented:content:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/panels.md

# Inspector

A trailing column that shows and edits the details of whatever is selected.

Also called: inspectorColumnWidth, InspectorCommands, info panel, properties panel, attributes inspector, right sidebar, trailing sidebar, details pane, NSSplitViewItem, Show Inspector.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `.inspector(isPresented:content:)` adds a column on the trailing edge of the window, beside your content.
- It shows the details of the current selection and updates as the selection changes, like the inspector in Keynote.
- Put the button that shows and hides it in the toolbar, and add `InspectorCommands` so the menu bar has a command and ⌃⌘I for it too.

## Built from

NavigationStack
└── Editor
    ├── .toolbar
    │   └── Button("Inspector")
    └── .inspector
        └── Form

## Rules

- **Show the details of the current selection.** An inspector follows the selection: pick another item and it updates. For details that shouldn't change, open a separate window instead.
- **Keep it on the trailing side, with its button at the trailing end of the toolbar.** That's where people expect to find both. Toolbar items at the trailing end stay visible at every window size.
- **Prefer controls that adjust in one step.** Sliders and steppers change a value right away. Typing in a text field, or picking an item from a list, takes more steps.

## Pitfalls

- **SwiftUI remembers whether the inspector was open.** When it's a trailing column, its shown or hidden state is restored with the window.

**Note:** A real inspector in this page would open in this app's own window, so the examples below draw the window. The demo window has the real thing.

## Key APIs

- `.inspector(isPresented:content:)`: Adds a trailing inspector column.
- `.inspectorColumnWidth(min:ideal:max:)`: A width people can drag within.
- `.inspectorColumnWidth(_:)`: A fixed width.
- `InspectorCommands()`: A menu command with ⌃⌘I.
- `.interactiveDismissDisabled()`: Keeps people from dragging it shut.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@State private var showsInspector = true

NavigationStack {
    Text("Canvas")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
        .inspector(isPresented: $showsInspector) {
            Form {
                Text("Details of the selection")
            }
            .inspectorColumnWidth(min: 200, ideal: 240, max: 320)
        }
        .toolbar {
            Button("Inspector", systemImage: "sidebar.trailing") {
                showsInspector.toggle()
            }
        }
}
```

### Toggle it from the toolbar

Bind `isPresented` to a `Bool` and flip it from a button at the trailing end of the toolbar; try it in the drawn toolbar.

```swift
@State private var showsInspector = true

Text("Canvas")
    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
    .inspector(isPresented: $showsInspector) {
        Text("Inspector")
    }
    .toolbar {
        Button("Inspector", systemImage: "sidebar.trailing") {
            showsInspector.toggle()
        }
    }
```

### Details that follow the selection

Pass a binding to the selected item into the inspector, so picking another shape switches what it edits.

```swift
@State private var shapes = ShapeItem.samples
@State private var selection: ShapeItem.ID? = 1
@State private var showsInspector = true

List(shapes, selection: $selection) { shape in
    Label(shape.name, systemImage: "square.fill")
        .foregroundStyle(shape.color)
}
.inspector(isPresented: $showsInspector) {
    if let index = shapes.firstIndex(where: { $0.id == selection }) {
        Form {
            TextField("Name", text: $shapes[index].name)
            Slider(value: $shapes[index].opacity, in: 0...1) {
                Text("Opacity")
            }
            Slider(value: $shapes[index].cornerRadius, in: 0...40) {
                Text("Corners")
            }
        }
    } else {
        ContentUnavailableView("No Selection", systemImage: "square.dashed")
    }
}
```

**Note:** `ShapeItem` is a small `Identifiable` struct with a name, color, opacity, and corner radius.

### A width people can drag, or a fixed one

`.inspectorColumnWidth` with `min`, `ideal`, and `max` lets people resize the column within limits, and one number fixes the width.

```swift
@State private var showsInspector = true

Text("Canvas")
    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
    .inspector(isPresented: $showsInspector) {
        Form {
            Text("Details")
        }
        .inspectorColumnWidth(min: 200, ideal: 240, max: 320)
        // Or a fixed width that people can't drag shut:
        // .inspectorColumnWidth(240)
        // .interactiveDismissDisabled()
    }
```

**Important:** On the Mac, people can drag an inspector closed even at a fixed width. Add `.interactiveDismissDisabled()` to prevent it.

### Add the menu command

```swift
@main
struct ShapesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            EditorView()
        }
        .commands {
            InspectorCommands()
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`split-views`, `toolbar`, `navigation-split-view`, `form`


<!-- topic: window-group -->
---
id: window-group
title: WindowGroup
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/windowgroup.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows.md
---

# WindowGroup

The scene for your app's main windows, where people can open as many as they need.

Also called: window, windows, multiple windows, new window, File > New Window, scene, WindowGroup(for:), open in new window, state restoration, restorationBehavior.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `WindowGroup` is the scene most Mac apps start with.
- Its content is a template: every window people open from it gets its own copy of the view, with its own state.
- On the Mac you get File > New Window, a list of open windows in the Window menu, and windows that people can merge into tabs, without writing any code.
- For a window there should only ever be one of, use `Window` instead.

## Built from

App
├── WindowGroup          main windows
└── WindowGroup(for:)    one per value
    └── $value binding

## Rules

- **Call it a window.** The system calls every window a window. Words like “scene” or “view” for the same thing only confuse people.
- **Open new windows when they help, not by default.** A second window is great for comparing or keeping context, like a draft beside your inbox. Opening one for every click fills the screen and makes the app harder to follow.
- **Offer “Open in New Window” as a choice.** Put it in the item's context menu or the File menu, so people who want a separate window can have one.
- **Make windows work at any size.** People resize and arrange windows constantly on the Mac. Set a sensible minimum size and let the layout grow from there.

## Pitfalls

- **Closing the last window doesn't quit the app.** An app built on a `WindowGroup` keeps running with no windows open. One whose only scene is a `Window` quits when it closes.
- **Each window starts with fresh `@State`.** Keep data that every window should see in a shared model, passed in through the environment.

## Key APIs

- `WindowGroup { }`: Main windows. People can open many.
- `WindowGroup(for:) { $value in }`: One window per value, like a note's ID.
- `WindowGroup(_:id:)`: A title for menus, and an ID to open it by.
- `defaultValue:`: The value File > New Window passes instead of `nil`.
- `@Environment(\.openWindow)`: Opens a window from your code.
- `.navigationTitle(_:)`: Each window's own title.
- `.restorationBehavior(.disabled)`: Keeps a scene's windows from reopening at launch.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct NotesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
    }
}
```

### Every window has its own state

SwiftUI gives each new window fresh storage for its `@State`. Count in one window, and the other doesn't change.

```swift
struct ContentView: View {
    @State private var count = 0

    var body: some View {
        Stepper("Cups of tea: \(count)", value: $count)
            .padding()
    }
}
```

### A window per item

`WindowGroup(for:)` opens one window per value, like a note's ID. Open a note twice, and its window comes forward.

```swift
@main
struct NotesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            NoteList()
        }
        WindowGroup("Note", for: Note.ID.self) { $noteID in
            NoteView(noteID: noteID)
        }
    }
}

struct NoteRow: View {
    let note: Note
    @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

    var body: some View {
        Text(note.title)
            .contextMenu {
                Button("Open in New Window") {
                    openWindow(value: note.id)
                }
            }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The value must be `Hashable` and `Codable`. Pass an ID rather than the whole model: SwiftUI saves the value to restore the window later.

### New windows and restoring

```swift
WindowGroup("Note", for: Note.ID.self) { $noteID in
    NoteView(noteID: noteID)
} defaultValue: {
    store.makeNote().id
}
```

## Related

`window`, `opening-windows`, `document-group`, `window-style`, `windows-tabs`


<!-- topic: window -->
---
id: window
title: Window
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/window.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/panels.md
---

# Window

A single, unique window, like an activity viewer or a floating palette.

Also called: single window, singleton window, one window, auxiliary window, secondary window, UtilityWindow, utility window, floating window, palette, panel.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `Window` opens one window, never two.
- Asking for it again brings the open window to the front, and the Window menu lists it by title.
- `UtilityWindow` (macOS 15) is a kind of `Window` for tool palettes and inspectors: it floats above your main windows, hides when your app isn't active, and adds an item to show and hide it in the View menu.

## Built from

App
├── WindowGroup      main windows
├── Window           exactly one
└── UtilityWindow    floating palette

## Rules

- **Leave “panel” out of the menu item.** Name the command after the panel's title, as in Show Inspector or Show Colors. Short noun titles are easy to spot in a menu and on screen.
- **Use a panel for controls that follow the selection.** An inspector updates as people select different items. A window that always shows the same thing, like an Info window, should be a regular window.
- **Prefer sliders and steppers in panels.** Panels work best with direct adjustments. Typing text or picking items to act on takes extra steps in a small floating window.
- **Hide panels with your app, and skip the minimize button.** Panels appear when needed and disappear when your app isn't active. `UtilityWindow` does both for you.

## Pitfalls

- **Every scene ID must be unique.** `Window` and `WindowGroup` share one set of IDs, and `openWindow(id:)` uses it to find the scene.
- **The Window menu lists it for you.** People can bring a `Window` back from the Window menu by its title, so it doesn't need its own menu item.

## Key APIs

- `Window(_:id:) { }`: One unique window, listed in the Window menu.
- `UtilityWindow(_:id:) { }`: A floating palette that follows the active window.
- `openWindow(id:)`: Shows the window, or brings it to the front.
- `@Environment(\.dismiss)`: Closes the window from inside it.
- `@FocusedValue`: Reads the focused main window's selection.
- `.windowLevel(.floating)`: Keeps any window above normal windows.
- `.defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)`: Opens it at launch, like a welcome window.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct PhotosApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        Window("Activity", id: "activity") {
            ActivityView()
        }
    }
}
```

### Show it from a button

Call `openWindow(id:)` with the window's ID. If the window is already open, it comes to the front.

```swift
struct ShowActivityButton: View {
    @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

    var body: some View {
        Button("Show Activity") {
            openWindow(id: "activity")
        }
    }
}
```

### A floating palette

`UtilityWindow` floats above your main windows. Read the active window's selection with `@FocusedValue`, and it updates as people switch windows.

```swift
extension FocusedValues {
    @Entry var selectedPhotoCount: Int?
}

@main
struct PhotosApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            PhotoGrid()
        }
        UtilityWindow("Photo Info", id: "photo-info") {
            PhotoInfo()
        }
    }
}

struct PhotoGrid: View {
    @State private var selection = Set<Int>()

    var body: some View {
        Text("\(selection.count) photos selected")
            .focusedSceneValue(\.selectedPhotoCount, selection.count)
    }
}

struct PhotoInfo: View {
    @FocusedValue(\.selectedPhotoCount) private var count

    var body: some View {
        Text("\(count ?? 0) photos selected")
            .padding()
    }
}
```

**Note:** A utility window isn't minimizable by default, and when it's focused, Esc closes it. It takes focus only when it needs to, like when people click its title bar or a text field in it.

### A window as the whole app

For an app that should never have two windows, like one built around the camera, make a `Window` the only scene.

```swift
@main
struct VideoCallApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        Window("Video Call", id: "main") {
            CallView()
        }
    }
}
```

**Important:** When that window closes, the app quits. For most apps, start with a `WindowGroup` instead, and add a `Window` beside it.

## Related

`window-group`, `opening-windows`, `settings-scene`, `window-style`, `menu-bar-extra`


<!-- topic: settings-scene -->
---
id: settings-scene
title: Settings
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/settings.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/settings.md
---

# Settings

The app's Settings window, opened from the app menu or with ⌘,.

Also called: preferences, settings window, command comma, ⌘,, SettingsLink, openSettings, NSPreferences, options.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `Settings` is a scene, like `WindowGroup`.
- It gives your app one Settings window, the Settings… item in the app menu, and ⌘, to open it.
- Put a `Form` inside for a single pane, or a `TabView` to split settings into panes that switch from the window's toolbar.

## Built from

Settings
└── TabView
    ├── Tab("General")
    │   └── Form
    └── Tab("Advanced")
        └── Form

## Rules

- **Open settings from the app menu, not a toolbar button.** People look for Settings… in the app menu and press ⌘,. A gear in the toolbar takes space from the commands people use all the time.
- **Keep it short, and keep task options with the task.** Settings are for things people change rarely. Options like sorting or showing a sidebar belong in the window they affect.
- **Reopen the pane people used last.** People often come back to change a related setting. Store the selected tab with `@AppStorage`, as in the example below.
- **Don't repeat system settings.** Appearance, scrolling, and accessibility belong to System Settings. A copy in your app suggests the system choice doesn't apply.

## Pitfalls

- **You get the menu item and ⌘, for free.** Adding a `Settings` scene puts Settings… in the app menu and wires up the shortcut.
- **Settings is a window like any other.** Use `@AppStorage` so a change shows up in every open window right away.

## Key APIs

- `Settings { }`: The scene for the app's Settings window.
- `TabView`: Inside `Settings`, a toolbar of panes.
- `SettingsLink`: A button that opens the Settings window.
- `@Environment(\.openSettings)`: Opens Settings from your own code.
- `@AppStorage`: Saves a setting and keeps windows in sync.
- `.formStyle(.grouped)`: Rows in rounded groups, like System Settings.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct ReaderApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        Settings {
            SettingsView()
        }
    }
}
```

### One pane

With a handful of settings, use a single grouped `Form` and give the window a fixed width.

```swift
struct SettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("showsPreview") private var showsPreview = true
    @AppStorage("fontSize") private var fontSize = 14.0

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Toggle("Show preview", isOn: $showsPreview)
            Slider(value: $fontSize, in: 10...24) {
                Text("Font size")
            }
        }
        .formStyle(.grouped)
        .frame(width: 400)
    }
}
```

**Note:** With one pane, the HIG suggests titling the window “App Name Settings”.

### Panes that remember where you were

A `TabView` inside `Settings` becomes the toolbar of panes. Bind it to `@AppStorage` so it reopens on the last pane.

```swift
enum SettingsPane: String {
    case general, advanced
}

struct SettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("settingsPane") private var pane = SettingsPane.general

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $pane) {
            Tab("General", systemImage: "gearshape", value: .general) {
                Form { Toggle("Show preview", isOn: .constant(true)) }
            }
            Tab("Advanced", systemImage: "gearshape.2", value: .advanced) {
                Form { Toggle("Enable logging", isOn: .constant(false)) }
            }
        }
        .frame(width: 440)
    }
}
```

### Open Settings from your own UI

Use `SettingsLink` for a button, or `@Environment(\.openSettings)` from code, like a link in an empty state.

```swift
ContentUnavailableView {
    Label("No Accounts", systemImage: "person.crop.circle")
} description: {
    Text("Add an account in Settings to start syncing.")
} actions: {
    SettingsLink {
        Text("Open Settings")
    }
}
```

## Related

`toggle`


<!-- topic: menu-bar-extra -->
---
id: menu-bar-extra
title: MenuBarExtra
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/menubarextra.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar.md
---

# MenuBarExtra

A menu bar icon that opens a menu or a small window, whichever app is in front.

Also called: menu bar extra, status item, status bar item, NSStatusItem, NSStatusBar, menu bar app, menulet, tray icon, system tray, LSUIElement.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `MenuBarExtra` is a scene that puts an icon at the trailing end of the menu bar.
- It stays there while your app runs, even when another app is in front.
- Clicking it shows a menu, or with `.menuBarExtraStyle(.window)`, a small window of controls.
- Add it beside your `WindowGroup`, or make it the only scene for an app that lives in the menu bar.

## Built from

App
├── WindowGroup
└── MenuBarExtra("Weather", systemImage:)
    └── Button, Toggle, Divider…

## Rules

- **Use a symbol for the icon.** The system tints a symbol or template image so it suits light and dark menu bars and the selected state. A full-color picture can't adapt.
- **Show a menu, not a popover.** A menu is what people expect from a menu bar icon. Save the `.window` style for features too rich for a menu.
- **Let people decide whether it appears.** Add a setting to turn it on or off in your Settings window, and consider offering the choice during setup.
- **Don't count on it being visible.** The system hides menu bar extras when space runs short. Offer the same features somewhere else too, like a Dock menu.

## Pitfalls

- **Removing it quits a menu bar–only app.** If the extra is the app's only scene and someone removes it from the menu bar, the system ends the app.
- **The menu bar is 24 points tall.** Size a custom icon to fit, or use an SF Symbol, which already does.

**Note:** A menu bar extra is a scene, so a page can't add one to this app. The previews below are drawings with live content; the code is the real thing.

## Key APIs

- `MenuBarExtra(_:systemImage:) { }`: An icon and title, with a menu.
- `MenuBarExtra(…, isInserted:)`: Shown only while the binding is true.
- `.menuBarExtraStyle(.menu)`: The content as a menu that pulls down.
- `.menuBarExtraStyle(.window)`: The content in a small, popover-like window.
- `@Environment(\.openWindow)`: Opens one of your app's windows from the menu.
- `LSUIElement`: Info.plist key that hides the Dock icon.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct WeatherApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        MenuBarExtra("Weather", systemImage: "cloud.sun") {
            Button("Refresh") { }
            Divider()
            Button("Open Weather") { }
        }
    }
}
```

### A menu

By default, the content is a menu that pulls down from the icon. Use buttons, toggles, and dividers, as in any menu.

```swift
@State private var isPaused = false

MenuBarExtra("Timer", systemImage: "timer") {
    Button("Start Focus Session") { }
    Toggle("Pause Notifications", isOn: $isPaused)
    Divider()
    SettingsLink {
        Text("Settings…")
    }
}
```

### A small window

With `.menuBarExtraStyle(.window)`, the content shows in a popover-like window, laid out like controls in a normal window.

```swift
MenuBarExtra("Weather", systemImage: "cloud.sun") {
    WeatherPanel()
}
.menuBarExtraStyle(.window)

struct WeatherPanel: View {
    @State private var usesCelsius = true

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
            Label("18°  Partly Cloudy", systemImage: "cloud.sun")
                .font(.title2)
            Gauge(value: 0.4) { Text("Rain") }
            Toggle("Celsius", isOn: $usesCelsius)
        }
        .padding()
        .frame(width: 240)
    }
}
```

### Let people turn it off

Pass `isInserted:` a binding, like an `@AppStorage` value, and put a toggle for it in your Settings window.

```swift
@main
struct WeatherApp: App {
    @AppStorage("showsInMenuBar") private var showsInMenuBar = true

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        MenuBarExtra("Weather", systemImage: "cloud.sun", isInserted: $showsInMenuBar) {
            Button("Refresh") { }
        }
        Settings {
            Form {
                Toggle("Show in menu bar", isOn: $showsInMenuBar)
            }
            .padding()
        }
    }
}
```

### An app that lives in the menu bar

```swift
@main
struct ClipboardApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        MenuBarExtra("Clipboard", systemImage: "list.clipboard") {
            ClipboardMenu()
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`menu-bar-utility`, `settings-scene`, `window`, `commands`, `menu-bar-conventions`


<!-- topic: document-group -->
---
id: document-group
title: DocumentGroup
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/documentgroup.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management.md
---

# DocumentGroup

The scene for document-based apps, with New, Open, and Save built in.

Also called: document-based app, document app, documents, NSDocument, NSDocumentController, FileDocument, ReferenceFileDocument, open panel, save panel, NSOpenPanel.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `DocumentGroup` makes your app document-based.
- You give it a document type and the view that edits it.
- SwiftUI adds File > New and the standard document commands, shows the system's open and save panels, opens each document in its own window, and writes the file back when people save.
- Model the document as a struct that conforms to `FileDocument`, and SwiftUI registers undo for every change.
- If it has to be a class, use `ReferenceFileDocument` and register undo yourself.

## Built from

DocumentGroup(newDocument:)
└── editor view
    └── file.$document

## Rules

- **Start new documents as “Untitled”.** That's the name the system gives a new document until people pick one in the save panel. Keep it, rather than inventing your own.
- **Save people's work without asking.** Save periodically while people edit, and when they close the document or switch apps, so work isn't lost.
- **Use the system's open and save panels.** People know them from every other Mac app. Build your own file browser only for a strong reason.
- **Hide file extensions by default.** Let people show them if they want, and respect that choice in every open and save panel.

## Pitfalls

- **Every document-based app declares its types.** List the content types your app opens under Document Types (`CFBundleDocumentTypes`) in the target's Info pane.
- **With several document groups, order matters.** SwiftUI opens a file with the first group whose types match it, so put more specific types first.

**Note:** Apple's documentation marks `FileDocument` deprecated in macOS 27.2, in favor of the new `Document` protocol, which needs macOS 27. For an app that also runs on earlier versions, `FileDocument` is still the one to use.

## Key APIs

- `DocumentGroup(newDocument:editor:)`: Creates, opens, and edits one document type.
- `FileDocument`: A struct document. Undo comes for free.
- `ReferenceFileDocument`: A class document. You register undo.
- `readableContentTypes`: The file types the document opens.
- `init(configuration:)`: Reads the document from a file.
- `fileWrapper(configuration:)`: Writes the document to a file.
- `file.$document`: A binding that edits the open document.
- `file.fileURL`: Where it's saved; `nil` until the first save.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct EditorApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        DocumentGroup(newDocument: TextFile()) { file in
            TextEditor(text: file.$document.text)
        }
    }
}
```

### A plain-text document

A `FileDocument` lists the types it reads, loads itself in `init(configuration:)`, and writes itself in `fileWrapper(configuration:)`.

```swift
import SwiftUI
import UniformTypeIdentifiers

struct TextFile: FileDocument {
    static let readableContentTypes = [UTType.plainText]
    var text = ""

    init() {}

    init(configuration: ReadConfiguration) throws {
        guard let data = configuration.file.regularFileContents else {
            throw CocoaError(.fileReadCorruptFile)
        }
        text = String(decoding: data, as: UTF8.self)
    }

    func fileWrapper(configuration: WriteConfiguration) throws -> FileWrapper {
        FileWrapper(regularFileWithContents: Data(text.utf8))
    }
}
```

**Important:** SwiftUI reads and writes documents on a background thread. Don't update the interface from those two methods.

### Show where the file is saved

The editor closure also gets `fileURL`, which is `nil` until the first save. Use it for display, and let the document read and write the file.

```swift
DocumentGroup(newDocument: TextFile()) { file in
    TextEditor(text: file.$document.text)
        .safeAreaInset(edge: .bottom) {
            Text(file.fileURL?.lastPathComponent ?? "Not saved yet")
                .font(.caption)
                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
                .padding(6)
        }
}
```

### Your own file type

```swift
extension UTType {
    static let checklist = UTType(exportedAs: "com.example.checklist")
}

struct ChecklistFile: FileDocument {
    static let readableContentTypes = [UTType.checklist]
    var items: [String] = []

    init() {}

    init(configuration: ReadConfiguration) throws {
        let data = configuration.file.regularFileContents ?? Data()
        items = try JSONDecoder().decode([String].self, from: data)
    }

    func fileWrapper(configuration: WriteConfiguration) throws -> FileWrapper {
        FileWrapper(regularFileWithContents: try JSONEncoder().encode(items))
    }
}
```

## Related

`file-import-export`, `document-editor`, `undo-redo`, `app-sandbox`, `window-group`


<!-- topic: window-style -->
---
id: window-style
title: Window style & sizing
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/windows.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows.md
---

# Window style & sizing

Scene modifiers for a window's title bar, toolbar style, size, and position.

Also called: windowStyle, hiddenTitleBar, title bar, titlebar, transparent title bar, windowToolbarStyle, unified toolbar, expanded toolbar, defaultSize, window size.

## Contents

- Use when
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- These modifiers go on a scene in your `App`, like a `WindowGroup`, not on a view.
- They decide how new windows start out.
- People can still move and resize them, within the limits you set.
- A few window behaviors are view modifiers instead, like `.containerBackground(_:for:)` with `.window`, so you can set them from inside the window.

## Rules

- **Keep the system's window frame.** People know how standard windows look and behave. A homemade frame or window buttons that don't match exactly make the app feel broken.
- **Let windows adapt to any size.** People arrange windows side by side and resize them all the time. Set a minimum that keeps your layout intact, and let it grow from there.
- **Keep important things out of a bottom bar.** People often move a window so its bottom edge is off screen. Use a bottom bar only for a little status, like Finder's item count.
- **Keep the system's look for each window state.** People tell the active window apart by its colored window buttons and materials. Standard backgrounds and controls change with the state; custom ones have to do it themselves.

## Pitfalls

- **Settings windows fit their content by default.** With `.automatic` resizability, a `Settings` window uses `.contentSize` and every other scene uses `.contentMinSize`.
- **These are starting values.** When the system restores a window, it comes back at the size and place people left it.

## Key APIs

- `.defaultSize(width:height:)`: The size a new window opens at.
- `.windowResizability(.contentSize)`: Sizes the window from its content's frame.
- `.defaultPosition(.topTrailing)`: Where the first window appears on screen.
- `.windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)`: Hides the title and the title bar's backing.
- `.windowToolbarStyle(.unified)`: How the toolbar and title bar combine.
- `.containerBackground(_:for:)`: With `.window`, the window's background.
- `WindowDragGesture()`: Lets people drag the window by a view.
- `.windowResizeBehavior(.disabled)`: Turns off resizing from inside the window.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct LibraryApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
                .frame(minWidth: 480, minHeight: 320)
        }
        .defaultSize(width: 900, height: 600)
    }
}
```

### A minimum size and a starting size

A `frame(minWidth:minHeight:)` on the content sets how small the window can get. `.defaultSize` sets the size it opens at.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
        .frame(minWidth: 320, minHeight: 180)
}
.defaultSize(width: 440, height: 260)
```

**Note:** A default size outside what the window allows is clamped to fit.

### A window that fits its content

`.windowResizability(.contentSize)` takes the window's limits from the content's frame. A fixed frame makes a window people can't resize.

```swift
Window("About Notes", id: "about") {
    AboutView()
        .frame(width: 440, height: 560)
}
.windowResizability(.contentSize)
.defaultPosition(.center)
```

**Note:** To turn off resizing, minimizing, or full screen from inside a window, set `.windowResizeBehavior`, `.windowMinimizeBehavior`, and `.windowFullScreenBehavior` to `.disabled`, as the Timer window does.

### Where the window opens

The first window opens in the center of the screen. `.defaultPosition` picks another spot, given as a `UnitPoint`.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
}
.defaultPosition(.topTrailing)
```

### Toolbar styles

`.windowToolbarStyle` sets how the title and toolbar share the top of the window. Pick a style to compare.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
}
.windowToolbarStyle(.unifiedCompact)
```

### Hide the title bar

`.windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)` hides the title and the title bar's backing, so more of the content shows.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    PlayerView()
}
.windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)
.windowBackgroundDragBehavior(.enabled)
```

**Important:** Without a title bar, people need another place to grab the window. Set `.windowBackgroundDragBehavior` to `.enabled` so they can drag it by its background.

### A see-through window

From inside the window, `.containerBackground(_:for:)` with `.window` sets its background, and you can hide the toolbar's title and backing.

```swift
struct NowPlayingView: View {
    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Text("Now Playing")
                .font(.title)
        }
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
        .containerBackground(.thinMaterial, for: .window)
        .toolbarBackgroundVisibility(.hidden, for: .windowToolbar)
        .toolbar(removing: .title)
        .gesture(WindowDragGesture())
        .allowsWindowActivationEvents()
    }
}
```

**Note:** `WindowDragGesture` lets people move the window by dragging the view. `.allowsWindowActivationEvents()` lets the drag work even while the window is in the background.

## Related

`window-group`, `window`, `toolbar`, `materials`, `full-screen`, `windows-layout`


<!-- topic: opening-windows -->
---
id: opening-windows
title: Opening windows
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/openwindowaction.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows.md
---

# Opening windows

Open, bring forward, and close windows from your own code.

Also called: openWindow, OpenWindowAction, dismissWindow, DismissWindowAction, dismiss, pushWindow, close window, show window, new window, open in new window.

## Contents

- Use when
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- Read `openWindow` from the environment and call it with a scene's ID, a value, or both.
- A `Window` comes to the front.
- A `WindowGroup` opens a new window, unless one is already showing that value.
- To close a window, call `dismiss` from a view inside it, or `dismissWindow` with the scene's ID from anywhere in your app.

## Rules

- **Pick the moments that deserve a window.** A new window helps people compare or keep context, like a draft next to the inbox. Opening one for everything clutters the screen.
- **Make “Open in New Window” easy to find.** Offer it in the item's context menu or the File menu, so it's there for people who want it.

## Pitfalls

- **Opening the same value twice doesn't make two windows.** If a window already shows that value, SwiftUI brings it to the front.
- **`pushWindow` is visionOS only.** It swaps one window for another there. On the Mac, open the new window and dismiss the old one.

## Guide

Read `openWindow` from the environment and call it with a scene's ID, a value, or both. A `Window` comes to the front. A `WindowGroup` opens a new window, unless one is already showing that value.

To close a window, call `dismiss` from a view inside it, or `dismissWindow` with the scene's ID from anywhere in your app.

### Usage

```swift
struct ShowActivityButton: View {
    @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

    var body: some View {
        Button("Show Activity") {
            openWindow(id: "activity")
        }
    }
}
```

### Two groups, one type

If two window groups take the same type, like a `UUID` for both messages and accounts, give each an `id` and pass both to `openWindow`.

```swift
WindowGroup("Message", id: "message", for: UUID.self) { $id in
    MessageView(id: id)
}
WindowGroup("Account", id: "account", for: UUID.self) { $id in
    AccountView(id: id)
}

// Elsewhere:
openWindow(id: "account", value: account.id)
```

## Key APIs

- `@Environment(\.openWindow)`: The action that opens windows.
- `openWindow(id:)`: Opens a scene by its ID.
- `openWindow(value:)`: Opens the window group for that value's type.
- `openWindow(id:value:)`: Picks between groups that take the same type.
- `@Environment(\.dismiss)`: Closes the window this view is in.
- `@Environment(\.dismissWindow)`: Closes a window by ID or value.

## Variants

### Open and close by value

These buttons open real windows. Open a note twice and its window comes forward; close it with `dismissWindow(value:)`.

```swift
struct NoteControls: View {
    let note: Note
    @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow
    @Environment(\.dismissWindow) private var dismissWindow

    var body: some View {
        HStack {
            Button("Open") {
                openWindow(value: note.id)
            }
            Button("Close") {
                dismissWindow(value: note.id)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Close the window you're in

Inside a window, `dismiss` closes that window. Each note window above has a Close button that does this.

```swift
struct NoteView: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Text("Groceries")
            Button("Close") {
                dismiss()
            }
            .keyboardShortcut(.cancelAction)
        }
        .padding()
    }
}
```

**Important:** Called from a sheet or popover, `dismiss` closes that presentation, not the window.

### Open a window from the menu bar

Menu commands can read `openWindow` too. This app's About item in the app menu opens its About window this way.

```swift
struct AboutCommands: Commands {
    @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

    var body: some Commands {
        CommandGroup(replacing: .appInfo) {
            Button("About Notes") {
                openWindow(id: "about")
            }
        }
    }
}

// In your App:
// WindowGroup { … }
//     .commands { AboutCommands() }
```

## Related

`window-group`, `window`, `commands`, `context-menu`, `keyboard-shortcuts`


<!-- topic: search -->
---
id: search
title: Search
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 12.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/adding-a-search-interface-to-your-app.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/search-fields.md
---

# Search

A search field in the toolbar or sidebar, with suggestions and tokens.

Also called: searchable, search field, search bar, NSSearchField, filter, find, Command-F, ⌘F, searchSuggestions, searchCompletion.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- Add `.searchable(text:)` to a `NavigationSplitView` or `NavigationStack`, or a view inside one, and a search field appears at the trailing edge of the window's toolbar.
- You own the text, and filter your data with it; SwiftUI draws and manages the field.
- With `placement: .sidebar`, the field sits at the top of the sidebar instead, which suits search that filters the sidebar itself.

## Built from

NavigationSplitView
├── sidebar
├── detail
└── .searchable(text:)
    └── .searchSuggestions { }

## Rules

- **Say what people can search for.** Placeholder text like “Songs, Artists, Albums” tells people what the field covers before they type.
- **Put search at the trailing end of the toolbar.** It's the familiar spot in apps like Mail and Notes, and people can browse results while their selection stays visible in the detail.
- **Use the top of the sidebar for filtering the sidebar.** When search narrows down the sidebar's own items, like System Settings, a field at its top makes the link clear.
- **Suggest searches, and pair tokens with suggestions.** Recent or likely searches help people search faster, and suggestions teach which tokens exist.

## Pitfalls

- **Search as people type.** Filtering on every keystroke feels responsive. For slow searches, like ones over the network, wait for Return with `.onSubmit(of: .search)`.
- **This app does it.** Its sidebar search uses `placement: .sidebar`, and Go > Search (⌘F) focuses the field with `searchFocused`.

## Key APIs

`.searchable(text:prompt:)`, `placement: .sidebar`, `.searchSuggestions { }`, `.searchCompletion(_:)`, `.searchable(text:tokens:)`, `.searchFocused(_:)`, `.onSubmit(of: .search)`

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@State private var query = ""
let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry", "Mango"]

NavigationStack {
    List(fruits.filter { query.isEmpty || $0.localizedStandardContains(query) },
         id: \.self) { fruit in
        Text(fruit)
    }
    .searchable(text: $query, prompt: "Fruit")
}
```

### Filter as people type

Bind `.searchable` to a string and filter with it. `localizedStandardContains` ignores case and accents, as people expect.

```swift
@State private var query = ""
let books = ["Emma", "Dracula", "Middlemarch", "Persuasion", "Ulysses"]

var results: [String] {
    query.isEmpty ? books : books.filter { $0.localizedStandardContains(query) }
}

NavigationStack {
    List(results, id: \.self) { book in
        Label(book, systemImage: "book")
    }
    .searchable(text: $query, prompt: "Titles")
}
```

**Note:** A real search field in a page would join this app's own toolbar, so the preview draws the window around a live field. The Library window above is the real thing.

### Suggest searches

`.searchSuggestions` lists views below the field, and each one's `searchCompletion` is the text it fills in. Click the field to see them.

```swift
@State private var query = ""

NavigationStack {
    List { Text("Results") }
        .searchable(text: $query, prompt: "Titles")
        .searchSuggestions {
            Section("Recent") {
                Label("Emma", systemImage: "clock").searchCompletion("Emma")
                Label("Dracula", systemImage: "clock").searchCompletion("Dracula")
            }
        }
}
```

### Tokens

With `searchable(text:tokens:)`, a search term becomes a token people can remove as one piece. Offer tokens as suggestions so people find them.

```swift
enum Genre: String, Identifiable, CaseIterable {
    case novel, poetry, drama
    var id: Self { self }
}

@State private var query = ""
@State private var genres: [Genre] = []

NavigationStack {
    List { Text("Results") }
        .searchable(text: $query, tokens: $genres, prompt: "Titles") { genre in
            Text(genre.rawValue.capitalized)
        }
        .searchSuggestions {
            ForEach(Genre.allCases) { genre in
                Text(genre.rawValue.capitalized).searchCompletion(genre)
            }
        }
}
```

### Focus the field with a shortcut

`.searchFocused` binds the field's focus to a `@FocusState`. Publish an action that sets it, and call it from a Find command.

```swift
struct FindAction {
    let perform: @MainActor () -> Void
}

extension FocusedValues {
    @Entry var findAction: FindAction?
}

struct FindCommands: Commands {
    @FocusedValue(\.findAction) private var findAction

    var body: some Commands {
        CommandGroup(after: .textEditing) {
            Button("Find…") { findAction?.perform() }
                .keyboardShortcut("f")
                .disabled(findAction == nil)
        }
    }
}

struct LibraryView: View {
    @State private var query = ""
    @FocusState private var isSearchFocused: Bool

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List { Text("Results") }
                .searchable(text: $query)
                .searchFocused($isSearchFocused)
        }
        .focusedSceneValue(\.findAction, FindAction { isSearchFocused = true })
    }
}
```

**Note:** The Mac's standard shortcuts list ⌘F for Find and ⌥⌘F for jumping to the search field. The Library window uses ⌥⌘F, because this app's own Go > Search already takes ⌘F.

## Related

`toolbar`, `navigation-split-view`, `text-field`, `focus-keyboard`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `list-styles`


<!-- topic: commands -->
---
id: commands
title: Commands & menu bar
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/building-and-customizing-the-menu-bar-with-swiftui.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar.md
---

# Commands & menu bar

Add your own menus and menu items to the Mac's menu bar.

Also called: menu bar, menubar, main menu, CommandMenu, CommandGroup, Commands, FocusedValue, focusedSceneValue, NSMenu, NSMenuItem.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `.commands` adds menus and items to the menu bar from your `App`.
- `CommandMenu` makes a new menu, which the system puts between View and Window.
- `CommandGroup` adds items to a menu the system already has, or replaces some of them.
- Commands aren't inside any window, so they read `@FocusedValue` to find out what's in front and act on it.

## Built from

WindowGroup
└── .commands
    ├── CommandMenu("Story")
    │   ├── Button
    │   ├── Divider
    │   └── Toggle
    └── CommandGroup(after: .newItem)
        └── Button

## Rules

- **Dim commands that don't apply. Don't hide them.** A menu that keeps the same items teaches people what the app can do, even when a command isn't available right now.
- **End a command with an ellipsis when it asks for more.** The … tells people a window or dialog opens next, so choosing the item doesn't act right away.
- **Put every command in the menu bar.** People look there first when they're learning an app. A command in the menu bar can have a shortcut and works with Full Keyboard Access, even if it's also in a toolbar or context menu.
- **Keep menu titles short, and in the usual order.** One word fits best. Custom menus sit between View and Window, from the most general to the most specific.

## Pitfalls

- **Scenes bring the standard menus.** A `WindowGroup` already has Copy, Paste, and the window commands, and a `Settings` scene adds Settings… to the app menu. Add only what's yours.
- **Values in `FocusedValues` are always optional.** A value is `nil` while no focused window or view publishes it, which is your cue to disable the command.

**Note:** `CommandGroup(replacing:)` removes the system's items in that group. Replacing `.newItem` removes File > New.

## Key APIs

- `.commands { }`: Adds menus and items to a scene.
- `CommandMenu(_:)`: A new menu, after View.
- `CommandGroup(after:)`: Adds items to a standard menu.
- `CommandGroup(replacing:)`: Swaps out a standard group of items.
- `@FocusedValue`: Reads a value from the focused window or view.
- `.focusedSceneValue(_:_:)`: Publishes a value for the whole window.
- `.focusedValue(_:_:)`: Publishes a value while a view has focus.
- `SidebarCommands()`: Adds Show or Hide Sidebar to the View menu.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct WriterApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        .commands {
            CommandMenu("Story") {
                Button("New Chapter") { }
                    .keyboardShortcut("n", modifiers: [.command, .option])
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### A menu of your own

`CommandMenu` holds buttons, toggles, and `Menu` submenus, and shows each item's shortcut beside it.

```swift
@State private var showsWordCount = true

var body: some Scene {
    WindowGroup {
        ContentView()
    }
    .commands {
        CommandMenu("Story") {
            Button("New Chapter") { }
                .keyboardShortcut("n", modifiers: [.command, .option])
            Button("Split Chapter") { }
                .keyboardShortcut("k", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
            Divider()
            Toggle("Show Word Count", isOn: $showsWordCount)
            Menu("Export As") {
                Button("PDF…") { }
                Button("Plain Text…") { }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The preview draws a menu bar, and its Story menu is a real `Menu` with the same items. While this page is open, ⌥⌘N and ⇧⌘K run them too.

### More code

```swift
.commands {
    CommandGroup(after: .newItem) {
        Button("New from Clipboard") { }
    }
    CommandGroup(replacing: .help) {
        Button("Writer User Guide") { }
    }
}
```

### Act on what's in focus

Publish a value with `.focusedSceneValue` or `.focusedValue`, and read it in your commands with `@FocusedValue`.

```swift
extension FocusedValues {
    @Entry var note: Note?
}

struct NoteEditor: View {
    @State private var note = Note()

    var body: some View {
        TextEditor(text: $note.text)
            .focusedSceneValue(\.note, note)
    }
}

struct NoteCommands: Commands {
    @FocusedValue(\.note) private var note

    var body: some Commands {
        CommandMenu("Note") {
            Button("Pin Note") { note?.pin() }
                .keyboardShortcut("p", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
                .disabled(note == nil)
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** Click a field, then the button: it stands in for a menu item and reads the same kind of `@FocusedValue`, so it's dimmed until a field has focus. `.focusedSceneValue` would keep the value while focus moves elsewhere in the window.

## Related

`keyboard-shortcuts`, `context-menu`, `menu`, `menu-bar-conventions`, `settings-scene`


<!-- topic: keyboard-shortcuts -->
---
id: keyboard-shortcuts
title: Keyboard shortcuts
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/keyboardshortcut(_:modifiers:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/keyboards.md

# Keyboard shortcuts

Run a button or menu item from the keyboard, like ⌘S for Save.

Also called: hotkey, hot key, key equivalent, keyEquivalent, accelerator, keybinding, key binding, command key, KeyEquivalent, EventModifiers.

## Default code

```swift
Button("Mark as Read") {
    markAsRead()
}
.keyboardShortcut("k", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
```

**Important:** A capital letter adds Shift: `.keyboardShortcut("K")` is ⇧⌘K. Write the letter in lowercase and list the modifiers, so the code says what people press.

## Rules

- **Don't give a standard shortcut a new job.** People expect ⌘C, ⌘Z, ⌘W, and the rest to work the same in every app. Pick a new shortcut for your own command instead.
- **Add shortcuts only for the commands people use most.** A few well-chosen shortcuts speed people up. Too many new ones make the app feel hard to learn.
- **Lead with Command, and add Shift for a related command.** Use Option sparingly, for advanced commands. Avoid Control: the system uses it for moving focus, screenshots, and more.
- **Write modifiers in the order ⌃ ⌥ ⇧ ⌘.** Menus list them that way, so help text and tooltips should too.
- **Don't add a modifier to make an unrelated shortcut.** ⇧⌘Z means Redo because ⌘Z means Undo. Using it for something else breaks the pattern people rely on.

## Pitfalls

- **A shortcut works anywhere in the front window.** Pressing it is the same as clicking the control, even when the control doesn't have focus.
- **The first match wins.** SwiftUI looks in the key window, then the main window, then the menu bar, and runs the first control it finds with that shortcut.
- **Shortcuts adapt to other keyboards.** The system remaps ones that are hard to type on another layout, like ⌘[, and mirrors directional ones for right-to-left languages.

## Key APIs

- `.keyboardShortcut(_:modifiers:)`: A key plus modifiers; ⌘ by default.
- `.keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)`: Return, for the main button.
- `.keyboardShortcut(.cancelAction)`: Escape, for Cancel.
- `KeyEquivalent`: The key: a character, or `.return`, `.delete`, arrows.
- `EventModifiers`: `.command`, `.shift`, `.option`, `.control`.

## Variants

### Return and Escape in a dialog

`.defaultAction` binds Return to the main button and `.cancelAction` binds Escape to Cancel, like a dialog.

```swift
HStack {
    Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { dismiss() }
        .keyboardShortcut(.cancelAction)
    Button("Save") { save() }
        .keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)
}
```

### Shortcuts appear in menus

Add `.keyboardShortcut` to a button in a `Menu` or a `CommandMenu`, and the menu shows the keys beside it.

```swift
Menu("Message") {
    Button("Reply") { reply() }
        .keyboardShortcut("r")
    Button("Forward") { forward() }
        .keyboardShortcut("f", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
    Button("Mark as Unread") { markAsUnread() }
        .keyboardShortcut("u", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
}
```

**Note:** The shortcuts work while the button's window is in front, even with the menu closed. In a real app, put these in a `CommandMenu` so they work from the menu bar.

## Related

`commands`, `button`, `keyboard-access`, `focus-keyboard`


<!-- topic: tooltips -->
---
id: tooltips
title: Tooltips
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+

hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/offering-help.md

# Tooltips

A short phrase that appears when the pointer rests on a control.

Also called: help tag, toolTip, title attribute, hover text, help(_:), NSView toolTip, hint, icon button.

## Default code

```swift
Button("Restore Defaults", systemImage: "arrow.counterclockwise") {
    restoreDefaults()
}
.labelStyle(.iconOnly)
.help("Restore default settings")
```

**Important:** An icon on its own rarely says what a button does. Give every icon-only button a title for VoiceOver and a `.help` tooltip for everyone else.

## Rules

- **Say what the control does, in a few words.** Start with a verb, and keep it to 60 to 75 characters at most. A sentence fragment without articles is fine.
- **Don't repeat the control's name.** The name is already on screen or in the label. Use the space to explain what happens.
- **Describe only that control.** People hold the pointer over one control to learn about it, not about its neighbors or the whole task.
- **Use sentence case, and match the state.** Write “Pin note”, not “Pin Note”, and skip the final period. If the control changes, like Pin and Unpin, change the tooltip too.

## Pitfalls

- **`.help` is also the VoiceOver hint.** One modifier gives pointer users a tooltip and VoiceOver users a hint.
- **Tooltips wait for the pointer.** They appear only after the pointer rests on a control for a moment, so keep anything people must know in the window itself.

## Key APIs

- `.help(_:)`: Adds a tooltip and an accessibility hint.
- `.help(Text)`: The same, from a `Text`.
- `Button(_:systemImage:action:)`: A button with a title and a symbol.
- `.labelStyle(.iconOnly)`: Shows only a label's icon; the title stays for VoiceOver.

## Variants

### Icon-only toolbar buttons

Add `.help` to each icon-only toolbar button, so people can find out what it does before they click.

```swift
.toolbar {
    Button("New Note", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") { newNote() }
        .help("Create a note")
    Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { share() }
        .help("Send this note to someone")
    Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash") { delete() }
        .help("Move this note to the Trash")
}
```

**Note:** Hold the pointer over each symbol in the preview. A real `.toolbar` here would land in this window's own toolbar, so the preview draws one.

### A tooltip that follows the state

When a button switches between two actions, switch its `.help` text too, so it describes the next click.

```swift
@State private var isPinned = false

Button(isPinned ? "Unpin" : "Pin", systemImage: isPinned ? "pin.slash" : "pin") {
    isPinned.toggle()
}
.labelStyle(.iconOnly)
.help(isPinned ? "Unpin this note" : "Pin this note to the top")
```

## Related

`button`, `hover`, `toolbar`, `voiceover`


<!-- topic: hover -->
---
id: hover
title: Hover & pointer
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/onhover(perform:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices.md

# Hover & pointer

React when the pointer moves over a view, and show the right pointer.

Also called: :hover, mouseenter, mouseleave, mousemove, cursor, NSCursor, NSTrackingArea, onHover, onContinuousHover, pointerStyle.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isHovering = false

ProjectRow(project)
    .padding(8)
    .background(isHovering ? Color.secondary.opacity(0.15) : .clear,
                in: .rect(cornerRadius: 8))
    .onHover { isHovering = $0 }
```

**Note:** `.onHover` is like CSS `:hover`, except you store the state yourself and style the view from it.

## Rules

- **Show the pointer that matches what happens.** Each pointer has a meaning people know: a pointing hand for a link, an open hand for content they can pan, like a map, and a crosshair for precise selection. Don't use one for anything else.
- **Let the pointer bring back controls that fade away.** Controls that hide to keep the view calm, like playback controls over a video, should reappear when the pointer moves over them.
- **Keep every way of working consistent.** People switch between the pointer, the keyboard, and gestures without thinking. An action shouldn't work differently, or only work, with one of them.

## Pitfalls

- **The hover area is the view's frame.** Add padding before `.onHover` to make the area bigger.
- **`.pointerStyle` needs macOS 15.** `.onContinuousHover` needs macOS 14, and `.onHover` dates back to macOS 10.15.

## Key APIs

- `.onHover { isHovering in }`: Runs when the pointer enters or leaves.
- `.onContinuousHover { phase in }`: Reports the pointer's location as it moves.
- `.pointerStyle(_:)`: The pointer to show over a view.
- `.link`, `.grabIdle`, `.columnResize`: A few of the built-in pointer styles.
- `.pointerVisibility(.hidden)`: Hides the pointer over a view.

## Variants

### Show actions on the row under the pointer

Use `.onHover` to track the row under the pointer and show its buttons only there, so the list stays calm.

```swift
@State private var hoveredRow: Project.ID?

ForEach(projects) { project in
    HStack {
        Text(project.name)
        Spacer()
        if hoveredRow == project.id {
            Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { share(project) }
            Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash") { delete(project) }
        }
    }
    .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
    .buttonStyle(.borderless)
    .contentShape(.rect)
    .onHover { isHovering in
        hoveredRow = isHovering ? project.id : nil
    }
}
```

**Important:** Hover-only buttons are invisible to the keyboard and to VoiceOver until the pointer arrives. Put the same commands in a context menu or the menu bar.

### Follow the pointer

`.onContinuousHover` reports the pointer's location while it moves over a view, and `.ended` when it leaves.

```swift
@State private var spot: CGPoint?

SceneryView(.lake)
    .overlay {
        if let spot {
            Circle()
                .fill(.white.opacity(0.35))
                .frame(width: 60, height: 60)
                .position(spot)
        }
    }
    .onContinuousHover { phase in
        switch phase {
        case .active(let location): spot = location
        case .ended: spot = nil
        }
    }
```

### A resize pointer on a divider

`.pointerStyle(.columnResize)` shows the left-right resize pointer, so people know they can drag the divider.

```swift
@State private var sidebarWidth = 140.0

HStack(spacing: 0) {
    Sidebar()
        .frame(width: sidebarWidth)
    Rectangle()
        .fill(.separator)
        .frame(width: 1)
        .padding(.horizontal, 3)
        .contentShape(.rect)
        .pointerStyle(.columnResize)
        .gesture(DragGesture(coordinateSpace: .named("split")).onChanged { drag in
            sidebarWidth = min(max(drag.location.x, 100), 220)
        })
    Detail()
}
.coordinateSpace(.named("split"))
```

**Note:** For a real sidebar, `NavigationSplitView` gives you the divider and the pointer for free.

## Related

`tooltips`, `trackpad-gestures`, `drag-drop`, `button`


<!-- topic: drag-drop -->

id: drag-drop
title: Drag and drop
platforms: [macOS]

hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/drag-and-drop.md

# Drag and drop

Let people drag content within a window, between windows, and to other apps.

Also called: drag, drop, draggable, dropDestination, onDrag, onDrop, Transferable, NSDraggingSource, NSDraggingDestination, dataTransfer.

## Contents

- Use when
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `.draggable` turns a view into something people can drag, and `.dropDestination` makes a view accept drops.
- Both work with `Transferable` types, so the same code handles drags inside a window, between your app's windows, and to and from other apps.
- A type's transfer representations decide what it becomes: your own data when it lands in your app, and plain text or a file in apps that don't know your type.

## Rules

- **Support drag and drop wherever people might try it.** Most people know it and try it everywhere. Text fields and text views already support it.
- **Offer another way to do the same thing.** Some people can't or don't drag. Back every drag with menu commands, like Copy and Paste or Move To.
- **Show whether a destination accepts the drop.** Highlight a destination only while content is over it and only if it can take it. Remove the highlight as soon as the pointer leaves.
- **Move within a container, copy between containers.** Dropping in the same place, like reordering a list, moves the content. Dropping somewhere else copies it, and a drop into another app always copies.
- **Let people drag content to the Finder.** Give it a file format your app can open again, the way Calendar drags an event out as an .ics file.
- **Offer the richest version first.** List your type's representations from highest fidelity to lowest, so each destination takes the best one it understands.

## Pitfalls

- **Common types already work.** `String`, `URL`, and many other system types conform to `Transferable`, so you can drag them without extra code.
- **A drag offers a copy unless you allow a move.** Pass `DragConfiguration(allowMove: true)` to `.dragConfiguration(_:)`. People can then hold ⌘ to move, or ⌥ to copy.
- **This `.dropDestination` is new in macOS 26.** It replaces the version with an `isTargeted:` closure, which is deprecated.

## Guide

`.draggable` turns a view into something people can drag, and `.dropDestination` makes a view accept drops. Both work with `Transferable` types, so the same code handles drags inside a window, between your app's windows, and to and from other apps.

A type's transfer representations decide what it becomes: your own data when it lands in your app, and plain text or a file in apps that don't know your type.

### Usage

```swift
@State private var basket: [String] = []

Text("Sunflowers")
    .draggable("Sunflowers")

BasketView(items: basket)
    .dropDestination(for: String.self) { names, session in
        basket.append(contentsOf: names)
    }
```

## Key APIs

`.draggable(_:)`, `.draggable(_:preview:)`, `.dropDestination(for:)`, `.onDropSessionUpdated(_:)`, `Transferable`, `CodableRepresentation`, `ProxyRepresentation`, `.dragConfiguration(_:)`

## Variants

### Drag text onto a target

Make each chip `.draggable` and the box a `.dropDestination`, and highlight the box with `.onDropSessionUpdated` during a drag.

```swift
@State private var basket: [String] = []
@State private var isTargeted = false

HStack {
    ForEach(["Sunflowers", "Tulips", "Ferns"], id: \.self) { plant in
        Text(plant)
            .padding(8)
            .background(.tint.opacity(0.15), in: .capsule)
            .draggable(plant)
    }
}

Text(basket.isEmpty ? "Drop here" : basket.joined(separator: ", "))
    .frame(width: 300, height: 90)
    .background(isTargeted ? Color.accentColor.opacity(0.15) : .clear)
    .dropDestination(for: String.self) { plants, _ in
        basket.append(contentsOf: plants)
    }
    .onDropSessionUpdated { session in
        switch session.phase {
        case .entering, .active: isTargeted = true
        default: isTargeted = false
        }
    }
```

**Note:** Text from other apps works too: select a word in Notes or TextEdit and drag it into the box. Or open a second window above and drag between the two.

### Drag your own type

Make your type `Transferable`, so a card moves between columns as itself and lands in other apps as its title.

```swift
struct TodoCard: Identifiable, Codable, Transferable {
    var id = UUID()
    var title: String

    static var transferRepresentation: some TransferRepresentation {
        CodableRepresentation(contentType: .json)
        ProxyRepresentation(exporting: \.title)
    }
}

@State private var todo = [TodoCard(title: "Water the ferns")]
@State private var done: [TodoCard] = []

HStack {
    CardColumn("To Do", cards: todo)
        .dropDestination(for: TodoCard.self) { cards, _ in
            move(cards, to: \.todo)
        }
    CardColumn("Done", cards: done)
        .dropDestination(for: TodoCard.self) { cards, _ in
            move(cards, to: \.done)
        }
}
```

**Important:** A type only your app understands should use its own content type, declared with `UTType(exportedAs:)` and listed in your Info.plist. This example uses `.json` so it runs without that setup.

### Accept files from the Finder

Ask for `URL` to accept files and folders dragged from the Finder or another app.

```swift
@State private var files: [URL] = []

Label("Drop files here", systemImage: "tray.and.arrow.down")
    .frame(width: 300, height: 120)
    .dropDestination(for: URL.self) { urls, _ in
        files.append(contentsOf: urls)
    }
```

## Related

`copy-paste`, `file-import-export`, `share-link`, `hover`, `list-styles`

id: copy-paste
title: Copy & paste
platforms: [macOS]

hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/edit-menus.md

# Copy & paste

Connect the Edit menu's Cut, Copy, Paste, and Delete to your own views.

Also called: clipboard, pasteboard, NSPasteboard, copyable, cuttable, pasteDestination, onCopyCommand, onPasteCommand, onCutCommand, onDeleteCommand.

## Contents

- Use when
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- Every Mac app has an Edit menu with Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, and Select All, and text fields support them without any code.
- For your own views, `.copyable`, `.cuttable`, and `.pasteDestination` connect those menu items and their shortcuts to your data.
- They use `Transferable`, like drag and drop, so what people copy from your app pastes into other apps, and the other way around.

## Rules

- **Let the Edit menu do the work.** People expect Copy and Paste in the Edit menu and on ⌘C and ⌘V. Extra buttons for the same commands crowd the window.
- **Let people copy text they can't edit.** Content like a caption or an address is often worth pasting somewhere else. Make that text selectable, but not the labels of controls.
- **Call it Delete, not Erase or Clear.** Edit > Delete does what the Delete key does. Unlike Cut, it doesn't put anything on the Clipboard.
- **Support undo.** Menu commands act without asking first. Undo lets people recover from a paste or delete they didn't mean.

## Pitfalls

- **The commands follow focus.** Edit > Copy turns on when the focused view has something to copy, so people click the list first, then press ⌘C.
- **Prefer `Transferable` to item providers.** `.onCopyCommand` and `.onPasteCommand` work with `NSItemProvider`. Apple recommends the `Transferable` modifiers when you can use them.

## Guide

Every Mac app has an Edit menu with Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, and Select All, and text fields support them without any code. For your own views, `.copyable`, `.cuttable`, and `.pasteDestination` connect those menu items and their shortcuts to your data.

They use `Transferable`, like drag and drop, so what people copy from your app pastes into other apps, and the other way around.

### Usage

```swift
@State private var plants = ["Sunflowers", "Tulips", "Ferns"]
@State private var selection = Set<String>()

List(plants, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { plant in
    Text(plant)
}
.copyable(plants.filter { selection.contains($0) })
.pasteDestination(for: String.self) { pasted in
    plants.append(contentsOf: pasted)
}
```

## Key APIs

- `.copyable(_:)`: The items Edit > Copy puts on the Clipboard.
- `.cuttable(for:action:)`: Removes items and returns them for Cut.
- `.pasteDestination(for:action:)`: Accepts items from Edit > Paste.
- `.onDeleteCommand(perform:)`: Edit > Delete and the Delete key.
- `PasteButton(payloadType:)`: A Paste button for the Clipboard.
- `.textSelection(.enabled)`: Lets people select and copy a `Text`.

## Variants

### Cut, copy, and paste list rows

Give a selectable `List` all three modifiers, and let the `.pasteDestination` validator drop unwanted items, like empty lines.

```swift
@State private var plants = ["Sunflowers", "Tulips", "Ferns", "Basil"]
@State private var selection = Set<String>()

List(plants, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { plant in
    Text(plant)
}
.copyable(plants.filter { selection.contains($0) })
.cuttable(for: String.self) {
    let cut = plants.filter { selection.contains($0) }
    plants.removeAll { selection.contains($0) }
    return cut
}
.pasteDestination(for: String.self) { pasted in
    plants.append(contentsOf: pasted)
} validator: { pasted in
    pasted
        .map { $0.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines) }
        .filter { !$0.isEmpty }
}
```

**Note:** Click the list, select a row, and press ⌘C. Paste it into Notes, or copy a word from another app and press ⌘V here.

### The Delete key and Edit > Delete

`.onDeleteCommand` runs when people choose Edit > Delete or press Delete while the view has focus.

```swift
@State private var tags = ["garden", "summer", "seeds", "watering"]
@State private var selection = Set<String>()

List(tags, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { tag in
    Text(tag)
}
.onDeleteCommand {
    tags.removeAll { selection.contains($0) }
}
```

### A Paste button

`PasteButton` reads the Clipboard when clicked and hands you the values of the type you ask for.

```swift
@State private var pasted = ""

PasteButton(payloadType: String.self) { strings in
    pasted = strings.joined(separator: " ")
}
```

**Note:** Add one only where a visible button helps; people look for Edit > Paste and ⌘V first. For a Copy item of your own, like in a context menu, write to `NSPasteboard.general`, since SwiftUI's modifiers only answer the system's Copy command.

### Selectable text

`.textSelection(.enabled)` lets people select a `Text` and copy it with ⌘C or the Edit menu.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Order number")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Text("W-48213-7")
        .font(.title2.monospaced())
        .textSelection(.enabled)
}
```

## Related

`drag-drop`, `commands`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `undo-redo`, `text-label`


<!-- topic: trackpad-gestures -->
---
id: trackpad-gestures
title: Trackpad gestures
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/magnifygesture.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices.md
---

# Trackpad gestures

Zoom and rotate with trackpad gestures, plus a way to do both with a mouse.

Also called: pinch, zoom, magnify, rotate, MagnifyGesture, RotateGesture, MagnificationGesture, RotationGesture, NSMagnificationGestureRecognizer, multitouch.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var scale = 1.0
@State private var baseScale = 1.0

Image("photo")
    .scaleEffect(scale)
    .gesture(
        MagnifyGesture()
            .onChanged { value in
                scale = baseScale * value.magnification
            }
            .onEnded { _ in
                baseScale = scale
            }
    )
```

**Important:** `value.magnification` starts at 1 for every new pinch. Multiply it by the scale you saved at the end of the last one, or each pinch jumps back to the original size.

## Rules

- **Give mouse users another way.** Pinching and rotating need a trackpad. Add buttons or menu commands that zoom and rotate, so everyone can reach the same result.
- **Don't take over system gestures.** People expect gestures like swiping up for Mission Control to work in every app, and they can customize them in System Settings.
- **Make gestures behave as they do elsewhere.** People expect a gesture to do the same thing in every app, like swiping between pages. A familiar gesture with a new meaning surprises them.

## Pitfalls

- **Scrolling needs no code.** A `ScrollView` scrolls with a trackpad or a mouse; you only add gestures for zooming and rotating.
- **`MagnificationGesture` is deprecated.** So is `RotationGesture`. Use `MagnifyGesture` and `RotateGesture` instead.

## Key APIs

- `MagnifyGesture()`: Pinch with two fingers to zoom.
- `RotateGesture()`: Turn two fingers to rotate.
- `value.magnification`: The scale since the gesture began.
- `value.rotation`: The angle since the gesture began.
- `.simultaneously(with:)`: Zoom and rotate in one motion.
- `.onScrollPhaseChange(_:)`: Tells you when scrolling starts and stops.

## Variants

### Rotate and snap to a right angle

Follow `RotateGesture` while the fingers turn, then snap to the nearest 90° when they lift, like straightening a photo.

```swift
@State private var angle = Angle.zero
@State private var baseAngle = Angle.zero

Image("photo")
    .rotationEffect(angle)
    .gesture(
        RotateGesture()
            .onChanged { angle = baseAngle + $0.rotation }
            .onEnded { _ in
                let quarterTurns = (angle.degrees / 90).rounded()
                withAnimation(.snappy) {
                    angle = .degrees(quarterTurns * 90)
                }
                baseAngle = angle
            }
    )
```

### Know when scrolling stops

`.onScrollPhaseChange` reports when a scroll starts and ends, from a trackpad or a mouse wheel alike.

```swift
@State private var isScrolling = false

ScrollView {
    LazyVStack {
        ForEach(1...40, id: \.self) { Text("Row \($0)") }
    }
}
.onScrollPhaseChange { _, phase in
    isScrolling = phase.isScrolling
}
```

## Related

`hover`, `drag-drop`, `scroll-view`, `animation`


<!-- topic: file-import-export -->
---
id: file-import-export
title: File import & export
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
