docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/fileimporter(ispresented:allowedcontenttypes:oncompletion:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management.md
---

# File import & export

Show the Mac's open and save panels, and read or write the files people pick.

Also called: open panel, save panel, NSOpenPanel, NSSavePanel, file picker, <input type=file>, download, save as, export, import.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Use the system's open and save panels.** People know how to browse files from the Finder and other apps. Build your own file browser only for a strong reason.
- **Offer Open and New in the File menu.** People expect File > New and File > Open… with ⌘N and ⌘O, even when your window has buttons for them.
- **Name the main button for the task.** If the panel inserts a file rather than opening it, call the button Insert. `.fileDialogConfirmationLabel` sets it.
- **Save work automatically.** Don't make people choose Save to keep their work. Save as they go, and when they close the window or switch apps.

## Pitfalls

- **Canceling calls nothing.** If people cancel, SwiftUI sets the binding back to `false` and skips `onCompletion`. The file exporter calls `onCancellation` instead.
- **This app does it for real.** It has the user-selected read-write entitlement, so the examples below can read and write what you pick.

**Important:** Apple's docs ask you to pair every start call with a stop call. `defer` makes sure the stop call runs, even when reading fails.

## Key APIs

- `.fileImporter(isPresented:…)`: The open panel.
- `.fileExporter(isPresented:item:)`: The save panel, for a `Transferable` item.
- `.fileMover(isPresented:file:)`: A panel that moves a file somewhere else.
- `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()`: Opens access to a URL from a panel.
- `.fileDialogConfirmationLabel(_:)`: Renames the panel's main button.
- `.fileDialogMessage(_:)`: A message in the panel, like a title.
- `.fileDialogDefaultDirectory(_:)`: The folder the panel opens in.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@State private var isImporting = false
@State private var text = ""

Button("Open…") { isImporting = true }
    .fileImporter(isPresented: $isImporting,
                  allowedContentTypes: [.plainText]) { result in
        guard case .success(let url) = result else { return }
        let didAccess = url.startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()
        defer {
            if didAccess { url.stopAccessingSecurityScopedResource() }
        }
        text = (try? String(contentsOf: url, encoding: .utf8)) ?? ""
    }
```

### Pick several files

Pass `allowsMultipleSelection: true` to get an array of URLs, and set a message and button title that fit the task.

```swift
@State private var isImporting = false
@State private var picked: [String] = []

Button("Add Photos…") { isImporting = true }
    .fileImporter(isPresented: $isImporting,
                  allowedContentTypes: [.image],
                  allowsMultipleSelection: true) { result in
        guard case .success(let urls) = result else { return }
        picked = urls.map(\.lastPathComponent)
    }
    .fileDialogMessage("Choose photos for the garden journal.")
    .fileDialogConfirmationLabel("Add")
```

### Save text to a file

`.fileExporter(isPresented:item:)` saves any `Transferable` value, like this `String`.

```swift
@State private var note = "Plant the tulip bulbs before the first frost."
@State private var isExporting = false

Button("Export…") { isExporting = true }
    .fileExporter(isPresented: $isExporting,
                  item: note,
                  contentTypes: [.plainText],
                  defaultFilename: "Garden Note") { result in
        if case .failure(let error) = result {
            print(error.localizedDescription)
        }
    }
```

### Move a file

`.fileMover` asks where to move a file you already have, like a draft from your app's own folder.

```swift
@State private var draft: URL?
@State private var isMoving = false

Button("Move Draft…") { isMoving = true }
    .fileMover(isPresented: $isMoving, file: draft) { result in
        if case .success(let newURL) = result {
            draft = newURL
        }
    }
```

**Note:** The panel only appears when `file` isn't `nil`. Here the sample file starts in this app's temporary folder.

## Related

`app-sandbox`, `drag-drop`, `share-link`, `document-group`, `document-editor`


<!-- topic: state-binding -->
---
id: state-binding
title: State & Binding
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/state.md
---

# State & Binding

@State keeps a value a view owns, and @Binding lets another view change it.

Also called: @State, @Binding, state, binding, useState, props, two-way binding, v-model, source of truth, $.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Declare `@State` as `private`.** Apple's docs say so: setting it from an initializer can conflict with the storage SwiftUI manages for it.
- **With Xcode 27, `@State` is a macro.** It creates its starting value only the first time SwiftUI makes the view, so a model object in `@State` isn't rebuilt each time the parent redraws.
- **Only the owner says `@State`.** Every other view gets either a plain value to read or a `Binding` to write. Two `@State` properties for one value means two copies that drift apart.

## Guide

Every value a view shows has one owner, its **source of truth**. Mark it `@State` in the view that owns it, and SwiftUI stores it and redraws whatever reads it when it changes.

When another view needs to change that value, such as a button in the window's toolbar, pass it a **binding** with `$`. The child declares `@Binding` and reads and writes the owner's value directly, like a controlled input in React.

The window owns `isPlaying`. The play button in its toolbar only has a binding, yet clicking it changes what the window shows.

### Which one to use

- This view creates the value and changes it: `@State private var isPlaying = false`
- A child view changes the owner's value: `@Binding var isPlaying: Bool`, passed as `$isPlaying`
- A child view only shows it: A plain property: `let isPlaying: Bool`
- Several windows or many views share it: An Observable (`observable`) model class, kept in `@State` once

## Key APIs

- `@State private var`: A value this view owns and SwiftUI stores.
- `@Binding var`: Reads and writes a value another view owns.
- `$value`: The binding to a `@State` value, to pass along.
- `$draft.title`: A binding to one property of a struct.
- `ForEach($items) { $item in }`: A binding to each element of an array.
- `.constant(_:)`: A binding that never changes, for previews.

## Variants

### A view option the view owns

Use `@State` for a value only this view needs, like whether a list shows finished tasks. Controls take `$showsCompleted`.

```swift
@State private var showsCompleted = true

let tasks = ["Write outline", "Record intro", "Edit episode"]
let finished: Set = ["Write outline"]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Toggle("Show completed", isOn: $showsCompleted)
    ForEach(tasks, id: \.self) { task in
        if showsCompleted || !finished.contains(task) {
            Label(task, systemImage: finished.contains(task) ? "checkmark.circle.fill" : "circle")
        }
    }
}
```

### Selection is a binding too

`List(selection:)` writes the selected rows into your `@State`. With a `Set`, people can select several rows on the Mac without an edit mode.

```swift
struct Mailbox: Identifiable {
    let id: String
    let name: String
    let symbol: String
}

let mailboxes = [
    Mailbox(id: "inbox", name: "Inbox", symbol: "tray"),
    Mailbox(id: "flagged", name: "Flagged", symbol: "flag"),
    Mailbox(id: "drafts", name: "Drafts", symbol: "doc"),
    Mailbox(id: "sent", name: "Sent", symbol: "paperplane"),
]

@State private var selection: Set<Mailbox.ID> = ["inbox"]

List(mailboxes, selection: $selection) { mailbox in
    Label(mailbox.name, systemImage: mailbox.symbol)
}
Text("\(selection.count) selected")
```

**Note:** Bind to a single optional ID instead of a `Set` when only one row can be selected at a time.

### Bind to one property of a struct

Keep related fields in one struct in `@State`. `$draft.title` is a binding to just that field, so each control edits its own part.

```swift
struct NoteDraft {
    var title = "Weekly review"
    var isPinned = false
    var color = Color.yellow
}

@State private var draft = NoteDraft()

Form {
    TextField("Title", text: $draft.title)
    Toggle("Pin to top", isOn: $draft.isPinned)
    ColorPicker("Color", selection: $draft.color)
}
```

### A binding for each row

`ForEach($tasks) { $task in … }` hands every row a binding to its own element, so a checkbox can tick off one task in the array.

```swift
struct TaskItem: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
    var title: String
    var isDone = false
}

@State private var tasks = [
    TaskItem(title: "Export the audio"),
    TaskItem(title: "Write show notes", isDone: true),
    TaskItem(title: "Upload the episode"),
]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    ForEach($tasks) { $task in
        Toggle(task.title, isOn: $task.isDone)
    }
    Text("\(tasks.filter(\.isDone).count) of \(tasks.count) done")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
```

### Write your own control with @Binding

A reusable control declares `@Binding` and never owns the value. Pass `.constant(_:)` when you only need to show it, as in a preview.

```swift
struct RatingControl: View {
    @Binding var rating: Int

    var body: some View {
        HStack(spacing: 2) {
            ForEach(1...5, id: \.self) { star in
                Button("\(star) stars", systemImage: star <= rating ? "star.fill" : "star") {
                    rating = star
                }
                .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
                .buttonStyle(.borderless)
            }
        }
    }
}

@State private var rating = 3

VStack {
    RatingControl(rating: $rating)
    RatingControl(rating: .constant(5))
        .disabled(true)
}
```

**Important:** Don't add `@State` inside the control to copy the value. The copy stops following the owner, and the two disagree.

## Related

`observable`, `environment`, `toggle`, `table`


<!-- topic: animation -->
---
id: animation
title: Animation
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/animations.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md
---

# Animation

Springs and transitions that stay quick and quiet under a pointer and in big windows.

Also called: withAnimation, spring, transition, animate, ease in out, CSS transition, keyframes, hover, onHover, Reduce Motion.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var showsDetails = false

VStack {
    Button(showsDetails ? "Hide Details" : "Show Details") {
        withAnimation(.snappy) {
            showsDetails.toggle()
        }
    }
    if showsDetails {
        Text("Recorded on October 12")
            .transition(.opacity)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Change state inside `withAnimation`, not the view. SwiftUI works out what moved and animates it, like a CSS transition on whatever the change affects.

## Rules

- **Add motion for a reason.** Use it to show where something came from or that something changed. Motion just for show distracts people and can make some of them feel unwell.
- **Skip motion on things people do all the time.** Standard controls already animate on their own. A pointer passes over custom rows constantly, so keep their hover feedback brief or leave the motion out.
- **Never make people wait for an animation.** Let them click again, or move on, while it plays. Springs handle an interruption smoothly, so don't block input until one finishes.
- **Make motion optional.** With Reduce Motion on, swap slides and zooms for fades and calm the bounce. Don't let motion be the only way people learn something happened.

## Pitfalls

- **Springs keep their speed when interrupted.** Click again mid-move and the next spring starts from where the view is, moving as fast as it was.
- **`withAnimation` animates what the change touches.** Every view that redraws because of the state you change inside it animates, wherever it is in the window.

## Key APIs

- `withAnimation(.snappy) { }`: Animates the views a state change affects.
- `.animation(_:value:)`: Animates one view whenever `value` changes.
- `.spring(duration:bounce:)`: A spring you tune with two numbers.
- `.smooth`, `.snappy`, `.bouncy`: Ready-made springs, from calm to lively.
- `.transition(_:)`: How a view enters and leaves.
- `.onHover { }`: Runs when the pointer enters or leaves.
- `.contentTransition(_:)`: Animates text and symbols that change in place.
- `\.accessibilityReduceMotion`: True when people turn on Reduce Motion.

## Variants

### Quiet hover feedback

Use `.onHover` with a short `.animation(_:value:)` to highlight what's under the pointer. Keep it subtle: people pass over it all the time.

```swift
struct ProjectCard: View {
    let name: String
    @State private var isHovering = false

    var body: some View {
        Label(name, systemImage: "folder")
            .frame(width: 140, height: 60)
            .background(isHovering ? AnyShapeStyle(.fill.secondary) : AnyShapeStyle(.fill.quaternary),
                        in: .rect(cornerRadius: 10))
            .animation(.easeOut(duration: 0.12), value: isHovering)
            .onHover { isHovering = $0 }
    }
}

HStack {
    ProjectCard(name: "Website")
    ProjectCard(name: "App")
    ProjectCard(name: "Docs")
}
```

### Slide a panel in and out

Give the panel a `.transition`, then toggle it inside `withAnimation`. A move from the trailing edge matches where inspectors live.

```swift
@State private var showsInspector = true

HStack(spacing: 0) {
    Text("Canvas")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
    if showsInspector {
        Text("Inspector")
            .frame(width: 140)
            .frame(maxHeight: .infinity)
            .background(.background.secondary)
            .transition(.move(edge: .trailing))
    }
}
.clipped()

Button("Toggle Inspector", systemImage: "sidebar.right") {
    withAnimation(.snappy) {
        showsInspector.toggle()
    }
}
```

### Numbers that roll

`.contentTransition(.numericText(value:))` animates digits as a count changes, like a downloads badge or a timer.

```swift
@State private var downloads = 3

HStack {
    Text("\(downloads) downloads")
        .contentTransition(.numericText(value: Double(downloads)))
        .monospacedDigit()
    Stepper("Downloads", value: $downloads.animation(.snappy), in: 0...99)
        .labelsHidden()
}
```

### Fade instead of slide with Reduce Motion

Read `accessibilityReduceMotion` and pick a calmer transition when it's on. The checkbox here stands in for the system setting.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
@State private var showsBanner = false

VStack {
    Button("Show Banner") {
        withAnimation(.snappy) { showsBanner.toggle() }
    }
    if showsBanner {
        Label("Export finished", systemImage: "checkmark.circle.fill")
            .padding(10)
            .background(.fill.secondary, in: .capsule)
            .transition(reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .bottom).combined(with: .opacity))
    }
}
```

**Note:** To test the real setting, turn on Reduce motion in the Accessibility section of System Settings.

## Related

`hover`, `reduce-motion`, `motion`, `state-binding`


<!-- topic: charts-maps -->
---
id: charts-maps
title: Charts & Maps
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/charts.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/charts.md
---

# Charts & Maps

Swift Charts with a selectable plot, and a MapKit map that fills a window.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Say what the chart shows in words.** A short headline above the chart gives the main message at a glance, so people don't have to read the plot to get it.
- **Don't hide important values behind interaction.** Selecting a point to see its value is a nice extra. Anything people must know, like a total or a trend, belongs on the chart itself.
- **Keep charts simple.** Too much data in one chart buries what matters. Let people choose a range or a series when they want more detail.
- **Let people move around the map.** People expect to zoom and pan any map. Don't cover it with views that block those gestures, and keep the Apple logo and legal link visible.
- **Mute the map when your content is the point.** The muted emphasis style lowers the map's colors so your markers and overlays stand out.

## Pitfalls

- **Charts are accessible by default.** Swift Charts gives VoiceOver the marks and an Audio Graph; add a title and a short summary that say what the chart is for.
- **Maps load over the network.** A sandboxed app needs the Outgoing Connections (Client) entitlement. See App Sandbox (`app-sandbox`).

## Key APIs

`Chart(data) { }`, `LineMark`, `BarMark`, `PointMark`, `.chartXSelection(value:)`, `RuleMark(x:)`, `Map(initialPosition:) { }`, `Marker(_:systemImage:coordinate:)`, `.mapControls { }`, `.mapStyle(_:)`

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
import Charts

struct DayCount: Identifiable {
    let day: Date
    let downloads: Int
    var id: Date { day }
}

struct DownloadsChart: View {
    let days: [DayCount]

    var body: some View {
        Chart(days) { day in
            LineMark(
                x: .value("Day", day.day, unit: .day),
                y: .value("Downloads", day.downloads)
            )
        }
    }
}
```

### Select a day to see its value

Bind `.chartXSelection(value:)` to a `Date?`, then draw a `RuleMark` with an annotation at the selected day.

```swift
import Charts

@State private var selectedDay: Date?

Chart(days) { day in
    LineMark(
        x: .value("Day", day.day, unit: .day),
        y: .value("Downloads", day.downloads)
    )
    if let selectedDay {
        RuleMark(x: .value("Day", selectedDay, unit: .day))
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            .annotation(position: .top, overflowResolution: .init(x: .fit(to: .chart), y: .disabled)) {
                Text(selectedDay, format: .dateTime.month().day())
                    .font(.caption)
            }
    }
}
.chartXSelection(value: $selectedDay)
.frame(height: 200)
```

**Note:** The selection is a raw x value, not one of your data points. Look up the nearest day yourself to show its count.

### Compare categories with bars

Use `BarMark` to compare totals, and state the takeaway above the chart, the way the guidelines suggest.

```swift
import Charts

struct PlatformShare: Identifiable {
    let name: String
    let downloads: Int
    var id: String { name }
}

let shares = [
    PlatformShare(name: "Mac", downloads: 1840),
    PlatformShare(name: "iPhone", downloads: 1260),
    PlatformShare(name: "iPad", downloads: 610),
]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Most downloads come from the Mac")
        .font(.headline)
    Chart(shares) { share in
        BarMark(
            x: .value("Downloads", share.downloads),
            y: .value("Platform", share.name)
        )
        .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Platform", share.name))
    }
    .chartLegend(.hidden)
    .frame(height: 140)
}
```

### A map with your places

Give `Map` a starting region and list a `Marker` for each place. People can pan, zoom, and rotate it as in Maps.

```swift
import MapKit

struct Cafe: Identifiable {
    let name: String
    let coordinate: CLLocationCoordinate2D
    var id: String { name }
}

let cafes = [
    Cafe(name: "Ferry Building", coordinate: .init(latitude: 37.7955, longitude: -122.3937)),
    Cafe(name: "Union Square", coordinate: .init(latitude: 37.7880, longitude: -122.4075)),
]

let region = MKCoordinateRegion(
    center: .init(latitude: 37.79, longitude: -122.40),
    span: .init(latitudeDelta: 0.04, longitudeDelta: 0.04)
)

Map(initialPosition: .region(region)) {
    ForEach(cafes) { cafe in
        Marker(cafe.name, systemImage: "cup.and.saucer.fill", coordinate: cafe.coordinate)
            .tint(.brown)
    }
}
.mapStyle(.standard(emphasis: .muted))
.mapControls {
    MapZoomStepper()
    MapCompass()
    MapScaleView()
}
.frame(height: 260)
```

More variants, left out to keep this file short: A map that fills a window. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/charts.md

## Related

`hover`, `inspector`, `window-group`, `library-window`


<!-- topic: library-window -->
---
id: library-window
title: Library window
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/navigationsplitview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sidebars.md
---

# Library window

A sidebar, a sortable table, and an inspector: the classic window for browsing a library.

## Contents

- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Built from

NavigationSplitView
├── sidebar: List(selection:)
│   ├── Section("Library")
│   └── Section("Playlists")
└── detail: Table(selection:sortOrder:)
    ├── .searchable(text:)
    ├── .toolbar { … }
    └── .inspector(isPresented:)
        └── Form

## Rules

- **Use familiar symbols in the sidebar.** A symbol next to each item helps people scan the list and find a place again. Leave their color to the accent color people chose.
- **Keep the sidebar to two levels.** Use short section headers for the groups. If your data goes deeper, add a content column between the sidebar and the details.
- **Let people hide the side panes, but show them at first.** Some people want room for the content, so offer a toolbar button and a View menu command. Start with the sidebar visible so people find it.
- **Don't put key actions at the bottom of the sidebar.** People often move windows so the bottom edge is off screen.

## Pitfalls

- **The table doesn't sort for you.** It shows the sort in its headers and updates `sortOrder`, and you sort your array when that changes.
- **The inspector remembers itself.** A trailing-column inspector has its shown or hidden state restored for you.
- **Add the standard commands.** `SidebarCommands()` adds the built-in sidebar commands, and `InspectorCommands()` adds one that shows and hides the inspector with ⌃⌘I.

## Key APIs

`NavigationSplitView { } detail: { }`, `List(selection:)`, `Table(_:selection:sortOrder:)`, `TableColumn(_:value:)`, `.inspector(isPresented:)`, `.navigationSplitViewColumnWidth`, `SidebarCommands()`, `InspectorCommands()`

## Variants

### Sidebar, table, and inspector

A `NavigationSplitView` with a sidebar `List`, a `Table` in the detail column, and an `.inspector` on the table. The drawing is live; the window is the real thing.

```swift
struct Song: Identifiable, Hashable {
    let id = UUID()
    var title: String
    var artist: String
    var album: String
    var seconds: Int
    var isFavorite = false
}

enum Collection: String, Hashable, CaseIterable {
    case all = "Songs"
    case favorites = "Favorites"

    var symbol: String { self == .all ? "music.note" : "star" }
}

struct LibraryView: View {
    @State private var songs = [
        Song(title: "Blue Hour", artist: "The Lanterns", album: "City Lights", seconds: 214, isFavorite: true),
        Song(title: "Northbound", artist: "Mara Quinn", album: "Open Road", seconds: 187),
        Song(title: "Slow Tide", artist: "Okon", album: "Harbor", seconds: 305),
    ]
    @State private var collection: Collection? = .all
    @State private var selection = Set<Song.ID>()
    @State private var sortOrder = [KeyPathComparator(\Song.title)]
    @State private var searchText = ""
    @State private var showsInspector = true

    private var visibleSongs: [Song] {
        songs.filter { song in
            (collection != .favorites || song.isFavorite)
                && (searchText.isEmpty || song.title.localizedStandardContains(searchText))
        }
    }

    var body: some View {
        NavigationSplitView {
            List(selection: $collection) {
                Section("Library") {
                    ForEach(Collection.allCases, id: \.self) { item in
                        Label(item.rawValue, systemImage: item.symbol)
                    }
                }
            }
            .navigationSplitViewColumnWidth(min: 160, ideal: 200)
        } detail: {
            Table(visibleSongs, selection: $selection, sortOrder: $sortOrder) {
                TableColumn("Title", value: \.title)
                TableColumn("Artist", value: \.artist)
                TableColumn("Album", value: \.album)
                TableColumn("Time", value: \.seconds) { song in
                    Text(Duration.seconds(song.seconds), format: .time(pattern: .minuteSecond))
                }
                .width(60)
            }
            .onChange(of: sortOrder) {
                songs.sort(using: sortOrder)
            }
            .searchable(text: $searchText)
            .navigationTitle(collection?.rawValue ?? "Library")
            .inspector(isPresented: $showsInspector) {
                SongInspector(songs: $songs, selection: selection)
                    .inspectorColumnWidth(min: 220, ideal: 260)
            }
            .toolbar {
                Button("Inspector", systemImage: "info.circle") {
                    showsInspector.toggle()
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

struct SongInspector: View {
    @Binding var songs: [Song]
    let selection: Set<Song.ID>

    var body: some View {
        if selection.count == 1, let index = songs.firstIndex(where: { selection.contains($0.id) }) {
            Form {
                TextField("Title", text: $songs[index].title)
                TextField("Artist", text: $songs[index].artist)
                TextField("Album", text: $songs[index].album)
                Toggle("Favorite", isOn: $songs[index].isFavorite)
            }
        } else {
            ContentUnavailableView(
                selection.isEmpty ? "No Selection" : "\(selection.count) Songs",
                systemImage: "music.note"
            )
        }
    }
}
```

### Add it to your app

```swift
@main
struct MusicApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            LibraryView()
        }
        .commands {
            SidebarCommands()
            InspectorCommands()
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`navigation-split-view`, `table`, `inspector`, `search`, `toolbar`, `empty-states`


<!-- topic: settings-window -->
---
id: settings-window
title: Settings window
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/settings.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/settings.md
---

# Settings window

A Settings window with a toolbar of panes, ready to copy into your app.

Also called: preferences, preferences window, settings panes, settings tabs, ⌘,, command comma, AppStorage, UserDefaults, options, NSPreferencePane.

## Contents

- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Built from

Settings
└── SettingsView
    └── TabView(selection:)
        ├── Tab("General")
        │   └── Form
        ├── Tab("Accounts")
        │   └── List + add and remove
        └── Tab("Advanced")
            └── Form

## Rules

- **Don't copy system settings.** Scrolling, accessibility, and sign-in methods belong to System Settings. A copy in your app suggests the system choice doesn't apply.
- **Offer as few settings as you can.** Good defaults mean most people never open the window. Every extra option makes the one people want harder to find.
- **Keep the toolbar of panes still.** Don't let people customize it or hide it, and always show which pane is active. People find settings by where they are.
- **Reopen the last pane.** People often come back to adjust a related setting. Bind the `TabView` to `@AppStorage`, as the block does.
- **Leave task options in the window.** Sorting, filters, and showing a sidebar belong next to the content they change, not in Settings.

## Pitfalls

- **`@AppStorage` keeps every window in sync.** A setting changed here shows up in your other windows right away, and it's saved for the next launch.
- **The `TabView` becomes the toolbar.** Inside `Settings`, its tabs turn into the toolbar of panes, so you don't build that toolbar yourself.

## Key APIs

- `Settings { }`: The scene behind Settings… and ⌘,.
- `TabView(selection:)`: In `Settings`, the toolbar of panes.
- `Tab(_:systemImage:value:)`: One pane, with its icon and title.
- `@AppStorage`: Saves a setting in `UserDefaults`.
- `.formStyle(.grouped)`: Rows in rounded groups, like System Settings.
- `SettingsLink`: A button that opens the Settings window.

## Variants

### General, Accounts, and Advanced

Add `Settings { SettingsView() }` to your `App`. The `TabView` inside becomes the toolbar of panes.

```swift
@main
struct ReaderApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        Settings {
            SettingsView()
        }
    }
}

enum SettingsPane: String {
    case general, accounts, advanced
}

struct SettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("settingsPane") private var pane = SettingsPane.general

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $pane) {
            Tab("General", systemImage: "gearshape", value: .general) {
                GeneralSettingsView()
            }
            Tab("Accounts", systemImage: "at", value: .accounts) {
                AccountsSettingsView()
            }
            Tab("Advanced", systemImage: "gearshape.2", value: .advanced) {
                AdvancedSettingsView()
            }
        }
        .frame(width: 460)
    }
}

enum RefreshInterval: String, CaseIterable, Identifiable {
    case hourly = "Every hour"
    case daily = "Every day"
    case manually = "Manually"

    var id: Self { self }
}

struct GeneralSettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("refreshInterval") private var refreshInterval = RefreshInterval.hourly
    @AppStorage("opensLinksInBackground") private var opensLinksInBackground = false
    @AppStorage("fontSize") private var fontSize = 14.0

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Picker("Check for new articles", selection: $refreshInterval) {
                ForEach(RefreshInterval.allCases) { interval in
                    Text(interval.rawValue).tag(interval)
                }
            }
            Toggle("Open links in the background", isOn: $opensLinksInBackground)
            Slider(value: $fontSize, in: 10...24) {
                Text("Font size")
            }
        }
        .formStyle(.grouped)
    }
}

struct AccountsSettingsView: View {
    @State private var accounts = ["sam@example.com", "work@example.com"]
    @State private var selection: String?

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Section {
                List(accounts, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { account in
                    Label(account, systemImage: "person.crop.circle")
                }
                .frame(height: 120)
            } footer: {
                HStack {
                    Button("Add Account", systemImage: "plus") {
                        accounts.append("new@example.com")
                    }
                    Button("Remove Account", systemImage: "minus") {
                        accounts.removeAll { $0 == selection }
                    }
                    .disabled(selection == nil)
                }
                .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
                .buttonStyle(.borderless)
            }
        }
        .formStyle(.grouped)
    }
}

struct AdvancedSettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("showsDebugMenu") private var showsDebugMenu = false

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Toggle("Show Debug menu", isOn: $showsDebugMenu)
            LabeledContent("Cache") {
                Button("Clear Cache") { }
            }
        }
        .formStyle(.grouped)
    }
}
```

### Open a pane from elsewhere

```swift
struct AddAccountButton: View {
    @AppStorage("settingsPane") private var pane = SettingsPane.general
    @Environment(\.openSettings) private var openSettings

    var body: some View {
        Button("Add an Account…") {
            pane = .accounts
            openSettings()
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`settings-scene`, `settings-pattern`, `form`, `toggle`, `picker`


<!-- topic: menu-bar-utility -->
---
id: menu-bar-utility
title: Menu bar utility
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/menubarextra.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar.md
---

# Menu bar utility

A small app that lives in the menu bar and opens a panel when clicked.

Also called: MenuBarExtra, status item, status bar app, menu bar app, tray icon, NSStatusItem, agent app, LSUIElement, no Dock icon, popover from menu bar.

## Contents

- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Built from

MenuBarExtra("Focus", systemImage:)
├── .menuBarExtraStyle(.window)
└── FocusPanel
    ├── TimelineView (countdown)
    ├── Picker (length)
    ├── Button("Start")
    └── SettingsLink, Quit

## Rules

- **Use a symbol for the menu bar icon.** A template symbol is drawn in the menu bar's own colors, so it looks right in light and dark menu bars and when it's highlighted.
- **Show a menu unless you need more.** Clicking an extra usually opens a menu. Use the window style only when the feature is too rich for menu items, like this timer.
- **Let people choose to show it.** Put a “Show in menu bar” setting in Settings, and offer it during setup so people find it.
- **Don't count on it being visible.** The system hides extras when the menu bar runs out of room. Make the same features reachable from your app's windows or its Dock menu too.

## Pitfalls

- **No Dock icon.** For an app that lives only in the menu bar, set `LSUIElement` to `YES` in its Info.plist, so it stays out of the Dock and the app switcher.
- **Removing the extra quits the app.** When an app's only scene is a `MenuBarExtra` and people remove it from the menu bar, the system ends the app.

## Key APIs

- `MenuBarExtra(_:systemImage:)`: A scene that lives in the menu bar.
- `.menuBarExtraStyle(.window)`: Opens a panel of your own views.
- `.menuBarExtraStyle(.menu)`: Pulls down a regular menu.
- `MenuBarExtra(…isInserted:)`: Lets a setting show or hide the extra.
- `LSUIElement`: Info.plist key that hides the Dock icon.
- `SettingsLink`: Opens your Settings window from the panel.

## Variants

### A focus timer in the menu bar

`MenuBarExtra` with `.menuBarExtraStyle(.window)` shows your view in a panel under the icon. Start the timer to try it.

```swift
@main
struct FocusApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        MenuBarExtra("Focus", systemImage: "timer") {
            FocusPanel()
        }
        .menuBarExtraStyle(.window)

        Settings {
            Text("Focus Settings")
                .padding()
        }
    }
}

struct FocusPanel: View {
    @State private var minutes = 25
    @State private var endDate: Date?

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 14) {
            TimelineView(.periodic(from: .now, by: 1)) { context in
                Text(remaining(at: context.date), format: .time(pattern: .minuteSecond))
                    .font(.system(size: 44, weight: .semibold, design: .rounded))
                    .monospacedDigit()
            }
            Picker("Length", selection: $minutes) {
                Text("15 min").tag(15)
                Text("25 min").tag(25)
                Text("50 min").tag(50)
            }
            .pickerStyle(.segmented)
            .labelsHidden()
            .disabled(endDate != nil)

            Button(endDate == nil ? "Start" : "Stop") {
                endDate = endDate == nil ? .now.addingTimeInterval(Double(minutes * 60)) : nil
            }
            .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
            .keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)

            Divider()
            HStack {
                SettingsLink {
                    Text("Settings…")
                }
                Spacer()
                Button("Quit Focus") {
                    // Quits through AppKit.
                    NSApplication.shared.terminate(nil)
                }
            }
            .buttonStyle(.borderless)
        }
        .padding()
        .frame(width: 260)
    }

    private func remaining(at date: Date) -> Duration {
        guard let endDate else { return .seconds(minutes * 60) }
        return .seconds(max(0, endDate.timeIntervalSince(date)))
    }
}
```

**Note:** The Quit button calls AppKit's `NSApplication.shared.terminate(nil)`. Without a Dock icon, it's how people quit.

### A plain menu

For a handful of commands, use `.menuBarExtraStyle(.menu)`. Buttons become menu items, and `Divider` separates groups.

```swift
MenuBarExtra("Clipboard", systemImage: "list.clipboard") {
    Button("Paste Last Item") { }
    Button("Clear History") { }
    Divider()
    Button("Quit Clipboard") {
        NSApplication.shared.terminate(nil)
    }
    .keyboardShortcut("q")
}
.menuBarExtraStyle(.menu)
```

### Let people hide it

Pass `isInserted:` a binding to `@AppStorage`, and put the same key behind a checkbox in Settings.

```swift
@main
struct FocusApp: App {
    @AppStorage("showsMenuBarExtra") private var showsMenuBarExtra = true

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        MenuBarExtra("Focus", systemImage: "timer", isInserted: $showsMenuBarExtra) {
            FocusPanel()
        }
        .menuBarExtraStyle(.window)
        Settings {
            Form {
                Toggle("Show in menu bar", isOn: $showsMenuBarExtra)
            }
            .padding()
        }
    }
}
```

## Related

`menu-bar-extra`, `menu-bar-conventions`, `settings-scene`, `popover`


<!-- topic: document-editor -->
---
id: document-editor
title: Document editor
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 12.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/documentgroup.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management.md
---

# Document editor

A text editor that opens, saves, and creates files, with a toolbar for formatting.

Also called: DocumentGroup, FileDocument, document-based app, text editor, NSDocument, open and save, File menu, UTType, CFBundleDocumentTypes, plain text.

## Contents

- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Built from

DocumentGroup(newDocument:)
└── EditorView(document: $document)
    ├── TextEditor(text:)
    ├── .toolbar
    │   └── ControlGroup (text size)
    └── .navigationSubtitle (word count)

## Rules

- **Save for people.** Don't make people press Save to keep their work. Save as they go, and keep the toolbar for the tools they use while writing.
- **Create and open from the File menu.** People expect New and Open in the File menu with their usual shortcuts. A document app gets them without extra code.
- **Call a new document “Untitled”.** Let people name it when they save it, in the save panel, along with where it goes.
- **Use the standard open and save panels.** People know the Finder's way of browsing files. Build your own file browser only for a strong reason.

## Pitfalls

- **Every document app declares its types.** Add Document Types (`CFBundleDocumentTypes`) to the Info pane, so the Finder knows which files your app opens.
- **Use the binding, not the file.** `configuration.fileURL` is fine for showing a name, but read and write only through your `FileDocument`, or you'll fight SwiftUI for the file.
- **Sandboxed apps need file access.** Turn on User Selected File with read and write access in the App Sandbox capability. See App Sandbox (`app-sandbox`).

## Key APIs

- `DocumentGroup(newDocument:)`: A scene of document windows.
- `FileDocument`: Reads and writes your document as a value.
- `readableContentTypes`: The file types the document opens.
- `configuration.$document`: The binding your editor changes.
- `configuration.fileURL`: The file's location; `nil` until saved.
- `UTType(exportedAs:)`: Your own file type, declared in Info.plist.

## Variants

### A plain-text editor

A `FileDocument` for plain text, a `DocumentGroup` scene, and an editor with text size buttons in the toolbar and a word count under the title.

```swift
import SwiftUI
import UniformTypeIdentifiers

struct TextDocument: FileDocument {
    static let readableContentTypes: [UTType] = [.plainText]
    var text: String

    init(text: String = "") {
        self.text = text
    }

    init(configuration: ReadConfiguration) throws {
        guard let data = configuration.file.regularFileContents,
              let text = String(data: data, encoding: .utf8) else {
            throw CocoaError(.fileReadCorruptFile)
        }
        self.text = text
    }

    func fileWrapper(configuration: WriteConfiguration) throws -> FileWrapper {
        FileWrapper(regularFileWithContents: Data(text.utf8))
    }
}

@main
struct NotesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        DocumentGroup(newDocument: TextDocument()) { file in
            EditorView(document: file.$document)
        }
    }
}

struct EditorView: View {
    @Binding var document: TextDocument
    @AppStorage("fontSize") private var fontSize = 14.0

    private var wordCount: Int {
        document.text.split(whereSeparator: \.isWhitespace).count
    }

    var body: some View {
        TextEditor(text: $document.text)
            .font(.system(size: fontSize))
            .navigationSubtitle("\(wordCount) words")
            .toolbar {
                ControlGroup {
                    Button("Smaller", systemImage: "textformat.size.smaller") {
                        fontSize = max(10, fontSize - 1)
                    }
                    Button("Bigger", systemImage: "textformat.size.larger") {
                        fontSize = min(32, fontSize + 1)
                    }
                }
            }
    }
}
```

### Declare a custom type

For a format of your own, make a `UTType` with `exportedAs:` and list it in `readableContentTypes`. Declare the same identifier under Exported Type Identifiers in the Info pane.

```swift
import UniformTypeIdentifiers

extension UTType {
    static let outline = UTType(exportedAs: "com.example.outline")
}

struct OutlineDocument: FileDocument {
    static let readableContentTypes: [UTType] = [.outline]
    var data = Data()

    init() {}

    init(configuration: ReadConfiguration) throws {
        data = configuration.file.regularFileContents ?? Data()
    }

    func fileWrapper(configuration: WriteConfiguration) throws -> FileWrapper {
        FileWrapper(regularFileWithContents: data)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Give the type a file extension in its declaration, so the system knows which files belong to it.

## Related

`document-group`, `text-editor`, `toolbar`, `file-import-export`, `app-sandbox`, `welcome-window`


<!-- topic: welcome-window -->
---
id: welcome-window
title: Welcome window
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/scene/defaultlaunchbehavior(_:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/launching.md
---

# Welcome window

The window a document app shows at launch, with New, Open, and recent files.

Also called: welcome screen, start window, launcher, splash, recent documents, open recent, Xcode welcome, hiddenTitleBar, defaultLaunchBehavior, restorationBehavior.

## Contents

- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Built from

Window("Welcome to Notes", id:)
├── .windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)
├── .defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)
└── WelcomeView
    ├── icon, name, version
    ├── New and Open buttons
    └── List (recent documents)

## Rules

- **Put people back where they were.** If documents were open when people quit, reopen them instead of greeting them again. With `.presented`, the welcome window shows only when nothing comes back.
- **Offer recent files next to Open.** Most of the time people want what they had yesterday. A list of recent documents saves a trip through the open panel.
- **Get out of the way fast.** People want to start right away. Keep the window to a few ways in, so they can pick one and get to work.

## Pitfalls

- **It appears only when nothing is restored.** With `.defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)`, the welcome window shows at launch when no document windows come back, and when people click the Dock icon with no windows open.
- **Recent files come from AppKit.** SwiftUI has no list of recent documents, so the block reads AppKit's `NSDocumentController.shared.recentDocumentURLs`.

## Key APIs

`Window(_:id:)`, `.defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)`, `.restorationBehavior(.disabled)`, `.windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)`, `.windowBackgroundDragBehavior`, `\.newDocument`, `\.openDocument`, `\.dismissWindow`

## Variants

### Icon, actions, and recent files

A `Window` with a hidden title bar and a material background. `newDocument` and `openDocument` from the environment do the work.

```swift
@main
struct NotesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        DocumentGroup(newDocument: TextDocument()) { file in
            TextEditor(text: file.$document.text)
        }

        Window("Welcome to Notes", id: "welcome") {
            WelcomeView()
                .toolbar(removing: .title)
                .containerBackground(.thickMaterial, for: .window)
        }
        .windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)
        .windowResizability(.contentSize)
        .windowBackgroundDragBehavior(.enabled)
        .defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)
        .restorationBehavior(.disabled)
    }
}

struct WelcomeView: View {
    @Environment(\.newDocument) private var newDocument
    @Environment(\.openDocument) private var openDocument
    @Environment(\.dismissWindow) private var dismissWindow
    @State private var isImporting = false
    @State private var openError: String?

    // SwiftUI has no list of recent documents; AppKit keeps it.
    private let recents = NSDocumentController.shared.recentDocumentURLs

    var body: some View {
        HStack(spacing: 0) {
            VStack(spacing: 10) {
                Image(systemName: "note.text")
                    .font(.system(size: 64))
                    .foregroundStyle(.tint)
                Text("Notes")
                    .font(.largeTitle.bold())
                Text("Version 2.0")
                    .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
                VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
                    Button("Create New Document", systemImage: "plus") {
                        newDocument(TextDocument())
                        dismissWindow(id: "welcome")
                    }
                    Button("Open Existing Document…", systemImage: "folder") {
                        isImporting = true
                    }
                }
                .buttonStyle(.borderless)
                .padding(.top, 16)
            }
            .frame(width: 300)
            .padding(32)

            List(recents, id: \.self) { url in
                Button {
                    open(url)
                } label: {
                    Label {
                        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
                            Text(url.deletingPathExtension().lastPathComponent)
                            Text(url.deletingLastPathComponent().path(percentEncoded: false))
                                .font(.caption)
                                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
                        }
                    } icon: {
                        Image(systemName: "doc.text")
                    }
                }
                .buttonStyle(.plain)
            }
            .frame(width: 280)
        }
        .frame(height: 400)
        .fileImporter(isPresented: $isImporting, allowedContentTypes: [.plainText]) { result in
            if case .success(let url) = result {
                open(url)
            }
        }
        .alert("Couldn't Open the Document", isPresented: Binding {
            openError != nil
        } set: { isShown in
            if !isShown { openError = nil }
        }) {
            Button("OK") {}
        } message: {
            Text(openError ?? "")
        }
    }

    // Close the welcome window only once the document is open. A recent
    // file may have moved; keep the window so people can pick another.
    private func open(_ url: URL) {
        Task {
            do {
                try await openDocument(at: url)
                dismissWindow(id: "welcome")
            } catch {
                openError = error.localizedDescription
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The block uses the `TextDocument` from Document editor (`document-editor`).

## Related

`document-editor`, `window`, `window-style`, `opening-windows`, `onboarding`


<!-- topic: empty-states -->
---
id: empty-states
title: Empty states
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/contentunavailableview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/writing.md
---

# Empty states

What a sidebar, table, or search shows when there's nothing to show yet.

Also called: ContentUnavailableView, empty state, no results, no items, blank slate, zero state, placeholder, nothing selected, no selection, error state.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Say what to do next, and give a button for it.** An empty window is daunting when the next step isn't clear. Name the action and put it right there.
- **Show progress while loading, not an empty state.** “No Items” while data is still on its way looks like a problem. Show a progress indicator until you know the list is empty.
- **Keep important information out of it.** An empty state goes away as soon as there's content, and anything in it goes too.

## Pitfalls

- **Overlay it, don't replace the list.** Put `ContentUnavailableView` in an `.overlay` on the empty `List` or `Table`, so the column headers, toolbar, and search field stay put.
- **`.search` fills in the words for you.** `ContentUnavailableView.search(text:)` builds a no-results message that quotes what people typed.

## Key APIs

- `ContentUnavailableView(_:systemImage:)`: A title and symbol, for simple cases.
- `ContentUnavailableView { } description: { }`: Adds a line about what to do.
- `actions: { Button… }`: Buttons under the message.
- `.search(text:)`: The standard no-results message.
- `.overlay { }`: Shows it on top of the empty list or table.

## Variants

### An empty sidebar

Give a first-run sidebar a title, a short description, and the button that fills it. Click New Playlist to see the list take over.

```swift
@State private var playlists: [String] = []

List(playlists, id: \.self) { name in
    Label(name, systemImage: "music.note.list")
}
.overlay {
    if playlists.isEmpty {
        ContentUnavailableView {
            Label("No Playlists", systemImage: "music.note.list")
        } description: {
            Text("Playlists you make appear here.")
        } actions: {
            Button("New Playlist") {
                playlists.append("Untitled Playlist")
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### An empty table

Overlay the empty state on the `Table`, so its column headers stay in place and people can see what will fill it.

```swift
@State private var contacts: [Contact] = []

Table(contacts) {
    TableColumn("Name", value: \.name)
    TableColumn("Email", value: \.email)
}
.overlay {
    if contacts.isEmpty {
        ContentUnavailableView {
            Label("No Contacts", systemImage: "person.2")
        } description: {
            Text("Import a file or add someone by hand.")
        } actions: {
            Button("Import Contacts…") { }
        }
    }
}
```

### No search results

When a search finds nothing, show `ContentUnavailableView.search(text:)`. Clear the field, or type Ana, to bring rows back.

```swift
struct Contact: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
    let name: String
    let email: String
}

struct ContactsView: View {
    let contacts: [Contact]
    @State private var searchText = ""

    private var results: [Contact] {
        contacts.filter { searchText.isEmpty || $0.name.localizedStandardContains(searchText) }
    }

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            Table(results) {
                TableColumn("Name", value: \.name)
                TableColumn("Email", value: \.email)
            }
            .overlay {
                if results.isEmpty {
                    ContentUnavailableView.search(text: searchText)
                }
            }
            .searchable(text: $searchText)
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The drawing uses a text field in place of `.searchable`, which would put its field in this app's own toolbar. The Contacts window has the real one.

### Nothing selected

In the detail column of a split view, say what's missing in a few words. No button needed: the next step is clicking the list.

```swift
ContentUnavailableView("No Message Selected", systemImage: "envelope")
```

### Something went wrong

For a failed load, explain it plainly and offer Try Again in `actions:`. Keep the details short; people want the way out.

```swift
ContentUnavailableView {
    Label("Couldn't Load Photos", systemImage: "wifi.exclamationmark")
} description: {
    Text("Check your internet connection, then try again.")
} actions: {
    Button("Try Again") { }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
```

## Related

`library-window`, `search`, `table`, `navigation-split-view`, `writing`


<!-- topic: windows-layout -->
---
id: windows-layout
title: Windows & Layout
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/windows.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Windows & Layout

Lay out windows that people move, resize, and stack beside other apps.

Also called: window size, resize, resizing, margins, padding, layout, minimum size, default size, key window, main window.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Keep important controls away from the bottom edge.** People often drag a window partly below the screen, which hides whatever sits at its bottom. Put actions in the toolbar or near the top.
- **Put what matters most at the top leading corner.** People read a window from the top and from the leading side, so the first thing they should see goes there.
- **Use a bottom bar only for a little status.** A bottom bar suits a short summary of the window, like a count of items. If you have more to show, use an inspector instead.
- **Let the system draw the window.** People know the standard frame, buttons, and title bar. A custom copy that doesn't match exactly makes the whole app feel broken.
- **Open new windows when they help, not by default.** A second window is great for comparing or keeping context, like a draft beside the message it answers. Offer Open in New Window in the File menu or a context menu instead of opening one every time.
- **Call it a window.** In anything people read, say window, whatever kind it is. Words like scene describe your code, not what people see.

## Pitfalls

- **Try the smallest and largest sizes first.** Apple suggests testing the extremes before the sizes in between, since that's where clipping shows up.
- **People decide where windows go.** People typically run several apps at once, so don't count on your window filling the screen or staying where it opened.

## Guide

On the Mac, people keep several apps open at once. They move, resize, minimize, and stack windows to suit their work, so your layout has to hold up at any size you allow, next to windows from other apps.

### Parts of a window

- Frame: The top of the window, with the close, minimize, and zoom buttons and often a toolbar. People drag it to move the window.
- Body: Your content. People can usually resize the window by dragging its edges.
- Bottom bar: Rare. A thin strip under the content for a little status, like Finder's count of items and free space.

### Window states

Only one window takes your typing at a time. The Mac draws the three states differently, so people can tell which window is in front and which one gets their input.

- Key: The window that receives keyboard input. Its close, minimize, and zoom buttons are in color. Only one window on screen is key.
- Main: The app's frontmost window. It's usually also key, unless a panel such as Fonts is taking input.
- Inactive: Any window in the background. Its window buttons turn gray and it drops its materials, so it looks farther away.

**Note:** System controls switch appearance on their own. Custom views can read `appearsActive`, as in the last example below.

## Key APIs

`.defaultSize(width:height:)`, `.windowResizability(_:)`, `.frame(minWidth:minHeight:)`, `.scenePadding()`, `ViewThatFits`, `\.appearsActive`, `.backgroundExtensionEffect()`

## Variants

### Choose a starting size and a minimum

Use `.defaultSize(width:height:)` on the scene for the first launch, and a minimum `.frame` on the content so the layout never breaks.

```swift
@main
struct TripsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
                .frame(minWidth: 480, minHeight: 320)
        }
        .defaultSize(width: 900, height: 600)
    }
}
```

### Size the window to its content

Use `.windowResizability(.contentSize)` for a window that should stay the size of what's inside, like a small utility window.

```swift
Window("Converter", id: "converter") {
    ConverterView()
        .frame(width: 320, height: 160)
}
.windowResizability(.contentSize)
```

### Use the Mac's margins

Apply `.scenePadding()` to a window's root view for the recommended space around its content, instead of picking a number.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
    Text("Lisbon")
        .font(.title2)
    Text("4 nights · 2 travelers")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
.scenePadding()
```

### Rearrange when the window narrows

`ViewThatFits` tries each layout in order and keeps the first one that fits, so a narrow window stacks what a wide one shows side by side.

```swift
ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
    HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 20) {
        TripSummary()
        TripStops()
    }
    VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
        TripSummary()
        TripStops()
    }
}
```

**Note:** Keep the same features at every size. Only how many show at once should change, not what the window can do.

### Tone down custom accents in inactive windows

Read `appearsActive` in a custom view, and drop accent colors while the window isn't key, the way system controls do.

```swift
struct StatusPill: View {
    @Environment(\.appearsActive) private var appearsActive

    var body: some View {
        Text("Booked")
            .padding(.horizontal, 8)
            .padding(.vertical, 2)
            .foregroundStyle(appearsActive ? .white : .secondary)
            .background(appearsActive ? AnyShapeStyle(.tint) : AnyShapeStyle(.fill.tertiary), in: .capsule)
    }
}
```

## Related

`window-group`, `window-style`, `opening-windows`, `split-views`, `view-that-fits`, `toolbar`, `full-screen`


<!-- topic: color -->
---
id: color
title: Color & Accent
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/color.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/color.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Color & Accent

Semantic colors that adapt, and an accent color people choose for every app.

Also called: accent color, tint, AccentColor, brand color, theme, system colors, semantic colors, NSColor, labelColor, controlAccentColor.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Use semantic colors for what they're named for.** Each one is defined by its job, so it adapts correctly. Don't borrow the separator color for text, or a label color for a background.
- **Don't rely on color alone.** Pair color with a symbol or a word, so people who can't tell the colors apart still get the message.
- **Let the person's accent color lead.** People can pick an accent color that applies to every app. Use `Color.accentColor` and the default control styles, so buttons and selection follow their choice.
- **Give each color one meaning.** If your brand color marks things people can click, don't also use it for plain text. Mixed meanings make people guess.
- **Use color sparingly on Liquid Glass.** Symbols and text in a toolbar are monochrome by default. To call out the main action, color its background, as a prominent button does, rather than its symbol or text.
- **Use the system color picker.** If people choose colors in your app, `ColorPicker` opens the standard Colors panel, where their saved colors are waiting.

## Pitfalls

- **Never hard-code a system color's value.** Apple adjusts them between releases and for each appearance. Use `Color.red`, not the RGB numbers it has today.
- **Your accent shows only with Multicolor.** Check your app with a few other accent colors chosen in System Settings, since anyone who picks one sees your app that way.

## Guide

Mac colors are named for what they do, not how they look: label, separator, window background, selected content. Each one has values for light, dark, and Increase Contrast, so a window built from them adapts on its own. On top of that, people choose an **accent color** in System Settings, and it shows up in every app's buttons, selection, and sidebar icons.

### Your accent color or theirs

- Multicolor: When people leave the accent color on Multicolor, the system uses your app's accent color, from the `AccentColor` set in your asset catalog.
- Any other choice: Their color replaces yours everywhere: buttons, selection, and sidebar icons. A sidebar icon you gave a fixed color keeps it.
- .tint(_:): Always respected. Use it when a color carries meaning, like red for a destructive action, not to force your brand.

### Semantic colors

Live, in light and dark. The first ones are SwiftUI styles; the rest come from AppKit's `NSColor`.

### System colors

Each has its own light and dark value, tuned for contrast. Use them by name.

## Key APIs

- `Color.accentColor`: The person's accent color, or yours with Multicolor.
- `.tint(_:)`: A color with meaning that's always respected.
- `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`: Label colors that adapt: `.primary` to `.quaternary`.
- `.separator`, `.link`, `.selection`: Semantic styles for lines, links, and selection.
- `Color(nsColor:)`: AppKit's semantic colors, like `.textBackgroundColor`.
- `.listItemTint(_:)`: A fixed color for one sidebar icon.
- `ColorPicker`: The system's color well and Colors panel.

## Variants

### Use the accent color

A `.borderedProminent` button fills with `Color.accentColor`: yours with Multicolor, the person's choice otherwise.

```swift
HStack {
    Button("Cancel") { }
    Button("Book Trip") { }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
```

**Note:** Set your accent in the asset catalog's `AccentColor` color set. Xcode's templates name it for you.

### Give a control a fixed meaning

`.tint(.red)` keeps a destructive button red whatever accent color people pick.

```swift
HStack {
    Button("Keep Trip") { }
    Button("Delete Trip", role: .destructive) { }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        .tint(.red)
}
```

**Note:** On the Mac, `.borderedProminent` tints the button's background, and `.bordered` doesn't tint at all.

### Keep one sidebar icon's color

Sidebar icons follow the accent color, so save `.listItemTint(_:)` for the rare icon whose color means something.

```swift
List {
    Label("Inbox", systemImage: "tray")
    Label("Important", systemImage: "star")
        .listItemTint(.yellow)
    Label("Sent", systemImage: "paperplane")
}
.listStyle(.sidebar)
```

### Use AppKit's semantic colors

`Color(nsColor:)` brings in Mac colors SwiftUI doesn't name, like `.textBackgroundColor` behind editable text.

```swift
Text("Bring a light jacket for the evenings.")
    .padding(10)
    .frame(width: 260, height: 70, alignment: .topLeading)
    .background(Color(nsColor: .textBackgroundColor))
    .border(.separator)
```

## Related

`dark-mode`, `materials`, `color-picker`, `button`, `contrast-transparency`


<!-- topic: keyboard-access -->
---
id: keyboard-access
title: Keyboard access
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/focus.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/keyboards.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Keyboard access

Let people reach every control and command without touching the pointer.

Also called: Full Keyboard Access, keyboard navigation, tab order, focus order, focus ring, tabindex, FocusState, focusable, focusSection, onKeyPress.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Don't hide actions behind hover.** A button that only appears under the pointer can't be reached from the keyboard. Show it, put it in a menu, or both.
- **Keep standard shortcuts doing standard things.** People carry ⌘C, ⌘Z, and ⌘W from app to app. Give your own command a new shortcut instead of borrowing one people already know.
- **Build custom shortcuts on Command.** Use ⌘ first, add ⇧ for a related variant, and save ⌥ for rarer commands. Avoid ⌃: the system uses it for moving focus and other features.
- **Give shortcuts only to frequent commands.** A few well-chosen shortcuts are easy to learn. Dozens of new ones make the app feel hard, and every command is still reachable through the menu bar.
- **Let people move focus themselves.** Jumping focus somewhere on its own makes people hunt for it. Move it only in response to what they did, like pressing Return in a field.

## Pitfalls

- **Buttons join the Tab order only when keyboard navigation is on.** That's the Mac convention for button-like views, so test your windows with the setting both on and off.
- **Every menu item is keyboard access for free.** People can reach the menu bar from the keyboard, so a command that lives in a menu works for them even without its own shortcut.

## Guide

Many Mac users keep their hands on the keyboard, and some can't use a pointer at all. **Full Keyboard Access**, in the Accessibility section of System Settings, lets people move through windows, menus, and controls and use them with the keyboard alone. A lighter setting, **Keyboard navigation** in System Settings > Keyboard, lets Tab reach every control. Apple asks apps to support Full Keyboard Access, and SwiftUI does most of the work: standard controls already take part.

Your part is custom views, the order focus moves in, and making sure no action needs the pointer.

Click the Name field, then press Tab and ⇧Tab. The readout shows what has focus. Turn on Keyboard navigation in System Settings > Keyboard and try again: now the swatches and the Save button join in.

### Keys the system already uses

These come from the HIG's list of standard shortcuts. Test your window with them, and don't assign them to anything else.

- Tab and ⇧Tab: Move to the next or previous control.
- ⌃Tab: Move to the next group of controls, or out of a table where Tab moves between cells.
- ⌃F2 and ⌃F5: Move focus to the menu bar, or to the window's toolbar.
- ⌘`: Switch to the app's next window.
- Esc and ⌘.: Cancel the current action.

## Key APIs

- `.focusable(_:interactions:)`: Lets a custom view take keyboard focus.
- `@FocusState`: Reads and moves focus from your code.
- `.focused(_:equals:)`: Ties a view to a `@FocusState` value.
- `.defaultFocus(_:_:)`: Picks what has focus when the window opens.
- `.focusSection()`: Visits a group's views before moving on.
- `.onKeyPress(_:action:)`: Handles a key while the view has focus.
- `.keyboardShortcut(_:modifiers:)`: Gives a button or menu item a shortcut.

## Variants

### Make a custom control focusable

Add `.focusable()` so Tab can reach the view, then `.onKeyPress` to change it with the arrow keys.

```swift
@State private var rating = 3

HStack {
    ForEach(1...5, id: \.self) { star in
        Image(systemName: star <= rating ? "star.fill" : "star")
            .onTapGesture { rating = star }
    }
}
.foregroundStyle(.orange)
.focusable()
.onKeyPress(.leftArrow) {
    rating = max(rating - 1, 1)
    return .handled
}
.onKeyPress(.rightArrow) {
    rating = min(rating + 1, 5)
    return .handled
}
```

**Note:** Click the stars, then press ← and →. Built with the macOS 14 SDK or later, `.focusable()` takes focus even with keyboard navigation off.

### Move to the next field on Return

Tie each field to `@FocusState` with `.focused(_:equals:)`, set it in `.onSubmit`, and pick the first field with `.defaultFocus`.

```swift
enum Field: Hashable {
    case name, email
}

@State private var name = ""
@State private var email = ""
@FocusState private var focus: Field?

Form {
    TextField("Name", text: $name)
        .focused($focus, equals: .name)
        .onSubmit { focus = .email }
    TextField("Email", text: $email)
        .focused($focus, equals: .email)
}
.defaultFocus($focus, .name)
```

### Keep a column together

Tab moves across a row first, so add `.focusSection()` to each column to finish one before the next.

```swift
@State private var shipping = ["", ""]
@State private var billing = ["", ""]

HStack(alignment: .top) {
    VStack {
        TextField("Shipping street", text: $shipping[0])
        TextField("Shipping city", text: $shipping[1])
    }
    .focusSection()
    VStack {
        TextField("Billing street", text: $billing[0])
        TextField("Billing city", text: $billing[1])
    }
    .focusSection()
}
```

**Note:** Without `.focusSection()`, Tab would go from Shipping street to Billing street, across the row.

## Related

`focus-keyboard`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `commands`, `voiceover`, `menu-bar-conventions`


<!-- topic: contrast-transparency -->
---
id: contrast-transparency
title: Contrast & transparency
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environmentvalues/colorschemecontrast.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Contrast & transparency

Stay readable when people turn on Increase Contrast or Reduce Transparency.

Also called: Increase Contrast, Reduce Transparency, high contrast, prefers-contrast, prefers-reduced-transparency, colorSchemeContrast, accessibilityReduceTransparency, Differentiate Without Color, accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor, contrast ratio.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Prefer system colors.** System colors and styles already have versions for light, dark, and Increase Contrast. Custom colors need all of those from you.
- **Meet the minimum contrast.** Small text needs at least 4.5:1 against its background. Faint gray text may look elegant, but many people can't read it.
- **Never rely on color alone.** Some people can't tell red from green. Add a symbol, shape, or word so the meaning survives without the color.
- **Offer more contrast when people ask for it.** If your defaults are subtle, check `colorSchemeContrast` and strengthen borders, dividers, and secondary text when it's `.increased`.
- **Check both appearances.** A pairing that passes in light mode can fail in dark mode. Test each setting in both.

## Pitfalls

- **You can read these settings, not change them.** They belong to the person using the Mac, and SwiftUI redraws your views when they change.
- **Asset catalogs can do it without code.** If a color only needs a stronger version, give the color set a high-contrast variant instead of checking the setting in code.

## Guide

Two display settings change how much of your window people can make out. **Increase Contrast** sharpens the difference between foreground and background, and **Reduce Transparency** asks for solid backgrounds instead of see-through ones. Both are in System Settings > Accessibility > Display.

System colors already have versions for these settings. Read the settings yourself for anything custom: your own colors, borders, and translucent layers.

Turn the two settings on here to see what a custom card should do. The real settings on this Mac:

### Minimum contrast

Accessibility Inspector checks against these ratios, from WCAG level AA. Check them in light and dark.

- Text up to 17 points: At least **4.5:1**.
- Text 18 points and larger: At least **3:1**.
- Bold text at any size: At least **3:1**.

## Key APIs

- `\.colorSchemeContrast`: `.increased` when Increase Contrast is on.
- `\.accessibilityReduceTransparency`: True when backgrounds should be opaque.
- `\.accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor`: True when color alone isn't enough.
- `\.colorScheme`: Light or dark, to check alongside contrast.
- `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`: System styles that adapt on their own.

## Variants

### Strengthen a border

Read `colorSchemeContrast` and draw a heavier, darker outline when it's `.increased`.

```swift
@Environment(\.colorSchemeContrast) private var contrast

Text("Draft")
    .padding(.horizontal, 10)
    .padding(.vertical, 4)
    .overlay {
        Capsule().strokeBorder(
            contrast == .increased ? Color.primary : Color.secondary.opacity(0.4),
            lineWidth: contrast == .increased ? 2 : 1
        )
    }
```

**Note:** On this Mac, Increase Contrast is off, so the preview shows the light border.

### Make a translucent layer solid

Check `accessibilityReduceTransparency` and swap a see-through background for an opaque one.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceTransparency) private var reduceTransparency

Image("photo")
    .resizable()
    .scaledToFill()
    .overlay(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
        Text("Lake at sunset")
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .padding(8)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
            .background(.black.opacity(reduceTransparency ? 1 : 0.4))
    }
```

**Note:** On this Mac, Reduce Transparency is off.

### Add shapes when color isn't enough

When `accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor` is true, show a distinct symbol for each status, not only a colored dot.

```swift
@Environment(\.accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor) private var differentiate

HStack {
    if differentiate {
        Image(systemName: "exclamationmark.triangle.fill")
    } else {
        Circle().frame(width: 10, height: 10)
    }
    Text("Payment failed")
}
.foregroundStyle(.red)
```

## Related

`color`, `materials`, `dark-mode`, `voiceover`, `reduce-motion`


<!-- topic: menu-bar-conventions -->
---
id: menu-bar-conventions
title: The menu bar
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/building-and-customizing-the-menu-bar-with-swiftui.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# The menu bar

The standard menus, their order, and which commands belong in each.

Also called: main menu, NSMenu, app menu, File menu, Edit menu, View menu, Window menu, Help menu, Format menu, CommandMenu.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Keep the standard menus, in the standard order.** People expect App, File, Edit, Format, View, your menus, Window, and Help. Many standard items work without any code from you.
- **Disable items instead of hiding them.** A menu that keeps the same items teaches people what the app can do, even when a command doesn't apply right now.
- **Put every command in a menu.** Even rare and advanced commands. In a menu, people can find them, see their shortcuts, and reach them with Full Keyboard Access.
- **Use short, one-word menu titles.** The menu bar shares its space with menu bar extras and may truncate long titles. One word is quick to scan.
- **Name show and hide items for what they'll do.** When the toolbar is showing, the item says Hide Toolbar; when it's hidden, Show Toolbar.
- **Keep a Window menu, even with one window.** Its Minimize and Zoom items give keyboard users a way to do what the window buttons do.

## Pitfalls

- **People learn your app from its menus.** Opening each menu is how many people find out what an app can do, so a command that's only in a toolbar or a context menu is easy to miss.
- **This app's Go menu is a `CommandMenu`.** The system put it after View, where app-specific menus go.

## Guide

The menu bar is how people learn what a Mac app can do and find its commands. Every app uses the same menus in the same order, so people know where to look before they've opened yours: your app's menu, **File**, **Edit**, **Format**, **View**, any menus of your own, **Window**, and **Help**. The Apple menu sits before them, and menu bar extras sit at the far end.

### What goes where

Click a menu to see the items the HIG lists for it, in order. The app here is a notes app.

### What SwiftUI adds for you

Each scene brings its own menu items. Add the optional ones with `.commands`.

- WindowGroup: Hiding and quitting the app, Copy and Paste, and window management.
- Settings: The **Settings…** item in the app menu. See Settings (`settings-scene`).
- DocumentGroup: Document items like Save and Duplicate.
- SidebarCommands, ToolbarCommands, InspectorCommands: Items for the sidebar, the toolbar, and the inspector. Add the ones your windows have.
- TextFormattingCommands: The Format menu, for apps that edit styled text.

**Note:** A real `.commands` here would change this app's own menu bar, so the previews draw the menus.

## Key APIs

- `.commands { }`: Adds menus and items to a scene.
- `CommandMenu(_:)`: Your own menu, placed after View.
- `CommandGroup(after:)`: Adds items next to a standard group.
- `CommandGroup(replacing:)`: Swaps out a standard group, like Help.
- `SidebarCommands()`: The menu item that shows or hides the sidebar.
- `TextFormattingCommands()`: The Format menu, for styled text.
- `@FocusedValue`: Lets a command act on the frontmost window.

## Variants

### Add a menu of your own

`CommandMenu` adds a menu after View: fill it with buttons, and give only the frequent ones a shortcut.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
}
.commands {
    CommandMenu("Note") {
        Button("Pin Note") { }
        Button("Duplicate Note") { }
            .keyboardShortcut("d")
        Divider()
        Button("Show Note Info") { }
            .keyboardShortcut("i")
    }
}
```

### Add to a standard menu

`CommandGroup(after:)` puts items next to a standard group, like after New in the File menu.

```swift
.commands {
    CommandGroup(after: .newItem) {
        Button("New Note from Clipboard") { }
    }
}
```

### Turn on the standard extras

If a window has a sidebar or a customizable toolbar, add `SidebarCommands` and `ToolbarCommands` for their menu items.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
}
.commands {
```
