```swift
    SidebarCommands()
    ToolbarCommands()
}
```

### Act on the frontmost window

Publish the window's model with `.focusedSceneValue`, read it with `@FocusedValue`, and disable the item when there isn't one.

```swift
@Observable
final class NoteModel {
    var isPinned = false
}

struct NoteCommands: Commands {
    @FocusedValue(NoteModel.self) private var note

    var body: some Commands {
        CommandMenu("Note") {
            Button("Pin Note") { note?.isPinned.toggle() }
                .disabled(note == nil)
        }
    }
}

// In the window's view:
// .focusedSceneValue(model)
```

## Related

`commands`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `context-menu`, `settings-pattern`, `undo-redo`, `keyboard-access`


<!-- topic: settings-pattern -->
---
id: settings-pattern
title: What goes in Settings
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/settings.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/settings.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# What goes in Settings

Keep rare, app-wide options in Settings, and task options in the window they affect.

Also called: preferences, options, app settings, settings window, ⌘,, Command-Comma, view options, defaults, configuration, document settings.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Pick defaults that work for most people.** With good defaults, most people never need to open Settings before they get going.
- **Keep Settings short.** Every option makes the window harder to scan and the app feel less approachable. Cut the ones few people change.
- **Keep task options with the task.** Sorting, filtering, and showing parts of a view belong in the window, where people see the result right away.
- **Don't copy system settings.** Appearance, scrolling, and accessibility are set for the whole Mac. A copy in your app suggests the system choice doesn't apply.
- **Don't ask for what you can find out.** Read whether the Mac is in Dark Mode, or which devices are connected, instead of making people tell you.

## Pitfalls

- **Building the window is a separate page.** Settings (`settings-scene`) shows the `Settings` scene, panes, and `SettingsLink` in code.
- **People already know ⌘,.** It opens Settings in nearly every Mac app, and adding a `Settings` scene wires it up for you.

## Guide

A Mac app's **Settings window** opens from Settings… in the app menu or with ⌘,. It's for general options that affect the whole app and that people change rarely, like accounts or the default font for new documents. People have to stop what they're doing to open it, so anything they adjust while working belongs in the window instead.

### Where does it go?

Pick a home for each option in a notes app.

### The Settings window itself

When you do need one, the HIG asks for a few things on the Mac:

- Open it from the app menu: Put Settings… in the app menu, with ⌘, as its shortcut, rather than a button in the toolbar.
- Panes in a toolbar that stays put: Switch between groups of settings with toolbar buttons that people can't customize, and always show which pane is active.
- Title it after the pane: Show the current pane's name, or “App Name Settings” for a window with one pane.
- Come back to the last pane: People often adjust related settings more than once.
- Dim minimize and zoom: People reopen it quickly with ⌘,, and it sizes itself to the pane.

## Key APIs

- `Settings { }`: The scene behind Settings… and ⌘,.
- `@AppStorage`: Saves a setting and updates every window.
- `SettingsLink`: A button that opens the Settings window.
- `CommandGroup(after: .saveItem)`: A home for document options in File.
- `\.colorScheme`: Detects light or dark instead of asking.

## Variants

### View options in the toolbar

Put a `Picker` in a toolbar `Menu`, so people change the sort order where they see the result.

```swift
enum SortOrder: String, CaseIterable {
    case date = "Date Edited"
    case title = "Title"
}

@State private var sort = SortOrder.date

NavigationStack {
    NotesList(sort: sort)
        .toolbar {
            Menu("Sort", systemImage: "arrow.up.arrow.down") {
                Picker("Sort By", selection: $sort) {
                    ForEach(SortOrder.allCases, id: \.self) { order in
                        Text(order.rawValue)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
}
```

**Note:** A real `.toolbar` here would land in this app's own toolbar, so the preview draws the window.

### Document options in the File menu

Put options that belong to one document in the File menu with `CommandGroup(after: .saveItem)`, not in Settings.

```swift
DocumentGroup(newDocument: NoteDocument()) { file in
    NoteEditor(document: file.$document)
}
.commands {
    CommandGroup(after: .saveItem) {
        Button("Document Settings…") { }
    }
}
```

### Detect instead of asking

Read `colorScheme` and follow the Mac's appearance, rather than adding a light and dark choice of your own.

```swift
@Environment(\.colorScheme) private var colorScheme

Label(
    colorScheme == .dark ? "Night chart" : "Day chart",
    systemImage: colorScheme == .dark ? "moon.stars" : "sun.max"
)
```

## Related

`settings-scene`, `menu-bar-conventions`, `toolbars-pattern`, `onboarding`


<!-- topic: windows-tabs -->
---
id: windows-tabs
title: Windows & tabs
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/windowgroup.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Windows & tabs

More than one window, tabs that gather them, and windows that come back after a relaunch.

Also called: multiple windows, new window, open in new window, window tabs, tabbed windows, state restoration, SceneStorage, openWindow, WindowGroup, NSWindow.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Open a new window when it helps, not by default.** A second window is great for comparing or keeping context, like a draft beside the inbox. Opening one for everything buries people in clutter.
- **Offer Open in New Window.** Let people choose to see an item on its own, from a context menu or the File menu.
- **Call it a window.** People know windows. Scene is a word for your code, not for menus and help.
- **Use the system's windows.** People rely on the real title bar, buttons, and active and inactive looks. A homemade frame that's slightly off makes the app feel broken.
- **Bring windows back the way people left them.** After a relaunch, reopen windows in the same place and state, down to the scroll position, so people pick up where they stopped.
- **Keep important things out of a bottom bar.** People often push a window's bottom edge off screen. Use a bottom bar only for a little status about the window's content.

## Pitfalls

- **This app does it too.** Control-click a page in the sidebar and choose Open in New Window. Each window remembers its own tab and page with `@SceneStorage`.
- **Keep `@SceneStorage` small.** It's for things like a selection or a scroll position. The system decides when to save it, and throws it away when the window is closed.

## Guide

Mac users keep several windows open, move between them, and resize them to suit the job. A `WindowGroup` gives your app that for free: people can open more than one window, each with its own state, gather them into **tabs** in a single window, and find them all in the Window menu.

Your part is deciding when content deserves its own window, titling each one, and saving what each window needs to come back after a relaunch.

Open both note windows. Click a button again and the window that's already open comes to the front instead of a copy. People can merge windows like these into one tabbed window, for example with Window > Merge All Windows.

## Key APIs

- `WindowGroup(for:)`: A group of windows, one per value.
- `@Environment(\.openWindow)`: Opens a window from your code.
- `.navigationTitle(_:)`: Titles the window and its Window menu item.
- `@SceneStorage`: Per-window state that's restored on relaunch.
- `.restorationBehavior(.disabled)`: Keeps a window from reopening at launch.
- `\.supportsMultipleWindows`: Whether opening another window is possible.

## Variants

### Open an item in its own window

Give `WindowGroup` a value type, then call `openWindow(value:)` from a context menu to open that item's window.

```swift
struct Note: Identifiable, Hashable, Codable {
    var id: String
    var title: String
}

// In the App:
WindowGroup("Note", for: Note.ID.self) { $noteID in
    NoteView(noteID: noteID)
}

// In the list:
@Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

List(notes) { note in
    Text(note.title)
        .contextMenu {
            Button("Open in New Window") {
                openWindow(value: note.id)
            }
        }
}
```

**Note:** If a window for that value is already open, `openWindow` brings it forward instead of opening a second one.

### Bring each window back as it was

`@SceneStorage` works like `@State`, but each window saves its own value and gets it back after a relaunch.

```swift
struct NoteView: View {
    @SceneStorage("draft") private var draft = ""

    var body: some View {
        TextEditor(text: $draft)
            .navigationTitle("Trip Notes")
    }
}
```

**Note:** Window restoration is a systemwide choice in System Settings. SwiftUI follows it unless you say otherwise for a window.

### Don't reopen short-lived windows

For a window that's only useful in the moment, like a connection test, add `.restorationBehavior(.disabled)` to its scene.

```swift
Window("Connection Test", id: "connection-test") {
    ConnectionTestView()
}
.restorationBehavior(.disabled)
```

## Related

`window-group`, `opening-windows`, `window`, `document-group`, `full-screen`, `onboarding`


<!-- topic: toolbars-pattern -->
---
id: toolbars-pattern
title: Toolbars
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 13.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/toolbars.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toolbars.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Toolbars

Which commands earn a place in the toolbar, how to group them, and letting people customize.

Also called: NSToolbar, toolbar items, customize toolbar, toolbar customization, toolbar(id:), ToolbarItem, ToolbarSpacer, toolbar placement, window title, overflow menu.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Put the commands people use most in the toolbar.** Not every menu item needs a button. Pick the frequent ones, or the ones for the most important things people work with.
- **Make every toolbar item a menu command too.** People can hide or customize the toolbar, so it can't be the only place a command lives.
- **Use plain symbols.** Toolbar items don't need outlines or circles: the toolbar already groups them, and the system draws hover and selection.
- **Title the window with its content, not your app's name.** The title tells people where they are and tells windows apart. Keep it short, under about 15 characters.
- **Keep groups few and logical.** Group items by what they do, and aim for no more than three groups. Separate text buttons with space so they don't read as one.
- **Let people customize toolbars in apps they live in.** If you offer many items, or people use the app for hours, let them choose what's in the center.

## Pitfalls

- **On the Mac, `.primaryAction` sits at the leading edge.** On iPhone and iPad it's at the trailing edge, so check placements when you bring an iPad toolbar over.
- **Overflow is automatic.** When a window gets too narrow, the system moves center items into an overflow menu. Don't build your own.

## Guide

On the Mac, the toolbar sits at the top of the window, in or below the title bar. It holds the window's title, controls for getting around, and the actions people use most. Because people can hide it or customize it, the toolbar is a shortcut to commands that also live in the menu bar, never the only way to reach them.

### Three areas

Pick an area to see what the HIG puts there.

### Try a real one

This window's toolbar can be customized. Control-click the toolbar and choose **Customize Toolbar…**, then drag items in and out.

**Note:** A real `.toolbar` here would land in this app's own toolbar, so the previews draw the window. The editor above uses the first example's code.

## Key APIs

- `.toolbar(id:content:)`: A toolbar people can customize.
- `ToolbarItem(id:placement:)`: One item, with an ID for customization.
- `ToolbarSpacer(.fixed)`: A gap between groups of items, from macOS 26.
- `.navigation`: Leading edge, before the title.
- `.principal`: The center of the toolbar.
- `ToolbarCommands()`: Adds the toolbar's menu items, like Customize.

## Variants

### A toolbar people can customize

Use `.toolbar(id:)`, give each `ToolbarItem` an ID, and separate the groups with `ToolbarSpacer(.fixed)`.

```swift
@State private var text = ""
@State private var isBold = false
@State private var isItalic = false

TextEditor(text: $text)
    .toolbar(id: "editor") {
        ToolbarItem(id: "bold") {
            Toggle("Bold", systemImage: "bold", isOn: $isBold)
        }
        ToolbarItem(id: "italic") {
            Toggle("Italic", systemImage: "italic", isOn: $isItalic)
        }
        ToolbarSpacer(.fixed)
        ToolbarItem(id: "share") {
            Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { }
        }
    }
    .navigationTitle("Trip Notes")
```

**Note:** To offer customization in the menu bar too, add `ToolbarCommands()` to the scene's `.commands`.

### Place items by role

`.navigation` goes at the leading edge, before the title, and `.principal` in the center.

```swift
Text("Page")
    .toolbar {
        ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation) {
            Button("Back", systemImage: "chevron.backward") { }
        }
        ToolbarItem(placement: .principal) {
            Picker("View", selection: .constant(0)) {
                Text("Day").tag(0)
                Text("Week").tag(1)
            }
            .pickerStyle(.segmented)
        }
    }
```

### The same command in the menu bar

Give each toolbar action a menu item, with a shortcut if it's frequent, so it works with the toolbar hidden.

```swift
.commands {
    CommandMenu("Note") {
        Button("Share Note…") { }
        Button("Show Note Info") { }
            .keyboardShortcut("i")
    }
}
```

## Related

`toolbar`, `menu-bar-conventions`, `search`, `inspector`, `full-screen`


<!-- topic: full-screen -->
---
id: full-screen
title: Full screen
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 15.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/windowtoolbarfullscreenvisibility(_:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/going-full-screen.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Full screen

Let a window fill the screen for focused work, and keep what people need in reach.

Also called: full-screen mode, Enter Full Screen, ⌃⌘F, green button, zoom, presentation mode, distraction free, windowToolbarFullScreenVisibility, windowFullScreenBehavior, appearsActive.

## Rules

- **Offer full screen where focus helps.** Games, photos, video, slideshows, and deep work like writing benefit most from filling the screen.
- **Use the system's full screen.** The green button, View > Enter Full Screen, and ⌃⌘F already work and handle things like the camera housing on some Macs. Don't add a menu of your own window modes.
- **Adjust the layout, not the window.** Use the extra room for the content, with subtle changes so switching modes isn't jarring. Never resize the window from code.
- **Keep essential controls in reach.** People should finish their task without leaving full screen, like playback controls that are always there or easy to reveal.
- **Hide toolbars when content is the point, and bring them back on request.** For reading or viewing, tuck controls away, and show them when people move the pointer to the top of the screen.
- **Let people decide when to leave, and pause when they look away.** Don't end full screen on your own when something finishes. If people switch away, pause a game or slideshow so they don't miss anything.

## Pitfalls

- **Full screen comes with the window.** SwiftUI decides from the scene and its modifiers. With `.windowResizability`, the content's maximum size also decides whether a window can go full screen.
- **Option-click the green button to zoom instead.** The window grows to its maximum size, or as large as the display allows.

## Guide

Any Mac window that can grow can usually fill the screen in a space of its own: people click the green window button, choose **View > Enter Full Screen**, or press ⌃⌘F. The menu bar hides until the pointer reaches the top of the screen, and by default the window's toolbar stays at the top, above the content.

SwiftUI windows get this for free. Your part is the layout, deciding what to hide, and pausing when people switch away.

Open the slideshow, then click its green button. Its toolbar hides until you move the pointer to the top. Switch to another app and the slideshow pauses.

## Key APIs

- `.windowToolbarFullScreenVisibility(_:)`: Shows the toolbar only on hover in full screen.
- `.windowFullScreenBehavior(.disabled)`: Keeps a window out of full screen.
- `\.appearsActive`: False when the window isn't the active one.
- `.toolbarVisibility(_:for:)`: Hides the window's toolbar entirely.

## Variants

### Tuck the toolbar away in full screen

`.windowToolbarFullScreenVisibility(.onHover)` hides the toolbar in full screen until the pointer moves to the top.

```swift
SlideshowView()
    .toolbar {
        Button("Pause", systemImage: "pause") { }
    }
    .windowToolbarFullScreenVisibility(.onHover)
```

**Note:** It only affects the window it's in. The slideshow above uses it; the preview draws the result.

### Pause when the window isn't active

Run the timer only while `appearsActive` is true; it turns false when people switch to another window or app.

```swift
@Environment(\.appearsActive) private var appearsActive
@State private var slide = 0

Text("Slide \(slide + 1)")
    .task(id: appearsActive) {
        guard appearsActive else { return }
        while !Task.isCancelled {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(2))
            slide = (slide + 1) % 5
        }
    }
```

### Keep a utility window out of full screen

Add `.windowFullScreenBehavior(.disabled)` to a small panel's content, like a color mixer, that has no use for the whole screen.

```swift
Window("Color Mixer", id: "mixer") {
    ColorMixer()
        .windowFullScreenBehavior(.disabled)
}
```

## Related

`windows-tabs`, `toolbars-pattern`, `menu-bar-conventions`, `window-style`


<!-- topic: native-vs-catalyst -->
---
id: native-vs-catalyst
title: Native, Catalyst, or iPad App
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/configuring-a-multiplatform-app-target.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-macos.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Native, Catalyst, or iPad App

Three ways onto the Mac: a native Mac app, Mac Catalyst, or your iPad app as it is.

Also called: Mac Catalyst, Catalyst, UIKit for Mac, Designed for iPad, iPad app on Mac, iOS apps on Mac, Apple silicon, multiplatform, supported destinations, port to Mac.

## Rules

- **Check that your app makes sense on a Mac.** Apps that depend on a gyroscope, an accelerometer, the rear camera, HealthKit, or ARKit, or that exist mainly for marking up, handwriting, or navigation, may not suit the Mac.
- **Don't offer two versions on the Mac.** Apple lists an existing Mac version, built with AppKit or Catalyst, as a reason to stop offering your iPad app on the Mac.
- **Whichever path you pick, design for the Mac.** Even with Catalyst, Apple says to go beyond showing your iPad layout in a Mac window: menus, toolbars, and resizable windows are what people expect.

## Pitfalls

- **Your iPad app may already be on the Mac App Store.** Apple offers compatible iPhone and iPad apps on Macs with Apple silicon unless you turn that off in App Store Connect.
- **A native Mac app replaces it.** If your iPad app is on the Mac App Store and you add the macOS platform, releasing the Mac app takes its place, and existing users move to the Mac app.
- **Catalyst adds the sandbox for you.** Turning on Mac Catalyst adds the App Sandbox entitlement to the Mac build only.

## Guide

In Xcode, an app target's **Supported Destinations** offers three kinds of Mac destination. Each one is a different way to get onto the Mac, with different work and a different result.

### Compare the three

- What it is: A new Mac app built against the macOS SDK. It's the default Mac destination for multiplatform apps.
- Built with: SwiftUI and AppKit, with every macOS API available.
- Looks like: A Mac app: checkboxes, pop-up buttons, the menu bar, and Mac sizes.
- App Store: Add the macOS platform to your app record to sell it with your iOS app as one purchase.

### Which one to pick

- Your app is SwiftUI, or it's new: **Mac.** Apple suggests one multiplatform target when you use SwiftUI on both platforms. You get every macOS API, and the controls are real Mac controls.
- You have a large UIKit iPad app: **Mac Catalyst.** You keep one codebase and build it for the Mac, then adjust menus, toolbars, and layout.
- You want something on the Mac today: **Designed for iPad.** No porting at all, but it only runs on Macs with Apple silicon and keeps the iPad's look.
- UIKit on iPad, AppKit on the Mac: **Mac**, in its own target. Apple suggests separate targets when the two apps share little code.

### Catalyst's two looks

A Catalyst app starts with **Scale Interface to Match iPad**: iPad views and text shrink to 77%, so 17-point body text shows at 13 points. Switch to **Optimize Interface for Mac** for full-size text, sharper artwork, and controls that look and behave like AppKit's, then plan time to fix the layout.

**Important:** In the Mac idiom, a few UIKit controls change or go away. `UIPageControl` isn't available, and showing it throws an exception.

## Variants

### Add Mac-only scenes

In a multiplatform target, one `App` serves every platform, and `#if os(macOS)` adds Mac-only scenes like `Settings`.

```swift
@main
struct TripsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        #if os(macOS)
        Settings {
            SettingsView()
        }
        #endif
    }
}
```

**Note:** Apple's own example adds a `MenuBarExtra` the same way. Use `#if canImport(ARKit)` for a framework the Mac doesn't have.

## Related

`great-mac-app`, `ipad-app-in-window`, `universal-purchase`, `app-sandbox`


<!-- topic: great-mac-app -->
---
id: great-mac-app
title: What Makes a Great Mac App
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/commands.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-macos.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# What Makes a Great Mac App

Menus, the keyboard, windows, Settings, and drag and drop: what people expect on a Mac.

Also called: Mac-like, mac assed, feels native, menu bar, keyboard shortcuts, multiple windows, drag and drop, preferences, settings, full keyboard access.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Disable menu items instead of hiding them.** A menu that always shows the same items teaches people what your app can do, even when an item doesn't apply right now.
- **Use the big display.** Show more content with fewer nested levels and fewer modal steps, while keeping the density comfortable to read.
- **Let people shape their windows.** People resize, hide, show, and move windows to fit how they work, and expect full screen for focused work.
- **Reward precise input.** A pointer allows exact selection and editing, so support it alongside the keyboard.
- **Let people personalize.** Customizable toolbars, windows that show the views people use most, and their choice of colors and fonts all help.

## Pitfalls

- **Standard menus do a lot of the work.** The system implements many standard menu items for you, so keeping them pays off twice.
- **People switch between apps all day.** Expect your app to be one of several windows on screen, and to move smoothly between active and inactive.

## Guide

A Mac sits on a desk, a foot or three from someone's eyes, with a big display, a keyboard, and a pointer. People keep several apps open and spend anything from minutes to hours in one. Five things make an app feel at home there.

### 1. Every command in the menu bar

People learn what an app does by opening its menus. Keep the standard menus in their usual order, put your own menus between View and Window, and list every command there, even the ones that also have a button. See Commands (`commands`).

### 2. The keyboard does everything

Standard shortcuts like ⌘C, ⌘Z, and ⌘W should work as they do everywhere else. Add your own only for frequent commands, list modifiers as ⌃⌥⇧⌘, and support Full Keyboard Access so people can reach every control without a pointer. See Keyboard Shortcuts (`keyboard-shortcuts`).

### 3. Windows people control

Windows should adapt smoothly to any size. Where it helps people multitask, let them open content in a window of its own, the way Mail gives each new message its own window. Keep the system's window frame and controls: a custom imitation that doesn't match them exactly makes an app feel broken. See WindowGroup (`window-group`).

```swift
WindowGroup(for: Trip.ID.self) { $tripID in
    TripView(tripID: tripID)
}
.defaultSize(width: 900, height: 600)
```

### 4. Settings in the app menu

App-wide options go in a Settings window that opens from the app menu or with ⌘,. A `Settings` scene gives you both. Options for one window, like sorting, stay in that window. See Settings (`settings-scene`).

### 5. Drag and drop everywhere

People try drag and drop on everything: between your windows, to and from other apps, and into the Finder. Offer another way to do the same thing, like a menu command, for people who can't drag. See Drag and Drop (`drag-drop`).

## Variants

### Add an app-specific menu

`CommandMenu` adds a menu between View and Window, with shortcuts for the commands people use most.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
}
.commands {
    CommandMenu("Trip") {
        Button("New Stop") { addStop() }
            .keyboardShortcut("n", modifiers: [.shift, .command])
        Button("Show Map") { showMap() }
            .keyboardShortcut("m")
    }
}
```

### A shortcut on a button

`.keyboardShortcut(_:modifiers:)` clicks the button for you while its window is active, so press ⌥⌘K to try it.

```swift
@State private var stops = 0

Button("Add Stop") { stops += 1 }
    .keyboardShortcut("k", modifiers: [.option, .command])
```

### Drag a stop onto the trip

`.draggable(_:)` makes a view a drag source, and `.dropDestination(for:)` accepts what people drop on a view.

```swift
@State private var trip: [String] = []

HStack {
    ForEach(["Lisbon", "Porto", "Faro"], id: \.self) { city in
        Text(city)
            .padding(8)
            .background(.fill.tertiary, in: .capsule)
            .draggable(city)
    }
}
Text(trip.isEmpty ? "Drop stops here" : trip.joined(separator: " → "))
    .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 60)
    .background(.fill.quaternary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 10))
    .dropDestination(for: String.self) { cities, _ in
        trip.append(contentsOf: cities)
    }
```

## Related

`mac-native-checklist`, `ipad-app-in-window`, `commands`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `window-group`, `settings-scene`, `drag-drop`, `menu-bar-conventions`


<!-- topic: mac-native-checklist -->
---
id: mac-native-checklist
title: Mac-Native Checklist
platforms: [macOS]
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-macos.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Mac-Native Checklist

The details Mac users and reviewers notice, in one list to check before you ship.

Also called: checklist, Mac polish, pre-flight, menu bar, Window menu, View menu, context menu, full keyboard access, undo, full screen.

## Pitfalls

- **Check with the keyboard only.** Turn on Full Keyboard Access in System Settings, then try to reach every control and menu item without the pointer.
- **Open your app next to a Mac app you like.** Compare the menus item by item. Gaps show up fast.

## Guide

Each item comes from the macOS Human Interface Guidelines. None of them is an App Review rule on its own, but together they're the difference between an app that feels at home on the Mac and one that doesn't. Your checkmarks are saved on this Mac.

### Menu bar

- **Standard menus, in order**: Your app's menu, File, Edit, Format, View, your own menus, Window, Help. Leave out File and Format if they don't apply. (`commands`)
- **Every command is in a menu**: Even commands that also have a toolbar button or a context menu item.
- **Unavailable items are dimmed, not hidden**: The menus show the same items every time.
- **About comes first in the app menu**: With a short app name and no version number in the item's title.
- **A Window menu, even with one window**: With Minimize and Zoom, so Full Keyboard Access can reach them.
- **View menu items say what they'll do**: Show Sidebar when it's hidden, Hide Sidebar when it's showing.
- **A Help menu at the end**: Point it to your help or support page.

### Keyboard

- **Standard shortcuts work**: ⌘C, ⌘V, ⌘Z, ⌘W, ⌘Q, and the rest do what they do everywhere. (`keyboard-shortcuts`)
- **Custom shortcuts only for frequent commands**: And never a standard shortcut reused for something else.
- **Modifiers listed as ⌃⌥⇧⌘**: Control, Option, Shift, Command, in that order.
- **Every control works with Full Keyboard Access**: Tab and the arrow keys reach everything. (`keyboard-access`)

### Windows

- **Windows resize smoothly**: The layout adapts to any reasonable size, not one fixed iPad-sized frame. (`window-group`)
- **Content can open in its own window**: Where that helps people work on two things at once.
- **Full screen works**: Enter Full Screen in the View menu. (`full-screen`)
- **The system's window frame and controls**: No custom title bars or imitation window buttons.
- **Nothing critical in a bottom bar**: People often move windows partly off screen.

### Input and editing

- **Objects have context menus**: Mac users expect a Control-click on almost anything to offer actions. (`context-menu`)
- **Drag and drop works, including to the Finder**: With another way to do the same thing. (`drag-drop`)
- **Undo and Redo in the Edit menu**: With the action's name, like Undo Paste. (`undo-redo`)
- **Buttons sit near the content, not at screen edges**: Ergonomic bottom bars from the iPad don't apply on a Mac.

### Settings and system

- **Settings… in the app menu with ⌘,**: Only app-wide options. Window options stay in the window. (`settings-scene`)
- **Light and dark appearances both look right**: Use system colors and materials. (`dark-mode`)
- **A Mac version of your app icon**: Not the iPad icon. (`app-icons`)
- **No assumptions about who's signed in**: With fast user switching, several people can be active on one Mac.

## Related

`great-mac-app`, `ipad-app-in-window`, `commands`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `context-menu`, `settings-scene`, `undo-redo`, `full-screen`, `keyboard-access`, `drag-drop`


<!-- topic: ipad-app-in-window -->
---
id: ipad-app-in-window
title: Not an iPad App in a Window
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/navigationsplitview.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/mac-catalyst.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Not an iPad App in a Window

The signs of a port that wasn't adapted to the Mac, and what to do instead.

Also called: port, iPad port, Catalyst app, tab bar on Mac, bottom toolbar, page control, page dots, popover, inspector, sidebar.

## Rules

- **Swap the tab bar for a sidebar.** A split view with a sidebar follows Mac conventions. Each tab becomes a sidebar row, and using a sidebar on iPad too keeps the layout familiar.
- **Move bottom-edge buttons to the toolbar.** Buttons at the bottom of an iPad screen are easy to reach with a thumb. On a Mac, the most important actions belong at the top of the window.
- **Show details in an inspector, not a popover.** There's room beside the content on a Mac, so details can sit next to it instead of covering it.
- **Give paged content Previous and Next buttons.** Swiping between pages needs a trackpad. Buttons also work with a mouse and from the keyboard.
- **Let windows resize.** An iPad app that skips multitasking runs in a fixed-size window on the Mac. Build layouts that grow and shrink with the window.
- **Fix text and artwork size.** In Catalyst's iPad idiom, everything scales down to 77%. In the Mac idiom, text shows at full size and can look too big. Use text styles, not fixed font sizes.

## Pitfalls

- **Gestures still work, but they can't be the only way.** Taps become clicks and pinch still works on a trackpad, but many people use a mouse or the keyboard.
- **The Mac version needs its own icon.** Apple asks for a macOS version of your app icon, in the Mac's rendering style.

## Guide

Whether you start from Mac Catalyst, run your iPad app as is, or rebuild in SwiftUI, the same habits from the iPad give a port away. Apple's advice for Catalyst apps applies to every Mac app: go beyond showing the iPad layout in a Mac window.

The pairs below show several of them. Each Do differs from its Don't in one thing.

## Variants

### Replace a TabView with a split view

On the Mac, `NavigationSplitView` with a `List` in the sidebar does the job a tab bar does on iPad.

```swift
enum TripSection: String, CaseIterable, Identifiable {
    case upcoming, past, shared
    var id: Self { self }
}

struct TripsView: View {
    @State private var section: TripSection? = .upcoming

    var body: some View {
        NavigationSplitView {
            List(TripSection.allCases, selection: $section) { section in
                Label(section.rawValue.capitalized, systemImage: "suitcase")
            }
        } detail: {
            Text(section?.rawValue.capitalized ?? "Choose a section")
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** Also list the sections in the View menu, so people can switch with the keyboard. A real split view here would take over this window, so the preview is a drawing.

## Related

`native-vs-catalyst`, `mac-native-checklist`, `navigation-split-view`, `toolbar`, `inspector`, `toggle`


<!-- topic: app-sandbox -->
---
id: app-sandbox
title: App Sandbox
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/app-sandbox.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# App Sandbox

Every Mac App Store app runs in a sandbox, with only the access it asks for.

Also called: sandbox, sandboxing, entitlements, entitlement, com.apple.security.app-sandbox, container, Library/Containers, Operation not permitted, file access, security-scoped.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Ask only for the access you use.** The sandbox works by keeping your app to the smallest set of privileges it needs. Turn on what a feature uses, and turn it off when the feature goes.
- **Reach people's files through the open and save panels.** The sandbox keeps your app in its own container. A file people pick in a panel is the normal way to read or write anywhere else.

## Pitfalls

- **Your Debug builds are sandboxed too.** The entitlements apply whenever the app is signed, so you find missing access while developing, not in review.
- **Asking for an entitlement isn't the same as getting access.** Camera, microphone, and location still show the system's permission prompt.

## Guide

Guideline **2.4.5(i)** says apps on the Mac App Store must be appropriately sandboxed. Turn on the App Sandbox, then turn on only the access your features need: the network, files people pick, the camera, and so on.

The sandbox limits what a compromised app can do. If someone tricks your app into running bad code, it can still only reach its own folder and what you declared.

### Turn it on

1. In Xcode, select your app's target and open **Signing & Capabilities**.
2. Click **+ Capability** and add **App Sandbox**. Xcode adds `com.apple.security.app-sandbox` to your entitlements file.
3. Under App Sandbox, check each resource you use, like **Outgoing Connections (Client)** for network requests.
4. For **User Selected File**, choose **Read Only** or **Read/Write** if people open or save files.
5. Run the app, open Activity Monitor, and choose View > Columns > Sandbox. Your app should say **Yes**.

### What the entitlements file looks like

This app's own entitlements: the sandbox, outgoing network connections for photos and maps, and files people pick.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>com.apple.security.app-sandbox</key>
    <true/>
    <key>com.apple.security.network.client</key>
    <true/>
    <key>com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-write</key>
    <true/>
</dict>
</plist>
```

### Where your files live

- Your container: `~/Library/Containers/<bundle ID>`. The system makes it on first launch, and only your app can read and write it.
- Downloads, Pictures, and other folders: Off limits unless you add the matching entitlement. Without it you get “Operation not permitted.”
- Files people pick: Readable or writable when you add the user-selected file entitlement and they choose the file in a panel.

### Before you submit

- **App Sandbox is on**: `com.apple.security.app-sandbox` is in your entitlements.
- **Only the entitlements you use**: Remove leftovers from features you cut.
- **Network access if you load anything**: Outgoing Connections (Client) for images, APIs, and maps.
- **Files go through open and save panels**: Plus the user-selected file entitlement.
- **Activity Monitor shows Sandbox: Yes**: Check the build you're about to submit.

## Key APIs

- `com.apple.security.app-sandbox`: Turns the sandbox on. Required for the Mac App Store.
- `com.apple.security.network.client`: Outgoing connections, like loading images.
- `…files.user-selected.read-write`: Files people pick in an open or save panel.
- `.fileImporter(isPresented:…)`: Shows an open panel from SwiftUI.
- `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()`: Opens access to a file people picked.

## Variants

### Read a file from an open panel

`.fileImporter` shows the open panel. Wrap your reads in `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()` and its matching stop call.

```swift
import SwiftUI
import UniformTypeIdentifiers

struct OpenTextButton: View {
    @State private var isImporting = false
    @State private var text = ""

    var body: some View {
        Button("Open Text File…") { isImporting = true }
            .fileImporter(isPresented: $isImporting, allowedContentTypes: [.plainText]) { result in
                guard case .success(let url) = result else { return }
                let didAccess = url.startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()
                defer { if didAccess { url.stopAccessingSecurityScopedResource() } }
                text = (try? String(contentsOf: url, encoding: .utf8)) ?? ""
            }
    }
}
```

**Important:** Without the user-selected file entitlement, the open panel still appears, but reading the file fails.

## Related

`settings-scene`


<!-- topic: privacy-permissions -->
---
id: privacy-permissions
title: Privacy & Permissions
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/privacy-manifest-files.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Privacy & Permissions

Purpose strings, the privacy manifest, App Privacy answers, and the Mac's permission prompts.

## Rules

- **Write a purpose string that says what and why.** One short, complete, active sentence about how the app uses the data, with a period at the end. Vague or bossy text gives people no reason to agree.
- **Ask when people reach the feature, not at launch.** A request out of nowhere feels suspicious. Asking when someone clicks Scan makes the reason obvious.
- **Give an explainer one button, and make it open the prompt.** If you show your own window first, give it a single Continue button. A second way out, or a button titled Allow, steers people.
- **Have a plan for No.** Guideline 5.1.1(iv) asks for an alternative where possible, like typing an address when someone declines Location.

## Pitfalls

- **One set of App Privacy answers covers every platform.** With Universal Purchase, answer for whichever platform collects the most.
- **Required-reason APIs are an iOS-family rule.** The privacy manifest lists them for iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS; the data your app collects goes in it on every platform, the Mac included.
- **Several people can share one Mac.** With fast user switching, don't assume who's signed in.

## Guide

Guideline **5.1.1** sets the rules. Link a privacy policy in App Store Connect and inside the app **(i)**. Get consent before you collect data, and write purpose strings that clearly and completely explain the use **(ii)**. Ask only for data your core features need **(iii)**, and respect people's choices without tricking or pressuring them **(iv)**.

Under **5.1.2(i)**, you can't use or share personal data without permission, and you must say clearly when it goes to a third party, third-party AI included.

### Four places privacy shows up

- In the permission prompt: Your purpose string, from `Info.plist`, appears when the system asks for access.
- In the app bundle: `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, the privacy manifest, records the data your app and its SDKs collect.
- On the product page: Your App Privacy answers in App Store Connect, shown to people before they download.
- In your privacy policy: Required for Mac apps: a link in App Store Connect and one inside the app.

### Camera, microphone, and friends

On the Mac, protected hardware and data need two things before you ask: a purpose string in `Info.plist` and the matching entitlement under App Sandbox (or Hardened Runtime).

- Camera: `NSCameraUsageDescription` + `com.apple.security.device.camera`
- Microphone: `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` + `com.apple.security.device.audio-input`
- Contacts: `NSContactsUsageDescription` + `…personal-information.addressbook`
- Photos: `NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription` + `…personal-information.photos-library`

**Important:** For the camera and microphone, Apple says the system ends your app if the key or the entitlement is missing when it asks for access or starts capturing.

### Permissions people grant in System Settings

People review and change every choice in **System Settings > Privacy & Security**. Some lists, like **Full Disk Access** and **Accessibility**, let people add an app themselves with the add button. If a feature needs one of those, tell people exactly where to go, and keep the rest of the app working without it.

### The privacy manifest

Choose File > New File, then **App Privacy** under Resource. Xcode names it `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, the name the system requires. Record the data types you collect, and whether you track. Each third-party SDK can ship its own.

```xml
<key>NSPrivacyTracking</key>
<false/>
<key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes</key>
<array>
    <dict>
        <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
        <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeEmailAddress</string>
        <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
        <true/>
        <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
        <false/>
        <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
        <array>
            <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAppFunctionality</string>
        </array>
    </dict>
</array>
```

### App Privacy answers

1. In App Store Connect, open your app and click **App Privacy** in the sidebar.
2. Click **Get Started** and say whether you or your partners collect data.
3. If you do, pick every data type you and your third-party partners collect, then answer the questions for each.
4. Check the **Product Page Preview**, then click **Publish**. Update the answers whenever your app's data practices change.

### Before you submit

- **Privacy policy linked in two places**: In App Store Connect and somewhere easy to find in the app.
- **A purpose string for every protected resource**: Clear and complete, one sentence each.
- **A matching entitlement for each**: Under App Sandbox in Signing & Capabilities. (`app-sandbox`)
- **Requests happen when the feature is used**: Not all at once on first launch.
- **The app still works after No**: With another way to finish the task where possible.
- **Privacy manifest lists collected data**: And the SDKs you include ship their own.
- **App Privacy answers match the app**: Covering every platform in the record.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Ask when the feature starts. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/privacy-manifest-files.md

## Related

`app-sandbox`, `mac-app-review`, `universal-purchase`, `onboarding`


<!-- topic: mac-app-review -->
---
id: mac-app-review
title: Mac App Review
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Mac App Review

Guideline 2.4.5's extra Mac App Store rules, and the issues that most often stall review.

Also called: App Review, rejection, rejected, Mac App Store rules, license key, serial number, launch at login, login item, SMAppService, auto-update.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Open to your app, not a license screen.** Guideline 2.4.5(vi) rules out license screens at launch, license keys, and your own copy protection. The Mac App Store handles purchases; use In-App Purchase to unlock more.
- **Ask before starting at login.** Guideline 2.4.5(iii) needs consent before your app or its helpers run at startup or keep running after people quit. Make it a setting that's off until people turn it on.

## Pitfalls

- **2.1 is the big one.** Apple says over 40% of unresolved issues come from Guideline 2.1, App Completeness: crashes, placeholder content, and missing information.
- **Plug-ins are an exception to In-App Purchase.** Mac App Store apps may host plug-ins or extensions that are unlocked some other way.

## Guide

Mac apps go through the same App Review as iPhone apps, under the same guidelines. Guideline **2.4.5** adds nine rules for apps on the Mac App Store. Here they are in plain words.

### Guideline 2.4.5, in full

- (i) Sandboxed: Appropriately sandboxed, following the macOS file system documentation. Change other apps' data, like bookmarks, contacts, or calendar events, only through the APIs made for it. See App Sandbox (`app-sandbox`).
- (ii) Packaged with Xcode: Packaged and submitted with Xcode's tools, with no third-party installers. One self-contained app bundle that installs nothing in shared locations.
- (iii) Nothing runs without consent: No launching at startup or login, and no processes left running after quit, unless people agree. Don't add yourself to the Dock or leave shortcuts on the desktop.
- (iv) No downloaded features: Don't download or install other apps, kernel extensions, code, or resources that add features or change what App Review saw.
- (v) No root: Don't ask for root privileges or use setuid attributes.
- (vi) No licensing of your own: No license screen at launch, no license keys, and no custom copy protection.
- (vii) Updates through the store: The Mac App Store delivers every update; no other update mechanism. See Updates Outside the Store (`updates-outside-store`).
- (viii) Current macOS, current tech: Run on the currently shipping macOS, without deprecated or optionally installed technologies such as Java.
- (ix) Every language in one bundle: All localizations ship inside the single app bundle.

### Issues Apple sees most

Apple lists the most common reasons submissions get stuck. None are Mac-only, and Mac apps run into them just the same:

- Crashes and bugs · 2.1: Test thoroughly on the latest macOS and fix bugs before you submit.
- Broken links · 2.1, 5.1: Support and privacy policy links must work, in the app and in App Store Connect.
- Placeholder content · 2.1: Finish every image and every piece of text before you submit.
- Incomplete information · 2.1: Give App Review a demo account and any setup steps in App Review Information.
- Unclear data requests · 5.1.1(ii): Every protected resource needs a purpose string that clearly explains the use. See Privacy & Permissions (`privacy-permissions`).
- Inaccurate screenshots · 2.3.3: Show the app in use, not a title screen or splash. See Screenshots & Metadata (`mac-screenshots`).
- Not enough lasting value · 4.2: Offer enough features and content to be useful. A repackaged website or a set of links isn't enough.

### Rules Mac apps often meet elsewhere

- 2.5.1 Public APIs only: And the app must run on the currently shipping macOS.
- 2.5.2 Self-contained: Read and write only inside your container, and don't download code that changes your app's features.
- 3.1.1 In-App Purchase: Unlock features with In-App Purchase, not license keys or codes of your own.

### Before you submit

- **App Sandbox is on**: With only the entitlements you use. (`app-sandbox`)
- **Archived and uploaded with Xcode**: No installer package of your own.
- **Nothing starts at login without consent**: Login items are an opt-in setting.
- **No update checker in the store build**: Updates come from the Mac App Store. (`updates-outside-store`)
- **No license keys or license screens**: Use In-App Purchase to unlock features. (`pricing-category`)
- **Tested on the current macOS**: No deprecated or optionally installed technologies.
- **App Review Information is complete**: Demo account, notes, and a contact who answers.

## Variants

### An Open at Login setting

`SMAppService.mainApp` registers your app as a login item, so tie it to a toggle that's off until people turn it on.

```swift
import ServiceManagement
import SwiftUI

struct LoginItemToggle: View {
    @State private var opensAtLogin = SMAppService.mainApp.status == .enabled

    var body: some View {
        Toggle("Open at login", isOn: $opensAtLogin)
            .onChange(of: opensAtLogin) { _, isOn in
                do {
                    if isOn {
                        try SMAppService.mainApp.register()
                    } else {
                        try SMAppService.mainApp.unregister()
                    }
                } catch {
                    opensAtLogin = SMAppService.mainApp.status == .enabled
                }
            }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The preview's toggle doesn't change your login items. People can also review login items in System Settings, and `SMAppService.openSystemSettingsLoginItems()` opens that pane.

## Related

`app-sandbox`, `updates-outside-store`, `privacy-permissions`, `mac-screenshots`, `pricing-category`, `testflight-mac`


<!-- topic: universal-purchase -->
---
id: universal-purchase
title: Universal Purchase
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/create-an-app-record/add-platforms
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Universal Purchase

One App Store listing and one purchase for your iPhone, iPad, and Mac apps.

Also called: add platform, macOS platform, same bundle ID, bundle identifier, one listing, cross-platform purchase, app record, multiplatform, Mac App Store and App Store.

## Pitfalls

- **In-app purchases come along.** Universal Purchase lets people use your app and its in-app purchases on every platform after one purchase.
- **App Privacy answers are shared.** They're set once for the app record, so cover what every platform collects.
- **It's permanent.** Once two platform versions are approved, the app stays a universal purchase, and you can't remove a platform from the record.

## Guide

With Universal Purchase, your iOS and Mac apps live in one app record in App Store Connect. People buy once and get both, with one product page. You set it up by adding the **macOS** platform to your existing iOS app.

### What has to match

- Bundle ID: **The same** as the iOS app's. The macOS version also shares its Apple ID (the app identifier) and SKU.
- Version and build: **Can differ.** The Mac app has its own version number and build string.
- Mac Catalyst apps: Supported when built with Xcode 11.4 or later.
- Separate records: Can't be merged. Keep one, remove the others from sale, and add their platforms to the one you kept.

**Important:** Removing an app from sale makes its product page unavailable. You can't update it for existing users, and its ratings and reviews don't move to the new page.

### Add the macOS platform

1. In App Store Connect, open **Apps** and select your iOS app. You need the Account Holder, Admin, or App Manager role.
2. Click **Add Platform** in the sidebar.
3. Choose **macOS** and click **Add**. A macOS version 1.0 appears in the sidebar; change the number under App Information if you like.
4. Fill in the Mac version's metadata. Everything carries over from iOS except the **promotional text**, **description**, and **screenshots**.
5. In Xcode, set the Mac target's bundle ID to the iOS app's, then archive and upload the Mac build.
6. Submit the Mac version for review. Once App Review approves both platforms, the app is a universal purchase.

### The same bundle ID in Xcode

Whether the Mac app is its own target or a destination in a multiplatform target, check the bundle ID it builds with. In build settings:

```swift
// iOS target
PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.example.trips
MARKETING_VERSION = 2.4

// Mac target: same ID, its own version
PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.example.trips
MARKETING_VERSION = 1.0
```

### If your iPad app is already on the Mac

Apple offers compatible iPhone and iPad apps on Macs with Apple silicon. When you add the macOS platform and release the Mac app, it **replaces** the iOS app on the Mac App Store, and existing users of the iOS app are updated to the Mac app.

### Before you submit

- **One app record, macOS added**: Not a second record for the Mac.
- **Mac build uses the iOS bundle ID**: Check the archived build, not just the target.
- **Mac description and promotional text written**: They don't carry over from iOS.
- **Mac screenshots uploaded**: In a 16:10 size. (`mac-screenshots`)
- **App Privacy answers cover the Mac**: One set of answers for every platform. (`privacy-permissions`)
- **In-app purchases work on the Mac**: Buy on one platform, check it unlocks on the other.

## Related

`native-vs-catalyst`, `mac-screenshots`, `pricing-category`, `testflight-mac`, `privacy-permissions`


<!-- topic: mac-screenshots -->
---
id: mac-screenshots
title: Screenshots & Metadata
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-information/screenshot-specifications
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Screenshots & Metadata

Mac screenshot sizes, app previews, and the text on your Mac product page.

Also called: screenshots, screenshot size, 1280x800, 1440x900, 2560x1600, 2880x1800, 16:10, app preview, video, product page.

## Rules

- **Show the app in use.** Guideline 2.3.3 asks for screenshots of the app doing its job, not just title art, a sign-in window, or a splash screen. Text and image overlays are allowed.
- **Use fictional data.** Guideline 2.3.9 asks for made-up account details in screenshots, never a real person's data, and you need the rights to everything shown.
- **Keep it suitable for everyone, and about this app.** Screenshots must suit a 4+ audience even if the app is rated higher (2.3.8), and can't show the names or imagery of other mobile platforms (2.3.10).

## Pitfalls

- **Mac screenshots don't come from iOS.** When you add the macOS platform, the description, promotional text, and screenshots start empty.
- **Promotional text changes without a review.** Use its 170 characters for news; it appears above the description.

## Guide

Screenshots are required for a Mac app. Upload at least one, and up to 10, as `.jpeg`, `.jpg`, or `.png`, in one of four sizes. Every size has a 16:10 aspect ratio.

### Accepted sizes

- Sizes, in pixels: 1280 × 800, 1440 × 900, 2560 × 1600, or 2880 × 1800.
- How many: At least one, up to 10.
- Scaling: If your interface is the same at every size, provide the highest resolution; App Store Connect scales it down.

**Important:** Screenshots can't have an alpha channel or transparency. Flatten them before you upload.

### App previews

- Optional: Up to three per language for each size.
- Size and length: 1920 × 1080 pixels (16:9), 15 to 30 seconds, and up to 500 MB.
- Orientation: Landscape only for Mac apps.
- Formats: `.mov`, `.m4v`, or `.mp4` with H.264, or `.mov` with ProRes 422 (HQ only).
- Order: Previews always show before screenshots. A preview with a different aspect ratio from your screenshots, like 16:9 next to 16:10, appears in the “A Closer Look” section instead.
- Content: Only video captured from the app itself (Guideline 2.3.4). Narration and text overlays are fine.

### The text on the page

- Name: Up to 30 characters (Guideline 2.3.7), with no prices or unrelated terms.
- Promotional text: Up to 170 characters. Change it any time without a new version.
- Description: Up to 4000 characters of plain text. Required.
- Keywords: Up to 100 bytes, each word longer than two characters. No other apps' or companies' names. Required.
- Support URL: Must lead to real contact information. Required.
- Copyright: The year and the owner, like “2026 Example, Inc.” Required.
- What's New: Required for every version after the first. Describe significant changes specifically (2.3.12).

## Related

`universal-purchase`, `pricing-category`, `mac-app-review`, `app-icons`


<!-- topic: pricing-category -->
---
id: pricing-category
title: Pricing & Category
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/information-property-list/lsapplicationcategorytype.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Pricing & Category

Set your Mac app's category in Xcode and App Store Connect, then its price and countries.

Also called: LSApplicationCategoryType, App Category, INFOPLIST_KEY_LSApplicationCategoryType, public.app-category, primary category, secondary category, price, price points, base country, storefronts.

## Pitfalls

- **Categories decide where you show up.** On the Mac App Store, your primary category places the app when people browse or filter search results, and in the Categories tab.
- **Games get subcategories.** Choose Games and you can add up to two game subcategories, and Xcode has a value for each, like `…category.puzzle-games`.

## Guide

Before you submit, App Store Connect needs a primary category, a price, and the countries or regions where the app is sold. A Mac app also names its category in Xcode.

### Category: set it twice

Pick a primary and an optional secondary category in App Store Connect. A Mac app also declares its category in its `Info.plist` with `LSApplicationCategoryType`, and Apple says the primary category in App Store Connect should match it. Choose the one that best describes what the app does; Guideline **2.3.5** lets Apple change a category that's way off.

```xml
<key>LSApplicationCategoryType</key>
<string>public.app-category.productivity</string>
```

```swift
INFOPLIST_KEY_LSApplicationCategoryType = public.app-category.productivity
```

### Price

Set a price before you submit. A paid app needs the Account Holder to accept the **Paid Apps Agreement** first; until then, the app can only be free.

1. In App Store Connect, open your app. Under **Monetization** in the sidebar, click **Pricing and Availability**.
2. In **Price Schedule**, click **Add Pricing** and pick a base country or region.
3. Pick a price. You can choose from 800 price points, or request 100 higher ones, up to $10,000.
4. Review the prices Apple generated for the other 174 storefronts. Change any you want to manage yourself, then click **Next** and **Confirm**.

- Your base price: Never changed by Apple.
- Other storefronts: Apple adjusts them from time to time for taxes and exchange rates, and tells you first. Prices you set by hand stay as they are.
- Universal Purchase: One purchase covers every platform in the app record. See Universal Purchase (`universal-purchase`).

### Availability

Under **App Availability** on the same page, click **Set Up Availability** and choose one of three options:

- All countries or regions: All 175 App Store countries and regions, plus any added later.
- Specific countries or regions: Only the ones you pick, with an option to include new ones.
- Publish as Pre-Order: A release date, and the regions where people can order ahead.

### Unlocking features

Guideline **3.1.1** applies on the Mac too: unlock features with In-App Purchase, not license keys or codes of your own. To offer a free trial of a paid app, Apple describes a non-consumable in-app purchase at price tier 0 named like “14-day Trial”, and before the trial starts the app must say how long it lasts, what stops working when it ends, and what the full version costs.

## Related

`universal-purchase`, `mac-screenshots`, `mac-app-review`


<!-- topic: testflight-mac -->
---
id: testflight-mac
title: TestFlight for Mac
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/test-a-beta-version/testflight-overview
reviewed: October 2026
---

# TestFlight for Mac

Send Mac builds to testers with TestFlight, the same way as iPhone builds.

Also called: TestFlight, beta, beta testing, testers, internal testers, external testers, public link, Beta App Review, build number, Organizer.

## Pitfalls

- **Builds expire after 90 days.** Upload a new one before testers lose access.
- **Testers can send screenshots.** With TestFlight 2.3 or later on the Mac, testers send feedback from the TestFlight app or by taking a screenshot in your app.
- **Notarized builds are another option.** Apple also suggests giving testers an Apple-notarized build before you ship on the App Store.

## Guide

TestFlight works for Mac apps as it does on iPhone: upload a build, add testers, and they install it with the TestFlight app on their Mac. Build your Mac app with Xcode 13 or later.

Guideline **2.2** says demos and betas belong in TestFlight, not on the App Store, and a TestFlight build should be meant for public release and follow the guidelines.

### Upload a Mac build

1. In Xcode, choose **My Mac** as the run destination, then **Product > Archive**. A Catalyst app needs its own Mac archive.
2. In the Organizer that opens, select the archive and click **Distribute App**.
3. Choose **TestFlight & App Store**, or **TestFlight Internal Only** to keep the build to your team, then click **Distribute**.
4. Wait for the email that says processing finished. The build then shows up in the TestFlight tab in App Store Connect.

**Important:** Each upload needs a new build string; App Store Connect uses it to tell builds apart. Mac builds can have their own version and build numbers, separate from iOS.

### Testers

- Who: Up to 100 members of your team with the Account Holder, Admin, App Manager, Developer, or Marketing role.
- Review: Only builds for external testers go to App Review. You can send new builds to internal testers automatically.
- Devices: Each tester can install on up to 30 devices.

### Set up the test

1. In the **TestFlight** tab, add **Test Information**: a beta app description, what to test, and an email for feedback.
2. Create a group and add the Mac build to it.
3. Invite testers by email, or turn on a **public link**. You can limit who joins a public link, for example by device type and OS version.
4. Testers install **TestFlight** on their Mac, accept the invitation, and install your app.
5. Read feedback, crash reports, and screenshots in App Store Connect, filtered by platform if you like.

### Before you invite testers

- **The build is sandboxed**: Test the same entitlements you'll ship. (`app-sandbox`)
- **A new build number**: Every upload needs its own.
- **Test Information filled in**: Description, what to test, and a feedback email.
- **Beta App Review information ready**: Required before external testers can join.
- **What to Test says what changed**: Point testers at the Mac-specific features.

## Related

`universal-purchase`, `mac-app-review`, `developer-id-notarization`, `app-sandbox`


<!-- topic: hardened-runtime -->
---
id: hardened-runtime
title: Hardened Runtime
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/hardened-runtime.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Hardened Runtime

Runtime protections Apple requires before it notarizes your Mac app.

Also called: ENABLE_HARDENED_RUNTIME, --options=runtime, runtime exceptions, com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit, allow-unsigned-executable-memory, disable-library-validation, allow-dyld-environment-variables, JIT, code injection, dylib hijacking.

## Rules

- **Add only the exceptions you need.** Each exception turns off one protection. Some, like Disable Executable Memory Protection, remove core security barriers, so pick the narrowest one that works.

## Pitfalls

- **New Mac projects have it already.** Xcode adds the Hardened Runtime capability when you create a macOS app from a template.
- **Entitlements go on executables only.** Frameworks, shared libraries, and in-process plug-ins inherit the entitlements of the app that loads them.
- **Leave out what's false.** These entitlements default to false, so include one only when its value is true, as Xcode does.

## Guide

The Hardened Runtime is a set of restrictions the system enforces on your app. Together with System Integrity Protection, it blocks whole classes of attacks, like injecting code, hijacking a dynamic library, or tampering with the app's memory. Most apps run the same with it on.

### When you need it

- Outside the Mac App Store: **Required.** Apple notarizes only apps with the Hardened Runtime on, and Developer ID software must be notarized. See Developer ID & Notarization (`developer-id-notarization`).
- On the Mac App Store: You don't notarize App Store apps, because the submission process includes equivalent checks. Apple ties the Hardened Runtime requirement to notarization.

**Note:** On the store, Guideline 2.4.5(i) requires the App Sandbox. See App Sandbox (`app-sandbox`).

### Turn it on

1. Select your app's target in Xcode and open **Signing & Capabilities**.
2. Click **+ Capability** and choose **Hardened Runtime**. The build setting behind it is `ENABLE_HARDENED_RUNTIME`.
3. If your app needs one, check a **Runtime Exception** or a **Resource Access** item. Xcode adds the entitlement, set to true.
4. Archive and notarize. Without it, notarization fails with “The executable does not have the hardened runtime enabled.”

### Build your entitlements

Check what your app needs. The file below shows only the keys you checked, the way Xcode writes them.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <!-- No exceptions: every protection stays on. -->
</dict>
</plist>
```

### Resource access still asks first

A resource access entitlement, like Camera or Location, only lets your app ask. People still see the system's permission prompt, and your `Info.plist` still needs a purpose string. See Privacy & Permissions (`privacy-permissions`).

### Check a signed app

```swift
# Verify the signature as strictly as notarization does
codesign -vvv --deep --strict "Trips.app"

# List the entitlements the app was signed with
codesign -d --entitlements :- "Trips.app"
```

## Related

`developer-id-notarization`, `app-sandbox`, `privacy-permissions`, `updates-outside-store`


<!-- topic: developer-id-notarization -->
---
id: developer-id-notarization
title: Developer ID & Notarization
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/notarizing-macos-software-before-distribution.md
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Developer ID & Notarization

Ship outside the Mac App Store: sign with Developer ID, notarize, and staple the ticket.

Also called: Developer ID, notarization, notarize, notarytool, stapler, staple, Gatekeeper, direct distribution, outside the App Store, DMG.

## Pitfalls

- **Notarization isn't App Review.** It's an automated scan for malicious content and code signing problems. Most uploads finish within 5 minutes, and 98% within 15.
- **It protects you too.** If your Developer ID key leaks, Apple can revoke the tickets for versions you didn't make.
- **`altool` no longer works.** Since November 1, 2023, the notary service accepts uploads only from `notarytool` or Xcode 14 and later.

## Guide

You can sell or give away a Mac app from your own website. Gatekeeper checks apps from outside the Mac App Store for a **Developer ID** signature, and since macOS 10.15, Developer ID software built after June 1, 2019 must also be **notarized** by Apple to run.

### Store or direct

- App Sandbox: Required on the Mac App Store. Recommended outside it.
- Hosting and updates: Apple hosts App Store apps and their updates. Outside, you host both.
- In-App Purchase and Game Center: Available only on the Mac App Store.
- Payments and support: On the store, Apple processes payments and supports customers with billing and downloads. Outside, both are yours.
- Notarization: Required outside the store. Not needed for the store, whose submission does equivalent checks.

### What the notary service needs

- Signed code: Every executable you ship has a valid code signature.
- A Developer ID certificate: Developer ID Application, or Developer ID Installer for packages. Not a Mac Distribution or development certificate. Only the Account Holder can create one.
- Hardened Runtime: Turned on for your app and command-line targets. See Hardened Runtime (`hardened-runtime`).
- A secure timestamp: Xcode's distribution workflow adds it for you.
- No get-task-allow: `com.apple.security.get-task-allow` must not be true. Xcode strips it when you export.

### The easy way: Xcode

1. Choose **Product > Archive**. The Organizer opens with your archive selected.
2. Click **Distribute App** and choose **Direct Distribution**, or **Custom** then **Developer ID**.
3. Choose to **upload** to the notary service. Scanning usually takes less than an hour.
4. When it's done, Xcode staples the ticket to your archive. **Export** it to get the app to ship.

### From the command line

Scripts and CI use `notarytool` and `stapler`, both included with Xcode. You can't upload an `.app` directly: zip it, or use a disk image or flat installer package.

```swift
# Once: save an app-specific password to the keychain
xcrun notarytool store-credentials "notary" \
    --apple-id "you@example.com" --team-id "TEAMID" \
    --password "app-specific-password"

# Zip the exported app and submit it
ditto -c -k --keepParent "Trips.app" "Trips.zip"
xcrun notarytool submit "Trips.zip" --keychain-profile "notary" --wait

# If it fails, read the log
xcrun notarytool log <submission-id> --keychain-profile "notary"

# Staple the ticket to the app, then zip it again to ship
xcrun stapler staple "Trips.app"
```

**Important:** You can't staple a ticket to a zip file. Staple the app inside, then make a new zip. Disk images and installer packages can be stapled directly.

**Note:** Gatekeeper also finds the ticket online, but stapling lets it check without a network connection.

### Before you ship

- **Signed with a Developer ID certificate**: Not Mac Distribution or Apple Development.
- **Hardened Runtime on**: With only the exceptions you need. (`hardened-runtime`)
- **Notarization status is Accepted**: And the log has no warnings worth fixing.
- **Ticket stapled**: To the app, disk image, or package you ship.
- **Tested like a customer**: Download it on another Mac and open it.
- **An update path**: Every update needs signing and notarizing too. (`updates-outside-store`)

## Related

`hardened-runtime`, `updates-outside-store`, `app-sandbox`, `testflight-mac`


<!-- topic: updates-outside-store -->
---
id: updates-outside-store
title: Updates Outside the Store
platforms: [macOS]
docs: https://developer.apple.com/macos/distribution/
reviewed: October 2026
---

# Updates Outside the Store

Apps you distribute yourself deliver their own updates; Mac App Store apps must not.

Also called: updates, auto-update, software update, Check for Updates, updater, update feed, appcast, direct distribution, compilation condition, SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Leave Check for Updates out of the store build.** Guideline 2.4.5(vii) says Mac App Store apps get updates only through the store, so the store build can't have an updater of its own.

## Pitfalls

- **Store updates can install themselves.** People can opt in to always getting the latest version of Mac App Store apps automatically.
- **Every release goes through the same steps.** Sign each update with Developer ID, notarize it, and staple the ticket, just like the first version.

## Guide

On the Mac App Store, Apple hosts your updates and delivers them. Outside it, Apple's own comparison puts software updates in your hands: you host each new version and get it to people.

### The rules on the store

- 2.4.5(vii): Mac App Store apps must use the Mac App Store for updates. Other update mechanisms aren't allowed.
- 2.4.5(iv): They can't download or install apps, code, or resources that add features or change the app from what App Review saw.
- 2.5.2: Apps stay self-contained and don't download code that changes their features.

### One codebase, two builds

If you ship both ways, compile the updater only into the direct build. Add a flag like `DIRECT` to **Active Compilation Conditions** (`SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS`) in a build configuration you use only for Developer ID builds.

### A simple update check

The smallest updater asks your server for the latest version and, if it's newer, sends people to your download page. Whatever people download must be signed with your Developer ID and notarized, like every Developer ID release.

### Before you release an update

- **No updater in the Mac App Store build**: Check the app menu of the archive you submit.
- **Version number raised**: So the update check sees a newer version.
- **Signed with Developer ID and notarized**: And the ticket stapled. (`developer-id-notarization`)
- **The update feed points at the new download**: Update it after the download is live, not before.
- **Tested from the previous version**: Install the last release and update it the way people will.

## Variants

### A Check for Updates command, direct builds only

`CommandGroup(after: .appInfo)` puts the item under About in the app menu, and `#if DIRECT` keeps it out of the store build.

```swift
@main
struct TripsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
        }
        #if DIRECT
        .commands {
            CommandGroup(after: .appInfo) {
                CheckForUpdatesButton()
            }
        }
        #endif
    }
}
```

### Compare versions, then open the download page

Read your version from `CFBundleShortVersionString`, compare it with the server's using `.numeric`, and open the page with `openURL`.

```swift
struct Release: Decodable {
    let version: String
    let downloadURL: URL
}

struct CheckForUpdatesButton: View {
    @Environment(\.openURL) private var openURL
    @State private var isUpToDate = false

    var body: some View {
        Button("Check for Updates…") {
            Task { await check() }
        }
        .alert("You're up to date.", isPresented: $isUpToDate) {}
    }

    func check() async {
        let feed = URL(string: "https://example.com/trips/latest.json")!
        guard let (data, _) = try? await URLSession.shared.data(from: feed),
              let latest = try? JSONDecoder().decode(Release.self, from: data)
        else { return }
        let current = Bundle.main.object(forInfoDictionaryKey: "CFBundleShortVersionString") as? String ?? "0"
        if current.compare(latest.version, options: .numeric) == .orderedAscending {
            openURL(latest.downloadURL)
        } else {
            isUpToDate = true
        }
    }
}
```

**Note:** The preview compares two versions you type, without a network request.

`developer-id-notarization`, `hardened-runtime`, `mac-app-review`, `commands`
